Teachers like it because it shows clearly how rhythm and rhyme can create a mood. It is also quoted in countless travel books, mountaineering memoirs and weddings of outdoor lovers. Its two closing lines, about the heaven above and the road below, have become a kind of motto for anyone who loves to wander.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
Readers have loved "The Vagabond" first of all for its sheer energy. It is a poem you want to read at a walking pace. The beat is infectious, the lines are simple, and the mood is exhilarating. People who walk, hike and travel often say that it puts into words a feeling they have had on a ridge or a road at dawn: that for a while they need nothing more than they carry.

They love the clarity of its vision. The poem knows exactly what it wants. Heaven above, road below, bread and river. Few poems are so uncluttered. In a world of complicated demands, with careers, possessions and obligations, the poem offers a picture of radical simplicity, and many readers find that refreshing, even if they would never live that way themselves. It speaks to a wish that most people have felt at least once, to drop everything and walk away.

There is also admiration for the poem's courage. The refusal of "wealth, hope nor love" and the defiance of winter are bold things to say. Readers sense in them a rejection of fear. "Let the blow fall soon or late" is a line that people take as a personal motto when things are going badly. It expresses a stoic readiness that is very appealing in a hard moment.

Music lovers have a special devotion to it because of Vaughan Williams. The song is a staple of the English concert repertoire, and singers speak of it as exhilarating to perform. The marriage of verse and tune is so close that many cannot read the poem without hearing the melody. That, too, is a kind of reader's affection, one that comes from having carried the words in one's body.

Finally, readers feel the sincerity beneath the swagger. They know that Stevenson was not a tourist in his own poem. He had tramped through the mountains, slept out under the stars and sailed across the Pacific. He lived with illness and uncertainty, and his love of the road was partly a love of freedom from the sickroom. That background lends the poem a depth it would not otherwise have. When he says "there's the life for a man like me", readers believe him, and that belief is the poem's most precious gift.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
There has been little hostile criticism of "The Vagabond", partly because it is a song and partly because it is so frankly a performance. But a few reservations are consistently raised.

The first is about authenticity. Stevenson was not a real tramp. He was a well-educated, middle-class Scot from a family of lighthouse engineers, and he wrote this poem as a man with publishers, an income, a wife and, in his last years, a household of servants in Samoa. Critics have noted that the vagabond's poverty is a literary pose, and that the poem romanticizes a life that, for people who truly have no home, is hard and often frightening. Lines like "bread I dip in the river" look charming from a study, and they look rather different to someone who has no other food. This is the most substantial objection, and it applies to the whole tradition of the "gentleman tramp" in Victorian and Edwardian writing.

A second criticism concerns the extreme stance. The poem rejects not only wealth but "hope nor love" and friendship as well. Some readers find this a cold or even adolescent attitude. A life without love or friends is hardly a happy one, and the poem seems to ignore the people who depend on the wanderer. It is a very masculine fantasy, in which the free man leaves everyone else behind. Modern readers, alert to questions of responsibility and care, sometimes feel uneasy about it. Stevenson himself, who loved his wife and stepfamily deeply, did not live by this creed, and the gap between the poem and the poet is part of the story.

Then there are the literary complaints. The poem is repetitive, and it relies on a simple, rather stock set of images: stars, road, river, heaven. Some critics feel that it offers sentiment without much surprise, and that it belongs more to the world of popular song than to serious poetry. Others point to its heavy debt to earlier romantic writers on wandering and nature.

A related complaint is that the poem's philosophy is naive. It assumes that freedom and happiness are the same thing, and it offers no sense of what the road costs. The idea of defying winter, in particular, feels bravely unrealistic. Real vagabonds die of cold.

All the same, the criticisms tend to be offered affectionately. Most critics accept that the poem is a song of aspiration rather than a report of fact, and that its exaggerations are part of its charm. The poem is not claiming to be wise. It is claiming to be free, and for the length of a song it persuades us.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
The poem belongs to a very old tradition: the praise of the wanderer. In every literature there are figures who leave the settled world, whether pilgrims, minstrels, tramps or holy fools, and writers have often envied them. In English, the line runs back to medieval songs of the greenwood and the poems of outlaws, through Wordsworth's wandering pedlars and leech-gatherers, to the Romantic fascination with Gypsies and the open road. George Borrow's books about Romani life, popular in the Victorian period, fed that fascination, and Stevenson was a child of it.

It also has a close American cousin in Walt Whitman's "Song of the Open Road", with its famous cry of "Afoot and light-hearted I take to the open road". Whitman's poem is more expansive and democratic, inviting everyone to come along, while Stevenson's vagabond walks alone. But they share the belief that the road is a place of truth. Comparing the two shows how much more compressed and song-like Stevenson is.

Among the poem's descendants are the tramp poets of the early twentieth century, such as W. H. Davies, whose Autobiography of a Super-Tramp appeared in 1908, and the American hoboes celebrated by Carl Sandburg and others. In the later twentieth century, the Beat writers and the folk singers of the 1960s revived the figure of the wanderer with a new political edge. Songwriters from Woody Guthrie onward made the road a symbol of freedom. They are indirect heirs of the same impulse.

In music, the poem's closest companions are the songs of Vaughan Williams and his contemporaries, who set British poems to tunes that sounded like folk songs. Schubert, whose melody inspired it, wrote his own great cycles about wandering, such as Winterreise, but there the walker is broken and alone. Stevenson takes a similar journey and makes it triumphant. Read alongside Schubert's gloom, the poem looks like a deliberate act of optimism.

Why does it matter to read today? Because the question it asks is still alive. What do we really need, and what could we do without? The poem answers in the extreme, and no one is expected to follow it literally. But it reminds us that much of what we chase is optional, and that there are pleasures, like a night under stars or a walk along a river, that cost nothing. It is a poem to read before a journey, or at the end of a crowded day. In thirty-two lines it offers a small, bracing holiday for the mind.

essays.title: Of Studies
essays.author: Francis Bacon
essays.epigraph: Some books are to be tasted, others to be swallowed, and some few to be chewed and digested: the foundational Renaissance treatise on how reading shapes character and judgment.
essays.keyContext: Francis Bacon's "Of Studies" is one of the shortest famous essays in English, and one of the most quoted. Bacon was a lawyer, courtier and philosopher who rose to be Lord Chancellor of England under King James the First, then fell in disgrace in 1621 when he admitted taking gifts from people whose cases he judged. He first published a small book of essays in 1597, borrowing the idea from the French writer Montaigne, and kept expanding it for nearly thirty years. "Of Studies" is the most polished piece in that collection. It was written at a moment when printing had made books cheap and plentiful, and people needed advice on how to read them. Bacon's answer is brisk and practical. Reading is not decoration or an escape, he says. It is a tool for shaping judgment and character, and different books deserve different kinds of attention. Listen for his famous line about tasting, swallowing, and chewing books, and for how packed each sentence is.
paragraphs: Studies serve for delight, for ornament, and for ability. Their chief use for delight, is in privateness and retiring; for ornament, is in discourse; and for ability, is in the judgment and disposition of business. For expert men can execute, and perhaps judge of particulars, one by one; but the general counsels, and the plots and marshalling of affairs, come best from those that are learned. To spend too much time in studies is sloth; to use them too much for ornament, is affectation; to make judgment wholly by their rules, is the humor of a scholar. They perfect nature, and are perfected by experience: for natural abilities are like natural plants, that need proyning by study; and studies themselves do give forth directions too much at large, except they be bounded in by experience.

Crafty men contemn studies, simple men admire them, and wise men use them; for they teach not their own use; but that is a wisdom without them, and above them, won by observation. Read not to contradict and confute; nor to believe and take for granted; nor to find talk and discourse; but to weigh and consider. Some books are to be tasted, others to be swallowed, and some few to be chewed and digested; that is, some books are to be read only in parts; others to be read, but not curiously; and some few to be read wholly, and with diligence and attention. Some books also may be read by deputy, and extracts made of them by others; but that would be only in the less important arguments, and the meaner sort of books, else distilled books are like common distilled waters, flashy things.

Reading maketh a full man; conference a ready man; and writing an exact man. And therefore, if a man write little, he had need have a great memory; if he confer little, he had need have a present wit: and if he read little, he had need have much cunning, to seem to know that he doth not. Histories make men wise; poets witty; the mathematics subtle; natural philosophy deep; moral grave; logic and rhetoric able to contend. Abeunt studia in mores: studies pass into and influence manners. Nay, there is no stond or impediment in the wit, but may be wrought out by fit studies; like as diseases of the body may have appropriate exercises.

Bowling is good for the stone and reins; shooting for the lungs and breast; gentle walking for the stomach; riding for the head; and the like. So if a man’s wit be wandering, let him study the mathematics; for in demonstrations, if his wit be called away never so little, he must begin again. If his wit be not apt to distinguish or find differences, let him study the schoolmen; for they are cymini sectores, splitters of hairs. If he be not apt to beat over matters, and to call up one thing to prove and illustrate another, let him study the lawyers’ cases. So every defect of the mind may have a special receipt.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
On the surface, "Of Studies" is a short list of advice about reading. Underneath, it is an argument about what knowledge is for. Bacon opens with three uses of study: delight, ornament, and ability. Delight is private, what you get alone in a quiet room. Ornament is public, the polish study gives your conversation. Ability is practical, the sound judgment you bring to real business. Then he ranks them without quite saying so. The whole essay leans toward ability, toward knowledge that changes how you act in the world.

He immediately warns against three ways of getting this wrong. "To spend too much time in studies is sloth; to use them too much for ornament, is affectation; to make judgment wholly by their rules, is the humor of a scholar." In other words, do not hide in books, do not show off with them, and do not let them replace your own eyes. Then comes one of his best images. Natural abilities are like plants that need pruning, and books are the pruning knife. But books alone give directions "too much at large," meaning too general, until experience bounds them in. Reading and living have to correct each other.

The next paragraph is the famous one. "Crafty men contemn studies, simple men admire them, and wise men use them." Notice that he does not sneer only at the ignorant. The cunning dismiss books because they trust their own tricks, the simple worship books because they cannot judge them, and only the wise treat them as instruments. He adds that studies "teach not their own use." Nobody can learn from a book how to apply books. That wisdom comes "by observation," from paying attention to life.

Then the rules for reading itself. "Read not to contradict and confute; nor to believe and take for granted; nor to find talk and discourse; but to weigh and consider." Four bad motives, one good one: weighing. The tasting, swallowing and chewing line follows, which is really a lesson in budgeting attention. Most books deserve a sample. Some can be gulped. A very few deserve slow, complete digestion. He even allows reading "by deputy," having someone else summarize minor books, though he sniffs that such distilled books are like cheap distilled water, "flashy things."

The last third is about transformation. "Reading maketh a full man; conference a ready man; and writing an exact man." Each activity builds something different: stock, speed, precision. Then comes a catalogue: history makes men wise, poetry witty, mathematics subtle, and so on, ending in the Latin tag "Abeunt studia in mores," studies pass into character. His closing comparison, that every mental defect has its special remedy in study the way bowling is good for the kidneys and shooting for the lungs, treats the mind as a body to be trained. The reader a first-time listener might miss is that this is a self-improvement manual from an age that was only just inventing the idea.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
As craft, "Of Studies" is close to flawless, and that is also the source of its limits. Bacon writes in what critics call the aphoristic or "curt" style: short, balanced, self-contained sentences that each feel like a coin. "Reading maketh a full man; conference a ready man; and writing an exact man" works because of its rhythm, three clauses with the verb dropped in the second and third, so the reader supplies the pattern. The three-part structure, the antitheses, the compression, all make the essay unusually memorable. It is hard to think of a piece of prose of its length that has donated so many lines to the language.

The tasting-and-chewing metaphor is the best single stroke. It does in a handful of words what a modern book on reading strategy takes chapters to say, and it is physical, so it sticks. The pruning image for natural ability is nearly as good. Even the slightly strange medical comparison at the end has a logic: if the mind has weaknesses, you can prescribe reading the way a doctor prescribes exercise. Bacon's examples there, such as the wandering mind being cured by mathematics, are clever and a little funny.

But the same compression has costs. Because every sentence is a verdict, the essay has almost no room for doubt, complication or personal voice. Compare Montaigne, who thinks out loud, contradicts himself and tells you about his kidney stones. Bacon never lets you see him struggle. He sounds like a judge reading out a ruling, and in a sense he is. The cataloguing in the final section, with each subject matched to a single virtue, feels neat to the point of glibness. Is it really true that poets make men "witty" and logicians able to "contend," and that is all? It reads more like a sorting exercise than an observation.

There is also a question of dated assumptions. The essay speaks of "men" throughout and assumes a reader preparing for public affairs, law and counsel, which was the audience of a Jacobean gentleman. Its snobbery shows in the line about "the meaner sort of books." And its confidence that books can be ranked by how much attention they deserve sits uneasily with how readers actually behave. We often discover what deserves chewing only after we have swallowed it.

Finally, a modern reader may find the utilitarian streak a bit narrow. Delight gets one sentence of respect and is then overshadowed by use. A work that treats reading mostly as career and character development leaves out the sheer joy and strangeness that other essayists celebrate. Still, these are the faults of a very sharp tool. It does one job superbly, and the job is persuading you to read with a purpose.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
The most visible impact of "Of Studies" is on the language itself. Phrases from it have lived far beyond the essay: reading makes a full man, some books are to be tasted and some chewed and digested, studies pass into manners. They appear in school mottoes, graduation speeches, library walls and the front pages of countless study-skills guides. Few essays have been quoted so often by people who have never read the rest of the book they came from.

For Bacon's own career, the essay belongs to a double life. He is remembered above all as a founder of the modern scientific method, through works like the Novum Organum of 1620, which argued that knowledge should come from careful observation and experiment, not from repeating ancient authorities. The essays were his lighter, more personal work, but they carry the same attitude. Notice that "Of Studies" insists wisdom is "won by observation" and that book learning needs to be "bounded in by experience." That is the empirical program in miniature. Readers who found the Novum Organum heavy often met his thinking first through the essays.

In literary history, Bacon is often credited with establishing the essay in English. Montaigne's French Essais came first and Bacon openly borrowed the word, but he turned the form in a different direction: not a wandering self-portrait but a distilled piece of counsel. The two models, the personal and the aphoristic, shaped everything that followed. Later English essayists such as Addison and Steele, Samuel Johnson, Charles Lamb, and Hazlitt each leaned toward one pole or the other, and Bacon was the standard-bearer for compression and authority.

The essay also became a permanent fixture in education. For centuries it was a staple of schoolbooks and examinations in Britain and its former colonies, where it was learned, parsed and sometimes memorized. Its Latin tag and its sorting of books helped shape how many generations were taught to think of reading as a discipline. Even today, when someone advises skimming some books and studying others closely, they are repeating Bacon, usually without knowing it.

Its modern afterlife includes everything from self-help to media studies. Writers on speed reading, note-taking and "reading for understanding" regularly start from his three categories. Advocates of the "great books" tradition use him as an ancestor, while those who defend skimming and summaries point to his permission to read "by deputy." The essay has become a kind of common property, which is perhaps the highest compliment an essay can earn. It is also worth noting that it has been repeatedly adapted for classroom use, set for translation exercises and used to teach rhetoric, since its parallel clauses are a gift to anyone teaching how sentences are built.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
Readers have loved "Of Studies" first for its density. In about five hundred words it manages to give a theory of knowledge, a lesson in reading, a map of the disciplines, and a promise about self-transformation. People who value economy see in it a model: nothing wasted, nothing apologized for. It is the opposite of padding, and that is a rare pleasure in any age.

They have loved it, too, for the gift of permission. Most people feel guilty about books they have not finished. Bacon says plainly that some books are only meant to be tasted, and that is not a failing but a skill. Readers who were taught that every book must be read cover to cover often find this liberating. At the same time, he sets a high bar for the "few" that deserve chewing, which flatters the serious reader. The essay is generous and demanding at once.

Writers have admired how it combines practical wisdom with a feel for the physical. The idea that books are food, that the mind is a body with weaknesses and exercises, makes abstract advice concrete. Teachers of writing often point to the sentence "Reading maketh a full man; conference a ready man; and writing an exact man" as a model of parallel structure and of an idea that can be tested in your own life. Anyone who has tried to explain something and discovered that they did not really understand it knows that writing makes you exact.

There is also a deeper appeal. The essay treats study as a moral activity, something that "passes into manners." That gives modest daily habits a large meaning. To read a little each evening is not just a pastime but a way of building the person you will be. Readers in every century who feel their lives are scattered and hurried have found comfort and direction in the idea that attention, steadily applied, adds up to character.

Finally, there is the sheer sound of it. Many readers say they love the music of Bacon's sentences: the balance, the stress on the last word, the confident rhythm of "tasted... swallowed... chewed and digested." Read aloud, which is how you may be hearing it now, the essay has a cadence that sticks in the ear. It is the kind of prose that wants to be spoken and remembered. That quality helps explain why it has been learned by heart by so many schoolchildren, and why adults who haven't thought of it for decades can still recite its best lines. People rarely forget a piece of writing that taught them how to eat a book.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
Objections to "Of Studies" tend to cluster around three things: its coldness, its narrowness, and the gap between the author and his advice.

The first is tone. Many readers, even admirers, find Bacon chilly. Where Montaigne invites you into his tower and tells you his fears, Bacon issues rulings. Later critics have noted that his essays often seem written from outside the human heart, concerned with advantage, management and appearances rather than with feeling. In "Of Studies," even the pleasures of reading are quickly turned into uses. It has been a common complaint that the essays offer wisdom without warmth.

The second is narrowness. The essay's picture of study is practical and classically masculine: it imagines a man preparing for law, government and counsel. It has little to say about reading for consolation, for wonder, for grief or for fun. Modern readers, especially those who came to reading from outside the circles of power, sometimes find it limited. Virginia Woolf, in her own essay on how to read, took a much more open and playful view, and the contrast shows how much Bacon leaves out. His ranking of books, with a "meaner sort" that may be read by deputy, has also struck some as snobbish.

Third, there is the old charge about the man himself. Bacon was convicted of corruption in 1621, after admitting he had accepted gifts from litigants, though he maintained that they had not influenced his judgments. He lost his office and was fined and briefly imprisoned. Critics have long delighted in the irony that the author of so much advice on wisdom and judgment fell so far through a lapse of both. Alexander Pope's famous line calling him "the wisest, brightest, meanest of mankind" captures this view, though historians today tend to see the picture as more complicated, since gift-taking was widespread in the legal system of his day.

There are also intellectual quarrels. Some scholars point out that Bacon's neat sorting of subjects into effects, such as mathematics making men "subtle," is more a rhetorical flourish than a claim anyone could test, which is ironic for a champion of experiment. And a few critics have argued that his model of reading as pruning or digestion makes books too passive, as if they were raw material and the reader the only active force. Readers who think of reading as an encounter or conversation may find that the metaphors flatten what actually happens when a mind meets a text. Still, it is notable that most of these complaints are about what the essay leaves out, rather than about whether what it says is true.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
"Of Studies" sits at the meeting point of three traditions. The first is classical moral philosophy. Bacon's talk of character formed by habit and study echoes Roman writers like Seneca and Cicero, and the Latin phrase "Abeunt studia in mores" is itself borrowed from the Roman poet Ovid. The second is the Renaissance humanist belief that education makes a person fit for public life. And the third is the new, restless, practical spirit that would become modern science. Bacon holds all three together, which is why the essay feels both ancient and strangely modern.

Within the history of the essay, it descends from Montaigne but argues with him. Montaigne essayed, meaning he tried and tested himself, and his writing meanders. Bacon takes the new form and sharpens it into a weapon. Together they define the two poles of the genre. If you follow the line forward you find Samuel Johnson's moral compression, Emerson's thunderclap sentences, and the pithy self-help essays of the modern era on one side, and Lamb, Hazlitt, Woolf and the confessional essayists on the other.

Comparing it with other essays on reading is illuminating. Montaigne's "Of Idleness" is about what a mind does when it is not occupied and why he began to write. Virginia Woolf's "How Should One Read a Book?" treats reading as a freedom and an act of imagination, and explicitly resists the authority that Bacon's confident rules might seem to carry. William James on habit supplies the psychology that explains why Bacon's claim that studies pass into character might be true. Reading Bacon next to these is like hearing the same question answered in four different voices.

His descendants outside the essay include the entire modern genre of advice writing, from Benjamin Franklin's maxims to contemporary productivity books, and the empirical tradition in philosophy and science that leads through the Royal Society to the present. Franklin in particular, with his tidy rules for self-improvement, writes in a recognizably Baconian register.

Why does it still matter? Partly because the problem he addressed is back, in a new form. Bacon wrote when printing had made books abundant, and readers felt overwhelmed. Today the flood is digital and far larger. His advice to choose, to read with a purpose, to weigh instead of swallow or merely argue, has become more useful, not less. And partly because it is simply a pleasure: a five-minute piece that rewards slow reading, in which almost every sentence can be taken out and held up to the light. It also reminds us that a good argument does not need to be long. If you read only one essay a night, this is one that gives you more each time you return to it.

essays.title: Nature
essays.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
essays.epigraph: Our age is retrospective; it builds the sepulchres of the fathers—Emerson's revolutionary call to step out under the stars and behold the universe firsthand.
essays.keyContext: Ralph Waldo Emerson's "Nature" is the founding text of American Transcendentalism, a movement that believed people can know truth directly, through intuition and experience, rather than through inherited authority. It appeared anonymously in Boston in 1836, a short book written by a man in his early thirties who had resigned from the Unitarian ministry and lost his first wife, his brother, and his old sense of purpose. After a trip to Europe, where he met Wordsworth, Coleridge and Carlyle, he settled in Concord, Massachusetts, and began to ask what a truly American thought might look like. What you are about to hear is the book's opening, the declaration of independence and the first chapter. It asks why every generation should live on secondhand religion, secondhand poetry and secondhand wisdom when the sun still shines and the woods are still there. Emerson's answer is that nature, truly seen, restores us to ourselves, and that this renewal is available to anyone who learns to look.
paragraphs: Our age is retrospective. It builds the sepulchres of the fathers. It writes biographies, histories, and criticism. The foregoing generations beheld God and nature face to face; we, through their eyes. Why should not we also enjoy an original relation to the universe? Why should not we have a poetry and philosophy of insight and not of tradition, and a religion by revelation to us, and not the history of theirs? Embosomed for a season in nature, whose floods of life stream around and through us, and invite us by the powers they supply, to action proportioned to nature, why should we grope among the dry bones of the past, or put the living generation into masquerade out of its faded wardrobe? The sun shines to-day also. There is more wool and flax in the fields. There are new lands, new men, new thoughts. Let us demand our own works and laws and worship.

To go into solitude, a man needs to retire as much from his chamber as from society. I am not solitary whilst I read and write, though nobody is with me. But if a man would be alone, let him look at the stars. The rays that come from those heavenly worlds, will separate between him and what he touches. One might think the atmosphere was made transparent with this design, to give man, in the heavenly bodies, the perpetual presence of the sublime. Seen in the streets of cities, how great they are! If the stars should appear one night in a thousand years, how would men believe and adore; and preserve for many generations the remembrance of the city of God which had been shown! But every night come out these envoys of beauty, and light the universe with their admonishing smile.

The stars awaken a certain reverence, because though always present, they are inaccessible; but all natural objects make a kindred impression, when the mind is open to their influence. Nature never wears a mean appearance. Neither does the wisest man extort her secret, and lose his curiosity by finding out all her perfection. Nature never became a toy to a wise spirit. The flowers, the animals, the mountains, reflected the wisdom of his best hour, as much as they had delighted the simplicity of his childhood.

When we speak of nature in this manner, we have a distinct but most poetical sense in the mind. We mean the integrity of impression made by manifold natural objects. It is this which distinguishes the stick of timber of the wood-cutter, from the tree of the poet. The charming landscape which I saw this morning, is indubitably made up of some twenty or thirty farms. Miller owns this field, Locke that, and Manning the woodland beyond. But none of them owns the landscape. There is a property in the horizon which no man has but he whose eye can integrate all the parts, that is, the poet. This is the best part of these men’s farms, yet to this their warranty-deeds give no title.

To speak truly, few adult persons can see nature. Most persons do not see the sun. At least they have a very superficial seeing. The sun illuminates only the eye of the man, but shines into the eye and the heart of the child. The lover of nature is he whose inward and outward senses are still truly adjusted to each other; who has retained the spirit of infancy even into the era of manhood. His intercourse with heaven and earth, becomes part of his daily food. In the presence of nature, a wild delight runs through the man, in spite of real sorrows. Nature says,—he is my creature, and maugre all his impertinent griefs, he shall be glad with me.

Not the sun or the summer alone, but every hour and season yields its tribute of delight; for every hour and change corresponds to and authorizes a different state of the mind, from breathless noon to grimmest midnight. Nature is a setting that fits equally well a comic or a mourning piece. In good health, the air is a cordial of incredible virtue. Crossing a bare common, in snow puddles, at twilight, under a clouded sky, without having in my thoughts any occurrence of special good fortune, I have enjoyed a perfect exhilaration. I am glad to the brink of fear. In the woods too, a man casts off his years, as the snake his slough, and at what period soever of life, is always a child. In the woods, is perpetual youth. Within these plantations of God, a decorum and sanctity reign, a perennial festival is dressed, and the guest sees not how he should tire of them in a thousand years.

In the woods, we return to reason and faith. There I feel that nothing can befal me in life,—no disgrace, no calamity, (leaving me my eyes,) which nature cannot repair. Standing on the bare ground,—my head bathed by the blithe air, and uplifted into infinite space,—all mean egotism vanishes. I become a transparent eye-ball; I am nothing; I see all; the currents of the Universal Being circulate through me; I am part or parcel of God. The name of the nearest friend sounds then foreign and accidental: to be brothers, to be acquaintances,—master or servant, is then a trifle and a disturbance. I am the lover of uncontained and immortal beauty. In the wilderness, I find something more dear and connate than in streets or villages. In the tranquil landscape, and especially in the distant line of the horizon, man beholds somewhat as beautiful as his own nature.

The greatest delight which the fields and woods minister, is the suggestion of an occult relation between man and the vegetable. I am not alone and unacknowledged. They nod to me, and I to them. The waving of the boughs in the storm, is new to me and old. It takes me by surprise, and yet is not unknown. Its effect is like that of a higher thought or a better emotion coming over me, when I deemed I was thinking justly or doing right.

Yet it is certain that the power to produce this delight, does not reside in nature, but in man, or in a harmony of both. It is necessary to use these pleasures with great temperance. For, nature is not always tricked in holiday attire, but the same scene which yesterday breathed perfume and glittered as for the frolic of the nymphs, is overspread with melancholy today. Nature always wears the colors of the spirit. To a man laboring under calamity, the heat of his own fire hath sadness in it. Then, there is a kind of contempt of the landscape felt by him who has just lost by death a dear friend. The sky is less grand as it shuts down over less worth in the population.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
The piece you have just heard is really two things welded together: a manifesto and a meditation. The manifesto comes first. "Our age is retrospective. It builds the sepulchres of the fathers." Emerson is saying that his generation spends its energy on biographies, histories and criticism, looking at God and nature through other people's eyes. His question is simple and radical: "Why should not we also enjoy an original relation to the universe?" Notice the phrase "dry bones of the past" and the image of putting the living generation into "masquerade out of its faded wardrobe." The past, in this picture, is a costume closet. You can dress in it, but you are then an actor, not yourself. The paragraph ends in a rally: "The sun shines to-day also."

The meditation begins with solitude. To be alone, he says, you must leave your room as well as other people, because even reading and writing keep company. So "let him look at the stars." Then the great thought experiment: if the stars appeared only one night in a thousand years, people would adore them and remember the vision for generations. But because they come out every night, we hardly look up. The point is about habit, the way constant gifts become invisible. The stars here are "envoys of beauty" with an "admonishing smile," a gentle rebuke to our inattention.

Next he distinguishes between the ordinary and the poetic way of seeing. The woodcutter sees a stick of timber, the poet sees a tree. And in his small parable of the landscape, several farmers own the fields, but none owns the view. "There is a property in the horizon which no man has but he whose eye can integrate all the parts." That "integration" is key. Real seeing is not counting objects but taking in the whole, and it is a kind of ownership no deed can record. "Few adult persons can see nature," he says, because the sun shines only on the eye of the adult but "into the eye and the heart of the child."

Then comes the most famous moment, usually remembered as "the transparent eye-ball." Standing on bare ground, with his head "bathed by the blithe air," his "mean egotism vanishes." "I become a transparent eye-ball; I am nothing; I see all; the currents of the Universal Being circulate through me." It sounds odd, and it was mocked for it, but he means something fairly precise: the ordinary self, with its worries about reputation, shrinks away, and what is left is pure perception, a feeling of belonging to something larger.

The last paragraph is the one many readers miss. Emerson pulls back and admits that the delight "does not reside in nature, but in man, or in a harmony of both." Nature is not always cheerful. To someone who has just lost a friend, "the sky is less grand." That sentence comes from a man who knew grief intimately, and it quietly corrects the sunny tone of everything before it.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
The strongest quality of this passage is its sentences. Emerson writes in short, strong, quotable units, and the first paragraph alone contains several that have lasted: the sepulchres of the fathers, the dry bones of the past, the masquerade of the faded wardrobe. The rhythm of the opening questions, each beginning "Why should not we..." builds like a drumbeat, and the turn to plain fact, "There is more wool and flax in the fields," is a masterstroke. After lofty abstractions, he reminds us of wool and flax. It is the voice of a preacher who has left the pulpit but kept the music.

The stars passage is probably the best-built thought in the whole excerpt. It uses a hypothetical, makes a surprising reversal, and lands on an image, the "admonishing smile," that is both beautiful and slightly stern. The parable of the farms and the horizon is similarly efficient and a little witty: the owners Miller, Locke and Manning are named like characters in a miniature fable. And the closing turn to grief, where he lets the weather of the soul override the weather of the sky, gives the piece a depth that pure nature-worship lacks.

The weaknesses are real, though. Emerson does not argue so much as assert. He moves from claim to claim by association, and the connection between them often rests on the reader's willingness to be carried along. The "transparent eye-ball" passage is the clearest example. It is thrilling when you are in sympathy with it, and faintly ridiculous when you are not. Even the author seems to have known this; the image became a favorite target for caricature almost at once. A reader who wants to know how one gets from the woods to the "Universal Being" will find an experience described rather than a path laid out.

There is also a certain privilege in the vision. The solitary walker with a free afternoon and a head full of Latin and Plato does not have much to say to someone working a field, or to anyone for whom nature is a source of labor and danger, not of epiphany. Emerson's farmers do not own the landscape, but they also do not seem to see it, and the essay is a little condescending about them. The line that "most persons do not see the sun" is flattering to the person who thinks they do.

Finally, the prose can be gaseous. Phrases like "integrity of impression" and "inward and outward senses... truly adjusted" gesture toward ideas that are never defined. This is the price of the style: the aphorism lights up and then leaves you to work out its meaning. Many readers find this exhilarating. Others finish a page of Emerson feeling uplifted and unable to say what they have been told. Both reactions are fair, and the essay is more honest about the second than its reputation suggests, since it ends by admitting that nature can fail us when we are sad.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
The immediate reception of "Nature" was modest. It was published without Emerson's name in September 1836, in a small printing, and it took years to sell out. But among a small group of readers in and around Boston and Concord it landed like a flare. Within weeks of its appearance, the group that came to be called the Transcendental Club was gathering, and the book gave that circle a vocabulary and a confidence. Margaret Fuller, Bronson Alcott, and the younger Henry David Thoreau were all within its orbit.

Emerson's own career grew directly from it. Two years later he gave the Divinity School Address at Harvard, which scandalized the Unitarian establishment by urging young ministers to trust their own intuition over church doctrine, and which got him effectively barred from speaking at Harvard for decades. "The American Scholar," delivered in 1837 and often called America's intellectual declaration of independence, picks up the opening cry of "Nature" and widens it. "Self-Reliance," from 1841, carries the same idea into private conduct. Everything he wrote afterward can be read as an expansion of the first paragraph you heard.

The influence on other writers is hard to overstate. Thoreau went to live at Walden Pond on land Emerson owned, and Walden is in many ways an extended experiment in the proposition that one can have an original relation to the universe. Walt Whitman said that Emerson's essays had brought him to a boil, and the first edition of Leaves of Grass drew a famous letter of praise from Emerson in return. Emily Dickinson, though she rarely left her home, absorbed his ideas. Later, the naturalist John Muir admired Emerson, who visited Yosemite in 1871, and the American conservation movement inherits some of its language of wilderness as spiritual renewal from this tradition. Overseas, readers such as Nietzsche found a kindred voice in his hymns to self-overcoming.

In wider culture, the book helped define an American attitude: suspicion of inherited authority, trust in direct experience, belief that landscape can heal. You can hear it in the nature writing of the twentieth century, in the outdoors movement, in the spiritual-but-not-religious outlook that so many people now share, and in countless graduation speeches. When someone says they feel closer to God in the woods than in church, they are echoing the "wilderness" passage you just heard.

In classrooms, "Nature" is a standard text in American literature courses, usually taught as the founding document of Transcendentalism and often read alongside "Self-Reliance." It has also been used by scholars of environmental history, who see in it the beginnings of both American ecological thought and its tendency to treat wilderness as a place for human self-discovery.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
What readers have loved most is the sense of permission. Emerson's opening says, in effect, that you do not need a degree, a priesthood, or a tradition's blessing to stand in front of the world and feel its meaning. For a young country in the 1830s that was intoxicating, and for an individual reader at any date it is still a relief. People tend to remember where they were when they first encountered "an original relation to the universe." It sounds like an invitation, and it is meant to be one.

Another source of affection is the sheer beauty of particular images. The stars that come out every night and light the universe with their "admonishing smile" has lodged in many memories, as has the idea that one can walk past a field owned by three men and own the best part of it by looking. Readers who like the essay often say it taught them to look up, literally. It is rare for a philosophical text to change the way a person spends five minutes on a walk, but this one does so reliably.

Writers and thinkers have loved its confidence. Thoreau, Whitman and many others took from Emerson the conviction that an American voice was possible. Whitman's remark that Emerson started him boiling is the best-known tribute, but the line of admirers runs through the whole nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Readers who find themselves stuck in rules and expectations often discover in this passage a kind of second wind.

The "transparent eye-ball" passage has its own devotees. Those who have ever stood in a forest, on a mountain or beside the sea and felt their ordinary worries thin out will recognize what he is describing. For them, the oddness of the phrase is a sign of honesty: he was trying to put into words a state that does not fit ordinary language. Even skeptics often admit that he captured something genuinely felt.

Finally, there is a loyalty to the essay's emotional honesty at the end. For all his serenity, Emerson allows the plain fact that delight is not guaranteed, that grief can dim the sky. Readers who come to the piece in hard times often say that this last paragraph is what keeps the optimism from feeling cheap. The passage promises that nature "can repair" any disgrace or calamity, and then admits that this depends on the state of the person looking. That mixture of hope and realism is what lets people go on returning to it long after they have outgrown the youthful thrill of the opening.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
From the start, "Nature" drew mockery as well as admiration. The most famous target was the "transparent eye-ball." Within a few years the image was being parodied, and the painter and Transcendentalist Christopher Cranch drew a well-known cartoon of a giant walking eyeball on legs. Critics outside the movement used the phrase as shorthand for everything they considered fuzzy about the group. Edgar Allan Poe, for one, was openly scornful of the Transcendentalists, and Nathaniel Hawthorne, who knew many of them, treated their utopian enthusiasms with gentle skepticism in his fiction.

More seriously, religious conservatives objected to what the book implied. If God can be met directly in the woods, what is the church for? If each person has "revelation to us, and not the history of theirs," what becomes of scripture? The same alarm greeted Emerson's Divinity School Address two years later, and it is part of why some of the Unitarian establishment treated him as a danger. The charge, essentially, was pantheism: that he had blurred God into nature and the self.

Philosophers and scientists have had different complaints. Some say his thinking is not rigorous: it is poetry dressed as argument, moving by flashes of insight with no demonstration. Others note that his picture of nature is highly selective. The nature of this passage is serene, nourishing and always at the service of the human mind, with little room for storms, predators, disease or indifference. Later readers, especially after Darwin, found this view of a benevolent, mind-friendly natural world hard to sustain. Even within the excerpt, a careful reader will notice that Emerson's claim that "nature never wears a mean appearance" is tested by his own admission at the end.

There are also social and political criticisms. Modern readers have asked who gets to stand alone in the woods with a bare head and a clear mind. Emerson wrote as a comfortable New England man at a time when millions of enslaved people could not walk anywhere freely, and critics have pointed out that his early work, with its focus on private spiritual independence, says little about the structural injustices around him. To be fair, Emerson became a significant antislavery voice in the following decades, but the silence of this early text is noticeable. Likewise, the celebration of landscape as an emptiness for the self to fill has been questioned by historians who note that the "wilderness" was already inhabited, and that the cult of it often overlooked the people who lived there.

Last, some have simply found the idealism tiresome: the claim that "the power to produce this delight does not reside in nature, but in man" can read as a retreat into the mind, a way of making the world a mirror. For readers who prefer the world to be stubbornly itself, that is a flaw, not a feature.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
Emerson's "Nature" belongs to the great tradition of Romanticism, the movement that swept Europe and America around 1800 to 1850 and insisted on feeling, imagination and the individual against the cool rationalism of the Enlightenment. Its direct ancestors are the English Romantics Wordsworth and Coleridge, whom Emerson visited, and the German idealists who shaped Coleridge's thinking, along with Kant, whose notion that the mind actively shapes what it perceives gave Transcendentalism its name. There is also an older strand of Neoplatonism and of Swedenborg, the Swedish mystic whom Emerson admired, running through the book's belief that natural things are signs of spiritual ones.

What descends from it is enormous. In American literature, the line runs from Thoreau and Whitman through Dickinson, and into the modern traditions of nature writing, from John Muir to Annie Dillard and beyond. The idea that wild places are a source of spiritual health underlies the national parks and the conservation movement. In philosophy, Emerson fed into American pragmatism: William James, the author of the essay on habit, was his godson, and his view that truth is something lived and tested has Emersonian roots. In Europe, Nietzsche kept a copy of Emerson close at hand.

It is useful to compare "Nature" with other pieces on reading and attention. Bacon's "Of Studies" says wisdom is won by observation and tempered by experience, and Emerson takes that proposition and pushes it into a vision, trusting the individual much more than Bacon would. Montaigne also withdrew to solitude, but he found the mind a noisy place that needed discipline; Emerson finds in solitude something like grace. Thoreau, who learned from Emerson, did the experiment that the older man proposed. Woolf's call for readers to trust their own judgment in the library is, in a sense, Emerson's call in a different room.

One thing to remember is that this is only the opening of a larger book, in which Emerson goes on to discuss commodity, beauty, language, discipline, idealism and spirit. What you have here is the doorway, and its job is to unsettle the reader's habits of looking.

Why read it now? Because the problem it names, living through other people's eyes, has become sharper. We experience much of life through screens, reviews and summaries, in an age more retrospective than he could have imagined. His invitation to stand outside, look up, and see the stars as if they appeared once in a thousand years may be the most practical advice in the essay. It costs nothing, takes five minutes, and, as Emerson promises, it does not wear out.

essays.title: Of Idleness
essays.author: Michel de Montaigne
essays.epigraph: Retiring to his château tower to let his mind rest in total idleness, Montaigne discovers that an unoccupied mind behaves like a runaway horse and breeds fantastic monsters—until he begins to write.
essays.keyContext: Michel de Montaigne's "Of Idleness" is a tiny essay with a huge consequence: it explains why the personal essay exists. Montaigne was a French nobleman and magistrate who, in 1571, at thirty-eight, retired from public life to his family estate, hoping to spend the rest of his days in peaceful reading. France was tearing itself apart in religious civil war, and he was exhausted. He had a round tower library, a thousand books, and the memory of his dearest friend, who had died years before. What he found, to his surprise, was that an idle mind does not rest. It runs wild. So he began writing his thoughts down to examine them, and called the results essais, meaning attempts or trials. This short chapter, from the first book he published in 1580, is the moment the habit begins. It is only a few hundred words, but it contains the seed of a form that includes nearly every personal essay, memoir and blog written since.
paragraphs: As we see some grounds that have long lain idle and untilled, when grown rich and fertile by rest, to abound with and spend their virtue in the product of innumerable sorts of weeds and wild herbs that are unprofitable, and that to make them perform their true office, we are to cultivate and prepare them for such seeds as are proper for our service; and as we see women that, without knowledge of man, do sometimes of themselves bring forth inanimate and formless lumps of flesh, but that to cause a natural and perfect generation they are to be husbanded with another kind of seed: even so it is with minds, which if not applied to some certain study that may fix and restrain them, run into a thousand extravagances, eternally roving here and there in the vague expanse of the imagination—

Sicut aqua tremulum labris ubi lumen ahenis, Sole repercussum, aut radiantis imagine lunae, Omnia pervolitat late loca; jamque sub auras Erigitur, summique ferit laquearia tecti. [“As when in brazen vats of water the trembling beams of light, reflected from the sun, or from the image of the radiant moon, swiftly float over every place around, and now are darted up on high, and strike the ceilings of the upmost roof.”—AEneid, viii. 22.] —in which wild agitation there is no folly, nor idle fancy they do not light upon:— Velut aegri somnia, vanae Finguntur species. [“As a sick man’s dreams, creating vain phantasms.”—Hor., De Arte Poetica, 7.] The soul that has no established aim loses itself, for, as it is said— Quisquis ubique habitat, Maxime, nusquam habitat. [“He who lives everywhere, lives nowhere.”—Martial, vii. 73.]

When I lately retired to my own house, with a resolution, as much as possibly I could, to avoid all manner of concern in affairs, and to spend in privacy and repose the little remainder of time I have to live, I fancied I could not more oblige my mind than to suffer it at full leisure to entertain and divert itself, which I now hoped it might henceforth do, as being by time become more settled and mature; but I find— Variam semper dant otia mentem, [“Leisure ever creates varied thought.”—Lucan, iv. 704] that, quite contrary, it is like a horse that has broke from his rider, who voluntarily runs into a much more violent career than any horseman would put him to, and creates me so many chimaeras and fantastic monsters, one upon another, without order or design, that, the better at leisure to contemplate their strangeness and absurdity, I have begun to commit them to writing, hoping in time to make it ashamed of itself.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
The essay is a single, tightly built thought, and it is worth walking through slowly. Montaigne begins with a comparison to land. Ground that has "long lain idle and untilled," he says, grows rich by resting, and then it fills with "innumerable sorts of weeds and wild herbs that are unprofitable." Fertility without direction does not produce a harvest; it produces a jungle. To get something useful, the farmer must "cultivate and prepare" the soil with "such seeds as are proper for our service."

Then he pushes the point further with an image that is startling, and not very comfortable to a modern ear. Women who have conceived without a man sometimes bring forth "formless lumps of flesh," whereas a proper birth requires the right seed. He is applying an old and mistaken piece of medical folklore, but his meaning is clear: the mind, left to itself, generates only shapeless matter, and real thought needs something to fertilize it, some subject or purpose.

The rest of the essay shows the same thing in the author's own life. A mind not "applied to some certain study that may fix and restrain" it runs into "a thousand extravagances, eternally roving here and there in the vague expanse of the imagination." To illustrate this he borrows a passage from the Roman poet Virgil, in which trembling light, reflected off a bronze basin of water, flickers across the walls and ceiling of a room. That is what an unoccupied mind looks like: bright, restless, and landing everywhere and nowhere. He adds a line from Horace comparing such thoughts to a sick man's dreams, and one from Martial: "He who lives everywhere, lives nowhere."

Then comes the personal confession. When he "lately retired" to his own house, intending "as much as possibly I could, to avoid all manner of concern in affairs," he assumed the kindest thing he could do for his mind was to let it entertain itself. Instead, "it is like a horse that has broke from his rider," running into "a much more violent career than any horseman would put him to." It creates "chimaeras and fantastic monsters, one upon another, without order or design."

The final sentence is the hinge of the whole essay and one of the most important in the history of writing. To "contemplate their strangeness and absurdity," he says, "I have begun to commit them to writing, hoping in time to make it ashamed of itself." Here is the entire invention: writing as a way of catching your own thoughts in the act. A thought on the page can be looked at, mocked, corrected. The aim is partly therapeutic and partly comic, since the goal is to make the mind blush. What looks like a note about laziness is actually the birth announcement of a new kind of book.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
As a piece of writing, "Of Idleness" is quietly excellent, though it is also an early and slightly rough version of what Montaigne would later do better. Its strongest quality is the way it moves from general principle to private confession. The first half sounds almost like a gardening manual or a bit of moral philosophy. Then, with the words "When I lately retired," the voice becomes intimate and the argument becomes a story about the author. That turn, from a doctrine to a person, is the move that defines the personal essay, and he makes it in a few sentences.

The imagery is also vivid and well chosen. The weedy field is simple and exact. The runaway horse is the best of the three, because it contains a small irony: he thought he was giving his mind a gift of freedom, and it galloped away with him. The picture of light dancing across the ceiling, borrowed from Virgil, is gorgeous, and it makes a point about the mind that no abstract term would. A reader who has ever lain awake at night with thoughts bouncing around will recognize it at once.

There is wit here, too. The idea that he might write down his chimeras to make his mind "ashamed of itself" is both a serious method and a joke, and the tone, half rueful and half proud, is why people feel they know him. Montaigne never preaches that idleness is wicked; he reports an experiment that did not turn out as planned.

But the essay is uneven in places. The sentence about women and "formless lumps of flesh" is a weak point. It rests on an outdated notion, and the comparison is awkward, since the metaphor turns a human body into a mere illustration. It sits oddly beside the tender observation of his own mind. Modern readers often wince, and it is fair to say the image has aged badly.

There is also a mild overdependence on quotation. Four Latin tags in an essay of this length can feel like decoration, and in the version you heard they come with bracketed translations that interrupt the flow. In Montaigne's own time, this was a mark of learning and an invitation to share a classical heritage with the reader, but it can feel like clutter now. Finally, the essay is more of an announcement than a developed argument. It says that a mind needs an occupation, but it does not tell us what the right occupation would be, and its answer, writing, is delivered almost in passing. The mature Montaigne of the later essays, who wanders further and explores more, is a richer companion. Still, this small piece has the great virtue of showing the form being born.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
The influence of "Of Idleness" is the influence of Montaigne's project as a whole, and this short chapter is its origin story. Montaigne's Essais, first published in 1580 and expanded repeatedly until his death in 1592, created a genre. Before him, there were treatises, sermons, letters, and collections of maxims. Nobody had written a book in which the main subject was the author's own mind, changing from page to page. By naming the practice essai, he gave later writers a word, and the word became the English "essay."

The direct line to English literature is traceable. Francis Bacon borrowed the title and form for his own essays, though he took them in a more compressed and public direction. The English translation by John Florio, published in 1603, was read by Shakespeare, and scholars have long seen echoes of Montaigne in some of his plays, most famously in the speech by Gonzalo in The Tempest, which draws on the essay on cannibals. Later, Montaigne's example runs through the essays of Hazlitt and Lamb, and onward.

In France, his legacy was immense. Pascal admired and argued with him, and Rousseau's Confessions, with its promise to show a man as he is, is unthinkable without him, though Rousseau claimed to be doing something unprecedented. Philosophers of skepticism, from Descartes onward, were shaped by the habits of doubt that Montaigne made fashionable. In the twentieth century, writers such as Virginia Woolf wrote lovingly about him, and the essayists of the personal and confessional kind, from Orwell to James Baldwin to Joan Didion, work in a house he built.

Culturally, the essay's idea, that writing is a way to look at yourself, has become so ordinary that we forget someone had to discover it. Journals, memoirs, blogs and even modern therapeutic practices that encourage writing down anxious thoughts all rest on the same insight. The popular biography by Sarah Bakewell, published in 2010 as How to Live, helped introduce a new generation to Montaigne as a kind of friend and guide.

In education, "Of Idleness" is often taught as an origin text. Teachers use it to show how the essay form began, how classical quotation worked in the Renaissance, and how a short piece can hold a large idea. It is also, increasingly, assigned in discussions of attention and mental health, because its central observation, that an unoccupied mind is not automatically a calm one, sounds uncannily modern in an age of restlessness and distraction.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
Readers have loved this essay, and Montaigne generally, because he tells the truth about the inside of a head. Most writers of his time presented themselves as authorities. Montaigne presents himself as a man who tried to retire, expected peace, and got chaos. That admission is endearing. We recognize ourselves in the scene: the person who finally clears the calendar and then cannot stop worrying, or who sits down to rest and finds the mind racing through a thousand imagined conversations.

They love the images. The runaway horse, the unplowed field and the shimmering light on the ceiling have all stayed vivid for centuries because they turn a vague experience into something you can see. The comparison of the mind to light reflected from water in a basin is especially admired. Readers often say it feels like a photograph of what it is to be distracted.

They love the humor and humility of the ending. The idea that he writes in order to make his mind "ashamed of itself" captures a gentle self-mockery that runs through the Essais. He does not set himself up as a model. Over and over in the book, he says he is writing about himself because he is the subject he knows best, and that there is no reason to take him as an authority. For many readers this is a relief after more solemn moral writing.

There is also a deep appeal in the way the essay recasts idleness. People often think of idleness as a failing to be cured by effort. Montaigne's answer is more interesting: the problem is not that you are not busy, but that your mind has no object. The solution is not frantic activity but attention, giving thought a shape. Readers have found this useful, especially those who live with anxiety or who struggle to relax.

Finally, the essay is loved for its sense of friendship across time. Montaigne wrote in a tower in the sixteenth century, during a civil war, and yet the voice feels warm and immediate. Many readers describe it as being addressed to them personally. It is common to hear people say that reading Montaigne is like talking with a clever, honest friend who happens to have lived four hundred years ago. This short chapter is where that friendship begins.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
Montaigne has always had critics, and some of their objections apply here. The most famous came from the French thinker Blaise Pascal, who admired much in him but wrote of "the foolish project he had of portraying himself." To Pascal, a deeply religious man, a book that makes the author's own mind the subject was self-indulgent, and distracting from God. Other moralists, including some in the seventeenth-century Catholic tradition, felt his emphasis on the self and his easygoing skepticism were dangerous. The Essais were placed on the Catholic Church's Index of banned books in 1676.

A second charge is privilege. Montaigne could retire at thirty-eight because he owned an estate, had servants, and had inherited wealth. His complaint that idleness produces monsters is the complaint of a man for whom idleness was available. A farmer or a laborer in sixteenth-century France was not worried about having too little to do. Critics have noted that the essay's picture of leisure as a problem to be solved by thoughtful writing is a very aristocratic worry, and that the great themes of the surrounding violence, the wars of religion that were killing his neighbors, are almost absent from this passage.

Third, there is the question of method. Some readers have found that the essay is thin as philosophy. It makes an observation and offers a remedy, but the remedy is not argued, and it quietly assumes that writing will improve the mind. Anyone who has seen a journal turn into an exercise in rumination might doubt it. Writing down monsters can feed them as easily as tame them. The essay does not entertain that possibility.

Then there are specific details that have aged badly. The metaphor of women producing "formless lumps of flesh" draws on a medical belief that is false, and it casts women as passive vessels in an essay about the mind. Even sympathetic readers tend to skip past it. And the heavy use of classical quotation, a normal practice in the Renaissance, has been seen by some as a way of hiding behind authority, which is ironic in a writer who claims to be exploring himself.

Finally, there is a view that the essay overstates its own originality. Montaigne is often credited with inventing the essay, but he drew on Plutarch, Seneca, and a rich tradition of commonplace books. In this reading, "Of Idleness" is less a birth than a clever repackaging. That is probably too harsh, but it is a reminder that nothing begins entirely from nothing.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
Montaigne belongs to Renaissance humanism, the movement that revived Greek and Roman writing and placed human experience at the center of study. His particular school was a skeptical, practical one, influenced by Stoics such as Seneca, by Plutarch's lively biographies and moral essays, and by the ancient skeptics whose doubts he brought into French. Within this tradition, "Of Idleness" is typical in drawing on Latin poets for its illustrations and on classical ideas about the discipline of the mind.

What came after is much of modern literature. The personal essay, the memoir, the confessional poem, the diary, and the autobiographical novel all have some debt. In English, the line runs from Bacon through Addison and Johnson to Lamb, Hazlitt, Orwell and Woolf, and in America to Emerson, Thoreau, and the present-day personal essayists. In French, from Pascal through Rousseau to Proust, who turns the study of a single mind into a whole novel.

It is revealing to compare Montaigne with the other writers on reading and attention in this tradition. Bacon, who borrowed the form, uses it to give counsel; Montaigne uses it to ask questions. Where Bacon is a judge, Montaigne is a fellow patient. William James, studying habit, explains in scientific terms why a mind without settled channels runs wild, which is what Montaigne describes in his tower. Emerson, in the woods, finds in solitude a joy that Montaigne found only chaos in, until he started to write. Woolf, who adored Montaigne, shares his belief that a person is best understood through the shifting surface of daily thought.

Why does "Of Idleness" still matter? Partly because it is the beginning of something. If you want to know where the voice of the first-person essay came from, here is the room, the tower, and the moment. But also because it offers a surprisingly current insight. We live in a time when many people are, in a sense, retired from patience, with endless free moments filled by screens, and often they are not rested but agitated. Montaigne would not be surprised. His advice is not to stop thinking but to give thought something to hold. Writing is one remedy, and you may find another. What matters is the discovery that the mind, left alone, is not a quiet room but a crowded and curious one, and that you can learn a great deal by writing down who is inside.

essays.title: Habit
essays.author: William James
essays.epigraph: Could the young but realize how soon they will become mere walking bundles of habits, they would give more heed to their conduct while in the plastic state: we are spinning our own fates, good or evil, and never to be undone.
essays.keyContext: William James's "Habit" is the chapter of a famous science book that escaped into everyday life. James was a Harvard physician turned psychologist and philosopher, the older brother of the novelist Henry James, and he spent twelve years writing his two-volume Principles of Psychology, published in 1890. This chapter was first printed as a magazine article, and it shows. It is clear, vivid and urgent, written for ordinary people, not specialists. James had his own reasons for caring. In his late twenties he fell into a deep depression, convinced that science had made human beings into helpless machines, and he climbed out by deciding to treat his own choices as real. Habit, for him, is both the machinery and the escape route. The brain is physically shaped by what we repeat, so repetition can trap us or free us. His chapter explains how, and ends with practical rules for building good habits and breaking bad ones.
paragraphs: When we look at living creatures from an outward point of view, one of the first things that strike us is that they are bundles of habits. In wild animals, the usual round of daily behavior seems a necessity implanted at birth; in animals domesticated, and especially in man, it seems, to a great extent, to be the result of education. The habits to which there is an innate tendency are called instincts; some of those due to education would by most persons be called acts of reason. It thus appears that habit covers a very large part of life, and that one engaged in studying the objective manifestations of mind is bound at the very outset to define clearly just what its limits are.

The moment one tries to define what habit is, one is led to the fundamental properties of matter. The laws of Nature are nothing but the immutable habits which the different elementary sorts of matter follow in their actions and reactions upon each other. In the organic world, however, the habits are more variable than this. Even instincts vary from one individual to another of a kind; and are modified in the same individual, as we shall later see, to suit the exigencies of the case. Plasticity, then, in the wide sense of the word, means the possession of a structure weak enough to yield to an influence, but strong enough not to yield all at once. Each relatively stable phase of equilibrium in such a structure is marked by what we may call a new set of habits. Organic matter, especially nervous tissue, seems endowed with a very extraordinary degree of plasticity of this sort; so that we may without hesitation lay down as our first proposition the following, that the phenomena of habit in living beings are due to the plasticity of the organic materials of which their bodies are composed.

If habits are due to the plasticity of materials to outward agents, we can immediately see to what outward influences, if to any, the brain-matter is plastic. Not to mechanical pressures, not to thermal changes, not to any of the forces to which all the other organs of our body are exposed; for nature has carefully shut up our brain and spinal cord in bony boxes, where no influences of this sort can get at them. She has floated them in fluid so that only the severest shocks can give them a concussion, and blanketed and wrapped them about in an altogether exceptional way. The only impressions that can be made upon them are through the blood, on the one hand, and through the sensory nerve-roots, on the other; and it is to the infinitely attenuated currents that pour in through these latter channels that the hemispherical cortex shows itself to be so peculiarly susceptible. The currents, once in, must find a way out. In getting out they leave their traces in the paths which they take. The only thing they can do, in short, is to deepen old paths or to make new ones; and the whole plasticity of the brain sums itself up in two words when we call it an organ in which currents pouring in from the sense-organs make with extreme facility paths which do not easily disappear.

Habit is thus the enormous fly-wheel of society, its most precious conservative agent. It alone is what keeps us all within the bounds of ordinance, and saves the children of fortune from the envious uprisings of the poor. It alone prevents the hardest and most repulsive walks of life from being deserted by those brought up to tread therein. It keeps the fisherman and the deck-hand at sea through the winter; it holds the miner in his darkness, and nails the countryman to his log-cabin and his lonely farm through all the months of snow; it protects us from invasion by the natives of the desert and the frozen zone. It dooms us all to fight out the battle of life upon the lines of our nurture or our early choice, and to make the best of a pursuit that disagrees, because there is no other for which we are fitted, and it is too late to begin again. It keeps different social strata from mixing. Already at the age of twenty-five you see the professional mannerism settling down on the young commercial traveller, on the young doctor, on the young minister, on the young counsellor-at-law. You see the little lines of cleavage running through the character, the tricks of thought, the prejudices, the ways of the 'shop,' in a word, from which the man can by-and-by no more escape than his coat-sleeve can suddenly fall into a new set of folds. On the whole, it is best he should not escape. It is well for the world that in most of us, by the age of thirty, the character has set like plaster, and will never soften again.

The great thing, then, in all education, is to make our nervous system our ally instead of our enemy. It is to fund and capitalize our acquisitions, and live at ease upon the interest of the fund. For this we must make automatic and habitual, as early as possible, as many useful actions as we can, and guard against the growing into ways that are likely to be disadvantageous to us, as we should guard against the plague. The more of the details of our daily life we can hand over to the effortless custody of automatism, the more our higher powers of mind will be set free for their own proper work. There is no more miserable human being than one in whom nothing is habitual but indecision, and for whom the lighting of every cigar, the drinking of every cup, the time of rising and going to bed every day, and the beginning of every bit of work, are subjects of express volitional deliberation. Full half the time of such a man goes to the deciding, or regretting, of matters which ought to be so ingrained in him as practically not to exist for his consciousness at all. If there be such daily duties not yet ingrained in any one of my readers, let him begin this very hour to set the matter right.

In Professor Bain's chapter on 'The Moral Habits' there are some admirable practical remarks laid down. Two great maxims emerge from his treatment. The first is that in the acquisition of a new habit, or the leaving off of an old one, we must take care to launch ourselves with as strong and decided an initiative as possible. Accumulate all the possible circumstances which shall re-enforce the right motives; put yourself assiduously in conditions that encourage the new way; make engagements incompatible with the old; take a public pledge, if the case allows; in short, envelop your resolution with every aid you know. This will give your new beginning such a momentum that the temptation to break down will not occur as soon as it otherwise might; and every day during which a breakdown is postponed adds to the chances of its not occurring at all.

The second maxim is: Never suffer an exception to occur till the new habit is securely rooted in your life. Each lapse is like the letting fall of a ball of string which one is carefully winding up; a single slip undoes more than a great many turns will wind again. Continuity of training is the great means of making the nervous system act infallibly right.

A third maxim may be added to the preceding pair: Seize the very first possible opportunity to act on every resolution you make, and on every emotional prompting you may experience in the direction of the habits you aspire to gain.
