It is not in the moment of their forming, but in the moment of their producing motor effects, that resolves and aspirations communicate the new 'set' to the brain. No matter how full a reservoir of maxims one may possess, and no matter how good one's sentiments may be, if one have not taken advantage of every concrete opportunity to act, one's character may remain entirely unaffected for the better. With mere good intentions, hell is proverbially paved. And this is an obvious consequence of the principles we have laid down. A 'character,' as J. S. Mill says, 'is a completely fashioned will'; and a will, in the sense in which he means it, is an aggregate of tendencies to act in a firm and prompt and definite way upon all the principal emergencies of life. A tendency to act only becomes effectively ingrained in us in proportion to the uninterrupted frequency with which the actions actually occur, and the brain 'grows' to their use. Every time a resolve or a fine glow of feeling evaporates without bearing practical fruit is worse than a chance lost; it works so as positively to hinder future resolutions and emotions from taking the normal path of discharge. There is no more contemptible type of human character than that of the nerveless sentimentalist and dreamer, who spends his life in a weltering sea of sensibility and emotion, but who never does a manly concrete deed. Rousseau, inflaming all the mothers of France, by his eloquence, to follow Nature and nurse their babies themselves, while he sends his own children to the foundling hospital, is the classical example of what I mean.

Keep the faculty of effort alive in you by a little gratuitous exercise every day. That is, be systematically ascetic or heroic in little unnecessary points, do every day or two something for no other reason than that you would rather not do it, so that when the hour of dire need draws nigh, it may find you not unnerved and untrained to stand the test. Asceticism of this sort is like the insurance which a man pays on his house and goods. The tax does him no good at the time, and possibly may never bring him a return. But if the fire does come, his having paid it will be his salvation from ruin. So with the man who has daily inured himself to habits of concentrated attention, energetic volition, and self-denial in unnecessary things. He will stand like a tower when everything rocks around him, and when his softer fellow-mortals are winnowed like chaff in the blast.

The physiological study of mental conditions is thus the most powerful ally of hortatory ethics. The hell to be endured hereafter, of which theology tells, is no worse than the hell we make for ourselves in this world by habitually fashioning our characters in the wrong way. Could the young but realize how soon they will become mere walking bundles of habits, they would give more heed to their conduct while in the plastic state. We are spinning our own fates, good or evil, and never to be undone. Every smallest stroke of virtue or of vice leaves its never so little scar. The drunken Rip Van Winkle, in Jefferson's play, excuses himself for every fresh dereliction by saying, 'I won't count this time!' Well! he may not count it, and a kind Heaven may not count it; but it is being counted none the less. Down among his nerve-cells and fibres the molecules are counting it, registering and storing it up to be used against him when the next temptation comes. Nothing we ever do is, in strict scientific literalness, wiped out. Of course, this has its good side as well as its bad one. As we become permanent drunkards by so many separate drinks, so we become saints in the moral, and authorities and experts in the practical and scientific spheres, by so many separate acts and hours of work. Let no youth have any anxiety about the upshot of his education, whatever the line of it may be. If he keep faithfully busy each hour of the working-day, he may safely leave the final result to itself. He can with perfect certainty count on waking up some fine morning, to find himself one of the competent ones of his generation, in whatever pursuit he may have singled out. Silently, between all the details of his business, the power of judging in all that class of matter will have built itself up within him as a possession that will never pass away. Young people should know this truth in advance. The ignorance of it has probably engendered more discouragement and faint-heartedness in youths embarking on arduous careers than all other causes put together.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
James begins from a simple observation: living creatures are "bundles of habits." Watch an animal and you see a round of routine. Watch yourself and you will see the same: the way you dress, speak, walk, think. His question is what habit actually is, and his answer is physical. The brain is made of living material that is "plastic," meaning it can take a shape and keep it. Just as a sheet of paper, once folded, tends to fold along the same crease, nerve tissue that has carried a current once finds it easier to carry it again. He sums it up: the brain is "an organ in which currents pouring in from the sense-organs make with extreme facility paths which do not easily disappear." Repeated actions wear paths, and the paths make the next repetition easier.

From that single idea, James builds a whole picture of society and character. Habit, he says, is "the enormous fly-wheel of society, its most precious conservative agent." A flywheel is a heavy wheel that keeps a machine turning steadily. Habit keeps people at their jobs, in their routines, within the bounds of ordinary life. It keeps the fisherman going out in the cold and the laborer at his trade, which is why the world does not collapse into chaos. He also says that by the age of thirty "the character has set like plaster, and will never soften again." That is a striking line, and we will come back to whether it is true.

Then the chapter turns to advice, and this is where it becomes memorable. The great thing in education, he says, is "to make our nervous system our ally instead of our enemy." Think of habit as a bank account. Make useful actions automatic early, and you "live at ease upon the interest of the fund." The more details of daily life we hand over to automatic routine, the more mental energy remains for higher things. People who have to decide every morning whether to get up or how to dress are wasting their best attention.

Then come the rules. Start a new habit with as strong and decided an initiative as possible. Never let an exception occur until the habit is rooted, because a lapse is like dropping a ball of string you are carefully winding: "a single slip undoes more than a great many turns will wind again." Seize every chance to act on a resolution, since good intentions alone do nothing; "hell is proverbially paved" with them. And do something every day or two "for no other reason than that you would rather not do it," so that when real hardship comes you stand "like a tower."

The final point is moral and sobering. Every action leaves a trace. "We are spinning our own fates, good or evil, and never to be undone." Even the small lapse leaves "its never so little scar." That is the layer first-time readers sometimes miss: this is not only a productivity manual, but a warning that you are always becoming someone.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
As popular science writing, "Habit" is superb. James does what the best explainers do: he finds a handful of images and sticks to them. The paper crease, the flywheel, the bank account, the ball of string, the plaster setting. Each one is physical, each can be remembered in a sentence, and together they cover the whole argument. The ball of string in particular is a gem, because it captures something true and counterintuitive about habit formation: the cost of a lapse is out of proportion to the lapse itself.

His structure is also admirable. He moves from a general fact, to a physical mechanism, to a social consequence, to a personal program, and each step feels earned. The chapter reads like a lecture from a charismatic teacher who is trying not only to inform but to change what you do tomorrow morning. There is real humor, too, in the portrait of the dreamer who is moved to tears by a tragedy at the theater but never helps anyone, and in the swipe at Rousseau, who urged French mothers to nurse their babies while sending his own children to a foundling hospital.

But the chapter has weaknesses that become clearer with time. The neurological language is more confident than the evidence of 1890 could support. James had no way of seeing neurons change, and "paths" and "currents" are metaphors, not findings. He is guessing intelligently, and he turned out to be broadly right, but it is a guess. A reader who treats the chapter as a scientific report, and not as a brilliant piece of reasoning, will be misled.

The claim that character "sets like plaster" by thirty is the clearest overstatement. It is memorable and rhetorically useful, but we now know that adult brains remain far more adaptable than that, and James himself spent much of the chapter urging people to change. There is a tension in his message: on one hand, you are shaping your fate irreversibly; on the other, here is how to remake yourself. He never fully reconciles the two, and the dire passages about irreversible scars can read as heavy-handed, even a bit Victorian in their moral gloom.

There is also a class tone. The idea that habit "saves the children of fortune from the envious uprisings of the poor" and keeps people content in their stations reveals the outlook of a comfortable professional. He calls habit a conservative force with evident approval. And the ending, which urges a kind of daily asceticism, assumes that suffering in small things is character-building in itself, an assumption many readers now question. Still, the best parts of the chapter outweigh these flaws by a wide margin.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
The chapter's influence has been broad and long. Within psychology, it helped establish habit as a central subject. James's Principles of Psychology became the standard text of the young science in America, and this chapter was one of its most read parts. Later schools drew on it in different ways. The behaviorists, who studied learning through repeated stimulus and response, saw in James an ancestor, and his picture of paths worn by repetition anticipates what we now call learning by reinforcement. Later neuroscientists, who showed that connections between neurons strengthen with use, found that his guess about plasticity had been remarkably close. The slogan "cells that fire together wire together" is often used to summarize what James described in different words.

In philosophy, the chapter belongs to the development of pragmatism, the distinctively American school of thought, led by James, Charles Peirce and later John Dewey, that judges ideas by their consequences in practice. Dewey's book Human Nature and Conduct, published in 1922, is a long meditation on habit that clearly builds on James's work. European thinkers took notice as well, and the French philosopher Henri Bergson was in conversation with James about the nature of mental life.

Culturally, the effect has been enormous, though often invisible. When a teacher says "practice makes permanent," when a coach talks about building routines, or when a self-help book tells you to start small and never miss twice, James is in the background. Modern bestsellers on habit, such as Charles Duhigg's The Power of Habit and James Clear's Atomic Habits, cover territory this chapter mapped, and his ball-of-string maxim is essentially the "never miss twice" rule.

The chapter also shaped how educators think. James gave lectures to teachers, published as Talks to Teachers, in which he applied the psychology of habit to the classroom. The idea that education is largely a matter of building useful automatic skills, such as reading, arithmetic, and manners, owes something to him.

In the broader culture of self-improvement, the chapter gave moral authority to the idea that character is built in small daily acts. This is the basis of countless routines, from morning disciplines to training regimens. It is taught today in courses on psychology, philosophy and education, and is a frequent selection in anthologies of American essays, usually as an example of how a scientist can write for the public with force and grace.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
People love this chapter for its usefulness. Few pieces of nineteenth-century science can be read as a practical guide, and fewer still hold up. Readers who pick it up expecting a dry old textbook are often startled to find that its advice is exactly what they would hear from a good coach today. Start strong. Do not allow exceptions. Act on your resolutions at once. Practice small acts of effort. These rules are easy to remember and demanding to follow.

They also love the images. The ball of string is the favorite, since anyone who has tried to get up early, keep a diet, or write every day knows how a single slip can unwind a week's work. The bank account of habit, from which we "live at ease upon the interest," gives a hopeful, almost financial way to think about discipline: it is an investment, not a punishment. The flywheel gives a sense of the dignity of routine. These are metaphors a reader can carry into the day.

Another source of affection is James's tone. He writes like a friend who is on your side, warm and direct, with flashes of humor. He addresses the reader openly: "let him begin this very hour." He does not scold from a height; he explains why the mechanism works so that you can use it. Many readers say that learning the reason behind the advice, that your brain is actually changing, made the advice feel more real.

The chapter has also been loved for its hope. Its final warning about irreversible scars could be read as grim, but the heart of the chapter is that you can make your own nervous system an ally. The reader who is stuck is told that the stuckness is not fate but a pattern, and patterns are made of repetition. That is why it has so often been quoted to people in difficult times. James himself had climbed out of a deep despair by acting as if his choices counted, and readers sense that the chapter comes from someone who has tested it on himself.

Finally, writers and scientists have admired the ambition: a short chapter that links the behavior of atoms, the structure of the brain, the order of society and the building of a personal character. It is rare to find an essay that moves so confidently from the small to the large.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
The pushback on "Habit" falls into a few groups. The first is scientific. Later researchers pointed out that James's picture of the brain was speculative and that his claims about fixed paths were too simple. Habit formation, it turns out, involves several brain systems, and habits can be changed later in life far more readily than "set like plaster" suggests. The idea that adults cannot change after thirty has been widely rejected, and many modern writers on habit treat the line as an example of how not to think about aging. Some also note that modern popular claims, such as that it takes a fixed number of days to form a habit, are not found in James and have little evidence behind them; his version is more careful than much of what has followed.

The second is philosophical. James was a champion of free will, yet his chapter leans heavily on a mechanical picture of the nervous system. Critics have asked whether he could consistently believe both that we are bundles of habit and that we freely choose our paths. He took the question seriously, and elsewhere in the Principles he defends the power of attention and effort, but the chapter itself does not resolve it, and some readers feel it hovers between determinism and exhortation.

The third is moral and social. The statement that habit keeps the poor from rising against the rich has struck many later readers as complacent. James presents habit as a conservative force that holds society together, and his picture of people settling into their stations by thirty implies a rather fixed social order. Readers sensitive to inequality have noticed how much of the chapter assumes an educated reader with the freedom to arrange his own days. For a worker with unpredictable shifts or a caregiver with no free hour, advice to begin "this very hour" may feel remote.

There is also the charge of moralism. The ascetic advice to do something every day because you would rather not has been criticized as joyless, and the language about hell and scars can feel like a sermon in scientific dress. Modern psychologists often prefer to emphasize making good behavior easy and pleasant, not building willpower through small hardships.

Finally, some critics see a certain smugness in the swipes at "sentimentalists" who feel deeply but do nothing. The attack on Rousseau, though funny, is personal, and it contains an idea, that feeling without action corrupts, which some think is too harsh on emotional people. These objections do not undo the chapter's value, but they remind us that it is a lively and opinionated work, not a neutral report.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
James's "Habit" sits at the crossroads of science, philosophy and moral advice. Its deepest ancestor is Aristotle, who argued in the Nicomachean Ethics that we become just by doing just acts and brave by doing brave acts, so that character is built by repetition. The philosopher David Hume wrote of "custom" as the great guide of human life, and the British psychologist Alexander Bain, whom James cites in the text, laid out practical maxims for forming moral habits that James adopts and sharpens. What is new in James is the physical grounding: he takes the old moral doctrine and ties it to the living tissue of the brain, at a moment when physiology was just becoming a science.

Its descendants are plentiful. In psychology, it feeds into behaviorism and learning theory, and later into cognitive neuroscience. In philosophy, it is part of pragmatism, with Dewey's later book on habit its most direct heir. In public life, it underlies the modern self-help and productivity industry, as well as serious fields like habit-formation research in public health.

Comparing it with the other essays on reading and attention is rewarding. Bacon, in "Of Studies," made a very similar claim three centuries earlier, that studies "pass into manners," meaning that what you read and practice becomes who you are. James supplies the mechanism that Bacon only asserted. Montaigne's runaway mind, galloping without direction, is what James would call a nervous system without grooves, and Montaigne's remedy of writing is a habit in James's sense. Emerson's call for an original relation to the universe depends on a self not dragged by routine, and James would say you earn that freedom by automating the routine so that attention is free. And Woolf's description of how to read as an acquired skill, built with practice, is a Jamesian picture too.

Why still read it? Because it is one of the few older science texts that is also a manual for living. It says clearly what many people now spend money to learn: that the quality of a life is the sum of what you do repeatedly. It offers a way of thinking about change that is neither magical nor hopeless. And it is a pleasure to read, direct, witty and humane. You may disagree with details, but you will probably find yourself noticing, tomorrow morning, which of your actions are paths and which are choices.

essays.title: How Should One Read a Book?
essays.author: Virginia Woolf
essays.epigraph: The only advice, indeed, that one person can give another about reading is to take no advice, to follow your own instincts, to use your own reason, to come to your own conclusions.
essays.keyContext: Virginia Woolf's "How Should One Read a Book?" began as a talk to schoolgirls at a school in Kent in January 1926, and was later published in a magazine and gathered into a book of essays in 1932. Woolf was by then one of the leading figures of English modernism, the writer of Mrs. Dalloway and soon of To the Lighthouse, and a central member of the Bloomsbury circle of writers and artists. She had never been to university, while her brothers had, and she educated herself by wandering through her father's enormous library. That history lies behind the essay. She borrows from Samuel Johnson the idea of the "common reader," an ordinary person who reads for pleasure, and she defends that person's authority against professors and critics. Her advice is startlingly short: trust yourself, read openly first, judge later. The essay ends with a funny, tender picture of what readers are really for.
paragraphs: In the first place, I want to emphasize the note of interrogation at the end of my title. Even if I could answer the question for myself, the answer would apply only to me and not to you. The only advice, indeed, that one person can give another about reading is to take no advice, to follow your own instincts, to use your own reason, to come to your own conclusions. If this is agreed between us, then I feel at liberty to put forward a few ideas and suggestions because you will not allow them to fetter that independence which is the most important quality that a reader can possess. After all, what laws can be laid down about books? The battle of Waterloo was certainly fought on a certain day; but is Hamlet a better play than Lear? Nobody can say. Each must decide that question for himself. To admit authorities, however heavily furred and gowned, into our libraries and let them tell us how to read, what to read, what value to place upon what we read, is to destroy the spirit of freedom which is the breath of those sanctuaries. Everywhere else we may be bound by laws and conventions—there we have none.

But to enjoy freedom, if the platitude is pardonable, we have of course to control ourselves. We must not squander our powers, helplessly and ignorantly, squirting half the house in order to water a single rose-bush; we must train them, exactly and powerfully, here on the very spot. This, it may be, is one of the first difficulties that faces us in a library. What is “the very spot?” There may well seem to be nothing but a conglomeration and huddle of confusion. Poems and novels, histories and memories, dictionaries and blue-books; books written in all languages by men and women of all tempers, races, and ages jostle each other on the shelf. And outside the donkey brays, the women gossip at the pump, the colts gallop across the fields. Where are we to begin? How are we to bring order into this multitudinous chaos and so get the deepest and widest pleasure from what we read?

It is simple enough to say that since books have classes—fiction, biography, poetry—we should separate them and take from each what it is right that each should give us. Yet few people ask from books what books can give us. Most commonly we come to books with blurred and divided minds, asking of fiction that it shall be true, of poetry that it shall be false, of biography that it shall be flattering, of history that it shall enforce our own prejudices. If we could banish all such preconceptions when we read, that would be an admirable beginning. Do not dictate to your author; try to become him. Be his fellow-worker and accomplice. If you hang back, and reserve and criticize at first, you are preventing yourself from getting the fullest possible value from what you read. But if you open your mind as widely as possible, then signs and hints of almost imperceptible fineness, from the twist and turn of the first sentences, will bring you into the presence of a human being unlike any other. Steep yourself in this, acquaint yourself with this, and soon you will find that your author is giving you, or attempting to give you, something far more definite. The thirty chapters of a novel—if we consider how to read a novel first—are an attempt to make something as formed and controlled as a building: but words are more impalpable than bricks; reading is a longer and more complicated process than seeing. Perhaps the quickest way to understand the elements of what a novelist is doing is not to read, but to write; to make your own experiment with the dangers and difficulties of words. Recall, then, some event that has left a distinct impression on you—how at the corner of the street, perhaps, you passed two people talking. A tree shook; an electric light danced; the tone of the talk was comic, but also tragic; a whole vision, an entire conception, seemed contained in that moment.

But when you attempt to reconstruct it in words, you will find that it breaks into a thousand conflicting impressions. Some must be subdued; others emphasized; in the process you will lose, probably, all grasp upon the emotion itself. Then turn from your blurred and littered pages to the opening pages of some great novelist—Defoe, Jane Austen, Hardy. Now you will be better able to appreciate their mastery. It is not merely that we are in the presence of a different person—Defoe, Jane Austen, or Thomas Hardy—but that we are living in a different world. Here, in Robinson Crusoe, we are trudging a plain high road; one thing happens after another; the fact and the order of the fact is enough. But if the open air and adventure mean everything to Defoe they mean nothing to Jane Austen. Hers is the drawing-room, and people talking, and by the many mirrors of their talk revealing their characters. And if, when we have accustomed ourselves to the drawing-room and its reflections, we turn to Hardy, we are once more spun round. The moors are round us and the stars are above our heads. The other side of the mind is now exposed—the dark side that comes uppermost in solitude, not the light side that shows in company. Our relations are not towards people, but towards Nature and destiny. Yet different as these worlds are, each is consistent with itself. The maker of each is careful to observe the laws of his own perspective, and however great a strain they may put upon us they will never confuse us, as lesser writers so frequently do, by introducing two different kinds of reality into the same book. Thus to go from one great novelist to another—from Jane Austen to Hardy, from Peacock to Trollope, from Scott to Meredith—is to be wrenched and uprooted; to be thrown this way and then that. To read a novel is a difficult and complex art. You must be capable not only of great fineness of perception, but of great boldness of imagination if you are going to make use of all that the novelist—the great artist—gives you.

But a glance at the heterogeneous company on the shelf will show you that writers are very seldom “great artists;” far more often a book makes no claim to be a work of art at all. These biographies and autobiographies, for example, lives of great men, of men long dead and forgotten, that stand cheek by jowl with the novels and poems, are we to refuse to read them because they are not “art?” Or shall we read them, but read them in a different way, with a different aim? Shall we read them in the first place to satisfy that curiosity which possesses us sometimes when in the evening we linger in front of a house where the lights are lit and the blinds not yet drawn, and each floor of the house shows us a different section of human life in being? Then we are consumed with curiosity about the lives of these people—the servants gossiping, the gentlemen dining, the girl dressing for a party, the old woman at the window with her knitting. Who are they, what are they, what are their names, their occupations, their thoughts, and adventures?

Also we can read such books with another aim, not to throw light on literature, not to become familiar with famous people, but to refresh and exercise our own creative powers. Is there not an open window on the right hand of the bookcase? How delightful to stop reading and look out! How stimulating the scene is, in its unconsciousness, its irrelevance, its perpetual movement—the colts galloping round the field, the woman filling her pail at the well, the donkey throwing back his head and emitting his long, acrid moan. The greater part of any library is nothing but the record of such fleeting moments in the lives of men, women, and donkeys. Every literature, as it grows old, has its rubbish-heap, its record of vanished moments and forgotten lives told in faltering and feeble accents that have perished. But if you give yourself up to the delight of rubbish-reading you will be surprised, indeed you will be overcome, by the relics of human life that have been cast out to molder. It may be one letter—but what a vision it gives! It may be a few sentences—but what vistas they suggest! Sometimes a whole story will come together with such beautiful humor and pathos and completeness that it seems as if a great novelist had been at work, yet it is only an old actor, Tate Wilkinson, remembering the strange story of Captain Jones; it is only a young subaltern serving under Arthur Wellesley and falling in love with a pretty girl at Lisbon; it is only Maria Allen letting fall her sewing in the empty drawing-room and sighing how she wishes she had taken Dr Burney's good advice and had never eloped with her Rishy. None of this has any value; it is negligible in the extreme; yet how absorbing it is now and again to go through the rubbish-heaps and find rings and scissors and broken noses buried in the huge past and try to piece them together while the colt gallops round the field, the woman fills her pail at the well, and the donkey brays.

But we tire of rubbish-reading in the long run. We tire of searching for what is needed to complete the half-truth which is all that the Wilkinsons, the Bunburys and the Maria Allens are able to offer us. They had not the artist's power of mastering and eliminating; they could not tell the whole truth even about their own lives; they have disfigured the story that might have been so shapely. Facts are all that they can offer us, and facts are a very inferior form of fiction. Thus the desire grows upon us to have done with half-statements and approximations; to cease from searching out the minute shades of human character, to enjoy the greater abstractness, the purer truth of fiction. Thus we create the mood, intense and generalized, unaware of detail, but stressed by some regular, recurrent beat, whose natural expression is poetry; and that is the time to read poetry when we are almost able to write it.

The impact of poetry is so hard and direct that for the moment there is no other sensation except that of the poem itself. What profound depths we visit then—how sudden and complete is our immersion! There is nothing here to catch hold of; nothing to stay us in our flight. The illusion of fiction is gradual; its effects are prepared; but who when they read these four lines stops to ask who wrote them, or conjures up the thought of Donne's house or Sidney's secretary; or enmeshes them in the intricacy of the past and the succession of generations? The poet is always our contemporary. Our being for the moment is centered and constricted, as in any violent shock of personal emotion. Afterwards, it is true, the sensation begins to spread in wider rings through our minds; remoter senses are reached; these begin to sound and to comment and we are aware of echoes and reflections. The intensity of poetry covers an immense range of emotion.

“We have only to compare”—with those words the cat is out of the bag, and the true complexity of reading is admitted. The first process, to receive impressions with the utmost understanding, is only half the process of reading; it must be completed, if we are to get the whole pleasure from a book, by another. We must pass judgment upon these multitudinous impressions; we must make of these fleeting shapes one that is hard and lasting. But not directly. Wait for the dust of reading to settle; for the conflict and the questioning to die down; walk, talk, pull the dead petals from a rose, or fall asleep. Then suddenly without our willing it, for it is thus that Nature undertakes these transitions, the book will return, but differently. It will float to the top of the mind as a whole. And the book as a whole is different from the book received currently in separate phrases. Details now fit themselves into their places. We see the shape from start to finish; it is a barn, a pig-sty, or a cathedral. Now then we can compare book with book as we compare building with building. But this act of comparison means that our attitude has changed; we are no longer the friends of the writer, but his judges; and just as we cannot be too sympathetic as friends, so as judges we cannot be too severe. Are they not criminals, books that have wasted our time and sympathy; are they not the most insidious enemies of society, corrupters, defilers, the writers of false books, faked books, books that fill the air with decay and disease? Let us then be severe in our judgments; let us compare each book with the greatest of its kind. There they hang in the mind the shapes of the books we have read solidified by the judgments we have passed on them—Robinson Crusoe, Emma, The Return of the Native. Compare the novels with these—even the latest and least of novels has a right to be judged with the best. And so with poetry when the intoxication of rhythm has died down and the splendor of words has faded, a visionary shape will return to us and this must be compared with Lear, with Phèdre, with The Prelude; or if not with these, with whatever is the best or seems to us to be the best in its own kind. And we may be sure that the newness of new poetry and fiction is its most superficial quality and that we have only to alter slightly, not to recast, the standards by which we have judged the old.

It would be foolish, then, to pretend that the second part of reading, to judge, to compare, is as simple as the first—to open the mind wide to the fast flocking of innumerable impressions. To continue reading without the book before you, to hold one shadow-shape against another, to have read widely enough and with enough understanding to make such comparisons alive and illuminating—that is difficult; it is still more difficult to press further and to say, “Not only is the book of this sort, but it is of this value; here it fails; here it succeeds; this is bad; that is good.” To carry out this part of a reader's duty needs such imagination, insight, and learning that it is hard to conceive any one mind sufficiently endowed; impossible for the most self-confident to find more than the seeds of such powers in himself. Would it not be wiser, then, to remit this part of reading and to allow the critics, the gowned and furred authorities of the library, to decide the question of the book's absolute value for us? Yet how impossible! We may stress the value of sympathy; we may try to sink our own identity as we read. But we know that we cannot sympathize wholly or immerse ourselves wholly; there is always a demon in us who whispers, “I hate, I love,” and we cannot silence him. Indeed, it is precisely because we hate and we love that our relation with the poets and novelists is so intimate that we find the presence of another person intolerable. And even if the results are abhorrent and our judgments are wrong, still our taste, the nerve of sensation that sends shocks through us, is our chief illuminant; we learn through feeling; we cannot suppress our own idiosyncrasy without impoverishing it. But as time goes on perhaps we can train our taste; perhaps we can make it submit to some control. When it has fed greedily and lavishly upon books of all sorts—poetry, fiction, history, biography—and has stopped reading and looked for long spaces upon the variety, the incongruity of the living world, we shall find that it is changing a little; it is not so greedy, it is more reflective. It will begin to bring us not merely judgments on particular books, but it will tell us that there is a quality common to certain books. Listen, it will say, what shall we call this? And it will read us perhaps Lear and then perhaps the Agamemnon in order to bring out that common quality. Thus, with our taste to guide us, we shall venture beyond the particular book in search of qualities that group books together; we shall give them names and thus frame a rule that brings order into our perceptions. We shall gain a further and a rarer pleasure from that discrimination. But as a rule only lives when it is perpetually broken by contact with the books themselves—nothing is easier and more stultifying than to make rules which exist out of touch with facts, in a vacuum—now at last, in order to steady ourselves in this difficult attempt, it may be well to turn to the very rare writers who are able to enlighten us upon literature as an art. Coleridge and Dryden and Johnson, in their considered criticism, the poets and novelists themselves in their unconsidered sayings, are often surprisingly relevant; they light up and solidify the vague ideas that have been tumbling in the misty depths of our minds. But they are only able to help us if we come to them laden with questions and suggestions won honestly in the course of our own reading. They can do nothing for us if we herd ourselves under their authority and lie down like sheep in the shade of a hedge. We can only understand their ruling when it comes in conflict with our own and vanquishes it.

If this is so, if to read a book as it should be read calls for the rarest qualities of imagination, insight, and judgment, you may perhaps conclude that literature is a very complex art and that it is unlikely that we shall be able, even after a lifetime of reading, to make any valuable contribution to its criticism. We must remain readers; we shall not put on the further glory that belongs to those rare beings who are also critics. But still we have our responsibilities as readers and even our importance. The standards we raise and the judgments we pass steal into the air and become part of the atmosphere which writers breathe as they work. An influence is created which tells upon them even if it never finds its way into print. And that influence, if it were well instructed, vigorous and individual and sincere, might be of great value now when criticism is necessarily in abeyance; when books pass in review like the procession of animals in a shooting gallery, and the critic has only one second in which to load and aim and shoot and may well be pardoned if he mistakes rabbits for tigers, eagles for barndoor fowls, or misses altogether and wastes his shot upon some peaceful cow grazing in a further field. If behind the erratic gunfire of the press the author felt that there was another kind of criticism, the opinion of people reading for the love of reading, slowly and unprofessionally, and judging with great sympathy and yet with great severity, might this not improve the quality of his work? And if by our means books were to become stronger, richer, and more varied, that would be an end worth reaching.

Yet who reads to bring about an end, however desirable? Are there not some pursuits that we practice because they are good in themselves, and some pleasures that are final? And is not this among them? I have sometimes dreamt, at least, that when the Day of Judgment dawns and the great conquerors and lawyers and statesmen come to receive their rewards—their crowns, their laurels, their names carved indelibly upon imperishable marble—the Almighty will turn to Peter and will say, not without a certain envy when He sees us coming with our books under our arms, “Look, these need no reward. We have nothing to give them here. They have loved reading.”

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
Woolf begins by putting a question mark on her own title. She says she cannot tell you how to read, because any answer she gave would apply only to her. "The only advice, indeed, that one person can give another about reading is to take no advice, to follow your own instincts, to use your own reason, to come to your own conclusions." It is a wonderful trick: an advice talk whose first piece of advice is to ignore advice. She justifies it with an example. The battle of Waterloo was fought on a certain day, but "is Hamlet a better play than Lear? Nobody can say." Facts can be looked up. Literary value has to be decided by each reader, and to let authorities "however heavily furred and gowned" tell us what to read "is to destroy the spirit of freedom which is the breath of those sanctuaries."

But freedom, she says, needs discipline. We must not squander our powers "squirting half the house in order to water a single rose-bush." The reader's problem is that a library is a chaos of voices, and the first step is to ask what each kind of book can give. Most of us come to books with "blurred and divided minds," demanding that fiction be true, poetry false, biography flattering and history agreeable to our prejudices. Her cure is the heart of the essay: "Do not dictate to your author; try to become him. Be his fellow-worker and accomplice." Open your mind as widely as possible, and the "twist and turn of the first sentences" will start to reveal a person.

To show why reading is hard, she asks you to try writing. Describe a moment you saw, two people talking as a tree shook and an electric light danced, and you will find it "breaks into a thousand conflicting impressions." After that failure, go back to Defoe, Jane Austen or Hardy, and their mastery shines. Robinson Crusoe is a plain high road where one thing follows another. Austen is a world of social nuance. Each great novelist builds a different world, and to read well you must live in it on its terms.

She then moves down the shelf. Lives, letters and memoirs, the "rubbish" of ordinary people like Tate Wilkinson or Maria Allen, are not art, but they let us look through "the open window" into rooms and lives long gone, and they give our own imagination exercise. Poetry, on the other hand, is something to read when we are "almost able to write it," when the mind is stirred and ready for its concentrated impact.

Finally comes the second half of reading, which most people forget: comparison and judgment. First you receive, with all your understanding. Then, after the book is closed, you weigh what you read against the masterpieces. The essay closes with a joke that turns serious. On Judgment Day the Almighty will say to Peter, with a touch of envy, of the readers: "Look, these need no reward... They have loved reading." The reader who needs no prize is her final hero.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
This is an unusually well-made piece of occasional writing. Woolf had a gift for sounding as though she were thinking aloud, and the talk's structure is cleverly hidden inside what feels like a stroll. She opens with a paradox, moves through a series of shelves, and ends with a joke and a vision. The speaking voice, intimate and a little teasing, makes it ideal for the ear. Lines such as "squirting half the house in order to water a single rose-bush" are funny and exact, and the picture of the Almighty envying readers is the kind of ending that makes an audience smile and then go quiet.

Her best idea, and the one that distinguishes the essay from a hundred others on reading, is the exercise of writing a scene yourself. By asking you to fail, deliberately, at capturing something you saw, she gives you an immediate, physical sense of how hard writing is, and therefore how much to admire it. This is better than any lecture on craft. The twin movement of reading, opening and then judging, is also a genuinely useful framework. It is simple, memorable, and true to experience: most readers either judge too early and spoil their pleasure or never judge at all.

The imagery of the shelf, with its open window, the colt galloping in the field, the woman filling her pail at the well, has the dreamlike detail of Woolf's fiction. It is a rare critical essay that doubles as a small prose poem.

But it is not flawless. The advice contains a quiet contradiction. Having told us to take no advice, she gives a good deal, and a firm hierarchy too: great artists at the top, memoirs and letters as a lesser pleasure, "rubbish-reading" that we eventually tire of. The phrase about tiring of rubbish reveals a certain snobbery, and the essay's assumption that poetry is the summit and that real readers will naturally move toward it is a taste dressed as a law. She also assumes a reader with leisure, a library and time to compare, which is not every reader's condition.

There is vagueness, too. What does it mean to "become" the author, or to compare a book with "the greatest" without absorbing the canon's authority? She warns against herding under authorities, and yet the standard she proposes, the masterpieces, is itself an authority, though a chosen one. Her suggestion that we reach a judgment by holding a "shadow-shape" of the book in our minds is evocative but hard to follow in practice. The essay is more inspiring than instructive, and it does not entirely resolve the tension between freedom and standards. Yet it is honest about difficulty, admitting that the second half of reading is much harder than the first.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
The essay's influence lies less in dramatic events than in a steady shaping of how people talk about reading. It is one of the best-known statements of the idea of the "common reader," an idea Woolf took from Samuel Johnson, who wrote that he rejoiced to concur with the common reader, as against the learned. She put it in the title of two collections of essays, in 1925 and 1932, and made it a banner for anyone who reads for love and not for a degree. Generations of general readers have taken comfort from it.

For Woolf's career, it belongs to a remarkable burst of work in the mid-1920s and after. Her essays of those years, along with the novels Mrs. Dalloway and To the Lighthouse and the book-length essay A Room of One's Own in 1929, make an argument that literature belongs to everyone, and that how we read is a matter of freedom. This piece is the plainest and friendliest version of that argument. It also reflects her work with the Hogarth Press, which she ran with her husband Leonard, and where she met writing as a craft with her own hands.

Among later critics and theorists, the essay is often cited as a forerunner of what came to be called reader-response criticism, which studies what happens in the reader's mind during reading and treats the reader as a partner in making meaning. Her picture of reading as an act of collaboration, "fellow-worker and accomplice," anticipates that way of thinking, though she would have scorned the jargon. Writers on how to read, from Nabokov in his lectures to Italo Calvino in his essay on why to read the classics, to modern popular guides, all work in a space she helped to open.

The essay is taught widely, in school and university courses on literature and on writing, often to encourage students to trust their own responses. It is also a staple in reading groups and book clubs, where its insistence on personal judgment is a common starting point. Its closing image has become a kind of motto among book lovers and is quoted on tote bags, library posters and bookshop walls.

Finally, the essay has helped legitimize a certain kind of writing, the informal critical essay that speaks of books as lived experience, which can be traced forward through essayists and reviewers who write as readers first and scholars second.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
What readers have loved above all is the freedom. Many people come to books with a vague guilt: they have not read the right things, they do not understand what the experts say, they like what they are told is lowbrow. Woolf answers with a flat declaration that the library is a place with no laws and that your own reading is the only authority that counts. For countless readers, this has felt like an unlocking of a door. It does not flatter laziness, since she insists on control and effort, but it gives dignity to the unprofessional reader.

They love the conversational warmth. Woolf here is not the experimental novelist of dense interior monologue but a friend who is charming, funny and clear. The talk is full of small domestic images that stay in the mind: the colt that gallops across the field, the old woman at the window with her knitting, the open window on the right of the bookcase. Readers often remark on how she can make a bookshelf feel like a street full of people.

They love the experiment with writing a scene. Many teachers and writers recall trying it and discovering exactly what she promised. After you have struggled to describe a passing moment, the great novelists seem miraculous, and your reading becomes more attentive. It is the sort of advice that can be used the same evening.

They love the generous view of lesser books. Her tour of letters, diaries and memoirs shows how an ordinary account of a life, such as Maria Allen dropping her sewing, can open a window on the past. This is an attractive idea to those who like to read about daily life, and it encourages curiosity about material that formal criticism ignores.

And above all, they love the ending. The thought that the Almighty will look at readers with envy, because they need no reward, has an affecting simplicity. It says that reading is one of the few activities done for its own sake, and that those who do it are, in a quiet way, blessed. In an age that asks every activity to prove its usefulness, this idea is both comforting and a little radical. It is the line many readers remember when they have forgotten everything else.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
The criticisms of Woolf's essay mostly circle around class, taste and consistency. The first is elitism. Although she presents herself as defending the ordinary reader, Woolf was a member of a highly educated, comfortable, interconnected circle, and her idea of what a reader should aspire to, the great novelists and above all poetry, reflects that background. The talk of "rubbish-reading" that one tires of, has struck some as condescending. Woolf herself was sensitive to charges of being a "highbrow," and she famously discussed the terms "highbrow" and "lowbrow" in other writing, but critics have noted that this essay still builds a ladder of taste and invites the reader to climb it.

The second is the contradiction between freedom and authority. Woolf tells us to bow to no authority, then proposes that we judge books by comparison with masterpieces, a canon assembled by earlier critics. Some readers find that she smuggles in the standards she claims to reject. Her answer, that we may use such standards only after testing them against our own response, is thoughtful, but it does not remove the tension.

Third, there is the question of who the "common reader" is. Many have pointed out that the person Woolf imagines has leisure, access to a library and the education to appreciate Defoe, Austen and Hardy. For a reader without those advantages, the invitation can ring hollow. Feminist and postcolonial critics have also asked whose books fill the imagined shelf; the examples here are overwhelmingly English and, apart from Austen, male, even though Woolf elsewhere wrote powerfully about neglected women writers.

Fourth, the essay is slight. It is a talk, brought into print, and some critics regard it as charming but thin compared with her other critical writing, such as A Room of One's Own. Those who want a method for interpreting literature, or a theory of why some books last, will find suggestions but no system.

Finally, the idea that the reader should "become" the author has been questioned by later theorists, who argue that reading is never a transparent merging with an author's mind. Today we are more aware that readers bring their own histories, and that a text can mean more than its author intended. Woolf's picture of sympathetic submission can sound naive in that light, though it is hard to find a reader who has not felt the experience she describes, of being briefly inside another mind.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
Woolf's essay stands in a long English tradition of the informal, personal essay on books and reading, running from Montaigne through Johnson, Lamb and Hazlitt, who all wrote about reading as a pleasure and a way of living. It is also tied to modernism, the early twentieth-century movement that rethought how fiction and poetry should work, and she was one of its central figures. The essay's emphasis on impressions, on the "thousand conflicting impressions" of a single moment, is the same interest that drives her novels, where consciousness is a shifting stream.

Its descendants include the whole body of writing that treats reading as an art. Nabokov's university lectures, which taught students to read with their spines as well as their minds, Ezra Pound's How to Read, Calvino's Why Read the Classics?, and Borges's essays on books can all be read in conversation with it. In academic criticism, reader-response theory takes up her idea that the reader is a partner in the work. In popular culture, book clubs and the modern reading community owe a good deal to her insistence that anyone can read well.

Seen alongside the other essays on reading in this tradition, her piece is the freest. Bacon, in "Of Studies," laid down rules about which books to taste and which to chew, and Woolf grants his premise that books deserve different kinds of attention but removes his tone of command. Montaigne retreated to a tower to read and found his mind restless; Woolf imagines readers who, with training, can make that restlessness productive. Emerson's cry for an original relation to the universe is echoed in her insistence on an original relation to books. William James's picture of habit could be called the practical side of her advice: readers become good by repeated attention.

Why does it still matter? Because the question mark in her title has not gone away. We have more to read than any age before us, with endless recommendations, ratings and summaries pressing us to let others decide. Her advice to trust your own response, to open yourself fully before you judge, and then to measure what you read against the best you know, is a manageable program for a lifetime. And because of its last image, which reminds us that the point of reading is not to win anything but to love it. It is a rare essay that makes you want to close it and pick up a book, and this is one of them.

essays.title: Walking
essays.author: Henry David Thoreau
essays.epigraph: I wish to speak a word for Nature, for absolute freedom and wildness: Thoreau's late masterpiece on the etymology of sauntering and why in Wildness is the preservation of the World.
essays.keyContext: Henry David Thoreau gave versions of this essay as lectures through the 1850s, and he was still revising it in the spring of 1862, when tuberculosis was killing him. It appeared in the Atlantic Monthly just weeks after he died at forty-four. That timing matters, because the essay reads like a last will: a plain-spoken argument for how to spend a life. Thoreau lived in Concord, Massachusetts, in a country that was building railroads, factories and cities at astonishing speed, and arguing bitterly with itself about slavery. His answer to all that busyness was radical in its simplicity. Walk, every day, for hours, with no destination and no errand. Along the way he plays with the word sauntering, and then pushes a bigger idea: that nature, and the wildness inside people, is where freedom and creativity come from. Listen for how he moves between jokes, scolding and sudden bursts of beauty. The essay's overall meaning is that a civilization stays alive only by staying in touch with what it has not tamed.
paragraphs: I wish to speak a word for Nature, for absolute freedom and wildness, as contrasted with a freedom and culture merely civil,—to regard man as an inhabitant, or a part and parcel of Nature, rather than a member of society. I wish to make an extreme statement, if so I may make an emphatic one, for there are enough champions of civilization: the minister and the school-committee and every one of you will take care of that.

I have met with but one or two persons in the course of my life who understood the art of Walking, that is, of taking walks,—who had a genius, so to speak, for sauntering: which word is beautifully derived 'from idle people who roved about the country, in the Middle Ages, and asked charity, under pretense of going à la Sainte Terre,' to the Holy Land, till the children exclaimed, 'There goes a Sainte-Terrer,' a Saunterer, a Holy-Lander. They who never go to the Holy Land in their walks, as they pretend, are indeed mere idlers and vagabonds; but they who do go there are saunterers in the good sense, such as I mean. Some, however, would derive the word from sans terre, without land or a home, which, therefore, in the good sense, will mean, having no particular home, but equally at home everywhere. For this is the secret of successful sauntering. He who sits still in a house all the time may be the greatest vagrant of all; but the saunterer, in the good sense, is no more vagrant than the meandering river, which is all the while sedulously seeking the shortest course to the sea.

I think that I cannot preserve my health and spirits, unless I spend four hours a day at least—and it is commonly more than that—sauntering through the woods and over the hills and fields, absolutely free from all worldly engagements. You may safely say, A penny for your thoughts, or a thousand pounds. When sometimes I am reminded that the mechanics and shopkeepers stay in their shops not only all the forenoon, but all the afternoon too, sitting with crossed legs, so many of them,—as if the legs were made to sit upon, and not to stand or walk upon,—I think that they deserve some credit for not having all committed suicide long ago.

Moreover, you must walk like a camel, which is said to be the only beast which ruminates when walking. When a traveler asked Wordsworth's servant to show him her master's study, she answered, 'Here is his library, but his study is out of doors.' Living much out of doors, in the sun and wind, will no doubt produce a certain roughness of character,—will cause a thicker cuticle to grow over some of the finer qualities of our nature, as on the face and hands, or as severe manual labor robs the hands of some of their delicate tactile power. So staying in the house, on the other hand, may produce a softness and smoothness, not to say thinness of skin, accompanied by an increased sensibility to certain impressions. Perhaps we should be more susceptible to some influences important to our intellectual and moral growth, if the sun had shone and the wind blown on us a little less; and no doubt it is a nice matter to proportion rightly the thick and thin skin. But methinks that is a scurf that will fall off fast enough,—that the natural remedy is to be found in the proportion which the night bears to the day, the winter to the year, thought to experience.

I am alarmed when it happens that I have walked a mile into the woods bodily, without getting there in spirit. In my afternoon walk I would fain forget all my morning occupations and my obligations to society. But it sometimes happens that I cannot easily shake off the village. The thought of some work will run in my head and I am not where my body is,—I am out of my senses. In my walks I would fain return to my senses. What business have I in the woods, if I am thinking of something out of the woods?

The West of which I speak is but another name for the Wild; and what I have been preparing to say is, that in Wildness is the preservation of the World. Every tree sends its fibers forth in search of the Wild. The cities import it at any price. Men plow and sail for it. From the forest and wilderness come the tonics and barks which brace mankind. Our ancestors were savages. The story of Romulus and Remus being suckled by a wolf is not a meaningless fable. The founders of every state which has risen to eminence have drawn their nourishment and vigor from a similar wild source. It was because the children of the Empire were not suckled by the wolf that they were conquered and displaced by the children of the northern forests who were.

Life consists with wildness. The most alive is the wildest. Not yet subdued to man, its presence refreshes him. One who pressed forward incessantly and never rested from his labors, who grew fast and made infinite demands on life, would always find himself in a new country or wilderness, and surrounded by the raw material of life. He would be climbing over the prostrate stems of primitive forest-trees. Hope and the future for me are not in lawns and cultivated fields, not in towns and cities, but in the impervious and quaking swamps.

In literature it is only the wild that attracts us. Dullness is but another name for tameness. It is the uncivilized free and wild thinking in Hamlet and The Iliad, in all the Scriptures and Mythologies, not learned in the schools, that delights us. As the wild duck is more swift and beautiful than the tame, so is the wild—the mallard—thought, which 'mid falling dews wings its solitary way above the marshes. A truly good book is something as natural, and as unexpectedly and unaccountably fair and perfect, as a wild flower discovered on the prairies of the West or in the jungles of the East. Genius is a light which makes the darkness visible, like the lightning's flash, which perchance shatters the temple of knowledge itself,—and not a taper lighted at the hearth-stone of the race, which pales before the light of common day.

We have heard of a Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge. It is said that knowledge is power; and the like. Methinks there is equal need of a Society for the Diffusion of Useful Ignorance, what we will call Beautiful Knowledge, a knowledge useful in a higher sense: for what is most of our boasted so-called knowledge but a conceit that we know something, which robs us of the advantage of our actual ignorance? What we call knowledge is often our positive ignorance; ignorance our negative knowledge. By long years of patient industry and reading of the newspapers,—for what are the libraries of science but files of newspapers?—a man accumulates a myriad facts, lays them up in his memory, and then when in some spring of his life he saunters abroad into the Great Fields of thought, he, as it were, goes to grass like a horse and leaves all his harness behind in the stable.

Above all, we cannot afford not to live in the present. He is blessed over all mortals who loses no moment of the passing life in remembering the past. Unless our philosophy hears the cock crow in every barn-yard within our horizon, it is belated. That sound commonly reminds us that we are growing rusty and antique in our employments and habits of thought. His philosophy comes down to a more recent time than ours. There is something suggested by it that is a newer testament,—the gospel according to this moment. So we saunter toward the Holy Land, till one day the sun shall shine more brightly than ever he has done, shall perchance shine into our minds and hearts, and light up our whole lives with a great awakening light, as warm and serene and golden as on a bankside in autumn.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
Thoreau opens by announcing that he wants to speak for Nature, for absolute freedom and wildness, as opposed to the kind of freedom that merely comes from living politely in society. He admits he is making an extreme statement on purpose, because there are plenty of people already speaking up for civilization. Notice the joke in that: the minister and the school committee will take care of it. From the first paragraph he is a man picking a fight with the respectable audience in the room.

Then comes the word that gives the essay its heart. He says he has met only one or two people who understood the art of walking, who had a genius for sauntering. He offers two possible origins of the word. One is that medieval wanderers claimed to be heading to the Holy Land, la Sainte Terre, so that children called them Sainte-Terrers, saunterers. The other is that it comes from sans terre, without land or home, which he reads as being at home everywhere. Whether or not the etymology is sound, the point is that a walk can be a pilgrimage. It does not matter whether you ever reach Jerusalem. What matters is that you set out as if something sacred were ahead of you.

This is why Thoreau says that a man who sits still in a house all the time may be the greatest vagrant of all. The restless, busy person who never really inhabits his own life is the true wanderer. The saunterer, by contrast, is like a meandering river, which looks aimless but is steadily finding its way to the sea.

Underneath the charm there is a serious claim. Thoreau thinks human beings are part of nature, not just members of a town or a church or a nation. Health, thought and morals all depend on contact with ground that nobody has fenced, planted or mortgaged. He says he cannot keep his health and spirits unless he spends at least four hours a day wandering the woods and fields, free of worldly engagements. He treats that as a requirement, like food.

Later the essay turns toward direction. He finds that his afternoon walks drift southwest, toward the open country and, symbolically, toward the future. Westward, he says, he goes free, while east means the past and the settled world. This can sound like a mere habit of his feet, but he lifts it into a theory about where the human spirit wants to go. It is also the part of the essay a modern reader has to handle with care, since westward expansion was bound up with the dispossession of Native peoples.

The essay's most quoted idea is that in wildness is the preservation of the world. He does not mean that everyone should live in a forest. He means that cultures grow stale unless something untamed feeds them, whether that is forest, swamp, or the unruly part of the imagination. He even says that hope for him lies not in lawns and cultivated fields but in the quaking swamps. The ending, with the setting sun lighting up the mind and heart, tells you the real subject. The walk is a way of preparing to be awake.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
As craft, "Walking" is both dazzling and uneven, and it is worth admitting both. Its best sentences are among the finest in American prose. Thoreau can take a plain observation and turn it into an image that stays in your head for years. The meandering river sentence is a good example: in a single comparison it defends the whole idea of the unhurried life and makes it sound purposeful. His humor is also underrated. He is a scold who knows he is a scold, and the exaggeration, the sly puns and the mock-heroic tone make a demanding argument easy to enjoy.

The essay's structure is its biggest weakness. It was stitched together from lectures, and you can feel the seams. The opening is tightly organized around sauntering, but the middle wanders into long discussions of America, the West, the supposed decline of European animals and plants in the New World, and the poetry of the wild. These sections do not build on one another so much as sit side by side. A listener hearing it aloud may feel the energy drop and rise rather than climb. You could argue that a walking essay should wander, and Thoreau might say so himself, but intentional looseness and plain looseness are not the same, and the essay does not always control the difference.

Some of his rhetoric has also aged badly. The claim that nature grows bigger and better in America, and that people and animals do too, is closer to patriotic boasting than observation, and it sits oddly beside his own scorn for national pride elsewhere. His hostility to nearly everyone who works for a living can read as snobbery. When he complains that most people are not really walking, he forgets that most people did not have four free hours every afternoon. The ideal of idle sauntering depends on leisure that Thoreau had, partly through the help of his family and friends, and partly through a willingness to live on very little.

There is also a gap between the lofty talk about wildness and the landscape he actually walked. The Concord countryside was farmland, old pasture and woodlots, shaped by centuries of human use. His wild was often a tamed place seen with a visionary eye. That is not necessarily a flaw, since the essay is about attention more than geography. But it makes his sharp contrast between wild and civil look a bit too neat.

Still, when the essay works, nothing quite matches it. The sunset ending, with its slow sentence that gathers light until it floods the mind, is a real piece of music. The piece succeeds less as an argument you can diagram than as a mood and a habit of mind you catch from him. It persuades by making you want to put the book down and go outside, and that is a rare test for an essay to pass. On balance it is a flawed masterpiece, brilliant in passages and patchy as a whole.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
The most direct legacy of "Walking" is the modern American conservation movement. Thoreau was not an organizer, and he did not found anything, but his phrase about the preservation of the world became a kind of motto. John Muir, who came a generation later and spent his life defending wild places like Yosemite, drew on the same current of thought, and the Sierra Club has long used Thoreau's line. When the United States passed the Wilderness Act in 1964, creating a legal category for land left essentially untouched, many people saw it as Thoreau's idea turning into law. The writer Wallace Stegner, in his famous letter defending wilderness, argued that we need wild country even if we never visit it, which is very much the Thoreauvian claim that wildness feeds a civilization from a distance.

The essay also shaped how people think about walking itself. It helped create the idea that walking is a form of thinking and a form of resistance. Later writers have followed that thread, from nature writers like Edward Abbey and Gary Snyder to modern cultural historians of walking such as Rebecca Solnit, who treats Thoreau as one of the central figures in the long story of people going on foot to think. The sense that a slow, unplugged walk is good for the mind has become so common that it is almost a cliché, and a good part of the origin of that cliché is here.

In the arts and politics the essay worked more quietly. Thoreau's other writings, especially the essay on civil disobedience, influenced Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr., and "Walking" belongs to the same habit of mind: trust your own conscience and your own legs over the opinions of the crowd. It does not preach political action directly, but it models a refusal to let institutions define what counts as a good life.

In literature classes the essay is taught as a prime example of American Transcendentalism, the movement that Ralph Waldo Emerson led, which held that the individual can know truth directly through intuition and through nature. It is also taught as a short, accessible entry into Thoreau for students who find Walden long. Teachers often pair it with nature writing, with environmental history, and with debates about what we mean when we say wilderness.

The essay has had a long afterlife outside the classroom as well. Outdoor brands, hiking clubs, mindfulness writers and anyone arguing against screens or constant productivity are likely to quote it. Thoreau's name sits on trails, lectures and nature centers. Because he died just as the essay appeared, it has also taken on the glow of a final statement, a last testament delivered by someone who knew time was short. That gave it a force that a casual lecture might not have carried, and it helped fix Thoreau in the public mind as the patron saint of the person who steps away to see clearly.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
Readers have loved "Walking" first for its permission. Thoreau tells you that the aimless afternoon is not wasted time, and that sitting in a room all day is the real waste. For anyone who feels guilty about not being productive, that is a profound relief. Many readers describe the essay as one that gave them language for something they already felt, that a walk without a goal is a way of becoming more fully alive.

They have also loved its voice. Thoreau is cranky, funny and unembarrassed. He is willing to say that most people do not know how to walk, and he says it with enough wit that the reader laughs at themselves rather than bristles. The extravagance is part of the pleasure. He is not careful or balanced, and he tells you so. A reader who is tired of hedged and cautious writing finds this bracing, like a cold swim.

The images are a third source of delight. The saunterer as a Holy-Lander, the river that looks aimless and is not, the swamp as a symbol of hope, the sun that finally shines into the mind and heart and lights the whole life: these are pictures that readers carry away and repeat. People who have never read the full essay often know a line or two of it, because the best phrases seem to float free and become part of the language. Thoreau had a gift for making ideas feel like things you could touch.

Naturalists and writers have admired the essay for its close attention to the actual world. Thoreau was a skilled observer who carried a notebook and spyglass, and some of that precision shows up in the way he names plants, light and weather even in a philosophical essay. For writers, this is a lesson: big ideas land best when anchored in the concrete.

Finally, readers respond to the feeling of urgency under the humor. Thoreau was dying as he finished the piece, and a thoughtful reader can sense that he is trying to get something essential said. There is no padding in the emotional core. When he writes about the evening light and the possibility of a great awakening, it reads as a man giving what he has left. This is part of why the essay is so often recommended to people at turning points in their lives, to students deciding what kind of life to build, and to anyone worn down by work and noise. They find in it a calm, stubborn encouragement to look up and walk out the door.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
Criticism of "Walking" has grown louder in recent decades, and much of it is fair. The most serious objection concerns the idea of wilderness itself. When Thoreau praises the untamed West and the unpeopled wild, he is writing as though those lands were empty, when they had been home to Native nations for thousands of years. Scholars of environmental history, most famously William Cronon in his essay on the trouble with wilderness, have argued that the notion of untouched nature is a cultural invention that helped justify pushing Indigenous people off their land and into reservations. Thoreau was not an enthusiastic participant in that, and in other writings he showed real interest in Native life, but "Walking" does lean on a frontier mythology that readers now find hard to ignore.

A second criticism is about privilege. The saunterer needs time and security, and Thoreau's contempt for people who work long hours can come across as disdain. He tells people to stop being slaves to business, but he does not much reckon with the fact that for many workers and for the enslaved people whose cause he elsewhere supported, there was no choice. Critics also point out that the sauntering ideal was mostly open to men. A woman walking alone in the nineteenth century faced dangers and rules that Thoreau never had to consider.

There are objections on the grounds of logic as well. The essay asserts rather than proves. Its claim that animals and men shrink in Europe and flourish in America is not backed by evidence and now looks like wishful nationalism. Even in his own day, friends and readers found him contrary and sometimes unfair. Emerson, in his eulogy, praised Thoreau's character and genius but also admitted a streak of stubborn opposition, a tendency to say no to almost everything, which shows in the essay's scolding side.

Some readers find the piece plain disorganized. Because it grew from lectures, it has digressions that go on a bit long, and repetition that a spoken version might forgive but a page does not. A modern reader may feel that the first third is brilliant and the rest is a lovely but rambling coda.

Finally, there is the charge of hypocrisy that has followed Thoreau all his life. He praises roaming free and condemns civilization, yet he walked home to a village, ate bread made by others, and relied on his family's pencil business and on neighbors for support. Defenders reply that he never claimed to be a hermit, and that the essay's point is about a way of attending, not a rule of life. The criticism is still useful, because it keeps the essay honest and reminds us to take the vision seriously without taking the man as a saint.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
"Walking" belongs to American Transcendentalism, a movement of the 1830s and 1840s centered around Concord. Its leader, Ralph Waldo Emerson, wrote that nature is a language through which the spirit speaks, and Thoreau took that idea literally and put on his boots. Transcendentalism itself grew from European Romanticism, in which poets such as Wordsworth and Coleridge turned to wild landscape as a source of truth and feeling. Wordsworth in particular was a famous walker, and it is fair to see Thoreau as an American version of that tradition, with more humor and more suspicion of institutions.

Behind both lies a much older tradition of the pilgrimage, which Thoreau slyly invokes with his Holy Land etymology, and of the philosopher who thinks while moving. Ancient Greek teachers walked and talked, and writers from Rousseau to Nietzsche have praised walking as the best condition for thought. "Walking" turns that long tradition into something both practical and democratic, because anyone with a pair of legs can try it.

Looking forward, the essay is a founding text of American nature writing and environmentalism. It sits in a line that runs through John Muir and John Burroughs, then Aldo Leopold, Rachel Carson, Edward Abbey, Annie Dillard, Gary Snyder and Wendell Berry. Each of them, in different ways, takes up Thoreau's insistence that attention to the natural world is a moral and spiritual act.
