They speak: "We are nothing; less than nothing, and dreams. We are only what might have been." The father wakes up in his bachelor armchair, with his sister Bridget beside him. John L. is gone for ever.

So the whole scene was a daydream. There are no children. The woman he courted did not marry him. The essay takes the reader through a warm illusion and ends with a bare room. The pen name Elia and the invented names hide real people: John was Lamb's actual brother, who died in 1821, and Bridget is his sister Mary, with whom he lived all his adult life. The woman he courted was based on Ann Simmons, who married someone else.

Readers sometimes miss the ghost story hidden in the middle. The great-grandmother is not frightened of the apparition of two infants gliding on the staircase, the ghosts of the Children in the Wood from the old ballad, because she says those innocents would do her no harm. The children in the essay, in a sense, are the same kind of spirit, harmless, sweet, and only half real. The essay is about wanting something so much that you can hold it for an evening, then let it go.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
The central structural idea is excellent: let the reader fall for the fiction, and only at the very end pull it away. Because the early paragraphs are so affectionate and detailed, the closing revelation is not just a twist but an emotional blow. Lamb also prepares it cleverly. The children interrupt, the father glances at their faces, Alice gives her mother's looks, John smiles when a joke lands. These small touches make the children vivid. When they dissolve, you feel as though you have lost real people, which is exactly the point.

The prose is a pleasure to read. Lamb writes in long sentences that wander and double back, with an old-fashioned flavor, and he rhymes humor with sorrow in a way that feels natural rather than staged. The aside about the foolish rich person who pulled down the carved wooden chimney-piece to put up a marble one with no story on it is both funny and revealing. The marble has no story, and Lamb is a man who lives for stories. The line about a great house's ornaments looking awkward when carried off, like tombs set up in a tawdry drawing-room, shows the same eye for how things lose meaning when they are moved from their place.

The deepest strength is emotional restraint. The central grief, that his brother died and that he is alone, is never stated at the outset. It comes out sideways, in the memory of the lame boy carried on a horseman's back and the admission that he did not make allowances for his brother's pain. That confession is the most moving passage because it does not ask for sympathy.

There are weaknesses, though, and a modern reader may feel them. The essay's prettiness can tip into sentiment. The children are almost too sweet, and the sorrow is occasionally cushioned by the very whimsy that makes it bearable. The line about "the tedious shores of Lethe", Lethe being the river of forgetfulness in Greek myth, is a touch ornate, and the final phrase, "only what might have been," is lovely but familiar. The devices of dreaming and waking were already well-worn, and some may feel Lamb leans on a literary convention rather than inventing one.

There is also an element of coyness. Lamb gives the real people initials and nicknames, hides the cause of Mary's illness entirely, and leaves most of the facts outside the frame. That reticence is part of the essay's dignity, but it can leave the sorrow feeling a little under-explained. If you did not know about Lamb's life, you might read the ending as mild wistfulness rather than as the cry of someone who gave up marriage to care for a sister.

Still, those faults are small against the effect. The essay is short, controlled and exact about the way memory edits what it keeps. It is more skillful than it first looks.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
Dream-Children is one of the pieces on which Lamb's reputation as the great English personal essayist was built. The Essays of Elia, published in 1823 with a second series in 1833, made him famous as a writer who could turn the small details of a clerk's life, a roast pig, old china, a visit to a theater, a memory of his schooldays, into literature. This essay was among the most anthologized of them, and for much of the nineteenth century it stood as a model of what the personal essay could do.

The impact on the form was lasting. Before Lamb, essays were often lessons or arguments. Lamb showed that an essay could be a performance of a particular sensibility, a character with moods, jokes, weak spots and sorrows. His invention of Elia, a half-disguised version of himself, allowed him to be intimate without being naked. Later essayists took up that lesson, writers such as Robert Louis Stevenson, Max Beerbohm, and in the twentieth century the many writers of the personal essay who treat memory and family with humor. Even people who have never read him write in a tradition he helped shape.

The essay also helped fix a certain image of Lamb himself. Victorian readers made a cult of Charles and Mary Lamb, the devoted brother and sister, the gentle bachelor and his troubled sister who had been through terrible events. Many readers came to the essays through the biography. The story of Lamb sacrificing marriage and family to care for Mary made the sorrow in Dream-Children feel real and noble. It is one of those cases where the life enriches the page, and the page in turn fills out the life.

In education, the essay has long been a staple of anthologies of English prose and courses on Romantic-era writing. It turns up in discussions of dreams and memory in literature, as an example of the "reverie" tradition, and in studies of the way essays present the self. Teachers use it to show how a piece can be both charming and devastating, and to show how an ending can recast everything before it.

It has less obvious screen or stage legacy than novels, but its central image, the unborn children who say they are only what might have been, has been echoed again and again in writing about regret, from poems about lost possibilities to stories where a dreamer meets the family he never had. Few readers forget the sight of those children shrinking into the distance.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
The first thing admirers praised in Lamb was his charm, a quality that is hard to define but easy to feel. His friends, a circle that included the poet Samuel Taylor Coleridge and the essayist William Hazlitt, treasured him as witty, kind and a little odd. Hazlitt, who was not an easy man to please, included Lamb among the figures he wrote about with affection. That personal love carried over to the essays. Victorian readers in particular adored what they called gentle Elia, and the phrase stuck for generations.

What they loved in Dream-Children specifically was its tenderness. The picture of a bachelor imagining the family he might have had touched readers because it is an experience many people know in some form: the sense of a life you did not lead sitting beside the one you did. People who had lost siblings, or who had given up a love for duty or circumstance, found their own feelings voiced with unusual delicacy. The essay never wallows. It treats the pain with a light hand, and that lightness is part of why it is believable.

Readers also loved the humor tucked inside the sadness. There is a funny, domestic quality to the scene: the children's reactions, the father catching Alice's foot dancing and looking grave until it stops, the gentle swipe at the rich person with the marble chimney-piece. The jokes make the ending hit harder, because they establish a world you do not want to leave.

Writers have admired the craft. The slow shift from anecdote to confession, and from confession to vision, is something later essayists have studied. The phrase "less than nothing, and dreams" has been quoted by readers who want to describe the pain of unrealized lives, and the closing line, with its quiet reference to John L. being gone for ever, is often cited as an example of how to end an emotional piece without overstatement.

There is also a more general affection for the idea of the essay as companionship. Lamb makes the reader feel like a guest at the fireside, trusted with a family story and some private feelings. Many readers say they first fell in love with essays through Lamb, and Dream-Children is a likely reason. It teaches that an essay can be a way of keeping company with someone who has been dead nearly two centuries, which is in its own way a kind of the dreaming the essay describes.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
Lamb has never lacked admirers, but he has also had critics, and their objections tend to circle around sentiment and style. The most persistent charge is that his writing can be too sweet and too self-consciously quaint. Readers influenced by modernist taste in the twentieth century, with its preference for plain, hard-edged prose, often found Lamb's antique diction, his fondness for old authors and his playful archaisms a bit precious. The fear is that the charm becomes a mannerism, a kind of performance of lovable eccentricity.

Dream-Children has drawn this complaint in particular, because its subject invites sentiment. Dead mothers, loving children and a lonely bachelor by the fire could easily be a recipe for sugar. Some critics have said that the essay relies on the reader's readiness to weep, and that the figures of the children are more emblems than people. Others point out that the ending depends on a familiar device, the dream that dissolves, and that it tidies up a very messy grief into a neat literary shape.

A second line of criticism concerns what the essay leaves out. Because Lamb protects his private world with initials and invented names, the essay can seem evasive. He mentions that his brother's death haunted him but says nothing of the other great catastrophe of his life, the death of his mother at his sister's hand. Readers wanting an unguarded confession may be frustrated. Defenders respond that the evasion is the whole point: Lamb was a man who survived by keeping his sorrows behind a smile, and the essay's restraint is a form of honesty about that.

There is also a historical point. Some contemporaries of Lamb disliked the Elia persona on political and moral grounds. Lamb was friendly with radicals and with religious doubters, and his easy, whimsical tone could be read as frivolous. Critics who preferred more public, argumentative writing felt that the personal essay was a minor form, a kind of literary chat. That prejudice has faded, but it shaped the early reception.

More recently, scholars have noted a certain social narrowness. The essay is about a bourgeois household and an old country house with servants and a housekeeper, and it takes for granted a world in which such memories and such leisure exist. Readers interested in broader questions of class or gender sometimes wonder about the women in the essay, who are mostly idealized figures: the pious grandmother, the pretty dead mother, the courted Alice. They are loved but seldom heard.

In fairness, most critics who object to the style still admit the force of the ending, which is hard to wave away.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
Dream-Children sits at the meeting point of two traditions. One is the English essay of the eighteenth century, the urbane, observant periodical writing of Joseph Addison and Richard Steele in The Spectator, which taught readers to enjoy character sketches and moral reflection in a conversational tone. The other is the Romantic emphasis on memory, childhood and the inner life, associated with Wordsworth, Coleridge and later writers. Lamb combined the two: the manners of the Spectator with the feeling of the Romantic poets.

Within the essay tradition, the dream vision or reverie has its own lineage. Addison's famous Vision of Mirza, in which the writer is shown human life as a bridge over a sea of mist, belongs here, as does the seventeenth-century prose of Sir Thomas Browne, whom Lamb adored. Dream-Children takes that old device of the dream and gives it a very private, domestic subject. Instead of the fate of mankind, it asks about one man's missing family.

What descends from it is the modern personal essay, the form that treats a writer's own life as legitimate material. Hazlitt's own essays, Virginia Woolf's essays on memory, E. B. White's reflections on family and time, and many later memoirists are in some sense cousins of Elia. The idea that a short piece can start in comedy and end in grief owes a good deal to Lamb. In fiction, the theme of the unlived life, the child who never was, the road not taken, appears in many forms, from ghost stories to the novels of regret that fill the library shelves.

Comparisons are illuminating. Wordsworth's Immortality Ode treats childhood as a lost radiance, but in poetry and with grand philosophy. Lamb does something humbler and perhaps more heartbreaking, giving the loss a table, a chair, a pair of children and a fire. Compare also Hazlitt, who in the same period wrote about his own feelings with fierce directness, where Lamb prefers disguise. Or compare Thomas Hardy, whose later poems about the missed chances of love cover similar ground with a bleaker tone. Lamb is softer and more consoling, but no less aware of time's cruelty.

Why read it now? Because its subject has not aged. People still imagine the families they might have had, the paths they did not take, and the people who are gone. The essay offers neither a cure nor a lecture, only a way of seeing the feeling clearly and then letting it go. And it is brief enough to read in a few minutes, and strange enough that, once you reach the ending, you will want to go back and read it again.

essays.title: On Going a Journey
essays.author: William Hazlitt
essays.epigraph: One of the pleasantest things in the world is going a journey; but I like to go by myself: Hazlitt's exuberant celebration of solitary walking, country inns, and throwing off our city identity.
essays.keyContext: On Going a Journey, by William Hazlitt, was published in January 1822 and collected that same year in his book Table-Talk. Hazlitt was one of the finest English essayists, a former painter turned critic and political radical, quick to argue and slow to compromise. In this piece he sets aside argument and simply tells you what he loves about taking a trip: going alone. Walking, he says, is for thinking, and conversation spoils it. The essay is full of vivid, almost greedy pleasure, in open roads, evening inns, supper plans and cheap books read by candlelight, and it ends with a sly remark about travel abroad. It is often described as the classic piece of writing about solitude on the road, and it helped create the modern idea of the walking trip as a kind of freedom. Listen for the energy of his sentences, and notice how a man who claims to want no company writes as though he is talking directly to you.
paragraphs: One of the pleasantest things in the world is going a journey; but I like to go by myself. I can enjoy society in a room; but out of doors, nature is company enough for me. I am then never less alone than when alone. “The fields his study, nature was his book.” I cannot see the wit of walking and talking at the same time. When I am in the country I wish to vegetate like the country. I am not for criticizing hedge-rows and black cattle. I go out of town in order to forget the town and all that is in it. There are those who for this purpose go to watering-places, and carry the metropolis with them. I like more elbow-room and fewer incumbrances. I like solitude, when I give myself up to it, for the sake of solitude; nor do I ask for “a friend in my retreat, Whom I may whisper solitude is sweet.”

The soul of a journey is liberty, perfect liberty, to think, feel, do, just as one pleases. We go a journey chiefly to be free of all impediments and of all inconveniences; to leave ourselves behind, much more to get rid of others. It is because I want a little breathing-space to muse on indifferent matters, where Contemplation “May plume her feathers and let grow her wings, That in the various bustle of resort Were all too ruffled, and sometimes impair'd,” that I absent myself from the town for a while, without feeling at a loss the moment I am left by myself. Instead of a friend in a post-chaise or in a Tilbury, to exchange good things with, and vary the same stale topics over again, for once let me have a truce with impertinence. Give me the clear blue sky over my head, and the green turf beneath my feet, a winding road before me, and a three hours' march to dinner—and then to thinking! It is hard if I cannot start some game on these lone heaths. I laugh, I run, I leap, I sing for joy. From the point of yonder rolling cloud I plunge into my past being, and revel there, as the sun-burnt Indian plunges headlong into the wave that wafts him to his native shore. Then long-forgotten things, like “sunken wrack and sumless treasuries,” burst upon my eager sight, and I begin to feel, think, and be myself again. Instead of an awkward silence, broken by attempts at wit or dull common-places, mine is that undisturbed silence of the heart which alone is perfect eloquence.

No one likes puns, alliterations, antitheses, argument, and analysis better than I do; but I sometimes had rather be without them. “Leave, oh, leave me to my repose!” I have just now other business in hand, which would seem idle to you, but is with me “very stuff of the conscience.” Is not this wild rose sweet without a comment? Does not this daisy leap to my heart set in its coat of emerald? Yet if I were to explain to you the circumstance that has so endeared it to me, you would only smile. Had I not better then keep it to myself, and let it serve me to brood over, from here to yonder craggy point, and from thence onward to the far-distant horizon? I should be but bad company all that way, and therefore prefer being alone. I have heard it said that you may, when the moody fit comes on, walk or ride on by yourself, and indulge your reveries. But this looks like a breach of manners, a neglect of others, and you are thinking all the time that you ought to rejoin your party. “Out upon such half-faced fellowship,” say I. I like to be either entirely to myself, or entirely at the disposal of others; to talk or be silent, to walk or sit still, to be sociable or solitary. I was pleased with an observation of Mr. Cobbett's, that “he thought it a bad French custom to drink our wine with our meals, and that an Englishman ought to do only one thing at a time.” So I cannot talk and think, or indulge in melancholy musing and lively conversation by fits and starts.

“Let me have a companion of my way,” says Sterne, “were it but to remark how the shadows lengthen as the sun declines.” It is beautifully said; but, in my opinion, this continual comparing of notes interferes with the involuntary impression of things upon the mind, and hurts the sentiment. If you only hint what you feel in a kind of dumb show, it is insipid: if you have to explain it, it is making a toil of a pleasure. You cannot read the book of nature without being perpetually put to the trouble of translating it for the benefit of others. I am for this synthetical method on a journey in preference to the analytical. I am content to lay in a stock of ideas then, and to examine and anatomise them afterwards. I want to see my vague notions float like the down of the thistle before the breeze, and not to have them entangled in the briars and thorns of controversy. For once, I like to have it all my own way; and this is impossible unless you are alone, or in such company as I do not covet. I have no objection to argue a point with any one for twenty miles of measured road, but not for pleasure. If you remark the scent of a bean-field crossing the road, perhaps your fellow-traveller has no smell. If you point to a distant object, perhaps he is short-sighted, and has to take out his glass to look at it. There is a feeling in the air, a tone in the colour of a cloud, which hits your fancy, but the effect of which you are unable to account for. There is then no sympathy, but an uneasy craving after it, and a dissatisfaction which pursues you on the way, and in the end probably produces ill-humour. Now I never quarrel with myself, and take all my own conclusions for granted till I find it necessary to defend them against objections.

In general, a good thing spoils out-of-door prospects: it should be reserved for Table-talk. Lamb is for this reason, I take it, the worst company in the world out of doors; because he is the best within. I grant, there is one subject on which it is pleasant to talk on a journey; and that is, what one shall have for supper when we get to our inn at night. The open air improves this sort of conversation or friendly altercation, by setting a keener edge on appetite. Every mile of the road heightens the flavour of the viands we expect at the end of it. How fine it is to enter some old town, walled and turreted, just at approach of nightfall, or to come to some straggling village, with the lights streaming through the surrounding gloom; and then, after inquiring for the best entertainment that the place affords, to “take one's ease at one's inn”! These eventful moments in our lives' history are too precious, too full of solid, heart-felt happiness to be frittered and dribbled away in imperfect sympathy. I would have them all to myself, and drain them to the last drop: they will do to talk of or to write about afterwards. What a delicate speculation it is, after drinking whole goblets of tea—“The cups that cheer, but not inebriate,”—and letting the fumes ascend into the brain, to sit considering what we shall have for supper—eggs and a rasher, a rabbit smothered in onions, or an excellent veal-cutlet! Sancho in such a situation once fixed upon cow-heel; and his choice, though he could not help it, is not to be disparaged. Then, in the intervals of pictured scenery and Shandean contemplation, to catch the preparation and the stir in the kitchen. Procul, O procul este profani! These hours are sacred to silence and to musing, to be treasured up in the memory, and to feed the source of smiling thoughts hereafter.

I would not waste them in idle talk; or if I must have the integrity of fancy broken in upon, I would rather it were by a stranger than a friend. A stranger takes his hue and character from the time and place; he is a part of the furniture and costume of an inn. If he is a Quaker, or from the West Riding of Yorkshire, so much the better. I do not even try to sympathise with him, and he breaks no squares. I associate nothing with my travelling companion but present objects and passing events. In his ignorance of me and my affairs, I in a manner forget myself. But a friend reminds one of other things, rips up old grievances, and destroys the abstraction of the scene. He comes in ungraciously between us and our imaginary character. Something is dropped in the course of conversation that gives a hint of your profession and pursuits; or from having some one with you that knows the less sublime portions of your history, it seems that other people do. You are no longer a citizen of the world; but your “unhoused free condition is put into circumscription and confine.” The incognito of an inn is one of its striking privileges—“lord of one's self, uncumber'd with a name.” Oh! it is great to shake off the trammels of the world and of public opinion—to lose our importunate, tormenting, everlasting personal identity in the elements of nature, and become the creature of the moment, clear of all ties—to hold to the universe only by a dish of sweet-breads, and to owe nothing but the score of the evening—and no longer seeking for applause and meeting with contempt, to be known by no other title than the Gentleman in the parlour! One may take one's choice of all characters in this romantic state of uncertainty as to one's real pretensions, and become indefinitely respectable and negatively right-worshipful. We baffle prejudice and disappoint conjecture; and from being so to others, begin to be objects of curiosity and wonder even to ourselves. We are no more those hackneyed common-places that we appear in the world; an inn restores us to the level of nature, and quits scores with society!

I have certainly spent some enviable hours at inns—sometimes when I have been left entirely to myself, and have tried to solve some metaphysical problem, as once at Witham-common, where I found out the proof that likeness is not a case of the association of ideas—at other times, when there have been pictures in the room, as at St. Neot's (I think it was), where I first met with Gribelin's engravings of the Cartoons, into which I entered at once, and at a little inn on the borders of Wales, where there happened to be hanging some of Westall's drawings, which I compared triumphantly (for a theory that I had, not for the admired artist) with the figure of a girl who had ferried me over the Severn, standing up in the boat between me and the twilight—at other times I might mention luxuriating in books, with a peculiar interest in this way, as I remember sitting up half the night to read Paul and Virginia, which I picked up at an inn at Bridgewater, after being drenched in the rain all day; and at the same place I got through two volumes of Madame D'Arblay's Camilla. It was on the tenth of April, 1798, that I sat down to a volume of the New Eloise, at the inn at Llangollen, over a bottle of sherry and a cold chicken. The letter I chose was that in which St. Preux describes his feelings as he first caught a glimpse from the heights of the Jura of the Pays de Vaud, which I had brought with me as a bon bouche to crown the evening with. It was my birth-day, and I had for the first time come from a place in the neighbourhood to visit this delightful spot.

There is undoubtedly a sensation in travelling into foreign parts that is to be had nowhere else; but it is more pleasing at the time than lasting. It is too remote from our habitual associations to be a common topic of discourse or reference, and, like a dream or another state of existence, does not piece into our daily modes of life. It is an animated but a momentary hallucination. It demands an effort to exchange our actual for our ideal identity; and to feel the pulse of our old transports revive very keenly, we must “jump” all our present comforts and connexions. Our romantic and itinerant character is not to be domesticated. Dr. Johnson remarked how little foreign travel added to the facilities of conversation in those who had been abroad. In fact, the time we have spent there is both delightful, and in one sense instructive; but it appears to be cut out of our substantial, downright existence, and never to join kindly on to it. We are not the same, but another, and perhaps more enviable individual, all the time we are out of our own country. We are lost to ourselves, as well as our friends. So the poet somewhat quaintly sings, “Out of my country and myself I go.” Those who wish to forget painful thoughts, do well to absent themselves for a while from the ties and objects that recall them; but we can be said only to fulfil our destiny in the place that gave us birth. I should on this account like well enough to spend the whole of my life in travelling abroad, if I could anywhere borrow another life to spend afterwards at home!

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
Hazlitt begins with a blunt declaration: "One of the pleasantest things in the world is going a journey; but I like to go by myself." Everything else in the essay is a defense of that taste, delivered with the confidence of a man who knows he may be called antisocial and does not much care.

His central claim is that the soul of a journey is liberty, "perfect liberty, to think, feel, do, just as one pleases." We do not travel to see sights or to meet people. We travel to leave behind the town, our habits, and even ourselves. A walking companion, however pleasant, interferes. If you notice the scent of a bean-field, your friend may have no sense of smell. If you point at a distant object, he may be short-sighted. Hazlitt does not just dislike chatter; he thinks that explaining a feeling turns pleasure into labor. You cannot read the book of nature, he says, without being constantly put to the trouble of translating it for someone else.

That is what he means by preferring the "synthetical" method to the "analytical." On the road, gather impressions and let them float like thistledown. Afterward, at leisure, take them apart and think them through. It is a theory of how experience works: first absorb, then analyze. The essay is a gentle argument that modern life has this order backwards.

The details are warm and funny. He is willing to talk on the road on exactly one subject, what to have for supper, because the open air sharpens the appetite and every mile improves the meal in imagination. He loves the moment of coming into a walled old town at nightfall and "taking one's ease at one's inn." And he loves the anonymity of that inn. A stranger beside you in the parlor is part of the furniture, but a friend brings your whole history with him. Hazlitt delights in being known as nothing but "the Gentleman in the parlour," free of reputation and obligation, owing nothing but the evening's bill.

The less obvious layer is about identity. Hazlitt was a man whose life was full of public quarrels, political enemies and private disappointment. To be a nameless walker is to be released from being William Hazlitt. The essay's most vivid moments are really about escape from the burdens of self, the "importunate, tormenting, everlasting personal identity."

The final paragraphs turn the idea around. Travel abroad is intoxicating, he admits, but it is a momentary hallucination that does not join onto ordinary life. One becomes another, perhaps more enviable person, then comes home and cannot piece the two lives together. His closing joke is that he would happily spend his whole life travelling abroad, if he could borrow another life to spend afterwards at home. Behind the joke is a serious thought: that we belong to the place we come from, and travel is a vacation from the self, not a replacement.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
As a piece of prose, the essay is a treat. Hazlitt writes in a style that mixes the casual and the grand: a sentence about a wild rose will be followed by a quotation from Milton and a joke about veal-cutlets. The sentences are long, rolling and propulsive, matching the rhythm of walking, and then suddenly a short one snaps shut, like "I laugh, I run, I leap, I sing for joy." His enthusiasm is infectious, and it is rooted in particular things. We get the three hours' march to dinner, the cups that cheer but not inebriate, the glimpse of lights in a village in the dark, the girl standing up in the ferry boat on the Severn against the twilight. Those images are why the essay feels like a lived experience rather than a thesis.

It is also cleverly constructed. The opening argument, that company ruins a walk, gradually deepens into a statement about self and freedom, and the final turn to foreign travel gives the whole thing an unexpected philosophical edge. The joke at the very end is superb, the sort of finishing touch that makes you reread the piece.

Still, the essay has real flaws. It is extremely self-indulgent. Hazlitt is wonderfully sure of his own taste, and the reader may feel the pleasure of being swept along mixed with a faint irritation at his certainty. Some of his claims are simply too absolute. Is conversation really always a barrier to feeling? Plenty of people find that a shared glance at a view doubles the pleasure. He admits as much indirectly: the most obvious contradiction in the essay is that it is a lively piece of talk addressed to a reader, and he praises the walking-and-silence life in pages crowded with other people's words.

That brings up the quotations. The essay is crowded with them, from Shakespeare, Milton, Sterne and others, often used from memory and not always necessary. In a modern reader this can feel like showing off, or like a barrier. A listener, especially, may lose track of who is speaking in these borrowed lines. The Latin interjection "Procul, O procul este profani," which means roughly keep away, you who are not initiated, is a joke about being left alone, but it does leave the unlearned reader outside.

There is also a narrowness of experience. Hazlitt's journey is a leisurely one for a man with enough money and time to wander and lodge at inns. The poor traveler walking for work is invisible here. And the praise of the inn's anonymity, the thrill of being "indefinitely respectable and negatively right-worshipful," is a joke at the expense of social vanity, but it depends on a man being able to pass as a gentleman.

None of this destroys the essay. It simply means the piece is best taken as a mood and a manifesto, brilliantly expressed, rather than as a balanced account of travel. That, after all, is exactly what its author would say it is.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
On Going a Journey is among the pieces that made Hazlitt's reputation as a writer of the familiar essay, a form in which a lively, opinionated voice talks to the reader about ordinary experience. Table-Talk, the collection where it appeared in 1822, contained several of his best pieces and established him, alongside his friend Charles Lamb, as a master of a style that mixed learning with plain feeling. The essay confirmed that he could write about pleasure as well as he could about politics and painting.

Its longest influence has been on the literature of walking. In the nineteenth century, the cult of the walking tour grew rapidly, and this essay was one of its touchstones. Robert Louis Stevenson, in his own essay Walking Tours in 1876, writes in the same tone of delighted solitude, and he openly admired Hazlitt as a master of English prose. The idea that walking alone is a path to thought, a way of letting the mind loosen, runs from Hazlitt through Stevenson and Leslie Stephen's In Praise of Walking, and on into modern books by writers such as Rebecca Solnit, who has written about the history of walking, and the many contemporary memoirs of long walks and pilgrimages.

It also helped shape the idea of travel as a state of mind. The notion that the real purpose of a journey is not to see monuments but to be free of one's usual role is now so common that we forget it had to be invented. When people today talk about a digital detox, a solo trip or a walk to clear the head, they are speaking a language Hazlitt helped formulate.

Within Hazlitt's own career, the essay marks a high point of the confident, assertive voice that suited the magazine culture of his day. The New Monthly Magazine, where it first appeared, was part of a thriving market for essays, and Hazlitt's pieces for such periodicals made him one of the most widely read prose writers of the 1820s. Even so, he died in relative poverty in 1830, and his reputation went through ups and downs. It took later admirers, including George Orwell and many literary critics, to restore him to a place among the greatest English essayists.

In teaching, it appears in anthologies of English prose and in courses on the essay as a form, usually as an example of how to write about taste and experience with vitality. It is also a favorite among people who simply love walking. Many a hiker has carried a line or two of it in their head, perhaps without knowing where it came from.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
Readers love the enthusiasm. It is rare to find a writer so openly delighted by small things: a bowl of tea, the thought of a rabbit smothered in onions, a cheap volume picked up at an inn. Hazlitt lets you in on a secret that most people eventually learn, that happiness is often made of ordinary pleasures attended to with full attention. His sentences carry that attention. When he describes the stir and preparation in the inn's kitchen as a kind of sacred hour, he makes you want to be there.

They also love the honesty about wanting to be alone. Many people feel guilty about needing solitude, especially in a culture that treats sociability as a virtue and solitude as a problem. Hazlitt says boldly that he is never less alone than when alone, and that solitude is not a lack but a fullness. Readers who share that temperament feel suddenly understood. The essay gives them permission, and a vocabulary.

Another source of affection is its portrait of the mind in motion. Hazlitt describes how, on a lonely heath, "long-forgotten things, like sunken wrack and sumless treasuries, burst upon my eager sight," and he begins to "feel, think, and be myself again." Anyone who has found memories rising during a long walk will recognize that. It is one of the best short descriptions in English of how walking loosens thought.

There is also pleasure in the humor, which is sly and self-aware. He teases Lamb, noting that Lamb is the worst company in the world out of doors because he is the best within. He quotes Cobbett's remark that an Englishman should do only one thing at a time. He jokes that Sancho Panza, faced with the choice of supper, picked cow-heel. These touches keep the manifesto from becoming a sermon.

Writers admire the technique of the closing section. The turn to foreign travel, with its subtle suggestion that exotic experience does not truly become part of us, feels both fresh and strangely modern. People who have come home from a long trip and found that it seems like a dream will recognize exactly what he means. And the last sentence, about borrowing another life to spend at home, is a favorite among readers. It is the kind of line that people quote because it compresses a whole attitude into a smile.

Finally, readers love the sense of freedom that the essay gives. It reminds you that you can step out of your usual self for an afternoon, with nothing but a road and a destination of supper.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
Hazlitt was a controversial figure in his own time, and much of the hostility toward him was political. He was a lifelong defender of the French Revolution and an admirer of Napoleon at a time when most of the English establishment despised both. Conservative magazines such as Blackwood's and the Quarterly Review attacked him viciously, partly for his radical opinions and partly as a member of what they sneeringly called the Cockney School of writers. Because of that, the reception of his essays was often colored by his politics, and a charming essay on walking could be dismissed because of the author's views.

In more purely literary terms, critics have long noted that Hazlitt is sometimes prolix and careless. He wrote quickly and for money, often quoting from memory, and he repeated himself. On Going a Journey shows some of that. The abundance of quotation, and the sometimes strained flourishes, can be tiresome, and some modern readers feel the essay would be stronger if shorter.

A more philosophical objection concerns its stance. The praise of solitude and the dislike of conversation can seem extreme, even a little selfish. Several readers have pointed out the paradox that Hazlitt, one of the great talkers and arguers of his day, attacks conversation on the road while building a reputation as a brilliant commentator on everything. Some see this as a charming inconsistency, others as a form of posturing. The essay's enthusiasm for the incognito, for being known as no one in particular, sits oddly with a writer who very much wanted to be known and admired.

There is also the objection that the essay is a fantasy of male leisure. The traveler is an educated, unattached man with time to spare, roaming freely and treating others, including the girl at the ferry, as scenery for his reflections. Contemporary readers sometimes remark that women and the working poor appear in these pages only as figures in a landscape. That is not unusual for the period, but it limits how universal the essay's account of freedom can be.

There is a final, more biographical caution. Hazlitt's private life was turbulent. He had a failed marriage and a painful infatuation with a young woman, which he would describe in his book Liber Amoris a year later. Readers who know that story sometimes read the longing for escape in this essay as more desperate than the cheerful surface suggests. Some critics argue that the polished joy conceals loneliness. Whether that makes the essay weaker or deeper is a matter of taste, but it does complicate its advertised serenity.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
Hazlitt belongs to the generation of English Romantic writers who valued feeling, nature and the individual voice. He was a younger friend of Coleridge and Wordsworth, whose poetry he admired and whose political drift he came to despise, and he shared with them the conviction that walking in nature was a source of imaginative life. Coleridge and Wordsworth were famous walkers who composed poems on foot, and Hazlitt's own first meeting with Coleridge, which he described in another essay, began a decisive moment in his life. The date he mentions in this essay, the tenth of April, 1798, falls in the very year that Lyrical Ballads, the book that launched English Romantic poetry, was published.

In the essay tradition, he descends from Montaigne, who taught writers that their own taste and moods were worthy subjects, and from the periodical essayists of the eighteenth century such as Addison and Steele. He stands beside Lamb, whose essays are quieter and more disguised, and De Quincey, whose prose is more dreamy. Hazlitt's particular contribution is energy: he writes as though thinking and feeling were athletic.

What descends from him is considerable. The line of walking essays is clear: Stevenson, Leslie Stephen, Thoreau's essay Walking, the travel writing of the twentieth century and today's nature writing. Thoreau, writing in America a generation later, makes a similar claim for walking as a spiritual discipline, though with a more philosophical, even sacred, tone. Hazlitt's version is more convivial and more gourmand: he wants his supper.

It is also worth comparing him with writers who take the opposite side. Dr. Johnson, whom Hazlitt cites, was fond of company and conversation, and James Boswell's biography of him shows an entire philosophy of life built on talk. Sterne, whom Hazlitt quotes saying he wants a companion to remark how the shadows lengthen, represents the more sociable view of travel. Reading Hazlitt alongside them shows how the argument about whether to travel alone or together is really an old argument about what the self needs.

Why does it matter now? In an age of constant connection, when a phone follows you into the wilderness, the essay is oddly urgent. It asks what we are missing when we turn every experience into something to be shared. You do not have to accept all of it. But you may find, after reading it, that the next time you go for a walk you leave your companion, or at least your phone, behind for a mile or two, and notice the scent of a bean-field.

essays.title: A Meditation Upon a Broomstick
essays.author: Jonathan Swift
essays.epigraph: Surely mortal man is a broomstick! Swift's wickedly brilliant parody of pious meditations turns a worn-out household broom into an upside-down mirror of human hypocrisy.
essays.keyContext: A Meditation Upon a Broomstick is a tiny piece of satire, barely four hundred words, by Jonathan Swift, the Irish-born writer who later gave the world Gulliver's Travels. Swift wrote it around 1703, while serving as chaplain, a kind of household clergyman, to the family of Lord Berkeley. It was printed in 1710. Its target is a style of writing popular then, the pious meditation, in which a thinker looks at an ordinary object and draws a solemn moral lesson from it. The most famous model was the scientist Robert Boyle, whose Occasional Reflections did exactly that, and Lady Berkeley liked having them read aloud. Swift decided to show how silly the formula could be. He picks a broomstick, an old, battered, upside-down tree, and announces that mankind is just like it. The result is a joke, but a bitter one, and it contains many of Swift's lifelong themes: human vanity, hypocrisy and decay.
paragraphs: This single stick, which you now behold ingloriously lying in that neglected corner, I once knew in a flourishing state in a forest. It was full of sap, full of leaves, and full of boughs; but now in vain does the busy art of man pretend to vie with nature, by tying that withered bundle of twigs to its sapless trunk; it is now at best but the reverse of what it was, a tree turned upside-down, the branches on the earth, and the root in the air; it is now handled by every dirty wench, condemned to do her drudgery, and, by a capricious kind of fate, destined to make other things clean, and be nasty itself; at length, worn to the stumps in the service of the maids, it is either thrown out of doors or condemned to the last use — of kindling a fire.

When I beheld this, I sighed, and said within myself, “Surely mortal man is a broomstick!” Nature sent him into the world strong and lusty, in a thriving condition, wearing his own hair on his head, the proper branches of this reasoning vegetable, till the axe of intemperance has lopped off his green boughs, and left him a withered trunk; he then flies to art, and puts on a periwig, valuing himself upon an unnatural bundle of hairs, all covered with powder, that never grew on his head; but now should this our broomstick pretend to enter the scene, proud of those birchen spoils it never bore, and all covered with dust, through the sweepings of the finest lady’s chamber, we should be apt to ridicule and despise its vanity. Partial judges that we are of our own excellencies, and other men’s defaults!

But a broomstick, perhaps you will say, is an emblem of a tree standing on its head; and pray what is a man but a topsy-turvy creature, his animal faculties perpetually mounted on his rational, his head where his heels should be, grovelling on the earth? And yet, with all his faults, he sets up to be a universal reformer and corrector of abuses, a remover of grievances, rakes into every slut’s corner of nature, bringing hidden corruptions to the light, and raises a mighty dust where there was none before, sharing deeply all the while in the very same pollutions he pretends to sweep away. His last days are spent in slavery to women, and generally the least deserving; till, worn to the stumps, like his brother besom, he is either kicked out of doors, or made use of to kindle flames for others to warm themselves by.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
The piece begins as though a preacher were speaking. "This single stick, which you now behold ingloriously lying in that neglected corner, I once knew in a flourishing state in a forest." There is a worn old broom in the corner, and the speaker remembers it as a living tree, full of sap, leaves and boughs. Now it is a clump of withered twigs tied to a dead trunk, a tree turned upside down, with its branches on the ground and its root in the air. It is used by every dirty housemaid to clean other things while being filthy itself, and when it is worn to stumps it is either thrown out of doors or used as kindling.

Then the speaker sighs and delivers the lesson: "Surely mortal man is a broomstick!" What follows is a rapid series of comparisons. Nature sent man into the world strong and healthy, with his own hair, the branches of what Swift calls a "reasoning vegetable." The axe of intemperance, meaning drink and excess, chops off those green boughs, and he is left a withered trunk. Then he turns to art, that is, artifice, and puts on a wig, a powdered mass of hair that never grew on his head. Swift asks you to picture a broomstick proudly displaying birch twigs it never grew, covered with the dust of a fine lady's bedroom, and says we would laugh at its vanity. Yet we are blind to our own.

The third paragraph twists the knife. Someone might say the broom is an emblem of a tree standing on its head, but what is a man except a topsy-turvy creature, his animal appetites riding on top of his reason, his head where his heels should be, grovelling on the earth? And yet this creature sets himself up as a universal reformer, raking into every slut's corner of nature, uncovering hidden corruptions and raising a mighty dust where there was none before, all the while sharing in the same pollutions he claims to sweep away. His last years are spent in slavery to women, generally the least deserving, until, worn to the stumps like his brother besom, he is kicked out of doors or burnt to warm others.

The layers a first reader might miss are two. First, the whole thing is a parody. The solemn form, "I beheld this, and I sighed, and said within myself," imitates Boyle's religious meditations, and the comic effect depends on the gap between a high-minded method and a ridiculous subject. Second, the target keeps shifting. Is Swift mocking vain people, the wig-wearers? Is he mocking reformers, who stir up dust? Or is he mocking the very habit of finding moral lessons in everything? He is mocking all of them at once, and the reader has no stable ground to stand on. The broomstick is humanity, but the speaker's grand moralizing is also a broomstick, raising a mighty dust.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
For something so small, it works brilliantly. The first great virtue is economy. In about four hundred words Swift sets up a parody, delivers a pun-laden central image, and extends it into three distinct satirical blows. There is no waste. Each paragraph escalates: the first describes the broom in pitiable detail, the second applies it to human vanity, and the third makes a sudden, sharper turn against reformers and against the gender politics of the age.

The language is also precise. Phrases like "a tree turned upside-down" and "to make other things clean, and be nasty itself" are both simple and nasty. The idea that the broom is condemned "by a capricious kind of fate" to clean while remaining dirty is a perfect compressed paradox, and it neatly foreshadows the point about reformers, who claim to clean up the world while sharing in its filth. The "reasoning vegetable" is a wonderful phrase, sneaking in a joke about the supposed dignity of reason by calling a human a kind of plant.

The structure is also admirably unstable. The pretense of solemnity cracks gradually. The opening is nearly sincere, almost tender toward the abandoned stick. Only as the comparison expands do we see that the preacher has the tone of a man who cannot resist a joke, and that the whole elaborate moral machinery is a trick. The reader is lured into nodding along before being hit.

But a critic should note limitations. As a parody, it depends heavily on knowing what is being parodied. A modern reader who has never encountered Boyle's Occasional Reflections, or the habit of pious analogy, may find the jokes of manner pass them by, and enjoy only the content. Out of context, the piece can seem a mildly cynical squib about human decay, which is much less interesting than the original satire of a literary fashion.

The final paragraph's reference to men being enslaved to women, "and generally the least deserving," is also a dated and rather cheap gibe. It fits the period's conventional misogyny, and the humor depends on contempt for women as housemaids, wenches and sluts, language that now reads as crude rather than daring. The joke about the housemaids using the broom, "every dirty wench," is likewise class-based snobbery. These are the weakest moments, not because they are offensive alone but because they let Swift's satire drop from a clever attack on human pretension into ordinary prejudice.

There is a further question of tone. Swift's misanthropy, his contempt for humanity as such, is here delivered without much leavening, and some readers find the piece a little glib in its pessimism. It lacks the complexity of his later work, where the narrators are themselves fools and the satire turns back on the reader.

Even so, as a miniature, it delivers its punch cleanly. It shows an early talent at work, and it is funny.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
The Meditation is one of Swift's early pieces, written years before the works that made him immortal, and its direct impact in his own career was modest but real. It gave him an early taste of the power of parody. He learned how adopting the voice and format of an established form, whether a pious meditation, a learned treatise or a charitable proposal, could expose its absurdities from within. That method runs through his greatest books. A Tale of a Tub, published in 1704, is a long satire in the voices of hack writers, and it grew from the same period of Swift's life. Gulliver's Travels in 1726 is narrated by a serious, dull traveler. A Modest Proposal in 1729 is delivered in the tone of a reasonable economist who suggests that the poor of Ireland should sell their babies as food. In each case the straight-faced mask is the weapon.

The piece also gave rise to a famous anecdote. According to the usual story, Lady Berkeley was fond of hearing Boyle's meditations read aloud, and Swift, finding them tiresome, wrote this mock-meditation and contrived for her to hear it read, pretending it was part of the volume. Her reaction, as the story goes, was amused. The truth of the details is hard to confirm, but the story has stuck because it suits Swift's reputation as an impish prankster who could not resist deflating pomposity.

More broadly, the Meditation has become a standard example in the study of parody and satire. It appears in anthologies of eighteenth-century literature and in courses on satire, often as a compact illustration of how a mock genre works. Teachers like it because it is short enough to read aloud and rich enough to discuss for an hour.

Its influence on later writers is mostly a matter of tone rather than direct borrowing. The tradition of the deadpan moral analogy that collapses into absurdity can be traced forward to comic writers such as Mark Twain, and the use of homely objects as emblems of human folly runs through writers as different as Samuel Johnson and, much later, humorists writing deliberately fake sermons and inspirational essays. Modern parodies of motivational writing, in which an author sees a life lesson in a coffee cup or a traffic jam, are the descendants of Swift's broom.

It is worth noting, finally, that the piece did not make Swift famous. It is a footnote to his career. But it shows that the sharpness and economy later admired in his masterpieces were already present in his youth, and that satire could be done on a very small canvas.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
Readers who enjoy Swift tend to love the Meditation for its audacity and compression. There is a sheer pleasure in watching a writer take a ridiculous image and push it as far as it will go. The idea of a human being as an upside-down tree, with his head, the seat of reason, where his heels should be, is silly and unforgettable. Readers often say the image lodges in the mind: after you have read it, you cannot see a broom without thinking of a wigged and withered old man.

They also love the surprise of its turn. The piece starts so solemnly that for a moment you may think it is a real sermon, and the shift into comedy is a delight. This is the pleasure of any good parody, in which you recognize the original and also see it undone. For readers who know Boyle, or who know the many other solemn essays of the time, the fun is even greater.

Another quality admired is the mixture of laughter and discomfort. The broomstick is amusing, but the description of the end of a human life, worn to the stumps, kicked out of doors or burned to warm others, is a grim truth underneath the joke. A reader might laugh and then feel slightly chastened, which is the effect Swift generally aims at. His satire works by inviting you to laugh at others before you realize you are included.

People also enjoy the portrait of the human reformer. The final paragraph's description of man as a creature who sets himself up as a universal corrector of abuses, raising a mighty dust and sharing in the pollutions he sweeps away, remains a favorite passage. It has been quoted whenever someone wants to describe a self-righteous crusader who makes a mess while pretending to clean. In a time of loud public moralizing, readers find the line fresh.

Finally, its brevity is a virtue. It can be read in two minutes, read aloud at a dinner party, and discussed afterward. It makes a good introduction to Swift for readers who might find Gulliver's Travels or his political pamphlets daunting. Within a few paragraphs you get his wit, his scorn and his love of a perfectly aimed sentence, and many readers find that taste is enough to send them looking for more.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
The Meditation has not been the subject of fierce controversy in the way Swift's larger works have, partly because it is so small. But it has met several kinds of resistance, and most of them are really objections to Swift's outlook as a whole.

The first is the charge of misanthropy. Swift himself wrote, in a letter to his friend Alexander Pope in 1725, that he hated and detested that animal called man, while loving individual people. Many readers, from his own day onward, have found his view of humanity too bleak, too ready to see people as filthy and foolish. The broomstick is an early sample. Man is born strong, then ruined by his own excess, then vainly covers the damage with a wig, then becomes a meddling nuisance, then is thrown away. There is little compassion in that story. Critics ask whether a satirist who sees only vanity and decay has understood human beings at all, or has merely settled on a joke that works every time.

The second is the complaint about its attitudes to women and the working classes, which I touched on earlier. The remark about being slaves to women, and the casual contempt for housemaids, are typical of the period but are hard to enjoy today. Feminist and social critics have pointed to such passages as evidence that Swift's satire often punches downward, turning ordinary servants and wives into emblems of dirt and corruption. Others defend him by noting that the target of satire is always the speaker's own pretension, but the passages in question remain uncomfortable.

A third criticism is about religion. Swift was a clergyman and a loyal member of the Church of England, yet a parody of pious meditation could be read as mocking religion itself. In his own time, and especially after the publication of A Tale of a Tub, some readers suspected him of irreverence, and this suspicion damaged his hopes for advancement in the Church. Defenders respond that he was attacking cheap, mechanical piety, not faith, and that his target here was a literary habit, not God. The debate shows how the same text can be seen as devout or mocking depending on the reader.

There is also the plain view that the piece is minor. Some critics regard it as a clever squib, amusing but slight, lacking the imaginative depth of Gulliver or the moral shock of A Modest Proposal. It is, they say, a joke dressed as an essay, and one that depends on knowing its target. That judgment is fair, although most would add that it is a very good joke.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
The Meditation belongs to the great age of English satire, the late seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries, when writers such as Swift, Alexander Pope, John Dryden and Daniel Defoe used wit as a political and moral weapon. It also belongs to the Augustan age, so called because writers admired the Roman poets of Augustus's time, and valued clarity, balance and the sharp, civilized insult. Swift is the fiercest of these writers, and this little piece is a compact example of his method.

It descends from a long tradition of mock forms. The Greek writer Lucian made fun of philosophers and gods. Erasmus's Praise of Folly, written in 1509, speaks in the voice of Folly herself. Rabelais, in sixteenth-century France, turned scholarship and religion into comic mayhem. Swift inherits their habit of attacking by imitation. In English, the immediate model is the practice of meditation on common things, which Boyle and many religious writers used, and which Swift lampoons.

What descends from it is the modern comic essay and the deadpan parody. Writers who imitate the voice of earnest authority to reveal its emptiness, from Mark Twain to the satirical newspapers of today, are working in a line that runs through Swift. The broomstick's final lesson, that the self-appointed reformer is as dirty as what he cleans, has an obvious afterlife in political satire, where a speaker's moral confidence is exposed as a cover for the same faults.

Comparison with Swift's other works is useful. A Modest Proposal takes the same approach of adopting a reasonable voice, but with devastating moral purpose and a specific political target, the poverty of Ireland and the indifference of the rich. Gulliver's Travels extends the idea of human absurdity across four voyages, with a far more complex narrator. Set beside them, the Meditation is a sketch, but a revealing one, showing the underlying structure of an image, a pious tone and a sudden drop into disgust.

Compare it also with the work of Robert Boyle himself, whose reflections were not meant to be silly; Boyle was a serious scientist and a devout man, and his meditations were sincere attempts to find God in everyday things. Swift's parody is a reminder that such sincerity can be mocked, and that mockery can have its own kind of seriousness.

Why read it now? Because it takes two minutes and leaves a mark. It is a lesson in how satire works, a sample of one of the great English prose styles, and a useful warning against the temptation to turn every small event into a sermon. And it might make you look at the broom in your own closet with new respect, and perhaps a little unease.

essays.title: Self-Reliance
essays.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
essays.epigraph: Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string. Whoso would be a man must be a nonconformist.
essays.keyContext: Self-Reliance, by Ralph Waldo Emerson, first appeared in 1841 in his book Essays: First Series, and it may be the most influential piece of prose in American intellectual life. Emerson had been a Unitarian minister in Boston, but he resigned his pulpit in 1832, uneasy with ritual and borrowed belief, and became a lecturer and writer. He was the leading voice of Transcendentalism, a loose New England movement that trusted intuition, nature and the individual conscience over tradition and institutions. This essay grew out of his lectures, and it reads like a series of sparks rather than a tidy argument. Its message is stark. Trust your own mind. Do not imitate others. Do not be frightened by the crowd, or by your own earlier opinions. It gave America some of its most famous phrases, and also some of its most debated ideas. As you listen, notice how often Emerson contradicts the comfortable and how little he apologizes for it.
paragraphs: I read the other day some verses written by an eminent painter which were original and not conventional. The soul always hears an admonition in such lines, let the subject be what it may. The sentiment they instil is of more value than any thought they may contain. To believe your own thought, to believe that what is true for you in your private heart is true for all men⁠—that is genius. Speak your latent conviction, and it shall be the universal sense; for the inmost in due time becomes the outmost, and our first thought is rendered back to us by the trumpets of the Last Judgment. Familiar as the voice of the mind is to each, the highest merit we ascribe to Moses, Plato and Milton is that they set at naught books and traditions, and spoke not what men, but what they thought. A man should learn to detect and watch that gleam of light which flashes across his mind from within, more than the lustre of the firmament of bards and sages. Yet he dismisses without notice his thought, because it is his. In every work of genius we recognize our own rejected thoughts; they come back to us with a certain alienated majesty. Great works of art have no more affecting lesson for us than this. They teach us to abide by our spontaneous impression with good-humored inflexibility then most when the whole cry of voices is on the other side. Else tomorrow a stranger will say with masterly good sense precisely what we have thought and felt all the time, and we shall be forced to take with shame our own opinion from another.

There is a time in every man’s education when he arrives at the conviction that envy is ignorance; that imitation is suicide; that he must take himself for better for worse as his portion; that though the wide universe is full of good, no kernel of nourishing corn can come to him but through his toil bestowed on that plot of ground which is given to him to till. The power which resides in him is new in nature, and none but he knows what that is which he can do, nor does he know until he has tried. Not for nothing one face, one character, one fact, makes much impression on him, and another none. This sculpture in the memory is not without preestablished harmony. The eye was placed where one ray should fall, that it might testify of that particular ray. We but half express ourselves, and are ashamed of that divine idea which each of us represents. It may be safely trusted as proportionate and of good issues, so it be faithfully imparted, but God will not have his work made manifest by cowards. A man is relieved and gay when he has put his heart into his work and done his best; but what he has said or done otherwise shall give him no peace. It is a deliverance which does not deliver. In the attempt his genius deserts him; no muse befriends; no invention, no hope.

Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string. Accept the place the divine providence has found for you, the society of your contemporaries, the connection of events. Great men have always done so, and confided themselves childlike to the genius of their age, betraying their perception that the absolutely trustworthy was seated at their heart, working through their hands, predominating in all their being. And we are now men, and must accept in the highest mind the same transcendent destiny; and not minors and invalids in a protected corner, not cowards fleeing before a revolution, but guides, redeemers and benefactors, obeying the Almighty effort and advancing on Chaos and the Dark.

What pretty oracles nature yields us on this text in the face and behavior of children, babes, and even brutes! That divided and rebel mind, that distrust of a sentiment because our arithmetic has computed the strength and means opposed to our purpose, these have not. Their mind being whole, their eye is as yet unconquered, and when we look in their faces we are disconcerted. Infancy conforms to nobody; all conform to it; so that one babe commonly makes four or five out of the adults who prattle and play to it. So God has armed youth and puberty and manhood no less with its own piquancy and charm, and made it enviable and gracious and its claims not to be put by, if it will stand by itself. Do not think the youth has no force, because he cannot speak to you and me. Hark! in the next room his voice is sufficiently clear and emphatic. It seems he knows how to speak to his contemporaries. Bashful or bold then, he will know how to make us seniors very unnecessary.

The nonchalance of boys who are sure of a dinner, and would disdain as much as a lord to do or say aught to conciliate one, is the healthy attitude of human nature. A boy is in the parlor what the pit is in the playhouse; independent, irresponsible, looking out from his corner on such people and facts as pass by, he tries and sentences them on their merits, in the swift, summary way of boys, as good, bad, interesting, silly, eloquent, troublesome. He cumbers himself never about consequences, about interests; he gives an independent, genuine verdict. You must court him; he does not court you. But the man is as it were clapped into jail by his consciousness. As soon as he has once acted or spoken with éclat he is a committed person, watched by the sympathy or the hatred of hundreds, whose affections must now enter into his account. There is no Lethe for this. Ah, that he could pass again into his neutrality! Who can thus avoid all pledges and, having observed, observe again from the same unaffected, unbiased, unbribable, unaffrighted innocence⁠—must always be formidable. He would utter opinions on all passing affairs, which being seen to be not private but necessary, would sink like darts into the ear of men and put them in fear.

These are the voices which we hear in solitude, but they grow faint and inaudible as we enter into the world. Society everywhere is in conspiracy against the manhood of every one of its members. Society is a joint-stock company, in which the members agree, for the better securing of his bread to each shareholder, to surrender the liberty and culture of the eater. The virtue in most request is conformity. Self-reliance is its aversion. It loves not realities and creators, but names and customs.

Whoso would be a man, must be a nonconformist. He who would gather immortal palms must not be hindered by the name of goodness, but must explore if it be goodness. Nothing is at last sacred but the integrity of your own mind. Absolve you to yourself, and you shall have the suffrage of the world. I remember an answer which when quite young I was prompted to make to a valued adviser who was wont to importune me with the dear old doctrines of the church. On my saying, What have I to do with the sacredness of traditions, if I live wholly from within? my friend suggested⁠—“But these impulses may be from below, not from above.” I replied, “They do not seem to me to be such; but if I am the Devil’s child, I will live then from the Devil.” No law can be sacred to me but that of my nature. Good and bad are but names very readily transferable to that or this; the only right is what is after my constitution; the only wrong what is against it. A man is to carry himself in the presence of all opposition as if everything were titular and ephemeral but he. I am ashamed to think how easily we capitulate to badges and names, to large societies and dead institutions. Every decent and well-spoken individual affects and sways me more than is right. I ought to go upright and vital, and speak the rude truth in all ways. If malice and vanity wear the coat of philanthropy, shall that pass? If an angry bigot assumes this bountiful cause of Abolition, and comes to me with his last news from Barbados, why should I not say to him, “Go love thy infant; love thy woodchopper; be good-natured and modest; have that grace; and never varnish your hard, uncharitable ambition with this incredible tenderness for black folk a thousand miles off. Thy love afar is spite at home.” Rough and graceless would be such greeting, but truth is handsomer than the affectation of love. Your goodness must have some edge to it⁠—else it is none. The doctrine of hatred must be preached, as the counteraction of the doctrine of love, when that pules and whines. I shun father and mother and wife and brother when my genius calls me. I would write on the lintels of the doorpost, Whim. I hope it is somewhat better than whim at last, but we cannot spend the day in explanation. Expect me not to show cause why I seek or why I exclude company. Then again, do not tell me, as a good man did today, of my obligation to put all poor men in good situations. Are they my poor? I tell thee, thou foolish philanthropist, that I grudge the dollar, the dime, the cent, I give to such men as do not belong to me and to whom I do not belong. There is a class of persons to whom by all spiritual affinity I am bought and sold; for them I will go to prison if need be; but your miscellaneous popular charities; the education at college of fools; the building of meetinghouses to the vain end to which many now stand; alms to sots, and the thousandfold Relief Societies;⁠—though I confess with shame I sometimes succumb and give the dollar, it is a wicked dollar which by and by I shall have the manhood to withhold.

Virtues are, in the popular estimate, rather the exception than the rule. There is the man and his virtues. Men do what is called a good action, as some piece of courage or charity, much as they would pay a fine in expiation of daily nonappearance on parade. Their works are done as an apology or extenuation of their living in the world⁠—as invalids and the insane pay a high board. Their virtues are penances. I do not wish to expiate, but to live. My life is for itself and not for a spectacle. I much prefer that it should be of a lower strain, so it be genuine and equal, than that it should be glittering and unsteady. I wish it to be sound and sweet, and not to need diet and bleeding. I ask primary evidence that you are a man, and refuse this appeal from the man to his actions. I know that for myself it makes no difference whether I do or forbear those actions which are reckoned excellent. I cannot consent to pay for a privilege where I have intrinsic right. Few and mean as my gifts may be, I actually am, and do not need for my own assurance or the assurance of my fellows any secondary testimony.

What I must do is all that concerns me, not what the people think. This rule, equally arduous in actual and in intellectual life, may serve for the whole distinction between greatness and meanness. It is the harder because you will always find those who think they know what is your duty better than you know it. It is easy in the world to live after the world’s opinion; it is easy in solitude to live after our own; but the great man is he who in the midst of the crowd keeps with perfect sweetness the independence of solitude.

The objection to conforming to usages that have become dead to you is that it scatters your force. It loses your time and blurs the impression of your character. If you maintain a dead church, contribute to a dead Bible-society, vote with a great party either for the government or against it, spread your table like base housekeepers⁠—under all these screens I have difficulty to detect the precise man you are: and of course so much force is withdrawn from your proper life. But do your work, and I shall know you. Do your work, and you shall reinforce yourself. A man must consider what a blindman’s buff is this game of conformity. If I know your sect, I anticipate your argument. I hear a preacher announce for his text and topic the expediency of one of the institutions of his church. Do I not know beforehand that not possibly can he say a new and spontaneous word? Do I not know that with all this ostentation of examining the grounds of the institution he will do no such thing? Do I not know that he is pledged to himself not to look but at one side, the permitted side, not as a man, but as a parish minister? He is a retained attorney, and these airs of the bench are the emptiest affectation. Well, most men have bound their eyes with one or another handkerchief, and attached themselves to some one of these communities of opinion. This conformity makes them not false in a few particulars, authors of a few lies, but false in all particulars. Their every truth is not quite true. Their two is not the real two, their four not the real four; so that every word they say chagrins us and we know not where to begin to set them right. Meantime nature is not slow to equip us in the prison-uniform of the party to which we adhere. We come to wear one cut of face and figure, and acquire by degrees the gentlest asinine expression. There is a mortifying experience in particular, which does not fail to wreak itself also in the general history; I mean “the foolish face of praise,” the forced smile which we put on in company where we do not feel at ease in answer to conversation which does not interest us. The muscles, not spontaneously moved but moved by a low usurping wilfulness, grow tight about the outline of the face with the most disagreeable sensation.

For nonconformity the world whips you with its displeasure. And therefore a man must know how to estimate a sour face. The bystanders look askance on him in the public street or in the friend’s parlor. If this aversation had its origin in contempt and resistance like his own he might well go home with a sad countenance; but the sour faces of the multitude, like their sweet faces, have no deep cause, but are put on and off as the wind blows and a newspaper directs. Yet is the discontent of the multitude more formidable than that of the senate and the college. It is easy enough for a firm man who knows the world to brook the rage of the cultivated classes. Their rage is decorous and prudent, for they are timid, as being very vulnerable themselves. But when to their feminine rage the indignation of the people is added, when the ignorant and the poor are aroused, when the unintelligent brute force that lies at the bottom of society is made to growl and mow, it needs the habit of magnanimity and religion to treat it godlike as a trifle of no concernment.

The other terror that scares us from self-trust is our consistency; a reverence for our past act or word because the eyes of others have no other data for computing our orbit than our past acts, and we are loath to disappoint them.

But why should you keep your head over your shoulder? Why drag about this corpse of your memory, lest you contradict somewhat you have stated in this or that public place? Suppose you should contradict yourself; what then? It seems to be a rule of wisdom never to rely on your memory alone, scarcely even in acts of pure memory, but to bring the past for judgment into the thousand-eyed present, and live ever in a new day. In your metaphysics you have denied personality to the Deity, yet when the devout motions of the soul come, yield to them heart and life, though they should clothe God with shape and color. Leave your theory, as Joseph his coat in the hand of the harlot, and flee.

A foolish consistency is the hobgoblin of little minds, adored by little statesmen and philosophers and divines. With consistency a great soul has simply nothing to do. He may as well concern himself with his shadow on the wall.
