Biographies and scholarly studies, such as Wilson Jeremiah Moses's work on Crummell and Black nationalism, have grown up around the figure Du Bois sketched.

The chapter also helped establish a model of the intellectual's life as a calling. Du Bois saw in Crummell a model of what a Black scholar might be, and the American Negro Academy, which Crummell founded in 1897 and in which Du Bois took part, was an early attempt to organize Black intellectuals as a body. The Academy sought to promote literature, science and art and to defend the race against its detractors. It was a forerunner of later efforts, from the writers' societies of the Harlem Renaissance to Black studies programs, to give Black thinkers an institutional home.

Crummell's own ideas about Africa and civilization, which Du Bois describes with sympathy, have affected the development of Pan-Africanism. Crummell believed that educated Black Americans had a duty to uplift Africa, and though his views are controversial today, they were an early expression of the feeling of a shared destiny among people of African descent. Du Bois himself would go on to organize Pan-African Congresses in the twentieth century, and it is not too much to say that the seed of that interest is visible in this chapter.

In the literary sense, the chapter belongs to a tradition of tribute writing in African American literature, the memorial essay that honors a teacher or elder. Later writers drew on that model, including Baldwin in his reckoning with his mentor Richard Wright. The chapter also set a pattern for treating the Black clergyman as a figure of learning and moral authority, a theme that would reappear in fiction and in the history of the civil rights movement. Within classrooms, it is often read alongside Du Bois's chapter on Booker T. Washington, since the two portraits, of a man he admired and a man he criticized, show how he thought about leadership and what he wanted from it.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
Readers have loved, above all, the tenderness of the portrait. Du Bois was known as a cool and sometimes forbidding person, and it is moving to see him speak openly of bowing before a man as one bows before the prophets of the world. The opening description of Crummell, tall, frail and black, with a calm courtesy and the sweetness of his strength, makes the reader feel the encounter. Many have said that this is a rare example of Du Bois's capacity for reverence and affection.

They have loved, too, the pilgrim structure. The idea of three temptations, Hate, Despair and Doubt, gives readers an easy handle on the emotional life of anyone who faces injustice. Many have recognized themselves in it, because these are the three feelings that visit a person who is treated unfairly. The chapter suggests that the real victory is internal, in refusing to be turned into what the world expects, and readers find that inspiring.

The chapter's most quoted line, the claim that the tragedy of the age is that men know so little of men, is another reason for its appeal. It names something that readers across eras have felt, that the deepest problems are not material but problems of ignorance of each other. People who have worked for understanding across racial, religious or cultural lines have often cited the line, and it has a long life beyond the chapter.

Then there is the ending. The image of the rusty gate and the wind that blows it open is quiet and beautiful, and the final vision, in which the dead priest is greeted by Christ with the words Well done as the morning stars sing, brings the chapter to a close with real emotion. Readers who might be skeptical of the theology still respond to the human longing for a recognition that the world refused.

Finally, readers have valued the way the chapter honors a figure of intellect. At a time when Black Americans were widely portrayed as unlearned, Du Bois held up a man who had studied at Cambridge, commanded classical learning and carried himself like an aristocrat of the spirit. For students of history, the chapter is a reminder of how much Black learning and Black dignity existed in the nineteenth century despite the conditions around it.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
The strongest criticism concerns Crummell's own views. Crummell believed that Africa needed to be civilized by Christianity and Western learning, and he spoke of African customs in terms that many later readers find paternalistic or even contemptuous. Scholars have pointed out that his picture of an uplifting mission echoes the language of European colonialism, and that his views of ordinary African peoples were harsh. Du Bois, writing in 1903, passes lightly over this side of the man. Critics argue that the chapter's admiring portrait leaves out the troubling parts of the legacy it celebrates.

A second criticism is that the portrait is too idealized. Historians who have studied Crummell's life describe a stern, sometimes inflexible and elitist man, who quarreled with colleagues in Liberia and in the United States, who was suspicious of the Black masses, and who held to a stiff idea of culture. Du Bois's chapter smooths these edges into a legend. This is an understandable choice in a tribute, but it means that readers should not treat the chapter as a complete biography.

There is also the argument that the chapter reflects Du Bois's own preoccupations more than Crummell's. The story of a gifted man denied recognition, struggling against Hate, Despair and Doubt, sounds a good deal like the story Du Bois was telling about himself and his people, and some scholars read Crummell here as a mirror. The theme of the lonely intellectual who works with so little human sympathy might have been as much about Du Bois's own fears as about his subject. That does not make the portrait false, but it makes it partly a self-portrait.

Some readers, as noted, find the style heavy. The allegorical devices and the elevated diction can feel too much like a Victorian funeral oration, especially to those who prefer a more plainspoken biography. Others have wondered about the religious vision of the ending, in which Crummell is greeted by a pierced Jew, Christ, as it fits uneasily with Du Bois's own skepticism about organized religion. It has been suggested that he adopts the language of faith here as a literary gesture of respect.

Finally, there are those who feel that the chapter is slighter than the rest of the book, a respectful interlude rather than a great argument. Even many admirers concede that it does not have the intellectual drama of the chapters on Washington or on education, and that its value lies more in its feeling than in its ideas.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
The chapter belongs to the long tradition of the biographical tribute, the short life written as a monument. Its ancestors range from Plutarch's Lives to the memorial sketches of the Victorian era. Du Bois's version borrows from John Bunyan's The Pilgrim's Progress, the allegory of a Christian on his journey through valleys and temptations, which was familiar to nearly every reader of his day. By putting a Black priest into the role of the pilgrim, Du Bois quietly claims for him a central place in the Christian and literary tradition that had excluded him.

It also belongs to the heritage of African American intellectual life, and within that, to the tradition of what scholars call racial uplift, the nineteenth century belief that an educated elite should lead the people toward progress. Crummell was a major voice of that world, along with Frederick Douglass and Anna Julia Cooper, and Du Bois's own Talented Tenth idea descends from it. Readers who want to understand where the later quarrels over education and leadership began can find some of the roots here.

Looking ahead, the chapter's descendants include a family of elegies and appreciations written by Black writers for their teachers, such as Baldwin's essay on Richard Wright and the many tributes to Du Bois himself after his death in 1963. It also feeds into the story of Pan-Africanism, which Crummell helped inspire and Du Bois would lead. And its central worry, that societies fail by not knowing their own best people, has echoes in later writing about invisibility, the most famous being Ralph Ellison's Invisible Man.

Within The Souls of Black Folk the chapter forms a pair with the chapter on the death of the firstborn. Both are elegies, one for a child and one for an old man, and together they show the book's emotional range, the hope for the young and the weariness of the old, both lived under the Veil. They serve as personal anchors for the political and historical argument around them.

Why read it today? One reason is historical, since it introduces a figure many readers have never met and gives a window on the nineteenth century Black intellectual world. Another is moral: the line about men knowing so little of men is as relevant now as it was then, and the idea that a person's worth may go unseen is a timely reminder. And the chapter is an example of how to honor someone well, with feeling, with a sense of history and with a grace of language, even when the portrait is not the whole truth. Read it with a critical eye, but read it, for the sake of that last image of a gate swinging open in the wind.

essays.title: The Sorrow Songs
essays.author: W. E. B. Du Bois
essays.epigraph: They that walked in darkness sang songs in the olden days—Sorrow Songs—for they were weary at heart.
essays.keyContext: W. E. B. Du Bois ended The Souls of Black Folk, published in 1903, with this chapter about the music of enslaved Black Americans. Before each chapter of the book he had placed a few bars of one of these songs, which he calls the Sorrow Songs, and here he finally explains why. He first heard them as a child, and later at Fisk University in Nashville, where the Fisk Jubilee Singers had toured the world in the 1870s to raise money for the school. Du Bois makes an enormous claim, that these songs are the only true American folk music and the most beautiful expression of human experience born in the New World. He traces where they came from, what they say about sorrow and hope, and how they were nearly forgotten. It is both a work of music history and a closing statement, an argument that a people thought to have given nothing has given America its soul.
paragraphs: They that walked in darkness sang songs in the olden days⁠—Sorrow Songs⁠—for they were weary at heart. And so before each thought that I have written in this book I have set a phrase, a haunting echo of these weird old songs in which the soul of the black slave spoke to men. Ever since I was a child these songs have stirred me strangely. They came out of the South unknown to me, one by one, and yet at once I knew them as of me and of mine. Then in after years when I came to Nashville I saw the great temple builded of these songs towering over the pale city. To me Jubilee Hall seemed ever made of the songs themselves, and its bricks were red with the blood and dust of toil. Out of them rose for me morning, noon, and night, bursts of wonderful melody, full of the voices of my brothers and sisters, full of the voices of the past.

Little of beauty has America given the world save the rude grandeur God himself stamped on her bosom; the human spirit in this new world has expressed itself in vigor and ingenuity rather than in beauty. And so by fateful chance the Negro folksong⁠—the rhythmic cry of the slave⁠—stands today not simply as the sole American music, but as the most beautiful expression of human experience born this side the seas. It has been neglected, it has been, and is, half despised, and above all it has been persistently mistaken and misunderstood; but notwithstanding, it still remains as the singular spiritual heritage of the nation and the greatest gift of the Negro people.

Away back in the thirties the melody of these slave songs stirred the nation, but the songs were soon half forgotten. Some, like “Near the Lake Where Drooped the Willow,” passed into current airs and their source was forgotten; others were caricatured on the “minstrel” stage and their memory died away. Then in wartime came the singular Port Royal experiment after the capture of Hilton Head, and perhaps for the first time the North met the Southern slave face to face and heart to heart with no third witness. The Sea Islands of the Carolinas, where they met, were filled with a black folk of primitive type, touched and moulded less by the world about them than any others outside the Black Belt. Their appearance was uncouth, their language funny, but their hearts were human and their singing stirred men with a mighty power. Thomas Wentworth Higginson hastened to tell of these songs, and Miss McKim and others urged upon the world their rare beauty. But the world listened only half credulously until the Fisk Jubilee Singers sang the slave songs so deeply into the world’s heart that it can never wholly forget them again.

There was once a blacksmith’s son born at Cadiz, New York, who in the changes of time taught school in Ohio and helped defend Cincinnati from Kirby Smith. Then he fought at Chancellorsville and Gettysburg and finally served in the Freedmen’s Bureau at Nashville. Here he formed a Sunday-school class of black children in 1866, and sang with them and taught them to sing. And then they taught him to sing, and when once the glory of the Jubilee songs passed into the soul of George L. White, he knew his lifework was to let those Negroes sing to the world as they had sung to him. So in 1871 the pilgrimage of the Fisk Jubilee Singers began. North to Cincinnati they rode⁠—four half-clothed black boys and five girl-women⁠—led by a man with a cause and a purpose. They stopped at Wilberforce, the oldest of Negro schools, where a black bishop blessed them. Then they went, fighting cold and starvation, shut out of hotels, and cheerfully sneered at, ever northward; and ever the magic of their song kept thrilling hearts, until a burst of applause in the Congregational Council at Oberlin revealed them to the world. They came to New York and Henry Ward Beecher dared to welcome them, even though the metropolitan dailies sneered at his “Nigger Minstrels.” So their songs conquered till they sang across the land and across the sea, before Queen and Kaiser, in Scotland and Ireland, Holland and Switzerland. Seven years they sang, and brought back a hundred and fifty thousand dollars to found Fisk University.

Since their day they have been imitated⁠—sometimes well, by the singers of Hampton and Atlanta, sometimes ill, by straggling quartets. Caricature has sought again to spoil the quaint beauty of the music, and has filled the air with many debased melodies which vulgar ears scarce know from the real. But the true Negro folksong still lives in the hearts of those who have heard them truly sung and in the hearts of the Negro people.

What are these songs, and what do they mean? I know little of music and can say nothing in technical phrase, but I know something of men, and knowing them, I know that these songs are the articulate message of the slave to the world. They tell us in these eager days that life was joyous to the black slave, careless and happy. I can easily believe this of some, of many. But not all the past South, though it rose from the dead, can gainsay the heart-touching witness of these songs. They are the music of an unhappy people, of the children of disappointment; they tell of death and suffering and unvoiced longing toward a truer world, of misty wanderings and hidden ways.

The songs are indeed the siftings of centuries; the music is far more ancient than the words, and in it we can trace here and there signs of development. My grandfather’s grandmother was seized by an evil Dutch trader two centuries ago; and coming to the valleys of the Hudson and Housatonic, black, little, and lithe, she shivered and shrank in the harsh north winds, looked longingly at the hills, and often crooned a heathen melody to the child between her knees, thus:

The child sang it to his children and they to their children’s children, and so two hundred years it has travelled down to us and we sing it to our children, knowing as little as our fathers what its words may mean, but knowing well the meaning of its music.
This was primitive African music; it may be seen in larger form in the strange chant which heralds “The Coming of John”:
“You may bury me in the East, You may bury me in the West, But I’ll hear the trumpet sound in that morning,”
—the voice of exile.

Ten master songs, more or less, one may pluck from the forest of melody-songs of undoubted Negro origin and wide popular currency, and songs peculiarly characteristic of the slave. One of these I have just mentioned. Another whose strains begin this book is “Nobody Knows the Trouble I’ve Seen.” When, struck with a sudden poverty, the United States refused to fulfill its promises of land to the freedmen, a brigadier-general went down to the Sea Islands to carry the news. An old woman on the outskirts of the throng began singing this song; all the mass joined with her, swaying. And the soldier wept.

The third song is the cradlesong of death which all men know⁠—“Swing Low, Sweet Chariot,”⁠—whose bars begin the life story of “Alexander Crummell.” Then there is the song of many waters, “Roll, Jordan, Roll,” a mighty chorus with minor cadences. There were many songs of the fugitive like that which opens “The Wings of Atalanta,” and the more familiar “Been A-Listening.” The seventh is the song of the End and the Beginning⁠—“My Lord, What a Mourning! When the Stars Begin to Fall”; a strain of this is placed before “The Dawn of Freedom.” The song of groping⁠—“My Way’s Cloudy”⁠—begins “The Meaning of Progress”; the ninth is the song of this chapter⁠—“Wrestlin’ Jacob, the Day Is A-Breaking,”⁠—a paean of hopeful strife. The last master song is the song of songs⁠—“Steal Away,”⁠—sprung from “The Faith of the Fathers.”

There are many others of the Negro folksongs as striking and characteristic as these, as, for instance, the three strains in the third, eighth, and ninth chapters; and others I am sure could easily make a selection on more scientific principles. There are, too, songs that seem to be a step removed from the more primitive types: there is the maze-like medley, “Bright Sparkles,” one phrase of which heads “The Black Belt”; the Easter carol, “Dust, Dust and Ashes”; the dirge, “My Mother’s Took Her Flight and Gone Home”; and that burst of melody hovering over “The Passing of the Firstborn”⁠—“I Hope My Mother Will Be There in That Beautiful World on High.”

These represent a third step in the development of the slave song, of which “You May Bury Me in the East” is the first, and songs like “March On” (Chapter VI) and “Steal Away” are the second. The first is African music, the second Afro-American, while the third is a blending of Negro music with the music heard in the foster land. The result is still distinctively Negro and the method of blending original, but the elements are both Negro and Caucasian. One might go further and find a fourth step in this development, where the songs of white America have been distinctively influenced by the slave songs or have incorporated whole phrases of Negro melody, as “Swanee River” and “Old Black Joe.” Side by side, too, with the growth has gone the debasements and imitations⁠—the Negro “minstrel” songs, many of the “gospel” hymns, and some of the contemporary “coon” songs⁠—a mass of music in which the novice may easily lose himself and never find the real Negro melodies.

In these songs, I have said, the slave spoke to the world. Such a message is naturally veiled and half articulate. Words and music have lost each other and new and cant phrases of a dimly understood theology have displaced the older sentiment. Once in a while we catch a strange word of an unknown tongue, as the “Mighty Myo,” which figures as a river of death; more often slight words or mere doggerel are joined to music of singular sweetness. Purely secular songs are few in number, partly because many of them were turned into hymns by a change of words, partly because the frolics were seldom heard by the stranger, and the music less often caught. Of nearly all the songs, however, the music is distinctly sorrowful. The ten master songs I have mentioned tell in word and music of trouble and exile, of strife and hiding; they grope toward some unseen power and sigh for rest in the End.

The words that are left to us are not without interest, and, cleared of evident dross, they conceal much of real poetry and meaning beneath conventional theology and unmeaning rhapsody. Like all primitive folk, the slave stood near to Nature’s heart. Life was a “Rough and Rolling Sea,” like the brown Atlantic of the Sea Islands; the “Wilderness” was the home of God, and the “Lonesome Valley” led to the way of life. “Winter’ll Soon Be Over,” was the picture of life and death to a tropical imagination. The sudden wild thunderstorms of the South awed and impressed the Negroes⁠—at times the rumbling seemed to them “mournful,” at times imperious:
“My Lord calls me, He calls me by the thunder, The trumpet sounds it in my soul.”
The monotonous toil and exposure is painted in many words. One sees the ploughmen in the hot, moist furrow, singing:
“Dere’s no rain to wet you, Dere’s no sun to burn you, Oh, push along, believer, I want to go home.”
The bowed and bent old man cries, with thrice-repeated wail:
“O Lord, keep me from sinking down,”
and he rebukes the devil of doubt who can whisper:
“Jesus is dead and God’s gone away.”
Yet the soul-hunger is there, the restlessness of the savage, the wail of the wanderer, and the plaint is put in one little phrase:

Over the inner thoughts of the slaves and their relations one with another the shadow of fear ever hung, so that we get but glimpses here and there, and also with them, eloquent omissions and silences. Mother and child are sung, but seldom father; fugitive and weary wanderer call for pity and affection, but there is little of wooing and wedding; the rocks and the mountains are well known, but home is unknown. Strange blending of love and helplessness sings through the refrain:
“Yonder’s my ole mudder, Been waggin’ at de hill so long; ’Bout time she cross over, Git home bime-by.”
Elsewhere comes the cry of the “Motherless” and the “Farewell, Farewell, My Only Child.”

Love-songs are scarce and fall into two categories⁠—the frivolous and light, and the sad. Of deep successful love there is ominous silence, and in one of the oldest of these songs there is a depth of history and meaning:
A black woman said of the song, “It can’t be sung without a full heart and a troubled sperrit.” The same voice sings here that sings in the German folksong:
“Jetz Geh i’ an’s brunele, trink’ aber net.”

Of death the Negro showed little fear, but talked of it familiarly and even fondly as simply a crossing of the waters, perhaps⁠—who knows?⁠—back to his ancient forests again. Later days transfigured his fatalism, and amid the dust and dirt the toiler sang:
“Dust, dust and ashes, fly over my grave, But the Lord shall bear my spirit home.”

The things evidently borrowed from the surrounding world undergo characteristic change when they enter the mouth of the slave. Especially is this true of Bible phrases. “Weep, O captive daughter of Zion,” is quaintly turned into “Zion, Weep-a-Low,” and the wheels of Ezekiel are turned every way in the mystic dreaming of the slave, till he says:
“There’s a little wheel a-turnin’ in-a-my heart.”

As in olden time, the words of these hymns were improvised by some leading minstrel of the religious band. The circumstances of the gathering, however, the rhythm of the songs, and the limitations of allowable thought, confined the poetry for the most part to single or double lines, and they seldom were expanded to quatrains or longer tales, although there are some few examples of sustained efforts, chiefly paraphrases of the Bible. Three short series of verses have always attracted me⁠—the one that heads this chapter, of one line of which Thomas Wentworth Higginson has fittingly said, “Never, it seems to me, since man first lived and suffered was his infinite longing for peace uttered more plaintively.” The second and third are descriptions of the Last Judgment⁠—the one a late improvisation, with some traces of outside influence:
“Oh, the stars in the elements are falling, And the moon drips away into blood, And the ransomed of the Lord are returning unto God, Blessed be the name of the Lord.”
And the other earlier and homelier picture from the low coast lands:

“Michael, haul the boat ashore, Then you’ll hear the horn they blow, Then you’ll hear the trumpet sound, Trumpet sound the world around, Trumpet sound for rich and poor, Trumpet sound the Jubilee, Trumpet sound for you and me.”

Through all the sorrow of the Sorrow Songs there breathes a hope⁠—a faith in the ultimate justice of things. The minor cadences of despair change often to triumph and calm confidence. Sometimes it is faith in life, sometimes a faith in death, sometimes assurance of boundless justice in some fair world beyond. But whichever it is, the meaning is always clear: that sometime, somewhere, men will judge men by their souls and not by their skins. Is such a hope justified? Do the Sorrow Songs sing true?

The silently growing assumption of this age is that the probation of races is past, and that the backward races of today are of proven inefficiency and not worth the saving. Such an assumption is the arrogance of peoples irreverent toward Time and ignorant of the deeds of men. A thousand years ago such an assumption, easily possible, would have made it difficult for the Teuton to prove his right to life. Two thousand years ago such dogmatism, readily welcome, would have scouted the idea of blond races ever leading civilization. So woefully unorganized is sociological knowledge that the meaning of progress, the meaning of “swift” and “slow” in human doing, and the limits of human perfectability, are veiled, unanswered sphinxes on the shores of science. Why should Aeschylus have sung two thousand years before Shakespeare was born? Why has civilization flourished in Europe, and flickered, flamed, and died in Africa? So long as the world stands meekly dumb before such questions, shall this nation proclaim its ignorance and unhallowed prejudices by denying freedom of opportunity to those who brought the Sorrow Songs to the Seats of the Mighty?

Your country? How came it yours? Before the Pilgrims landed we were here. Here we have brought our three gifts and mingled them with yours: a gift of story and song⁠—soft, stirring melody in an ill-harmonized and unmelodious land; the gift of sweat and brawn to beat back the wilderness, conquer the soil, and lay the foundations of this vast economic empire two hundred years earlier than your weak hands could have done it; the third, a gift of the Spirit. Around us the history of the land has centred for thrice a hundred years; out of the nation’s heart we have called all that was best to throttle and subdue all that was worst; fire and blood, prayer and sacrifice, have billowed over this people, and they have found peace only in the altars of the God of Right. Nor has our gift of the Spirit been merely passive. Actively we have woven ourselves with the very warp and woof of this nation⁠—we fought their battles, shared their sorrow, mingled our blood with theirs, and generation after generation have pleaded with a headstrong, careless people to despise not Justice, Mercy, and Truth, lest the nation be smitten with a curse. Our song, our toil, our cheer, and warning have been given to this nation in blood-brotherhood. Are not these gifts worth the giving? Is not this work and striving? Would America have been America without her Negro people?

Even so is the hope that sang in the songs of my fathers well sung. If somewhere in this whirl and chaos of things there dwells Eternal Good, pitiful yet masterful, then anon in His good time America shall rend the Veil and the prisoned shall go free. Free, free as the sunshine trickling down the morning into these high windows of mine, free as yonder fresh young voices welling up to me from the caverns of brick and mortar below⁠—swelling with song, instinct with life, tremulous treble and darkening bass. My children, my little children, are singing to the sunshine, and thus they sing:
And the traveller girds himself, and sets his face toward the Morning, and goes his way.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
Du Bois begins with a confession of love. Ever since he was a child these songs have stirred him strangely, and when he came to Nashville and saw Jubilee Hall, the building the Fisk Singers' tours had paid for, it seemed to him made of the songs themselves, its bricks red with the blood and dust of toil. This is the emotional key of the chapter. He is not writing as a detached scholar but as a man who recognizes in the music something that was his own before he knew it.

Then he makes the great claim. America, he says, has given the world little of beauty beyond the grandeur of her landscape. The human spirit in the new world has expressed itself in vigor and ingenuity rather than beauty. And so by a fateful chance the Negro folksong, the rhythmic cry of the slave, stands today as the only American music and the most beautiful expression of human experience born this side of the seas. He adds that it has been neglected, half despised and persistently misunderstood. To read this properly we have to remember the setting. In 1903 many white Americans thought of spirituals as quaint plantation tunes or entertainment, and many educated Black Americans were embarrassed by them as relics of slavery.

The middle of the chapter is a history. Du Bois tells how the songs first came to the attention of the world, through the collectors during the Civil War and after, and especially through the Fisk Jubilee Singers, who from 1871 sang them across the United States and Europe, and in seven years brought back a large sum to found the university. He divides the music into types, describing the oldest songs as having African roots, later ones in which African and European elements blend, and still later ones influenced by the white songs around them. He notices that the songs often carry a double meaning, their religious language masking a longing for freedom in this world as well as the next.

The final section reads the songs themselves. Their main theme is sorrow, the weariness, the hunger and the wandering, and Du Bois says the music is the voice of an unhappy people. But beneath the sorrow runs hope, a faith that in the end there will be justice and that the weary will rest. Their message, he says, is of the hope that sang in the songs of my fathers. He closes by arguing that Black Americans have given America not only labor but song, story and spirit, and he asks whether America would have been America without her Negro people. The final image is of children singing to the sunshine and a traveller who girds himself and sets his face toward the Morning. The meaning is that the songs are both a record of suffering and a promise of freedom, and that they are the nation's most valuable inheritance.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
As a concluding chapter, this is a very effective piece. It does the difficult thing of ending a book with both summary and release. After a volume of argument about politics, education and the color line, Du Bois turns to music, where the book's themes of suffering, dignity and hope can be felt rather than argued. The structure of the chapter, from personal memory to bold claim to history to interpretation to blessing, is clear and builds a gentle momentum. And the idea he introduced at the start of the book, placing a fragment of a song at the head of each chapter, pays off here, because the reader suddenly understands that the whole book has been framed by this music.

The chapter also has real critical achievement. Du Bois was one of the first major American writers to insist that the spirituals were art, not just folk curiosity, and his argument for their beauty was ahead of the thinking of his time. His observation that the songs carry hidden meaning is perceptive, and the line he draws between the songs as a record of the soul and as a form of social memory is a shrewd one. The warmth with which he writes about them gives the chapter a unique sincerity.

There are weak points, though, and a modern reader will notice them. Du Bois was not a trained musicologist, and his accounts of the origins and development of the songs are partly speculative. His classification of songs into African, blended and white-influenced types is rather schematic, and his claims about the African roots of particular songs are not well documented. Some of his statements about the music's history are now known to be incomplete, and he gives too little attention to the individual composers and singers who must have shaped the tradition.

The prose, as elsewhere in the book, can run high. Sentences about the beautiful expression of human experience or about the nation's singular spiritual heritage are stirring but a little grand, and there are stretches where he leans on abstractions instead of describing the music. A reader who comes expecting detailed musical analysis, rhythm and harmony and melody, will be disappointed. The chapter is more a work of cultural interpretation than of technical study.

There is also an awkwardness in the way he treats the music of white Americans, whom he says have given little of beauty, and the claim that the folksong is the sole American music is an exaggeration, however useful. Still, the chapter's strength is that it persuades through feeling. The passage about the songs rising from Jubilee Hall and the last page with the children singing are moving enough to carry the argument, and the final impression is of a writer who has found the right way to end.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
The chapter's influence has been profound, because it helped change how Americans think about their own culture. By declaring the spirituals the nation's greatest music, Du Bois offered a way to value African American art at a time when it was largely dismissed. This claim became a foundation of the Harlem Renaissance in the 1920s, when writers, composers and singers set out to honor and transform the folk heritage. James Weldon Johnson's collections of the spirituals, Alain Locke's essays on the Negro spirituals as American music, and the concert arrangements of Harry Burleigh and later Paul Robeson's recitals all worked in this spirit. Locke called the spirituals the most characteristic product of the race genius, a view that echoes Du Bois.

The chapter also contributed to the scholarly study of African American music. It stands near the beginning of a long line of work, from the early collections such as Slave Songs of the United States, published in 1867, to the studies of folklorists like John and Alan Lomax, and later historians of gospel, blues and jazz. The idea that this music was not an accident but a deep cultural inheritance shaped these later efforts. Du Bois had in a sense set the question: what do these songs mean, and what do they tell us about the people who made them?

Beyond scholarship, the chapter helped lay a cultural groundwork for the civil rights movement. In the 1950s and 1960s, the old songs were reborn as freedom songs, with new words set to old tunes, sung in churches, marches and jails. The idea that these songs carried a hope for liberation was what Du Bois had said sixty years earlier, and the movement lived it out. The sense of the music as a national treasure also helped shape the way teachers, concert halls and public institutions came to treat the spirituals.

In education, the chapter is widely taught and often excerpted, especially its opening pages and its closing, and it is often read in conjunction with recordings of the Fisk Jubilee Singers, whose descendants still perform. Because the book ties each chapter to a song, many editions print the musical notation, and readers and teachers have long used the chapter as a way into the entire volume. Later writers such as Ralph Ellison and Amiri Baraka, whose Blues People is a major book on Black music, drew on and argued with the tradition that Du Bois helped begin, showing that the claim in this chapter set off a debate that continues.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
Readers have loved the chapter first for its passion. It is hard to read the opening without feeling the force of the author's attachment. The image of a great temple built of songs, with bricks red with blood and dust, gives a physical form to the idea that culture is built from suffering, and many readers have remembered it years later. The sincerity of the opening, the sense of a man hearing the music of his own people and knowing it as of me and of mine, touches readers who have felt their own roots through a song.

They have loved, too, the generosity of the claim. Du Bois does not merely defend the spirituals. He says that they are the finest contribution of America to world art. That boldness has inspired generations of Black readers, and also many white readers who have come to see the music as their own national heritage. There is a deep satisfaction in a writer who turns a thing that was despised into a thing that is revered.

The chapter has also been valued for the way it joins grief and hope. Du Bois dwells on the sorrow but lets the reader feel the faith that lies under it. The idea that the songs are the cry of a people who have been wronged but who still believe in justice is moving and instructive. Many readers have found the closing paragraphs, with their children singing to the sunshine, a profound expression of unbroken hope after a long book of hard facts.

Readers also love the way the chapter helps them listen. After reading it, many go back to the spirituals with fresh ears. Songs such as Swing Low, Steal Away and Nobody Knows the Trouble I've Seen, which Du Bois discusses with deep affection, take on new depth when one knows that they were sung by people who had every reason to despair. The chapter turns familiar melodies into a window onto history.

Finally, there is the pleasure of its history. The story of the Fisk Jubilee Singers, a group of young former slaves and their children who traveled in the cold and the face of prejudice to raise money for their school, and who ended up charming audiences from America to Europe, is one of the great stories of American music. Du Bois tells it with gratitude and pride, and that pride is catching. For many who have read the chapter, it was the first time they heard of these singers, and they have gone on to seek out their recordings.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
The chapter has drawn criticism on several fronts. The first is musicological. Scholars who study African American music have pointed out that Du Bois's accounts of origin and classification are impressionistic. He suggests that certain songs are directly African in origin, but his evidence is slight, and later research by folklorists and ethnomusicologists has painted a more complicated picture of how African, European and American elements combined. The large claim that these songs are the sole American music has also been questioned, since there are other genuine American folk traditions, and Du Bois's dismissal of white American song is more rhetorical than reasoned.

A second criticism is about who is speaking. Du Bois grew up in New England, far from the plantation South, and some have said that he describes the songs with the appreciation of a man who found them rather than one who grew up inside the tradition. Black critics in later generations, such as Zora Neale Hurston, argued that the concert spirituals, polished for formal audiences and the form in which Du Bois largely met the music, were a refined version of the living folk tradition, and that something of the rough power was lost in the arrangement. Hurston, in her essays on the spirituals, complained that the concert versions were not the real thing. This is a challenge to the chapter's picture of the Jubilee Singers as the fullest voice of the songs.

Some readers find the chapter's tone of sorrow too dominant. The title itself, Sorrow Songs, is a selective name. Many spirituals are joyful, defiant or humorous, and the tradition also includes work songs, play songs and other genres. Critics have said that Du Bois's emphasis on sorrow creates a one-sided image of Black musical expression, and that it risks reinforcing the idea of Black life as only suffering. Defenders reply that he was doing exactly what the title says, interpreting one strand of the music, and that he also stresses the hope within it.

There is a further objection about the concluding argument that Black Americans have given America song, toil and spirit and thus deserve full citizenship. Some find the form of the argument, which asks for rights as a reward for contributions, a little too much a plea to the nation to see its debt, and not enough a claim of right regardless of gifts. Du Bois's argument is part of the logic of his time, and one can reasonably read it as strategic. But it has been noted, as has the idea that the chapter's reverent treatment of the spirituals can sit uneasily next to its critique of Black religion in the preceding chapter. These are real tensions, yet they take little from the chapter's power.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
This chapter belongs to the great story of how the spirituals went from the slave quarters to the concert hall to the world. It follows the early collectors of the Civil War era, such as Thomas Wentworth Higginson, whom Du Bois quotes, and the editors of Slave Songs of the United States, and it follows the Fisk Jubilee Singers. It also stands alongside a wider interest at the turn of the century in folk song as the true expression of a people, an interest seen in Europe in the work of composers who built on folk melodies. Around the same period the Czech composer Antonin Dvorak, living in America, had suggested that the future of American concert music might lie in the spirituals, an idea that was much discussed and that Du Bois's claim takes further.

It descends, too, from the Romantic belief that the folk carry a nation's soul, an idea associated with thinkers such as Johann Gottfried Herder, whose work Du Bois would have met in his German education. Du Bois applies it to the American case with a twist. In his account the American folk soul is not that of the settler, but that of the enslaved.

What descends from it is wide. The Harlem Renaissance builds on it directly, as does the study of gospel, blues, jazz and later hip hop as expressions of a continuing tradition. Writers have drawn on its image of music as a vessel of history, from Ralph Ellison's essays to Toni Morrison's novels, and from Baraka to James Baldwin, whose story Sonny's Blues builds its meaning around the way music holds suffering. Even the civil rights movement's songs, We Shall Overcome among them, are in a sense its heirs.

Within The Souls of Black Folk it is the capstone. The book ends on music rather than on argument, which tells us how Du Bois thought about the final source of hope. The epigraphs that begin each chapter now become a hidden thread revealed, and the book's metaphor of the Veil gives way to the image of the Morning. The chapter's last lines about the traveller who sets his face toward the Morning are one of the great endings in American prose.

Why does it matter today? Because it asks us to listen to a tradition the nation too often forgot it had, and to recognize that the songs of the oppressed are a form of knowledge. Because it is a model of how to honor a culture without sentimentalizing it. And because its question, would America have been America without her Negro people, has the sort of answer that changes how one understands the country's history. Read it, and then go listen to the songs.

essays.title: Appearance and Reality
essays.author: Bertrand Russell
essays.epigraph: Is there any knowledge in the world which is so certain that no reasonable man could doubt it?
essays.keyContext: This is the opening chapter of The Problems of Philosophy, a small book Bertrand Russell wrote in 1911 and published in 1912 as a gentle introduction for ordinary readers. Russell was then one of the sharpest logicians alive, deep in his enormous work Principia Mathematica with Alfred North Whitehead, yet here he chose to speak plainly about the oldest puzzles there are. The book became one of the most widely read philosophy primers ever written, and this chapter is the reason why. It starts with something as dull as a table, and by the end you are no longer sure the table is what you thought it was. Russell asks a simple question: is there any knowledge so certain that no reasonable person could doubt it? His answer begins with the difference between how things appear to us and how they might really be. As you listen, notice how he never lectures. He just keeps asking you to look more closely at what you thought you already knew.
paragraphs: Is there any knowledge in the world which is so certain that no reasonable man could doubt it? This question, which at first sight might not seem difficult, is really one of the most difficult that can be asked. When we have realized the obstacles in the way of a straightforward and confident answer, we shall be well launched on the study of philosophy⁠—for philosophy is merely the attempt to answer such ultimate questions, not carelessly and dogmatically, as we do in ordinary life and even in the sciences, but critically, after exploring all that makes such questions puzzling, and after realizing all the vagueness and confusion that underlie our ordinary ideas.

In daily life, we assume as certain many things which, on a closer scrutiny, are found to be so full of apparent contradictions that only a great amount of thought enables us to know what it is that we really may believe. In the search for certainty, it is natural to begin with our present experiences, and in some sense, no doubt, knowledge is to be derived from them. But any statement as to what it is that our immediate experiences make us know is very likely to be wrong. It seems to me that I am now sitting in a chair, at a table of a certain shape, on which I see sheets of paper with writing or print. By turning my head I see out of the window buildings and clouds and the sun. I believe that the sun is about ninety-three million miles from the earth; that it is a hot globe many times bigger than the earth; that, owing to the earth’s rotation, it rises every morning, and will continue to do so for an indefinite time in the future. I believe that, if any other normal person comes into my room, he will see the same chairs and tables and books and papers as I see, and that the table which I see is the same as the table which I feel pressing against my arm. All this seems to be so evident as to be hardly worth stating, except in answer to a man who doubts whether I know anything. Yet all this may be reasonably doubted, and all of it requires much careful discussion before we can be sure that we have stated it in a form that is wholly true.

To make our difficulties plain, let us concentrate attention on the table. To the eye it is oblong, brown and shiny, to the touch it is smooth and cool and hard; when I tap it, it gives out a wooden sound. Anyone else who sees and feels and hears the table will agree with this description, so that it might seem as if no difficulty would arise; but as soon as we try to be more precise our troubles begin. Although I believe that the table is “really” of the same colour all over, the parts that reflect the light look much brighter than the other parts, and some parts look white because of reflected light. I know that, if I move, the parts that reflect the light will be different, so that the apparent distribution of colours on the table will change. It follows that if several people are looking at the table at the same moment, no two of them will see exactly the same distribution of colours, because no two can see it from exactly the same point of view, and any change in the point of view makes some change in the way the light is reflected.

For most practical purposes these differences are unimportant, but to the painter they are all-important: the painter has to unlearn the habit of thinking that things seem to have the colour which common sense says they “really” have, and to learn the habit of seeing things as they appear. Here we have already the beginning of one of the distinctions that cause most trouble in philosophy⁠—the distinction between “appearance” and “reality,” between what things seem to be and what they are. The painter wants to know what things seem to be, the practical man and the philosopher want to know what they are; but the philosopher’s wish to know this is stronger than the practical man’s, and is more troubled by knowledge as to the difficulties of answering the question.

To return to the table. It is evident from what we have found, that there is no colour which preeminently appears to be the colour of the table, or even of any one particular part of the table⁠—it appears to be of different colours from different points of view, and there is no reason for regarding some of these as more really its colour than others. And we know that even from a given point of view the colour will seem different by artificial light, or to a colour-blind man, or to a man wearing blue spectacles, while in the dark there will be no colour at all, though to touch and hearing the table will be unchanged. This colour is not something which is inherent in the table, but something depending upon the table and the spectator and the way the light falls on the table. When, in ordinary life, we speak of the colour of the table, we only mean the sort of colour which it will seem to have to a normal spectator from an ordinary point of view under usual conditions of light. But the other colours which appear under other conditions have just as good a right to be considered real; and therefore, to avoid favouritism, we are compelled to deny that, in itself, the table has any one particular colour.

The same thing applies to the texture. With the naked eye one can see the grain, but otherwise the table looks smooth and even. If we looked at it through a microscope, we should see roughnesses and hills and valleys, and all sorts of differences that are imperceptible to the naked eye. Which of these is the “real” table? We are naturally tempted to say that what we see through the microscope is more real, but that in turn would be changed by a still more powerful microscope. If, then, we cannot trust what we see with the naked eye, why should we trust what we see through a microscope? Thus, again, the confidence in our senses with which we began deserts us.

The shape of the table is no better. We are all in the habit of judging as to the “real” shapes of things, and we do this so unreflectingly that we come to think we actually see the real shapes. But, in fact, as we all have to learn if we try to draw, a given thing looks different in shape from every different point of view. If our table is “really” rectangular, it will look, from almost all points of view, as if it had two acute angles and two obtuse angles. If opposite sides are parallel, they will look as if they converged to a point away from the spectator; if they are of equal length, they will look as if the nearer side were longer. All these things are not commonly noticed in looking at a table, because experience has taught us to construct the “real” shape from the apparent shape, and the “real” shape is what interests us as practical men. But the “real” shape is not what we see; it is something inferred from what we see. And what we see is constantly changing in shape as we move about the room; so that here again the senses seem not to give us the truth about the table itself, but only about the appearance of the table.

Similar difficulties arise when we consider the sense of touch. It is true that the table always gives us a sensation of hardness, and we feel that it resists pressure. But the sensation we obtain depends upon how hard we press the table and also upon what part of the body we press with; thus the various sensations due to various pressures or various parts of the body cannot be supposed to reveal directly any definite property of the table, but at most to be signs of some property which perhaps causes all the sensations, but is not actually apparent in any of them. And the same applies still more obviously to the sounds which can be elicited by rapping the table.

Thus it becomes evident that the real table, if there is one, is not the same as what we immediately experience by sight or touch or hearing. The real table, if there is one, is not immediately known to us at all, but must be an inference from what is immediately known. Hence, two very difficult questions at once arise; namely, (1) Is there a real table at all? (2) If so, what sort of object can it be?

It will help us in considering these questions to have a few simple terms of which the meaning is definite and clear. Let us give the name of “sense-data” to the things that are immediately known in sensation: such things as colours, sounds, smells, hardnesses, roughnesses, and so on. We shall give the name “sensation” to the experience of being immediately aware of these things. Thus, whenever we see a colour, we have a sensation of the colour, but the colour itself is a sense-datum, not a sensation. The colour is that of which we are immediately aware, and the awareness itself is the sensation. It is plain that if we are to know anything about the table, it must be by means of the sense-data⁠—brown colour, oblong shape, smoothness, etc.⁠—which we associate with the table; but, for the reasons which have been given, we cannot say that the table is the sense-data, or even that the sense-data are directly properties of the table. Thus a problem arises as to the relation of the sense-data to the real table, supposing there is such a thing.

The real table, if it exists, we will call a “physical object.” Thus we have to consider the relation of sense-data to physical objects. The collection of all physical objects is called “matter.” Thus our two questions may be restated as follows:
Is there any such thing as matter?
If so, what is its nature?

The philosopher who first brought prominently forward the reasons for regarding the immediate objects of our senses as not existing independently of us was Bishop Berkeley (1685⁠–⁠1753). His Three Dialogues Between Hylas and Philonous, in Opposition to Sceptics and Atheists, undertake to prove that there is no such thing as matter at all, and that the world consists of nothing but minds and their ideas. Hylas has hitherto believed in matter, but he is no match for Philonous, who mercilessly drives him into contradictions and paradoxes, and makes his own denial of matter seem, in the end, as if it were almost common sense. The arguments employed are of very different value: some are important and sound, others are confused or quibbling. But Berkeley retains the merit of having shown that the existence of matter is capable of being denied without absurdity, and that if there are any things that exist independently of us they cannot be the immediate objects of our sensations.

There are two different questions involved when we ask whether matter exists, and it is important to keep them clear. We commonly mean by “matter” something which is opposed to “mind,” something which we think of as occupying space and as radically incapable of any sort of thought or consciousness. It is chiefly in this sense that Berkeley denies matter; that is to say, he does not deny that the sense-data which we commonly take as signs of the existence of the table are really signs of the existence of something independent of us, but he does deny that this something is non-mental, that it is neither mind nor ideas entertained by some mind. He admits that there must be something which continues to exist when we go out of the room or shut our eyes, and that what we call seeing the table does really give us reason for believing in something which persists even when we are not seeing it. But he thinks that this something cannot be radically different in nature from what we see, and cannot be independent of seeing altogether, though it must be independent of our seeing. He is thus led to regard the “real” table as an idea in the mind of God. Such an idea has the required permanence and independence of ourselves, without being⁠—as matter would otherwise be⁠—something quite unknowable, in the sense that we can only infer it, and can never be directly and immediately aware of it.

Other philosophers since Berkeley have also held that, although the table does not depend for its existence upon being seen by me, it does depend upon being seen (or otherwise apprehended in sensation) by some mind⁠—not necessarily the mind of God, but more often the whole collective mind of the universe. This they hold, as Berkeley does, chiefly because they think there can be nothing real⁠—or at any rate nothing known to be real except minds and their thoughts and feelings. We might state the argument by which they support their view in some such way as this: “Whatever can be thought of is an idea in the mind of the person thinking of it; therefore nothing can be thought of except ideas in minds; therefore anything else is inconceivable, and what is inconceivable cannot exist.”

Such an argument, in my opinion, is fallacious; and of course those who advance it do not put it so shortly or so crudely. But whether valid or not, the argument has been very widely advanced in one form or another; and very many philosophers, perhaps a majority, have held that there is nothing real except minds and their ideas. Such philosophers are called “idealists.” When they come to explaining matter, they either say, like Berkeley, that matter is really nothing but a collection of ideas, or they say, like Leibniz (1646⁠–⁠1716), that what appears as matter is really a collection of more or less rudimentary minds.

But these philosophers, though they deny matter as opposed to mind, nevertheless, in another sense, admit matter. It will be remembered that we asked two questions; namely, (1) Is there a real table at all? (2) If so, what sort of object can it be? Now both Berkeley and Leibniz admit that there is a real table, but Berkeley says it is certain ideas in the mind of God, and Leibniz says it is a colony of souls. Thus both of them answer our first question in the affirmative, and only diverge from the views of ordinary mortals in their answer to our second question. In fact, almost all philosophers seem to be agreed that there is a real table: they almost all agree that, however much our sense-data⁠—colour, shape, smoothness, etc.⁠—may depend upon us, yet their occurrence is a sign of something existing independently of us, something differing, perhaps, completely from our sense-data, and yet to be regarded as causing those sense-data whenever we are in a suitable relation to the real table.

Now obviously this point in which the philosophers are agreed⁠—the view that there is a real table, whatever its nature may be⁠—is vitally important, and it will be worth while to consider what reasons there are for accepting this view before we go on to the further question as to the nature of the real table. Our next chapter, therefore, will be concerned with the reasons for supposing that there is a real table at all.

Before we go farther it will be well to consider for a moment what it is that we have discovered so far. It has appeared that, if we take any common object of the sort that is supposed to be known by the senses, what the senses immediately tell us is not the truth about the object as it is apart from us, but only the truth about certain sense-data which, so far as we can see, depend upon the relations between us and the object. Thus what we directly see and feel is merely “appearance,” which we believe to be a sign of some “reality” behind. But if the reality is not what appears, have we any means of knowing whether there is any reality at all? And if so, have we any means of finding out what it is like?

Such questions are bewildering, and it is difficult to know that even the strangest hypotheses may not be true. Thus our familiar table, which has roused but the slightest thoughts in us hitherto, has become a problem full of surprising possibilities. The one thing we know about it is that it is not what it seems. Beyond this modest result, so far, we have the most complete liberty of conjecture. Leibniz tells us it is a community of souls; Berkeley tells us it is an idea in the mind of God; sober science, scarcely less wonderful, tells us it is a vast collection of electric charges in violent motion.

Among these surprising possibilities, doubt suggests that perhaps there is no table at all. Philosophy, if it cannot answer so many questions as we could wish, has at least the power of asking questions which increase the interest of the world, and show the strangeness and wonder lying just below the surface even in the commonest things of daily life.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
Russell begins with a question that sounds easy and turns out to be brutal: is there anything we know so surely that no reasonable person could doubt it? He says that once you feel how hard this question is, you are already doing philosophy. For him philosophy is not a body of secret doctrines. It is the attempt to answer the biggest questions carefully, after looking at everything that makes them puzzling, instead of carelessly, as we do in daily life.

He then picks the humblest possible example. He is sitting in a chair at a table. He believes the sun is about ninety-three million miles away, that other people entering the room would see the same table, and that the table he sees is the one he feels pressing on his arm. All of this seems too obvious to say. Then he starts looking at the table. Where the light falls, it looks bright and white. From another angle, parts of it look dark. If you and I stand in different places, we see different colours and different shapes. A painter knows this and trains herself to draw what she actually sees, not what she knows. Touch tells a similar story. The table feels hard, but press harder and you feel only more pressure, and under a microscope the smooth grain is rough and full of hills and valleys. So what is the real colour, texture and shape of the table? Russell's answer is that nobody can say, because what we are directly aware of keeps changing with our position, the lighting and our own bodies.

This is where he introduces his key term, sense-data. These are the things we are immediately aware of in sensation, such as a patch of colour, a hardness, a sound. The experience of seeing is the sensation, but the colour itself is the sense-datum. And the key insight is that the sense-datum is not the table. It depends on us as much as on the table. So the table, whatever it is, is something we reach only by inference, a sign of something behind the appearance.

That leaves a dizzying set of possibilities, and the chapter ends by lining them up. Leibniz said the table is a community of souls. Berkeley said it is an idea in the mind of God. Science says it is a vast collection of electric charges in violent motion. Russell is not endorsing any of these. His point is that the one thing we know about our familiar table is that it is not what it seems, and beyond that we have, in his words, the most complete liberty of conjecture.

The layer a first-time reader may miss is how carefully he distinguishes doubt from denial. He is not saying there is no table. He is saying the table we see is not automatically the table that exists, and that the gap between appearance and reality is where all the interesting thinking begins. The last lines turn this into a defence of the whole subject: philosophy may not answer many questions, but it can show the strangeness and wonder lying just below the surface of the commonest things.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
As a piece of teaching, this chapter is close to perfect, and it is worth saying exactly why. The central move is the choice of the table. Philosophers before Russell had used wax, dreams, and demons. A table is better because it is boring. The reader cannot say, I never worried about wax. Everyone has a table, and the argument arrives at the reader's own elbow. Russell's prose does the rest. Sentences are short, examples are concrete, there is no show of learning, and every term, like sense-datum, is defined the moment it appears. He also has the confidence to confess that his conclusions are modest. A weaker writer would have announced a system. Russell announces a puzzle and lets it do the work.

The structure is also elegant. He starts from what seems certain, shows that it is not, and ends on three rival pictures of the table that are each stranger than the last. That ending is rhetorical craft of a high order. You are left unsettled but not despairing, curious rather than defeated.

But the chapter has real weaknesses, and a fair assessment has to name them. The biggest is that the whole argument leans on the notion of sense-data, which he treats as obvious. In fact it is a substantial and contestable theory. Russell slides from the true observation that things look different from different angles to the stronger claim that what we are directly aware of is a private inner object, not the table itself. Those are not the same claim. A table that looks different from different angles may simply be a table seen from different angles. The step from perspective to a veil between us and the world is the very step a sceptical reader should refuse, and Russell makes it very smoothly.

A second weakness is the way he moves from the fact that the colour varies to the claim that there is no real colour. There are perfectly sensible ways of saying the table is brown under normal conditions in daylight, and Russell dismisses these a little quickly as favouring one set of circumstances without a reason. That is arguable, not decisive.

Third, the scientific picture is used as a kind of trump card against ordinary perception, as if talk of electric charges showed that the table of everyday life is somehow less real. Later philosophers, and many scientists, would say that the solid wooden table and the swarm of particles are two descriptions of one object at different scales, not rivals.

Finally, the chapter is very much a product of its moment. The physics is of 1911, the vocabulary of sensation is early Cambridge, and the sheer comfort with a split between mind and world feels dated. Still, being dated is not the same as being wrong, and these flaws are exactly what make it a good starting point for argument.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
It is hard to measure the impact of one chapter, but this one belongs to a book that did enormous work. The Problems of Philosophy came out in 1912 in the Home University Library, a series of short, cheap volumes meant for general readers. It has hardly been out of print since. For generations of English-speaking students it has been the first philosophy book they ever opened, and the table passage is often the first thing they remember. Teachers still assign it, and the table of sense-data has become a kind of shared opening scene for introductory courses.

For Russell himself, the book marked a turn from technical logic toward public philosophy. He had spent years on Principia Mathematica, written with Whitehead and published between 1910 and 1913, which tried to derive mathematics from logic. The little book on philosophy showed he could write for anyone. That gift would carry through his famous History of Western Philosophy, his popular essays, and eventually the Nobel Prize in Literature he received in 1950. The clear, dry, witty voice you hear in this chapter is the voice that made him a public figure.

Intellectually, the chapter helped set the terms of a long debate in twentieth-century Anglo-American philosophy. Sense-data became the standard vocabulary for discussing perception. G. E. Moore, C. D. Broad, H. H. Price and A. J. Ayer all wrote about them, sometimes defending and sometimes refining the idea. Russell himself pushed it further in his 1914 book Our Knowledge of the External World, where he tried to treat physical objects as logical constructions out of sense-data. The question he raises here, how perception connects us to a world beyond it, is now called the problem of perception, and it still organises a whole branch of the field.

The impact also runs backwards through a clear picture of Berkeley. Russell's brief summary of the three dialogues between Hylas and Philonous introduced many readers to the idea that matter might not exist, and presented it as a serious position instead of a joke.

The book has also seeped into general culture. Whenever someone asks whether your red is my red, or whether a tree falling in an empty forest makes a sound, they are standing on ground Russell helped make familiar. And the last paragraph, the line about the wonder lying just below the surface, has been quoted so often in defence of studying philosophy that it has almost become a motto. In that sense the chapter did what its author most wanted: it made doubt feel like a pleasure.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
What readers have loved most is the sense of being addressed as an intelligent adult. Russell does not talk down, and he does not show off. He gives you a table, a few observations, and the freedom to be puzzled, and the effect is a little like being let into a secret. Many people who later became philosophers say that this opening was the moment they first felt the vertigo of the subject, the moment the ordinary world went slightly strange. That feeling of the familiar turning unfamiliar is a rare thing for an argument to produce.

Readers also admire the plainness of the writing. There is hardly a sentence in the chapter that needs rereading. The paragraphs are built on observations anyone can check by moving their head or pressing a thumb into wood, so the reader is not asked to take anything on trust. Russell was famous for prose with an Enlightenment clarity, a dry wit, and a refusal of jargon, and this chapter is a good place to see why admirers praised his style as much as his logic. The final paragraph, with the Leibniz, Berkeley and science trio, is especially often cited. Russell sets out three astonishing pictures in a few lines and lets the reader feel their absurdity and their seriousness at once.

There is also the pleasure of honesty. Russell admits again and again that he cannot settle the matter yet. He does not pretend. For readers used to textbooks that bury the difficulty, this willingness to say, here is a real problem and I do not know the answer, is refreshing and, oddly, trust-building.

Another source of affection is the way the chapter turns an apparently useless activity into something worth the effort. Many people feel suspicious of philosophy as idle word-play. Russell answers that suspicion not by promising practical results but by arguing that the subject enlarges the world. A mind that has seriously asked whether the table exists, he suggests, will never look at the ordinary again quite as before. That promise, that the reward of thinking is wonder, speaks to a lot of readers, including those who never go on to read any more philosophy.

Lastly, there is the sheer usefulness of the vocabulary. Terms like appearance and reality, sense-datum and physical object give a beginner handles for thoughts that were previously foggy. Readers feel smarter afterwards, and that is a real gift from a book this short.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
The most serious criticism is aimed at the idea of sense-data itself. In the middle of the twentieth century, the Oxford philosopher J. L. Austin attacked the whole picture in lectures later published as Sense and Sensibilia. Austin argued that philosophers had been bewitched by a few misleading examples, such as a stick that looks bent in water, and had drawn from them a sweeping conclusion that we never really see material things. Ordinary language, he said, is more subtle: we do not say we are deceived every time the light changes. Many later thinkers agreed that the argument from variation, which Russell uses in this chapter, proves far less than it seems to.

A related complaint comes from direct realists, who hold that in normal perception we see the table itself, not a mental stand-in. They say Russell invents a gap between us and the world and then worries about how to cross it. Phenomenologists such as Husserl and Merleau-Ponty, working in another tradition, also objected that Russell starts from isolated, passive snapshots of experience, when real perceiving is an active, bodily engagement with a world that is already there. On this view the problem of how to get from inner data to outer objects is an artefact of a bad starting point.

Some critics have pointed to the way Russell talks about common sense. He treats the everyday assumptions of the first paragraph as naive and in need of repair, which can seem condescending. Defenders of common sense, following G. E. Moore, held that we are more certain of everyday facts, like having hands, than we could ever be of any philosophical premise, so any argument that leads to doubt about them should be suspected, not the facts.

Others complain about the tone of the popular approach. Because the book is so readable, some argue it makes hard questions look easy, giving beginners the impression that sense-data are a settled fact and that the central issue is the choice between three or four neat theories. Professional philosophers sometimes say that the book is brilliant but compresses a lot of controversy into a few confident turns.

There is also a more historical note. Russell's own views changed, and within a few years he moved away from some of the picture presented here. He later became sceptical of sense-data as private mental items and drifted toward a view in which mind and matter are made of the same neutral stuff. So even the author did not regard this chapter as the last word. Most of the objections, in other words, are not that the chapter is careless, but that its tidy starting assumptions carry heavier loads than they admit.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
This chapter belongs to the old tradition of epistemology, the study of knowledge, which stretches back through Descartes, Locke, Berkeley and Hume to the ancient sceptics. The method of beginning with doubt and asking what survives is Cartesian. The idea that the immediate objects of experience are ideas or impressions rather than things is British empiricism. Russell's special talent was to take these inherited puzzles and restate them in cleaner modern language, with logic as his tool.

Its closest relatives are Locke's distinction between primary and secondary qualities, Berkeley's Three Dialogues, and Hume's discussions of perception. Berkeley in particular is a companion here. Russell credits him with showing that the existence of matter can be denied without absurdity, and that if there are things independent of us they cannot be the immediate objects of our senses. Where Berkeley moved from this to the claim that only minds and ideas exist, Russell stays cautious and, in the next chapter, defends the view that there is matter behind our sense-data.

Looking forward, the chapter is a founding text for the analytic tradition's treatment of perception. Sense-data theory dominated English-language philosophy for roughly half a century, and its collapse under attack from Austin, Wittgenstein, Ryle and others became one of the great stories of the discipline. Modern debates still revolve around the questions Russell sets up, even when the vocabulary has changed. Contemporary philosophers of perception talk about representationalism, naive realism and disjunctivism, but they are in effect arguing about whether and how a gap like Russell's table gap exists.

Interestingly, the chapter also anticipates themes in physics and cognitive science. The point that our experience depends on our position and our bodies is echoed in modern theories of perception as an active construction of the brain. Russell's glance at the scientific table, a mass of electric charges, anticipates the later puzzle about how the manifest world of colour and solidity relates to the scientific image of the world, a puzzle philosophers such as Wilfrid Sellars made famous.

Compare it with other popular entry points: Plato's cave offers a similar shock, that the shadows we take for reality are not the whole story, and Descartes' first Meditation uses dreaming for a similar purpose. Russell's table is the plain, daylight version of these, with no story about a cave or an evil demon.

Why read it today? Because it still works. In under three thousand words you get a real philosophical problem, a vocabulary for it, and the sense that careful thinking can be exciting. Whether or not you accept sense-data, you will understand much better what the arguments are about, and you will have enjoyed the company of a writer who plainly loved the questions.

essays.title: The Existence of Matter
essays.author: Bertrand Russell
essays.epigraph: Every principle of simplicity urges us to adopt the natural view, that there really are objects other than ourselves and our sense-data which have an existence not dependent upon our perceiving them.
essays.keyContext: This chapter comes from The Problems of Philosophy, the short book Bertrand Russell wrote in 1911 and published in 1912 for readers with no training in the subject. It picks up exactly where the first chapter left us. There we learned that what we directly see and touch is not the table itself but only a kind of appearance. So here Russell asks the natural next question: is there any real table at all? He was a master logician at the time, finishing Principia Mathematica with Alfred North Whitehead, but he writes here like a patient friend. The chapter is famous for its cat, and for a very practical idea about how to reason when certainty is out of reach. Its overall meaning is that we cannot prove the outside world exists, but we have excellent reasons to believe it, and philosophy's job is to organise our deepest instinctive beliefs, not to throw them away. Listen for how modest and clever that conclusion is.
