The question we really have to ask is: “When two things have been found to be often associated, and no instance is known of the one occurring without the other, does the occurrence of one of the two, in a fresh instance, give any good ground for expecting the other?” On our answer to this question must depend the validity of the whole of our expectations as to the future, the whole of the results obtained by induction, and in fact practically all the beliefs upon which our daily life is based.

It must be conceded, to begin with, that the fact that two things have been found often together and never apart does not, by itself, suffice to prove demonstratively that they will be found together in the next case we examine. The most we can hope is that the oftener things are found together, the more probable it becomes that they will be found together another time, and that, if they have been found together often enough, the probability will amount almost to certainty. It can never quite reach certainty, because we know that in spite of frequent repetitions there sometimes is a failure at the last, as in the case of the chicken whose neck is wrung. Thus probability is all we ought to seek.

It might be urged, as against the view we are advocating, that we know all natural phenomena to be subject to the reign of law, and that sometimes, on the basis of observation, we can see that only one law can possibly fit the facts of the case. Now to this view there are two answers. The first is that, even if some law which has no exceptions applies to our case, we can never, in practice, be sure that we have discovered that law and not one to which there are exceptions. The second is that the reign of law would seem to be itself only probable, and that our belief that it will hold in the future, or in unexamined cases in the past, is itself based upon the very principle we are examining.
The principle we are examining may be called the principle of induction, and its two parts may be stated as follows:

When a thing of a certain sort A has been found to be associated with a thing of a certain other sort B, and has never been found dissociated from a thing of the sort B, the greater the number of cases in which A and B have been associated, the greater is the probability that they will be associated in a fresh case in which one of them is known to be present;
Under the same circumstances, a sufficient number of cases of association will make the probability of a fresh association nearly a certainty, and will make it approach certainty without limit.

As just stated, the principle applies only to the verification of our expectation in a single fresh instance. But we want also to know that there is a probability in favour of the general law that things of the sort A are always associated with things of the sort B, provided a sufficient number of cases of association are known, and no cases of failure of association are known. The probability of the general law is obviously less than the probability of the particular case, since if the general law is true, the particular case must also be true, whereas the particular case may be true without the general law being true. Nevertheless the probability of the general law is increased by repetitions, just as the probability of the particular case is. We may therefore repeat the two parts of our principle as regards the general law, thus:

The greater the number of cases in which a thing of the sort A has been found associated with a thing of the sort B, the more probable it is (if no cases of failure of association are known) that A is always associated with B;

Under the same circumstances, a sufficient number of cases of the association of A with B will make it nearly certain that A is always associated with B, and will make this general law approach certainty without limit.

It should be noted that probability is always relative to certain data. In our case, the data are merely the known cases of coexistence of A and B. There may be other data, which might be taken into account, which would gravely alter the probability. For example, a man who had seen a great many white swans might argue, by our principle, that on the data it was probable that all swans were white, and this might be a perfectly sound argument. The argument is not disproved by the fact that some swans are black, because a thing may very well happen in spite of the fact that some data render it improbable. In the case of the swans, a man might know that colour is a very variable characteristic in many species of animals, and that, therefore, an induction as to colour is peculiarly liable to error. But this knowledge would be a fresh datum, by no means proving that the probability relatively to our previous data had been wrongly estimated. The fact, therefore, that things often fail to fulfil our expectations is no evidence that our expectations will not probably be fulfilled in a given case or a given class of cases. Thus our inductive principle is at any rate not capable of being disproved by an appeal to experience.

The inductive principle, however, is equally incapable of being proved by an appeal to experience. Experience might conceivably confirm the inductive principle as regards the cases that have been already examined; but as regards unexamined cases, it is the inductive principle alone that can justify any inference from what has been examined to what has not been examined. All arguments which, on the basis of experience, argue as to the future or the unexperienced parts of the past or present, assume the inductive principle; hence we can never use experience to prove the inductive principle without begging the question. Thus we must either accept the inductive principle on the ground of its intrinsic evidence, or forgo all justification of our expectations about the future. If the principle is unsound, we have no reason to expect the sun to rise tomorrow, to expect bread to be more nourishing than a stone, or to expect that if we throw ourselves off the roof we shall fall. When we see what looks like our best friend approaching us, we shall have no reason to suppose that his body is not inhabited by the mind of our worst enemy or of some total stranger. All our conduct is based upon associations which have worked in the past, and which we therefore regard as likely to work in the future; and this likelihood is dependent for its validity upon the inductive principle.

The general principles of science, such as the belief in the reign of law, and the belief that every event must have a cause, are as completely dependent upon the inductive principle as are the beliefs of daily life. All such general principles are believed because mankind have found innumerable instances of their truth and no instances of their falsehood. But this affords no evidence for their truth in the future, unless the inductive principle is assumed.

Thus all knowledge which, on a basis of experience tells us something about what is not experienced, is based upon a belief which experience can neither confirm nor confute, yet which, at least in its more concrete applications, appears to be as firmly rooted in us as many of the facts of experience. The existence and justification of such beliefs⁠—for the inductive principle, as we shall see, is not the only example⁠—raises some of the most difficult and most debated problems of philosophy. We will, in the next chapter, consider briefly what may be said to account for such knowledge, and what is its scope and its degree of certainty.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
Russell begins with a plain observation: all of us believe the sun will rise tomorrow. He asks why. The natural answer is that it always has. But that answer, he points out, only moves the question one step further back. Why should the fact that something has always happened make it likely to happen again?

He first notes that our expectation of regularity is not a product of careful thought. Animals have it too. A domestic animal expects food when it sees the person who usually feeds it. Here comes the famous illustration, the chicken. The man who has fed the chicken every day of its life at last wrings its neck instead, which shows, Russell dryly remarks, that more refined views about the uniformity of nature would have been useful to the chicken. The point is that expecting repetition can mislead us, and yet we do it instinctively, so the real question is whether there is any way to tell a sound expectation from a foolish one.

To answer, he asks what general belief would be needed to justify our confidence. His answer is what he calls the principle of induction. It has two parts. First, the more often two things have been found together, and never apart, the more probable it is that they will be found together again. Second, with enough cases, that probability comes as near to certainty as we like. This principle is not itself a certainty, but if true, it would justify our ordinary expectations and the laws of science.

Now comes the trap, and it is the heart of the chapter. How do we know the principle of induction is true? Not by logic, since the future could logically differ from the past. Not by experience either, because experience can only tell us about the cases we have actually met. To say the principle has worked so far and so will keep working is to use the principle to prove itself. That is circular.

So Russell reaches a stark choice: either accept the principle on the strength of its own obviousness, or give up all justification of our expectations about the future. If we give it up, we lose not just the sun rising but bread nourishing us, the ground holding us up, and our best friend being our best friend, not an impostor in disguise. And the same goes for the great principles of science, such as the reign of law and the belief that every event has a cause.

The last paragraph widens the lesson. All knowledge that goes beyond what we have experienced rests on a belief that experience can neither confirm nor refute, and that belief is not the only one of its kind. That sets up the next chapter's search for knowledge that does not come from experience at all.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
This is among the clearest short treatments of the problem of induction ever written, and its craftsmanship is a pleasure to examine. The pacing is excellent. Russell starts with a belief too obvious to question, makes you feel why it is odd, then builds step by step toward the trap, and finally closes it with a short and slightly alarming paragraph about best friends and impostors. The chicken is perfect. It is darkly funny, memorable, and exact about the point, which is that regularity can be a reason for trust and, at the same time, a lulling prelude to disaster.

He also deserves credit for the care of his formulation. By splitting the principle of induction into two parts, he separates a modest claim, that repeated instances raise probability, from a larger one, that enough instances approach certainty. He also adds the condition that there must be no known case of failure. That is more precise than the usual slogan that the future will be like the past.

Yet there are real weaknesses. The most important is that he leaves the conclusion hanging. He says we must either accept the principle on its intrinsic evidence or give up on the future, and then, in effect, he accepts it. But what does intrinsic evidence mean here? To say it is as firmly rooted in us as many facts of experience is a description of psychology, not a justification. Russell has proved that induction cannot be proved by experience, which is Hume's point, and then waves toward an alternative without showing it works. A sceptical reader may feel that the chapter diagnoses the disease beautifully and prescribes only a shrug.

Second, the argument slides between probability and certainty in a way that is not fully worked out. Saying a principle makes something probable raises a question about what probability means, and that question is not addressed. Is it a degree of rational belief, a frequency, something else? The chapter only touches it, leaving the later technical work to others.

Third, the principle as stated is rather crude. It treats instances as simply piling up, whereas real scientific reasoning is far more selective. Which regularities count? Why do we generalise some patterns and not others? Russell's formulation does not say, and later philosophers found that these omissions were not minor but central.

Finally, readers may feel the chapter is somewhat dated in its confidence about natural law, and in its assumption that the reign of law is what science needs to justify. Even so, as an exposition, it is almost flawless.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
The chapter's influence comes from the clarity with which it dramatises a problem rather than from any solution. Most readers outside philosophy first meet the problem of induction through Russell, and that is a considerable cultural achievement. The chicken in particular has gone on to a remarkable second life. It is retold in popular books on risk and uncertainty, most prominently in Nassim Nicholas Taleb's writing on rare and unpredictable events, where a turkey replaces the chicken but the lesson is the same: a long record of calm is no guarantee against a sudden break. People who have never heard of Russell now use his story.

Within philosophy, the chapter helped keep Hume's old puzzle at the centre of the field at a moment when logic and science were advancing quickly. It also sits at the front of a line of twentieth-century work. John Maynard Keynes, a friend of Russell's, published his Treatise on Probability in 1921, trying to give a logical account of how evidence supports conclusions. Karl Popper, in the 1930s, took the harshest possible line, arguing that science does not rest on induction at all but on bold guesses subjected to attempts at refutation. Hans Reichenbach and others tried a pragmatic defence, and the Bayesian school developed mathematical rules for updating belief in the light of evidence. In 1955 Nelson Goodman gave the puzzle a new twist with his riddle about the colour called grue, showing that even deciding what counts as a pattern is a problem. All of these are in some sense replies to the difficulty that this chapter lays out.

For Russell himself, the problem never went away. In later works, particularly Human Knowledge, written in the 1940s, he returned to it and argued that science needs several unprovable assumptions, not just one. That shows the chapter was an early move in a lifelong effort.

In education, the chapter is a standard reading in courses on science, scepticism and reasoning. It is frequently used to show students why science is not simply a matter of piling up observations. Its influence also reaches the philosophy of science, where debates about confirmation, prediction and the nature of scientific laws all start from the worry Russell sets out.

Beyond the academy, the chapter has fed a general modern habit of mind: the awareness that confident extrapolation is risky, from financial markets to epidemics. Few philosophers have made a technical puzzle so useful for everyday caution.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
Readers love the chicken, and they should. It is one of those examples that lodges in the mind and never leaves. The image of the trusting bird, fed faithfully every day and then unexpectedly doomed, turns an abstract worry into a story with a pulse. Many people who have forgotten everything else in the book remember it, and that is the highest compliment a teaching example can earn.

They also appreciate the honest bleakness of the argument. Russell does not offer a cheerful trick to dispose of the problem. He says plainly that we cannot prove the sun will rise, and that nothing in daily experience can prove it. Readers who expect philosophy to be either empty or consoling are often struck that here it is simply truthful about a hard limit. There is a certain bracing pleasure in being told the real situation.

Another delight is the way he makes the problem feel personal. The line about a friend's body being inhabited by the mind of a stranger or an enemy is startling, and it shows in one stroke how much of ordinary trust depends on assuming that patterns continue. Readers often say this passage made them see that the problem is not remote and academic but the ground beneath every decision.

Scientists and students of science have been particularly receptive. Many have found in the chapter an articulation of something they half-knew, that for all its power, science relies on assuming that nature is regular. Some regard that as a humbling truth, others as an invitation to think more carefully about what science actually claims.

Finally, there is the quality of the prose. The chapter proceeds with a calm, unhurried logic, as if Russell were simply lighting each step of a staircase for the reader. He never raises his voice, never overstates, and never leaves a term undefined. Readers admire how much weight a plain and modest style can carry, and the chapter is often held up as a model of how to explain a difficult idea to someone who has never studied it. For many, it is the moment they realise that philosophy is not about vague mystery but about pressing hard on something you thought was solid.

It also helps that the chapter respects the reader's own experience. Everyone has felt, at some point, the small shock of a routine failing, the lift that does not come or the friend who does not appear. Russell's argument gives a name and a shape to that unease, and readers find a strange comfort in seeing it explained so plainly, even though the explanation offers no cure.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
The central complaint is that the chapter shows the problem but offers no real answer. Russell concludes that we must accept the principle of induction on its own evidence or give up expectations about the future, and then in practice he takes the first option. Critics say that declaring the principle self-evident is simply to stop arguing. Others had hoped he would offer a justification, as some later philosophers tried, instead of an acknowledgement of faith dressed as intuition.

A second objection comes from Karl Popper, who argued that Russell and the whole tradition had misdescribed science. Scientists, Popper said, do not collect instances and infer a law; they propose bold conjectures and try to refute them. On this view the problem of induction is real as a logical point but irrelevant to how science actually proceeds. Russell's emphasis on accumulating cases looks, to Popper's followers, like a mistaken picture of method.

Another line of criticism, associated with Nelson Goodman, is that the principle of induction is too vague to be useful. Every set of observations fits many patterns. Emeralds observed so far are all green, but they are equally all grue, a made-up colour that means green until some future date and blue afterward. The principle of induction, as Russell states it, cannot tell us which pattern to project. So the principle does not even do the job it was supposed to do.

Probability theorists have also raised problems. Bayesians argue that the chapter does not say how prior expectations enter the picture, while others object that treating probability as a measure of rational expectation raises questions Russell does not address. Some have pointed out that his formulation runs together a claim about frequencies in the world with a claim about how confident we should be.

There is also a more general complaint that the chapter is too pessimistic, that it inflates a logical possibility into a practical worry. Defenders of common sense say that the demand for a non-circular justification of induction is an impossible one, which no reasoning method could satisfy, so failing it should not count as a defect. Some philosophers have simply said that using induction is part of what it is to be rational, and that no further proof is either needed or possible.

Russell would probably accept much of this. The chapter was never meant to close the question, only to show why it matters.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
This chapter stands in a long line of work on the foundations of empirical knowledge, and its fountainhead is David Hume. In the Treatise of Human Nature, published in 1739 and 1740, and the later Enquiry, Hume argued that our belief that the future will resemble the past cannot be justified by reason, and that it comes instead from habit. Russell restates this clearly and gives it a modern frame, with the principle of induction set out in careful terms. The idea that human reasoning depends on something it cannot justify is one of the great discoveries of the Enlightenment, and Kant said that Hume woke him from his dogmatic slumber.

Looking back further, the chapter also touches on Francis Bacon's push for inductive method in science, and on Mill's nineteenth-century canons of induction. Russell's contribution is to ask what must be true for such methods to be justified at all. Looking forward, as the earlier section suggested, almost every later theory of scientific reasoning is a reply: Popper's falsificationism, Carnap's inductive logic, the Bayesian revival and Goodman's new riddle.

Within The Problems of Philosophy, the chapter does an important job. It follows the chapters on perception and the external world and leads to those on general principles and a priori knowledge. In effect it marks the moment when the book turns from asking how we know the world exists to asking what kind of knowledge goes beyond experience. Russell's response, in the next chapter, is that some knowledge is independent of experience, a rationalist note in an otherwise empiricist book.

Compare it with the older sceptical arguments of Sextus Empiricus, who also worried about whether generalising from particulars can be justified, or with modern worries in statistics and machine learning, where the question of whether a pattern found in past data will hold in new data is called generalisation, and is still imperfectly understood. The chicken has an unexpected cousin in every system that has to predict from a record of the past.

Why read it today? Because it states, in a few pages, a problem that nobody has fully solved, and because it does so without panic. It teaches intellectual humility without surrendering to doubt. In an age of forecasts, models and confident extrapolations, the lesson of the chicken is as useful as ever: past regularity is evidence, but never proof, and it is wise to know exactly what we are assuming when we trust it.

essays.title: The World of Universals
essays.author: Bertrand Russell
essays.epigraph: The world of universals may also be described as the world of being: it is unchangeable, rigid, exact, delightful to the mathematician, the logician, the builder of metaphysical systems.
essays.keyContext: This chapter comes from The Problems of Philosophy, Bertrand Russell's short 1912 introduction to the subject, written in 1911 for readers with no special training. It tackles a question that sounds technical but is actually about everything: when we say that two different things are both white, or that one city is north of another, what exactly are we talking about? Is there something real called whiteness, apart from white things? This is the ancient problem of universals, and it goes back to Plato, whom Russell openly admires here. Russell was at the time deep in Principia Mathematica, his great work with Alfred North Whitehead on the logical foundations of mathematics, and his love of logic and mathematics colours everything he says. His overall meaning is bold: general qualities and relations are real, they do not live in anyone's mind, and they belong to a timeless world that is just as important as the changing one we inhabit.
paragraphs: At the end of the preceding chapter we saw that such entities as relations appear to have a being which is in some way different from that of physical objects, and also different from that of minds and from that of sense-data. In the present chapter we have to consider what is the nature of this kind of being, and also what objects there are that have this kind of being. We will begin with the latter question.

The problem with which we are now concerned is a very old one, since it was brought into philosophy by Plato. Plato’s “theory of ideas” is an attempt to solve this very problem, and in my opinion it is one of the most successful attempts hitherto made. The theory to be advocated in what follows is largely Plato’s, with merely such modifications as time has shown to be necessary.

The way the problem arose for Plato was more or less as follows. Let us consider, say, such a notion as justice. If we ask ourselves what justice is, it is natural to proceed by considering this, that, and the other just act, with a view to discovering what they have in common. They must all, in some sense, partake of a common nature, which will be found in whatever is just and in nothing else. This common nature, in virtue of which they are all just, will be justice itself, the pure essence the admixture of which with facts of ordinary life produces the multiplicity of just acts. Similarly with any other word which may be applicable to common facts, such as “whiteness” for example. The word will be applicable to a number of particular things because they all participate in a common nature or essence. This pure essence is what Plato calls an “idea” or “form.” (It must not be supposed that “ideas,” in his sense, exist in minds, though they may be apprehended by minds.) The “idea” justice is not identical with anything that is just: it is something other than particular things, which particular things partake of. Not being particular, it cannot itself exist in the world of sense. Moreover it is not fleeting or changeable like the things of sense: it is eternally itself, immutable and indestructible.

Thus Plato is led to a supra-sensible world, more real than the common world of sense, the unchangeable world of ideas, which alone gives to the world of sense whatever pale reflection of reality may belong to it. The truly real world, for Plato, is the world of ideas; for whatever we may attempt to say about things in the world of sense, we can only succeed in saying that they participate in such and such ideas, which, therefore, constitute all their character. Hence it is easy to pass on into a mysticism. We may hope, in a mystic illumination, to see the ideas as we see objects of sense; and we may imagine that the ideas exist in heaven. These mystical developments are very natural, but the basis of the theory is in logic, and it is as based in logic that we have to consider it.

The word “idea” has acquired, in the course of time, many associations which are quite misleading when applied to Plato’s “ideas.” We shall therefore use the word “universal” instead of the word “idea,” to describe what Plato meant. The essence of the sort of entity that Plato meant is that it is opposed to the particular things that are given in sensation. We speak of whatever is given in sensation, or is of the same nature as things given in sensation, as a particular; by opposition to this, a universal will be anything which may be shared by many particulars, and has those characteristics which, as we saw, distinguish justice and whiteness from just acts and white things.

When we examine common words, we find that, broadly speaking, proper names stand for particulars, while other substantives, adjectives, prepositions, and verbs stand for universals. Pronouns stand for particulars, but are ambiguous: it is only by the context or the circumstances that we know what particulars they stand for. The word “now” stands for a particular, namely the present moment; but like pronouns, it stands for an ambiguous particular, because the present is always changing.

It will be seen that no sentence can be made up without at least one word which denotes a universal. The nearest approach would be some such statement as “I like this.” But even here the word “like” denotes a universal, for I may like other things, and other people may like things. Thus all truths involve universals, and all knowledge of truths involves acquaintance with universals.

Seeing that nearly all the words to be found in the dictionary stand for universals, it is strange that hardly anybody except students of philosophy ever realizes that there are such entities as universals. We do not naturally dwell upon those words in a sentence which do not stand for particulars; and if we are forced to dwell upon a word which stands for a universal, we naturally think of it as standing for some one of the particulars that come under the universal. When, for example, we hear the sentence, “Charles I’s head was cut off,” we may naturally enough think of Charles I, of Charles I’s head, and of the operation of cutting off his head, which are all particulars; but we do not naturally dwell upon what is meant by the word “head” or the word “cut,” which is a universal: We feel such words to be incomplete and insubstantial; they seem to demand a context before anything can be done with them. Hence we succeed in avoiding all notice of universals as such, until the study of philosophy forces them upon our attention.

Even among philosophers, we may say, broadly, that only those universals which are named by adjectives or substantives have been much or often recognized, while those named by verbs and prepositions have been usually overlooked. This omission has had a very great effect upon philosophy; it is hardly too much to say that most metaphysics, since Spinoza, has been largely determined by it. The way this has occurred is, in outline, as follows: Speaking generally, adjectives and common nouns express qualities or properties of single things, whereas prepositions and verbs tend to express relations between two or more things. Thus the neglect of prepositions and verbs led to the belief that every proposition can be regarded as attributing a property to a single thing, rather than as expressing a relation between two or more things. Hence it was supposed that, ultimately, there can be no such entities as relations between things. Hence either there can be only one thing in the universe, or, if there are many things, they cannot possibly interact in any way, since any interaction would be a relation, and relations are impossible.

The first of these views, advocated by Spinoza and held in our own day by Bradley and many other philosophers, is called monism; the second, advocated by Leibniz but not very common nowadays, is called monadism, because each of the isolated things is called a monad. Both these opposing philosophies, interesting as they are, result, in my opinion, from an undue attention to one sort of universals, namely the sort represented by adjectives and substantives rather than by verbs and prepositions.

As a matter of fact, if anyone were anxious to deny altogether that there are such things as universals, we should find that we cannot strictly prove that there are such entities as qualities, i.e. the universals represented by adjectives and substantives, whereas we can prove that there must be relations, i.e. the sort of universals generally represented by verbs and prepositions. Let us take in illustration the universal whiteness. If we believe that there is such a universal, we shall say that things are white because they have the quality of whiteness. This view, however, was strenuously denied by Berkeley and Hume, who have been followed in this by later empiricists. The form which their denial took was to deny that there are such things as “abstract ideas.” When we want to think of whiteness, they said, we form an image of some particular white thing, and reason concerning this particular, taking care not to deduce anything concerning it which we cannot see to be equally true of any other white thing. As an account of our actual mental processes, this is no doubt largely true. In geometry, for example, when we wish to prove something about all triangles, we draw a particular triangle and reason about it, taking care not to use any characteristic which it does not share with other triangles. The beginner, in order to avoid error, often finds it useful to draw several triangles, as unlike each other as possible, in order to make sure that his reasoning is equally applicable to all of them. But a difficulty emerges as soon as we ask ourselves how we know that a thing is white or a triangle. If we wish to avoid the universals whiteness and triangularity, we shall choose some particular patch of white or some particular triangle, and say that anything is white or a triangle if it has the right sort of resemblance to our chosen particular. But then the resemblance required will have to be a universal. Since there are many white things, the resemblance must hold between many pairs of particular white things; and this is the characteristic of a universal. It will be useless to say that there is a different resemblance for each pair, for then we shall have to say that these resemblances resemble each other, and thus at last we shall be forced to admit resemblance as a universal. The relation of resemblance, therefore, must be a true universal. And having been forced to admit this universal, we find that it is no longer worth while to invent difficult and unplausible theories to avoid the admission of such universals as whiteness and triangularity.

Berkeley and Hume failed to perceive this refutation of their rejection of “abstract ideas,” because, like their adversaries, they only thought of qualities, and altogether ignored relations as universals. We have therefore here another respect in which the rationalists appear to have been in the right as against the empiricists, although, owing to the neglect or denial of relations, the deductions made by rationalists were, if anything, more apt to be mistaken than those made by empiricists.

Having now seen that there must be such entities as universals, the next point to be proved is that their being is not merely mental. By this is meant that whatever being belongs to them is independent of their being thought of or in any way apprehended by minds. We have already touched on this subject at the end of the preceding chapter, but we must now consider more fully what sort of being it is that belongs to universals.

Consider such a proposition as “Edinburgh is north of London.” Here we have a relation between two places, and it seems plain that the relation subsists independently of our knowledge of it. When we come to know that Edinburgh is north of London, we come to know something which has to do only with Edinburgh and London: we do not cause the truth of the proposition by coming to know it, on the contrary we merely apprehend a fact which was there before we knew it. The part of the earth’s surface where Edinburgh stands would be north of the part where London stands, even if there were no human being to know about north and south, and even if there were no minds at all in the universe. This is, of course, denied by many philosophers, either for Berkeley’s reasons or for Kant’s. But we have already considered these reasons, and decided that they are inadequate. We may therefore now assume it to be true that nothing mental is presupposed in the fact that Edinburgh is north of London. But this fact involves the relation “north of,” which is a universal; and it would be impossible for the whole fact to involve nothing mental if the relation “north of,” which is a constituent part of the fact, did involve anything mental. Hence we must admit that the relation, like the terms it relates, is not dependent upon thought, but belongs to the independent world which thought apprehends but does not create.

This conclusion, however, is met by the difficulty that the relation “north of” does not seem to exist in the same sense in which Edinburgh and London exist. If we ask “Where and when does this relation exist?” the answer must be “Nowhere and nowhen.” There is no place or time where we can find the relation “north of.” It does not exist in Edinburgh any more than in London, for it relates the two and is neutral as between them. Nor can we say that it exists at any particular time. Now everything that can be apprehended by the senses or by introspection exists at some particular time. Hence the relation “north of” is radically different from such things. It is neither in space nor in time, neither material nor mental; yet it is something.

It is largely the very peculiar kind of being that belongs to universals which has led many people to suppose that they are really mental. We can think of a universal, and our thinking then exists in a perfectly ordinary sense, like any other mental act. Suppose, for example, that we are thinking of whiteness. Then in one sense it may be said that whiteness is “in our mind.” We have here the same ambiguity as we noted in discussing Berkeley in Chapter IV. In the strict sense, it is not whiteness that is in our mind, but the act of thinking of whiteness. The connected ambiguity in the word “idea,” which we noted at the same time, also causes confusion here. In one sense of this word, namely the sense in which it denotes the object of an act of thought, whiteness is an “idea.” Hence, if the ambiguity is not guarded against, we may come to think that whiteness is an “idea” in the other sense, i.e. an act of thought; and thus we come to think that whiteness is mental. But in so thinking, we rob it of its essential quality of universality. One man’s act of thought is necessarily a different thing from another man’s; one man’s act of thought at one time is necessarily a different thing from the same man’s act of thought at another time. Hence, if whiteness were the thought as opposed to its object, no two different men could think of it, and no one man could think of it twice. That which many different thoughts of whiteness have in common is their object, and this object is different from all of them. Thus universals are not thoughts, though when known they are the objects of thoughts.

We shall find it convenient only to speak of things existing when they are in time, that is to say, when we can point to some time at which they exist (not excluding the possibility of their existing at all times). Thus thoughts and feelings, minds and physical objects exist. But universals do not exist in this sense; we shall say that they subsist or have being, where “being” is opposed to “existence” as being timeless. The world of universals, therefore, may also be described as the world of being. The world of being is unchangeable, rigid, exact, delightful to the mathematician, the logician, the builder of metaphysical systems, and all who love perfection more than life. The world of existence is fleeting, vague, without sharp boundaries, without any clear plan or arrangement, but it contains all thoughts and feelings, all the data of sense, and all physical objects, everything that can do either good or harm, everything that makes any difference to the value of life and the world. According to our temperaments, we shall prefer the contemplation of the one or of the other. The one we do not prefer will probably seem to us a pale shadow of the one we prefer, and hardly worthy to be regarded as in any sense real. But the truth is that both have the same claim on our impartial attention, both are real, and both are important to the metaphysician. Indeed no sooner have we distinguished the two worlds than it becomes necessary to consider their relations.

But first of all we must examine our knowledge of universals. This consideration will occupy us in the following chapter, where we shall find that it solves the problem of a priori knowledge, from which we were first led to consider universals.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
Russell opens by noting that this is a very old problem, introduced into philosophy by Plato, and that Plato's theory of ideas is, in his opinion, one of the most successful attempts yet made to solve it. The problem is this. We use general words constantly: justice, whiteness, triangle, brother. A word like justice applies to many different acts, and we feel that they are all just because they share something. Plato called that shared something a form or idea, a pure essence that the many particular things take part in. Russell wants to keep the core of this, while pointing out that Plato's word idea is misleading, since the thing in question is not in anyone's mind.

He then draws his central distinction. A particular is something that exists in time, a thing you could point to, like a patch of white or a person. A universal is anything that can be shared by many particulars. And when you look at ordinary language, he says, you find that proper names stand for particulars, while other nouns, adjectives, prepositions and verbs stand for universals. Whiteness, triangularity, and relations like being north of are all universals.

Why believe in them? The most important argument concerns relations. Consider the statement that Edinburgh is north of London. This is true whether or not anyone knows it. We do not cause it by thinking it. We merely discover a fact that was there before we knew it. But the fact involves the relation north of, and that relation is not one particular thing, since it holds between many other places too. So it must be a universal, and it cannot depend on any mind.

Next he deals with the philosophers who said there are no universals. Berkeley and Hume, he reports, denied there are abstract ideas, claiming that when we think of whiteness we really picture some particular white thing. Russell's reply is that if you say something is white because it resembles a chosen white patch, then you need the resemblance, and resemblance holds among many pairs, so you have smuggled in a universal after all. Denying universals in one place just forces you to accept them in another.

Finally, he says that universals do not exist in the way particulars do, because they are not in time. They subsist, or have being. The world of being is unchanging, rigid and exact, delightful to the mathematician and the logician. The world of existence is fleeting and vague, but it contains everything that matters to life. Both are real, and both deserve our attention.

The overall shape of the argument, then, is a chain with three links. Language is full of general terms. Some of those terms, especially relations, cannot be explained away as mental pictures. Therefore there must be general things, which he calls universals, and these belong to a realm of their own, outside time and independent of us. Seen that way, the chapter is less a pile of examples than a single, tidy piece of reasoning, and it is worth listening for how each stage rests on the one before.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
The core of this chapter is a genuinely strong argument, and it is presented with great economy. The case from relations is the real achievement. Philosophers before Russell had mostly thought about universals as qualities, like redness. By turning to relations, such as north of, he picks examples that are difficult to reduce to our mental images. It is easy to say that redness is just a way we group similar patches in our minds. It is much harder to say that Edinburgh's being north of London is something we construct. That sharpening of the debate was a real contribution, and Russell is right to point out that both Berkeley and Hume overlooked it because they only considered qualities.

The resemblance argument is also neat. It shows in a few lines that the nominalist, who denies universals, cannot escape having to speak of some repeated feature. Even if the objection is not fatal, as some later thinkers argued, it forces the opponent to pay a price, and it is a good example of how philosophical argument works as a kind of accounting.

The prose rises, too, at the end. The passage about the world of being, rigid, exact, delightful to the mathematician, set against the fleeting and vague world of existence, is some of the most eloquent writing in the book. It reveals the temperament behind the argument, a love of perfection and permanence, and it is also fair to the other temperament, which prefers the living world.

But there are real weaknesses. First, the argument often proves less than it claims. That a relation holds between many pairs does not by itself show that there is a separate entity, the relation, existing in a realm of being. It might only show that our language needs general terms. Russell moves from the requirement that we speak generally to the claim that there is a world of general things, and that is a large leap.

Second, the notion of subsistence is obscure. He says universals have being but not existence, yet he gives little help in understanding what that being amounts to. How can something be real without being anywhere or at any time, and how do we come to know it? The chapter promises an answer in the next, but here the picture is more poetic than precise.

Third, the argument against the idea that universals are thoughts is quick. And finally, the chapter's confident dismissal of Berkeley and Kant by reference to earlier chapters feels a little breezy. Still, as an introductory case for a very old theory, it is strikingly effective.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
This chapter belongs to a stretch of Russell's career in which he was a convinced realist about universals, and it helped make that position a live option in twentieth-century philosophy. It was not unique to him. G. E. Moore, his Cambridge colleague, and others were also reacting against the idealism that had dominated British thought, and a revival of Platonism in logic and mathematics was in the air. But the book put the case before a very wide audience, and for many students it was their first encounter with the debate between realists and nominalists.

Within Russell's work, the position played a role in his logic. In Principia Mathematica, the notion of propositional functions, which are general forms with a slot to be filled, owes a debt to the idea that general features are real things we can talk about. His stance also supported a Platonist view of mathematics, in which numbers and logical truths are discovered, not invented. That view was shared by Gottlob Frege and later by Kurt Gödel, who defended a robust mathematical Platonism, and it remains one of the main positions in the philosophy of mathematics.

The debate that followed was lively. Frank Ramsey, a young Cambridge philosopher, wrote a famous short paper in 1925 arguing that the division between particulars and universals is not as clear as Russell supposed. In the middle of the century, Nelson Goodman and W. V. Quine defended nominalist scepticism about abstract entities, while D. C. Williams proposed that properties are particular instances, sometimes called tropes. In the 1970s and later, David Armstrong built an elaborate realism about universals grounded in science, in a direct line from Russell. Russell himself later modified some of these views, and in his later writings he took a more guarded stand on the particular and universal distinction.

The chapter also influenced the way the problem is taught. The terms particular and universal, and the examples of whiteness and being north of, are standard in introductory metaphysics. Whenever students are asked whether redness is a thing or just a way of talking, they are repeating a conversation that Russell's chapter helped to organise.

Beyond philosophy, the idea of a timeless realm of exact forms has had a long cultural echo, in mathematics, in aesthetics, and in the picture of science as the discovery of laws that hold whether or not anyone is there to know them.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
One thing readers admire is the sheer nerve of defending Plato. In an age that was supposed to have outgrown him, Russell says that Plato's theory is largely right, with merely such modifications as time has shown to be necessary. There is something refreshing about a modern logician treating a twenty-four-century-old idea as live. Readers who think philosophy only ever moves forward are often delighted to find that an ancient answer can still hold its own.

They also love the example of Edinburgh and London. It is homely and exact. The thought that north of is not something we make up, that it would hold even if no minds existed at all, produces a distinct, slightly giddy feeling that something real has been grasped. Students often report that this is the moment the whole subject clicks, when they see why anyone would believe in universals in the first place.

The eloquent passage near the end is another favourite. Russell is usually dry, but here he allows himself a glow of feeling for the world of being, which he calls delightful to the mathematician and all who love perfection more than life. Readers who have ever felt the beauty of a proof or a geometric truth recognise that sentiment immediately. And he is generous, adding that those who prefer the living, changing world should not look down on the other, since both have the same claim on our impartial attention.

There is, too, the satisfaction of the argument against Berkeley and Hume. Many readers have been taught to admire those two philosophers, and it is a treat to watch Russell find a hole in their view using only a humble example, the relation of resemblance. People who enjoy seeing a clever argument done in a few strokes have always valued this chapter.

Finally, readers appreciate how the chapter connects. It ties together earlier discussion of what we know, in the account of things and truths, with the coming discussion of how we know general truths, and it hints that the world of universals will solve the puzzle of knowledge not gained by experience. That sense of a plan unfolding gives the book momentum.

Many readers also value what the chapter does for the ordinary words they use every day. After reading it, a term like justice, or a phrase like to the left of, no longer feels like a throwaway. You begin to notice that every sentence you speak is full of general terms, and that you understand them without effort. Russell makes that quiet daily miracle visible, and readers often say the world looks a little richer afterwards.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
The main pushback comes from nominalists, who hold that only individual things exist and that general words are simply labels we apply to groups of similar things. They think Russell has multiplied entities beyond necessity. William of Ockham's old maxim, that entities should not be multiplied without need, is the usual weapon. On this view, Russell takes a fact about language, that we use general terms, and turns it into a population of mysterious objects. Quine and Goodman pressed this objection in the twentieth century, and their scepticism about abstract entities was widely shared.

The resemblance argument has been challenged directly. Some nominalists respond that resemblance does not need to be a universal; they say it is a primitive fact about the individual things, or that an endless regress of resemblances is harmless. Others argue that the argument assumes what it is meant to prove, that anything which holds between many pairs must be a thing in its own right. Frank Ramsey made a related point, saying that the supposed difference between names for particulars and words for universals is a matter of grammar, not of real kinds of being.

Wittgenstein, in his later philosophy, challenged the whole demand for something common to all cases. In his remarks on family resemblance, he argued that things we call by one word, like games, need not share a single essence. This undercuts the Platonic picture that Russell defends, in which each general word corresponds to one shared form.

Empiricists object to the epistemology. If universals exist outside space and time, how can we know them? We have no senses by which to meet a timeless object, and critics say the chapter gestures at the problem without solving it. This worry is sometimes put as a question about how Platonists can explain our contact with entities that cannot cause anything.

There are also complaints about the notion of subsistence. Critics find the distinction between being and existence an evasion, a way of having things both ways, and even sympathetic readers find it hard to say what it adds. Russell himself later became uneasy with some of this language.

Lastly, a more general objection holds that the chapter is simply too quick, covering centuries of dispute in a few pages and dismissing great philosophers in a sentence. That is an unavoidable cost of a popular book, and Russell would likely have said so himself.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
The problem of universals is among the oldest in philosophy, and this chapter is a short, vivid statement of one side of it. The realist side descends from Plato and runs through the medieval realists, such as Anselm, and later through the rationalists of the seventeenth century. The nominalist and conceptualist side runs from Ockham through Locke, Berkeley and Hume. Russell's chapter is explicitly an effort to reopen the case that the empiricists had closed, and he says that here the rationalists appear to have been in the right as against the empiricists.

That is a striking admission, because Russell is usually counted among the empiricists. The book as a whole is a blend, and this chapter shows its rationalist streak. It leads directly into the next chapter, on how we know universals, and from there to the claim that some knowledge, such as logic and arithmetic, is independent of experience. In that way the chapter is a hinge in the book's argument, answering the problem of a priori knowledge that the previous chapters left hanging.

In the larger picture, the chapter links to the revival of Platonism in the philosophy of mathematics, represented by Frege and Gödel, and to contemporary metaphysics, where the debate between realists and nominalists, with its newer options such as tropes and resemblance classes, is still very much alive. Science also supplies a modern angle: when physicists speak of laws that hold everywhere, they seem to rely on something like universals, and Armstrong's later work made this the centrepiece of his realism.

Compare it with the Platonic dialogues themselves, where the forms are presented with myth and poetry, or with Aristotle's more earthy view that universals exist only in the things that have them. Russell's version sits between mathematical rigour and Platonic enthusiasm, and it is more argumentative than either.

Why read it now? Because it asks what it means for general truths to be real, a question that comes up whenever we ask whether mathematics is discovered or invented, whether moral facts are objective, or whether categories like species and justice carve nature at its joints. The chapter will not settle those questions. But it gives a clear, memorable and spirited account of one answer, and it shows how a good argument can start from nothing more than a city map.

essays.title: On Intuitive Knowledge
essays.author: Bertrand Russell
essays.epigraph: All our knowledge of truths depends upon our intuitive knowledge; it is therefore important to consider the nature and scope of such knowledge.
essays.keyContext: This short chapter comes from Bertrand Russell's little book The Problems of Philosophy, published in 1912 and still one of the most widely read introductions to the subject. Russell was around forty, a leading logician who had just been working on the enormous Principia Mathematica with Alfred North Whitehead, and he wrote the book quickly, for ordinary readers rather than specialists. The chapter takes up a question every thinking person eventually bumps into. We feel we should be able to give reasons for what we believe. But reasons rest on other reasons, so where does the chain stop? Russell's answer is that it stops in things we simply see to be so: basic logical truths, simple arithmetic, what our senses show us right now, and our clear memories. He calls these self-evident, and then makes the interesting move of admitting that self-evidence comes in degrees and can sometimes mislead us. It is a quiet, careful chapter about what our knowledge is built on.
paragraphs: There is a common impression that everything that we believe ought to be capable of proof, or at least of being shown to be highly probable. It is felt by many that a belief for which no reason can be given is an unreasonable belief. In the main, this view is just. Almost all our common beliefs are either inferred, or capable of being inferred, from other beliefs which may be regarded as giving the reason for them. As a rule, the reason has been forgotten, or has even never been consciously present to our minds. Few of us ever ask ourselves, for example, what reason there is to suppose the food we are just going to eat will not turn out to be poison. Yet we feel, when challenged, that a perfectly good reason could be found, even if we are not ready with it at the moment. And in this belief we are usually justified.

But let us imagine some insistent Socrates, who, whatever reason we give him, continues to demand a reason for the reason. We must sooner or later, and probably before very long, be driven to a point where we cannot find any further reason, and where it becomes almost certain that no further reason is even theoretically discoverable. Starting with the common beliefs of daily life, we can be driven back from point to point, until we come to some general principle, or some instance of a general principle, which seems luminously evident, and is not itself capable of being deduced from anything more evident. In most questions of daily life, such as whether our food is likely to be nourishing and not poisonous, we shall be driven back to the inductive principle, which we discussed in Chapter VI. But beyond that, there seems to be no further regress. The principle itself is constantly used in our reasoning, sometimes consciously, sometimes unconsciously; but there is no reasoning which, starting from some simpler self-evident principle, leads us to the principle of induction as its conclusion. And the same holds for other logical principles. Their truth is evident to us, and we employ them in constructing demonstrations; but they themselves, or at least some of them, are incapable of demonstration.

Self-evidence, however, is not confined to those among general principles which are incapable of proof. When a certain number of logical principles have been admitted, the rest can be deduced from them; but the propositions deduced are often just as self-evident as those that were assumed without proof. All arithmetic, moreover, can be deduced from the general principles of logic, yet the simple propositions of arithmetic, such as “two and two are four,” are just as self-evident as the principles of logic.
It would seem, also, though this is more disputable, that there are some self-evident ethical principles, such as “we ought to pursue what is good.”

It should be observed that, in all cases of general principles, particular instances, dealing with familiar things, are more evident than the general principle. For example, the law of contradiction states that nothing can both have a certain property and not have it. This is evident as soon as it is understood, but it is not so evident as that a particular rose which we see cannot be both red and not red. (It is of course possible that parts of the rose may be red and parts not red, or that the rose may be of a shade of pink which we hardly know whether to call red or not; but in the former case it is plain that the rose as a whole is not red, while in the latter case the answer is theoretically definite as soon as we have decided on a precise definition of “red.”) It is usually through particular instances that we come to be able to see the general principle. Only those who are practised in dealing with abstractions can readily grasp a general principle without the help of instances.

In addition to general principles, the other kind of self-evident truths are those immediately derived from sensation. We will call such truths “truths of perception,” and the judgements expressing them we will call “judgements of perception.” But here a certain amount of care is required in getting at the precise nature of the truths that are self-evident. The actual sense-data are neither true nor false. A particular patch of colour which I see, for example, simply exists: it is not the sort of thing that is true or false. It is true that there is such a patch, true that it has a certain shape and degree of brightness, true that it is surrounded by certain other colours. But the patch itself, like everything else in the world of sense, is of a radically different kind from the things that are true or false, and therefore cannot properly be said to be true. Thus whatever self-evident truths may be obtained from our senses must be different from the sense-data from which they are obtained.

It would seem that there are two kinds of self-evident truths of perception, though perhaps in the last analysis the two kinds may coalesce. First, there is the kind which simply asserts the existence of the sense-datum, without in any way analysing it. We see a patch of red, and we judge “there is such-and-such a patch of red,” or more strictly “there is that”; this is one kind of intuitive judgement of perception. The other kind arises when the object of sense is complex, and we subject it to some degree of analysis. If, for instance, we see a “round” patch of red, we may judge “that patch of red is round.” This is again a judgement of perception, but it differs from our previous kind. In our present kind we have a single sense-datum which has both colour and shape: the colour is red and the shape is round. Our judgement analyses the datum into colour and shape, and then recombines them by stating that the red colour is round in shape. Another example of this kind of judgement is “this is to the right of that,” where “this” and “that” are seen simultaneously. In this kind of judgement the sense-datum contains constituents which have some relation to each other, and the judgement asserts that these constituents have this relation.

Another class of intuitive judgements, analogous to those of sense and yet quite distinct from them, are judgements of “memory.” There is some danger of confusion as to the nature of memory, owing to the fact that memory of an object is apt to be accompanied by an image of the object, and yet the image cannot be what constitutes memory. This is easily seen by merely noticing that the image is in the present, whereas what is remembered is known to be in the past. Moreover, we are certainly able to some extent to compare our image with the object remembered, so that we often know, within somewhat wide limits, how far our image is accurate; but this would be impossible, unless the object, as opposed to the image, were in some way before the mind. Thus the essence of memory is not constituted by the image, but by having immediately before the mind an object which is recognized as past. But for the fact of memory in this sense, we should not know that there ever was a past at all, nor should we be able to understand the word “past,” any more than a man born blind can understand the word “light.” Thus there must be intuitive judgements of memory, and it is upon them, ultimately, that all our knowledge of the past depends.

The case of memory, however, raises a difficulty, for it is notoriously fallacious, and thus throws doubt on the trustworthiness of intuitive judgements in general. This difficulty is no light one. But let us first narrow its scope as far as possible. Broadly speaking, memory is trustworthy in proportion to the vividness of the experience and to its nearness in time. If the house next door was struck by lightning half a minute ago, my memory of what I saw and heard will be so reliable that it would be preposterous to doubt whether there had been a flash at all. And the same applies to less vivid experiences, so long as they are recent. I am absolutely certain that half a minute ago I was sitting in the same chair in which I am sitting now. Going backward over the day, I find things of which I am quite certain, other things of which I am almost certain, other things of which I can become certain by thought and by calling up attendant circumstances, and some things of which I am by no means certain. I am quite certain that I ate my breakfast this morning, but if I were as indifferent to my breakfast as a philosopher should be, I should be doubtful. As to the conversation at breakfast, I can recall some of it easily, some with an effort, some only with a large element of doubt, and some not at all. Thus there is a continual gradation in the degree of self-evidence of what I remember, and a corresponding gradation in the trustworthiness of my memory.

Thus the first answer to the difficulty of fallacious memory is to say that memory has degrees of self-evidence, and that these correspond to the degrees of its trustworthiness, reaching a limit of perfect self-evidence and perfect trustworthiness in our memory of events which are recent and vivid.

It would seem, however, that there are cases of very firm belief in a memory which is wholly false. It is probable that, in these cases, what is really remembered, in the sense of being immediately before the mind, is something other than what is falsely believed in, though something generally associated with it. George IV is said to have at last believed that he was at the battle of Waterloo, because he had so often said that he was. In this case, what was immediately remembered was his repeated assertion; the belief in what he was asserting (if it existed) would be produced by association with the remembered assertion, and would therefore not be a genuine case of memory. It would seem that cases of fallacious memory can probably all be dealt with in this way, i.e. they can be shown to be not cases of memory in the strict sense at all.

One important point about self-evidence is made clear by the case of memory, and that is, that self-evidence has degrees: it is not a quality which is simply present or absent, but a quality which may be more or less present, in gradations ranging from absolute certainty down to an almost imperceptible faintness. Truths of perception and some of the principles of logic have the very highest degree of self-evidence; truths of immediate memory have an almost equally high degree. The inductive principle has less self-evidence than some of the other principles of logic, such as “what follows from a true premise must be true.” Memories have a diminishing self-evidence as they become remoter and fainter; the truths of logic and mathematics have (broadly speaking) less self-evidence as they become more complicated. Judgements of intrinsic ethical or aesthetic value are apt to have some self-evidence, but not much.

Degrees of self-evidence are important in the theory of knowledge, since, if propositions may (as seems likely) have some degree of self-evidence without being true, it will not be necessary to abandon all connection between self-evidence and truth, but merely to say that, where there is a conflict, the more self-evident proposition is to be retained and the less self-evident rejected.

It seems, however, highly probable that two different notions are combined in “self-evidence” as above explained; that one of them, which corresponds to the highest degree of self-evidence, is really an infallible guarantee of truth, while the other, which corresponds to all the other degrees, does not give an infallible guarantee, but only a greater or less presumption. This, however, is only a suggestion, which we cannot as yet develop further. After we have dealt with the nature of truth, we shall return to the subject of self-evidence, in connection with the distinction between knowledge and error.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
Start with the problem Russell is really facing. Most of us assume that a belief we cannot defend is a belief we should not hold. He begins by granting that this is mostly right. Nearly everything we believe could, in principle, be traced back to some other belief that supports it. His example is wonderfully ordinary: hardly any of us ask what reason we have for thinking the food in front of us is not poison, yet we feel that a good reason could be dug up if someone pressed us.

Then he introduces what he calls an insistent Socrates, a questioner who keeps asking for the reason behind the reason. This is the heart of the chapter, and it is something every child does to every parent. Why? Because. Why? Because. Russell's point is that the chain cannot go on forever. Sooner or later you reach a belief for which no further reason can be given, and not because you are lazy, but because there is nothing more basic to appeal to. In everyday life, he says, we are usually driven back to the principle of induction, the assumption that the future will resemble the past, which he had discussed earlier in the book. Nothing simpler stands behind it. We use it constantly, and we cannot prove it.

So what holds the whole structure up? Russell's answer is that some truths are self-evident. He means truths that, once we understand them, we simply see to be so. The first group is the basic principles of logic, such as the law of contradiction, which says that nothing can both have a property and lack it. The second group includes simple arithmetic: two and two are four. He adds, a little cautiously, that there may be self-evident ethical principles too, such as that we ought to pursue what is good, though he calls that more disputable.

The chapter then widens beyond abstract principles. He notes that particular cases are often more evident than the general rule. We are more certain that this particular rose cannot be both red and not red than we are of the abstract law that covers it. Next come what he calls truths of perception. Here he draws a careful line. The raw patch of colour you are looking at is neither true nor false; it simply exists. What can be true is your judgement about it, such as that there is a patch of red, or that it is round.

Finally he turns to memory, the shakiest of the foundations. His memorable example is George IV, who was said to have come to believe he had fought at Waterloo because he had told the story so often. Russell's explanation is subtle. What the king really remembered was his own repeated telling, and the false belief grew out of that. The lesson he draws is the chapter's most important idea: self-evidence is not an on-off switch. It runs from blazing certainty down to a faint glimmer, and when two beliefs conflict, we keep the more self-evident one. At its top level, he suggests, self-evidence may truly guarantee truth. Below that, it gives only a presumption, and that is a sober, honest place to stop.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
The great strength of this chapter is its honesty about where argument runs out. Many philosophers before Russell tried to prove everything from a single indisputable starting point. Russell simply says that you cannot prove everything, that you never could, and that this is no disaster. That is a mature and useful position. He also writes with a clarity that most philosophers never manage. The poisoned-food example, the insistent Socrates, the round patch of red and George IV at Waterloo each do real work. They make an abstract point feel like something you could check against your own mind.

His move toward degrees of self-evidence is the most original and defensible part. It rescues his theory from an obvious objection. If self-evidence guaranteed truth, then every false memory would refute the theory. By saying that self-evidence comes in grades, he can admit that we sometimes feel sure and are wrong, while still insisting that feeling sure is the best evidence we have. That is closer to how knowledge actually works for human beings than any all-or-nothing rule would be.

But the chapter has real weaknesses, and a fair reader should name them. The central difficulty is that self-evidence is a feeling, and feelings are not a very solid foundation. History is full of things that seemed self-evident to careful minds and turned out to be false. Euclid's geometry seemed beyond doubt until other geometries were found, and Russell himself discusses this in a neighbouring chapter. His own logic suffered a crushing blow when he discovered the paradox that bears his name, which showed that an apparently obvious principle about collections led to contradiction. A theory resting on what looks luminously evident has an awkward history to explain.

He half sees this, which is why he suggests, only as a tentative idea, that two different things may be hiding inside the word. One is a perfect guarantee, the other a mere presumption. But he does not say how we tell which one we are experiencing at any given moment, and that is exactly the question a critic would ask. If I cannot tell the infallible kind from the fallible kind from the inside, the distinction does me little good.

There is also a slightly dated feel in the vocabulary. Terms like sense-data and the whole picture of a mind confronting patches of colour belong to a particular moment in early analytic philosophy, and few philosophers today would describe perception that way. The ethical remark, that we simply see that we ought to pursue the good, is brief and hardly argued, and Russell himself later moved away from believing in objective ethical truths. Even so, as an introduction the chapter does what it sets out to do. It makes a hard problem vivid, it does not pretend to more than it can deliver, and it leaves the reader thinking.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
It is hard to point to one dramatic event caused by this particular chapter, because its influence is bound up with the book that contains it. The Problems of Philosophy was published in 1912 in the Home University Library, a series meant to bring serious learning to general readers, and it became one of the best-selling and longest-lived introductions to philosophy ever written. Generations of students, including many who never took another philosophy course, have met epistemology, the study of knowledge, through its pages. This chapter is a standard stop on that tour.

Within philosophy, the chapter belongs to a family of ideas about foundations. The picture it sketches, in which our knowledge rests on a small base of directly evident truths and everything else is built upward by inference, is known as foundationalism. It has been the dominant way of thinking about knowledge for much of the history of Western philosophy, from Descartes onward, and Russell gave it one of its clearest twentieth-century statements. Later philosophers spent decades arguing about whether such a base exists, whether it can be described without circularity, and what to do about the fallibility Russell admits. Much of the discussion of knowledge in the following century can be read as a conversation with, or a rebellion against, the picture found here.

The chapter also helped fix a way of talking. Russell's term sense-data, his distinction between the raw datum and the judgement we make about it, and his careful separation of what is merely there from what can be true or false, were absorbed into the working vocabulary of English-language philosophy for a good while. His student Ludwig Wittgenstein, and later figures such as A. J. Ayer, worked within or against these ideas. Ayer's famous book Language, Truth and Logic is unthinkable without this tradition.

On Russell's own career, the book was a bridge. He was already known among specialists as a logician. This little volume, written quickly and aimed at everyone, was the first step toward the public figure he later became, the author of popular books and essays, the campaigner, and the winner of the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1950. The habit of explaining hard things plainly, which this chapter shows so well, became his trademark.

As for how it is taught today, the chapter is often used as a gentle entry to the regress problem, the puzzle of how justification can ever come to rest. Teachers pair it with Descartes and with Hume, and then with modern critics of foundationalism, so that students can see both the attraction and the trouble of the idea.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
What readers have loved about Russell's book, and this chapter in particular, begins with the voice. He writes like a very clever friend who wants you to understand, not to be impressed. There is no fog of technical language. When a technical word appears, he stops to explain it. A reader who has never opened a philosophy book can follow the whole argument of this chapter from the first sentence to the last, and that is a rarer achievement than it sounds.

People also respond to how recognisable the problem is. Almost everyone has had the experience of being asked why they believe something and realizing, halfway through the answer, that they are not quite sure. Russell turns that uncomfortable moment into a topic. Readers often report a small shock of recognition when they meet the insistent Socrates, because they have been that questioner, or been questioned by one. The chapter takes an everyday feeling and shows that it points to a deep question.

Another source of affection is the tone of intellectual modesty. Russell was a formidable logician, and it would have been easy to write with swagger. Instead he repeatedly says that he is making a suggestion, that a point is disputable, or that something cannot yet be developed further. That candour builds trust. The reader feels they are being treated as an adult who can handle an unfinished answer, which is exactly what philosophy usually offers.

Fellow thinkers have admired the book as well. It is often named by working philosophers as the book that first drew them into the subject. Part of its charm is its confidence that these questions matter to everyone, not just to professors. Russell's belief that philosophy is for the general reader shines through, and later writers who tried to explain difficult ideas to a wide audience, in science as much as in philosophy, have often followed his example.

There is also real pleasure in the small, vivid touches.
