The decline of the birthrate in all civilized countries, which is pretty certain to continue, whatever economic system is adopted, suggests that, especially when the probable effects of the war are taken into account, the population of Western Europe is not likely to increase very much beyond its present level, and that of America is likely only to increase through immigration. Negroes may continue to increase in the tropics, but are not likely to be a serious menace to the white inhabitants of temperate regions. There remains, of course, the Yellow Peril; but by the time that begins to be serious it is quite likely that the birthrate will also have begun to decline among the races of Asia. If not, there are other means of dealing with this question; and in any case the whole matter is too conjectural to be set up seriously as a bar to our hopes. I conclude that, though no certain forecast is possible, there is not any valid reason for regarding the possible increase of population as a serious obstacle to Socialism.

Our discussion has led us to the belief that the communal ownership of land and capital, which constitutes the characteristic doctrine of Socialism and Anarchist Communism, is a necessary step toward the removal of the evils from which the world suffers at present and the creation of such a society as any humane man must wish to see realized. But, though a necessary step, Socialism alone is by no means sufficient. There are various forms of Socialism: the form in which the State is the employer, and all who work receive wages from it, involves dangers of tyranny and interference with progress which would make it, if possible, even worse than the present regime. On the other hand, Anarchism, which avoids the dangers of State Socialism, has dangers and difficulties of its own, which make it probable that, within any reasonable period of time, it could not last long even if it were established. Nevertheless, it remains an ideal to which we should wish to approach as nearly as possible, and which, in some distant age, we hope may be reached completely. Syndicalism shares many of the defects of Anarchism, and, like it, would prove unstable, since the need of a central government would make itself felt almost at once.

The system we have advocated is a form of Guild Socialism, leaning more, perhaps, towards Anarchism than the official Guildsman would wholly approve. It is in the matters that politicians usually ignore⁠—science and art, human relations, and the joy of life⁠—that Anarchism is strongest, and it is chiefly for the sake of these things that we included such more or less Anarchist proposals as the “vagabond’s wage.” It is by its effects outside economics and politics, at least as much as by effects inside them, that a social system should be judged. And if Socialism ever comes, it is only likely to prove beneficent if non-economic goods are valued and consciously pursued.

The world that we must seek is a world in which the creative spirit is alive, in which life is an adventure full of joy and hope, based rather upon the impulse to construct than upon the desire to retain what we possess or to seize what is possessed by others. It must be a world in which affection has free play, in which love is purged of the instinct for domination, in which cruelty and envy have been dispelled by happiness and the unfettered development of all the instincts that build up life and fill it with mental delights. Such a world is possible; it waits only for men to wish to create it.

Meantime, the world in which we exist has other aims. But it will pass away, burned up in the fire of its own hot passions; and from its ashes will spring a new and younger world, full of fresh hope, with the light of morning in its eyes.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
The chapter opens with a striking claim: in the daily lives of most people, fear plays a greater part than hope. We are busy guarding what others might take from us, rather than creating something good. Russell then says, in a short paragraph of one sentence, "It is not so that life should be lived." People whose lives are fruitful, he says, are inspired by hope and joy, they give affection freely, they work without jealousy, and in politics they aim to make the world less cruel. A life lived in this spirit, aimed at creating rather than possessing, has a fundamental happiness that bad luck cannot wholly rob.

But he does not stop with preaching, because he knows that sermons have not changed the world. The teaching of Christ, he notes, has been nominally accepted for centuries, yet those who follow it are still persecuted. So it is necessary to remove the causes of fear, to make a good life no longer an unsuccessful one in a worldly sense.

To do this he sorts the evils of life into three kinds: evils of physical nature, such as death, pain and the difficulty of getting food from the soil; evils of character, those that come from our own defects; and evils of power, those that come from being subject to the control of others. Science fights the first, education and free outlets for harmless impulses fight the second, and reform of political and economic institutions fights the third. He quotes the socialist thinker G. D. H. Cole to make a crucial point: poverty is the symptom, slavery the disease. The poor, Cole says, are not enslaved because they are poor, they are poor because they are enslaved.

The middle of the chapter lays out Russell's actual blueprint, which he sets down, as he says, without argument. Education should be compulsory to sixteen and free to twenty-one for anyone who wants it. Those who choose not to work should still be guaranteed a bare livelihood. The great majority, who will work, will do only a few hours a day, because science and the removal of wasteful competition and armaments make that possible. Industries will be governed by self-ruling guilds. Women's domestic work will be paid, giving wives economic independence. Children's costs will not fall on parents. Government and law will shrink to a minimum, though he argues that an international authority, strong enough to forbid the use of force by anyone else, is needed to secure peace.

Then he asks how this would affect the three evils. Character would improve, because economic fear and greed would no longer drive people to ruthlessness. Human relations would be freer, with marriages held together by affection alone. Physical evil would be lessened through healthier living and a freer science. He answers the worry about population briefly. The chapter closes with a hopeful image: the old world will be burned up in the fire of its own hot passions, and from its ashes a new world will spring, with the light of morning in its eyes.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
The chapter's greatest strength is its moral vision, stated with disarming simplicity. The opening paragraphs are beautifully done. The one-line paragraph, "It is not so that life should be lived," has the force of a quiet verdict. Russell's contrast between living by fear of loss and living by the impulse to create is a genuinely useful way of looking at both private life and politics, and it lifts the chapter above a mere policy list. The idea that a social system should be judged by non-economic goods, by science, art, human relations and the joy of life, is the real heart of the argument, and it is as fresh now as it was then.

The threefold division of evils is also an elegant bit of analysis. It gives the reader a map for sorting problems, and it shows why no single remedy, whether science, education or politics, can do everything. Quoting Cole's line that poverty is the symptom and slavery the disease is a shrewd choice, because it relocates the problem from having too little to having too little control, a shift that shaped much modern thinking about dignity at work.

Several of the practical proposals look surprisingly prescient. Paid domestic work, free education through the university years, a guaranteed floor of livelihood, shorter working hours, and a cut in the waste of competition and armaments all became live political ideas in the following century. The remark that people paid for willingness to work, not just work performed, is close to the logic of salaried employment today.

But there are real weaknesses. The proposals are offered, as Russell admits, without argument, and a reader who wants to know how any of it would work is left unsatisfied. How would the guilds and Parliament really share power? Who would decide what counts as a necessary good, and who would bear the cost if too few people chose to work? Russell's confidence on these points often rests on a hope that human nature will behave well once the pressure of economic fear is lifted. That may be too sunny.

The device of money that expires after a year is ingenious but a little fanciful, and the long run of administrative details in the middle sags compared with the rousing opening and close. The prose can drift into the manner of a committee report. There are also passages that have dated badly. The phrase about an international force for protection against uncivilized races reflects the colonial assumptions of its time, and the brief mention of the feebleminded uses the vocabulary of an era of eugenics that we now find troubling. And the ending, with its fire and ashes and morning light, is stirring but somewhat rhetorical, a poetic flourish in place of an argument. It is the weakest kind of ending for a rationalist, yet it is also what gives the chapter its emotional lift.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
The chapter's direct political influence was limited, but real in its way. Proposed Roads to Freedom was widely read on the British left after the First World War, and its closing chapter gave guild socialism, the movement for worker self-government of industry, one of its more attractive literary advocates. Guild socialism faded in the 1920s, overtaken by the rise of the Labour Party's more orthodox state-oriented approach, by the Russian Revolution's example, and by the movement's own internal splits. So the specific system never took root.

The influence of the ideas is easier to trace. The notion that education should be free through the university years and available to all who want it became a defining demand of the twentieth-century welfare state. The ideal of reducing the hours of work as productivity rises, an idea Russell would return to in his later essay In Praise of Idleness in 1932, fed into long debates about leisure and the working week. The thought that basic necessities might be guaranteed to everyone, so that no one is driven by destitution, is an ancestor of modern proposals for a basic income. The idea of economic independence for women through paid domestic work belongs to the long history of feminist argument about unpaid labour.

On international affairs, his sketch of a single authority strong enough to make all private use of force by states illegal anticipates the hopes that gathered around the League of Nations and later the United Nations. Russell himself pressed for world government after the atomic bomb, and his campaigns against nuclear weapons in the 1950s and 1960s grew from the same conviction expressed here: that peace requires an authority above nations.

On Russell's career, the chapter helped to define his public persona. The man who wrote it was soon to be jailed for his pacifism, and later became a leading voice of conscience on war, nuclear weapons, sexual morality and education. The earnest, hopeful moral voice that closes this chapter echoes through his later popular writing, and sits within the body of work for which he received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1950.

In classrooms, the chapter is read as a primary source on guild socialism and on the intellectual climate of the First World War, and also as an example of political philosophy that tries to describe a positive ideal rather than only criticise the present.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
What readers have loved most about this chapter is its hopefulness. Written in the middle of one of the bloodiest wars in history, it does not retreat into cynicism. It insists that life could be an adventure full of joy and hope, based on the impulse to construct rather than the desire to retain or seize. Many readers say they find in these pages a rare combination of realism about how bad things are and stubborn belief that they could be better. For people who are exhausted by despair in politics, that tone is a tonic.

They also love the generosity of Russell's vision of ordinary happiness. When he says that the serious happiness of most people, once their basic needs are met, depends on two things, their work and their human relations, he puts his finger on something almost everyone recognises. His picture of work as interesting, free and not excessive, and of relationships held together by affection rather than by property or fear, is touching because it describes what many of us already want from life. The sentence about people bowed down by forethought, no longer capable of lighthearted gaiety, hits home for anyone who has been worn down by worry about money.

Readers appreciate that the chapter takes the personal and the political together. Many political writings treat private life as an afterthought. Russell argues that systems of property shape the way we love, the way we raise children, and the way we fear one another. That link between economic arrangements and the quality of our inner lives has resonated with readers ever since.

There is also admiration for the clarity and calm of the prose. Russell has an ability to state large claims in short sentences without sounding grandiose. The short opening paragraph and the final image of a young world with morning in its eyes are justly remembered.

Finally, readers have valued the intellectual honesty of its structure. Russell does not just rail against the present. He sets out a specific picture, admits it can be disputed, and then tests it against the three evils he identified, asking in turn how it would affect physical hardship, character and power. Even readers who reject the conclusions often credit the method as a model of how to think constructively about politics.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
The first and most common objection is that the vision is utopian. Critics, then and now, have argued that Russell underestimates how stubborn human selfishness and scarcity are, and that a society without economic fear and ambition might lose the drive that produces wealth and invention. His own chapter raises this worry, asking whether people would become lazy and apathetic, but his answers are hopeful guesses rather than evidence. Economists and conservatives have long argued that markets, prices and property are not merely evils to be removed but tools for coordinating the knowledge and effort of millions.

A second objection is that the plan is thin on how it would actually be run. Who sets the pay for willingness to work? Who decides which trades are unpleasant enough to need higher pay? How would the guilds and Parliament be kept from fighting, or from merging into precisely the powerful bureaucracy Russell fears? Fellow socialists criticised guild socialism for just this vagueness, and the experience of Russia, which Russell himself visited in 1920 and found deeply disappointing, suggested that revolutionary regimes tend toward concentrated power, not the dispersed freedom he describes.

Third, there is the worry that he trusts too much in the effect of economic change on character. The idea that abolishing capitalism would transform human relations, ending jealousy and possessiveness in love, has struck many readers as naive. Psychology and history suggest that envy, pride and cruelty survive many changes in economic arrangement.

Fourth come the dated and uncomfortable passages. The language about uncivilized races and about the feebleminded reflects prejudices that Russell shared with many progressives of his day, and modern readers rightly wince. These phrases remind us that even an inspiring vision may carry assumptions we have since rejected.

A final criticism concerns the ending. Some readers find the rhetorical image of the old world burning in its own passions and a new one rising from its ashes uncomfortably close to the revolutionary romanticism that has justified much violence. Russell, a lifelong critic of violence, means something gentler, but the passage shows how easily hope for a new world can drift into apocalyptic language. And in a more practical vein, historians point out that the war's end and the postwar settlement brought not the morning he imagined but another generation of conflict, which makes the chapter's optimism look, in hindsight, poignant.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
This chapter belongs to the great tradition of utopian writing, in which authors imagine a better society in order to criticise the present one. The tradition runs from Plato's Republic and Thomas More's Utopia in 1516, through Edward Bellamy's Looking Backward in 1888 and William Morris's News from Nowhere in 1890, to H. G. Wells's A Modern Utopia in 1905. Compared with those, Russell's chapter is shorter and far less fictional. It contains no story and no fictional visitor, just an argument and a list. But it shares their purpose, which is to show that the world is not fixed and could be arranged differently.

It descends most directly from nineteenth-century socialism and anarchism: from Kropotkin's confidence in voluntary cooperation, from Morris's dream of work as joy, and from the guild socialists such as Cole who wanted workers to govern their own industries. It also draws on a liberal ethic of individual freedom that comes from John Stuart Mill, whose belief in the free development of each person's character runs through Russell's idea of evils of power and of the importance of creative impulse.

What descends from it? Modern arguments about the length of the working week, universal basic income, free higher education and the economic recognition of unpaid domestic labour all echo the proposals here. The faith in a global authority to prevent war points toward the post-1945 order. And in a larger sense, the book belongs to a line of liberal and democratic socialism that tried to combine economic fairness with personal liberty and that later found expression in post-war social democracy.

It is instructive to read it against the dystopias that followed. Yevgeny Zamyatin's We, Aldous Huxley's Brave New World and George Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four are, in a sense, nightmare versions of the very worries Russell raises: the state with too much power, the loss of freedom in the name of comfort. Russell's chapter and those novels belong together as hope and warning about the same tension.

Why read it today? Because its central question is still the right one: what is a society for? Russell's answer, that it should be judged by the creative, joyful and loving lives it makes possible rather than by output alone, still cuts against the grain of a world obsessed with growth and anxiety. You need not accept his guilds or his expiring money to find his central claim bracing. The measure of a good world is how little of life is spent in fear, and how much in making things worth having.

essays.title: On the Negative Spirit
essays.author: G. K. Chesterton
essays.epigraph: The human brain is a machine for coming to conclusions; if it cannot come to conclusions it is rusty.
essays.keyContext: In 1905 a thirty-one-year-old journalist named G. K. Chesterton published Heretics, a book that took on the leading thinkers of his day one at a time and argued with them like a friend arguing across a dinner table. This is the second chapter, and it is where he states his main complaint. Chesterton thought his age was wonderful at saying what is wrong and hopeless at saying what is right. Reformers talked about liberty, progress and education, but never said what people should be free for, progress toward, or educated into. To make the point, he compares a medieval monk, who at least dreams of perfect health, with the modern moralist, who only knows how to point at disease. His main example is the Norwegian playwright Henrik Ibsen, and he also takes a fond swipe at his friend H. G. Wells. The essay is funny, but it has a serious edge. It asks a question that still stings: what do you actually believe is good, and why?
paragraphs: Much has been said, and said truly, of the monkish morbidity, of the hysteria which has often gone with the visions of hermits or nuns. But let us never forget that this visionary religion is, in one sense, necessarily more wholesome than our modern and reasonable morality. It is more wholesome for this reason, that it can contemplate the idea of success or triumph in the hopeless fight towards the ethical ideal, in what Stevenson called, with his usual startling felicity, “the lost fight of virtue.” A modern morality, on the other hand, can only point with absolute conviction to the horrors that follow breaches of law; its only certainty is a certainty of ill. It can only point to imperfection. It has no perfection to point to. But the monk meditating upon Christ or Buddha has in his mind an image of perfect health, a thing of clear colours and clean air. He may contemplate this ideal wholeness and happiness far more than he ought; he may contemplate it to the neglect of exclusion of essential things; he may contemplate it until he has become a dreamer or a driveller; but still it is wholeness and happiness that he is contemplating. He may even go mad; but he is going mad for the love of sanity. But the modern student of ethics, even if he remains sane, remains sane from an insane dread of insanity.

The anchorite rolling on the stones in a frenzy of submission is a healthier person fundamentally than many a sober man in a silk hat who is walking down Cheapside. For many such are good only through a withering knowledge of evil. I am not at this moment claiming for the devotee anything more than this primary advantage, that though he may be making himself personally weak and miserable, he is still fixing his thoughts largely on gigantic strength and happiness, on a strength that has no limits, and a happiness that has no end. Doubtless there are other objections which can be urged without unreason against the influence of gods and visions in morality, whether in the cell or street. But this advantage the mystic morality must always have⁠—it is always jollier. A young man may keep himself from vice by continually thinking of disease. He may keep himself from it also by continually thinking of the Virgin Mary. There may be question about which method is the more reasonable, or even about which is the more efficient. But surely there can be no question about which is the more wholesome.

I remember a pamphlet by that able and sincere secularist, Mr. G. W. Foote, which contained a phrase sharply symbolizing and dividing these two methods. The pamphlet was called Beer and Bible, those two very noble things, all the nobler for a conjunction which Mr. Foote, in his stern old Puritan way, seemed to think sardonic, but which I confess to thinking appropriate and charming. I have not the work by me, but I remember that Mr. Foote dismissed very contemptuously any attempts to deal with the problem of strong drink by religious offices or intercessions, and said that a picture of a drunkard’s liver would be more efficacious in the matter of temperance than any prayer or praise. In that picturesque expression, it seems to me, is perfectly embodied the incurable morbidity of modern ethics. In that temple the lights are low, the crowds kneel, the solemn anthems are uplifted. But that upon the altar to which all men kneel is no longer the perfect flesh, the body and substance of the perfect man; it is still flesh, but it is diseased. It is the drunkard’s liver of the New Testament that is marred for us, which we take in remembrance of him.

Now, it is this great gap in modern ethics, the absence of vivid pictures of purity and spiritual triumph, which lies at the back of the real objection felt by so many sane men to the realistic literature of the nineteenth century. If any ordinary man ever said that he was horrified by the subjects discussed in Ibsen or Maupassant, or by the plain language in which they are spoken of, that ordinary man was lying. The average conversation of average men throughout the whole of modern civilization in every class or trade is such as Zola would never dream of printing. Nor is the habit of writing thus of these things a new habit. On the contrary, it is the Victorian prudery and silence which is new still, though it is already dying. The tradition of calling a spade a spade starts very early in our literature and comes down very late. But the truth is that the ordinary honest man, whatever vague account he may have given of his feelings, was not either disgusted or even annoyed at the candour of the moderns. What disgusted him, and very justly, was not the presence of a clear realism, but the absence of a clear idealism. Strong and genuine religious sentiment has never had any objection to realism; on the contrary, religion was the realistic thing, the brutal thing, the thing that called names. This is the great difference between some recent developments of Nonconformity and the great Puritanism of the seventeenth century. It was the whole point of the Puritans that they cared nothing for decency. Modern Nonconformist newspapers distinguish themselves by suppressing precisely those nouns and adjectives which the founders of Nonconformity distinguished themselves by flinging at kings and queens. But if it was a chief claim of religion that it spoke plainly about evil, it was the chief claim of all that it spoke plainly about good. The thing which is resented, and, as I think, rightly resented, in that great modern literature of which Ibsen is typical, is that while the eye that can perceive what are the wrong things increases in an uncanny and devouring clarity, the eye which sees what things are right is growing mistier and mistier every moment, till it goes almost blind with doubt. If we compare, let us say, the morality of the Divine Comedy with the morality of Ibsen’s Ghosts, we shall see all that modern ethics have really done. No one, I imagine, will accuse the author of the Inferno of an Early Victorian prudishness or a Podsnapian optimism. But Dante describes three moral instruments⁠—Heaven, Purgatory, and Hell, the vision of perfection, the vision of improvement, and the vision of failure. Ibsen has only one⁠—Hell. It is often said, and with perfect truth, that no one could read a play like Ghosts and remain indifferent to the necessity of an ethical self-command. That is quite true, and the same is to be said of the most monstrous and material descriptions of the eternal fire. It is quite certain the realists like Zola do in one sense promote morality⁠—they promote it in the sense in which the hangman promotes it, in the sense in which the devil promotes it. But they only affect that small minority which will accept any virtue of courage. Most healthy people dismiss these moral dangers as they dismiss the possibility of bombs or microbes. Modern realists are indeed Terrorists, like the dynamiters; and they fail just as much in their effort to create a thrill. Both realists and dynamiters are well-meaning people engaged in the task, so obviously ultimately hopeless, of using science to promote morality.

I do not wish the reader to confuse me for a moment with those vague persons who imagine that Ibsen is what they call a pessimist. There are plenty of wholesome people in Ibsen, plenty of good people, plenty of happy people, plenty of examples of men acting wisely and things ending well. That is not my meaning. My meaning is that Ibsen has throughout, and does not disguise, a certain vagueness and a changing attitude as well as a doubting attitude towards what is really wisdom and virtue in this life⁠—a vagueness which contrasts very remarkably with the decisiveness with which he pounces on something which he perceives to be a root of evil, some convention, some deception, some ignorance. We know that the hero of Ghosts is mad, and we know why he is mad. We do also know that Dr. Stockman is sane; but we do not know why he is sane. Ibsen does not profess to know how virtue and happiness are brought about, in the sense that he professes to know how our modern sexual tragedies are brought about. Falsehood works ruin in The Pillars of Society, but truth works equal ruin in The Wild Duck. There are no cardinal virtues of Ibsenism. There is no ideal man of Ibsen. All this is not only admitted, but vaunted in the most valuable and thoughtful of all the eulogies upon Ibsen, Mr. Bernard Shaw’s “Quintessence of Ibsenism.” Mr. Shaw sums up Ibsen’s teaching in the phrase, “The golden rule is that there is no golden rule.” In his eyes this absence of an enduring and positive ideal, this absence of a permanent key to virtue, is the one great Ibsen merit. I am not discussing now with any fullness whether this is so or not. All I venture to point out, with an increased firmness, is that this omission, good or bad, does leave us face to face with the problem of a human consciousness filled with very definite images of evil, and with no definite image of good. To us light must be henceforward the dark thing⁠—the thing of which we cannot speak. To us, as to Milton’s devils in Pandemonium, it is darkness that is visible. The human race, according to religion, fell once, and in falling gained knowledge of good and of evil. Now we have fallen a second time, and only the knowledge of evil remains to us.

A great silent collapse, an enormous unspoken disappointment, has in our time fallen on our Northern civilization. All previous ages have sweated and been crucified in an attempt to realize what is really the right life, what was really the good man. A definite part of the modern world has come beyond question to the conclusion that there is no answer to these questions, that the most that we can do is to set up a few notice-boards at places of obvious danger, to warn men, for instance, against drinking themselves to death, or ignoring the mere existence of their neighbours. Ibsen is the first to return from the baffled hunt to bring us the tidings of great failure.

Every one of the popular modern phrases and ideals is a dodge in order to shirk the problem of what is good. We are fond of talking about “liberty”; that, as we talk of it, is a dodge to avoid discussing what is good. We are fond of talking about “progress”; that is a dodge to avoid discussing what is good. We are fond of talking about “education”; that is a dodge to avoid discussing what is good. The modern man says, “Let us leave all these arbitrary standards and embrace liberty.” This is, logically rendered, “Let us not decide what is good, but let it be considered good not to decide it.” He says, “Away with your old moral formulae; I am for progress.” This, logically stated, means, “Let us not settle what is good; but let us settle whether we are getting more of it.” He says, “Neither in religion nor morality, my friend, lie the hopes of the race, but in education.” This, clearly expressed, means, “We cannot decide what is good, but let us give it to our children.”

Mr. H. G. Wells, that exceedingly clear-sighted man, has pointed out in a recent work that this has happened in connection with economic questions. The old economists, he says, made generalizations, and they were (in Mr. Wells’s view) mostly wrong. But the new economists, he says, seem to have lost the power of making any generalizations at all. And they cover this incapacity with a general claim to be, in specific cases, regarded as “experts,” a claim “proper enough in a hairdresser or a fashionable physician, but indecent in a philosopher or a man of science.” But in spite of the refreshing rationality with which Mr. Wells has indicated this, it must also be said that he himself has fallen into the same enormous modern error. In the opening pages of that excellent book Mankind in the Making, he dismisses the ideals of art, religion, abstract morality, and the rest, and says that he is going to consider men in their chief function, the function of parenthood. He is going to discuss life as a “tissue of births.” He is not going to ask what will produce satisfactory saints or satisfactory heroes, but what will produce satisfactory fathers and mothers. The whole is set forward so sensibly that it is a few moments at least before the reader realises that it is another example of unconscious shirking. What is the good of begetting a man until we have settled what is the good of being a man? You are merely handing on to him a problem you dare not settle yourself. It is as if a man were asked, “What is the use of a hammer?” and answered, “To make hammers”; and when asked, “And of those hammers, what is the use?” answered, “To make hammers again.” Just as such a man would be perpetually putting off the question of the ultimate use of carpentry, so Mr. Wells and all the rest of us are by these phrases successfully putting off the question of the ultimate value of the human life.

The case of the general talk of “progress” is, indeed, an extreme one. As enunciated today, “progress” is simply a comparative of which we have not settled the superlative. We meet every ideal of religion, patriotism, beauty, or brute pleasure with the alternative ideal of progress⁠—that is to say, we meet every proposal of getting something that we know about, with an alternative proposal of getting a great deal more of nobody knows what. Progress, properly understood, has, indeed, a most dignified and legitimate meaning. But as used in opposition to precise moral ideals, it is ludicrous. So far from it being the truth that the ideal of progress is to be set against that of ethical or religious finality, the reverse is the truth. Nobody has any business to use the word “progress” unless he has a definite creed and a cast-iron code of morals. Nobody can be progressive without being doctrinal; I might almost say that nobody can be progressive without being infallible⁠—at any rate, without believing in some infallibility. For progress by its very name indicates a direction; and the moment we are in the least doubtful about the direction, we become in the same degree doubtful about the progress. Never perhaps since the beginning of the world has there been an age that had less right to use the word “progress” than we. In the Catholic twelfth century, in the philosophic eighteenth century, the direction may have been a good or a bad one, men may have differed more or less about how far they went, and in what direction, but about the direction they did in the main agree, and consequently they had the genuine sensation of progress. But it is precisely about the direction that we disagree. Whether the future excellence lies in more law or less law, in more liberty or less liberty; whether property will be finally concentrated or finally cut up; whether sexual passion will reach its sanest in an almost virgin intellectualism or in a full animal freedom; whether we should love everybody with Tolstoy, or spare nobody with Nietzsche;⁠—these are the things about which we are actually fighting most. It is not merely true that the age which has settled least what is progress is this “progressive” age. It is, moreover, true that the people who have settled least what is progress are the most “progressive” people in it. The ordinary mass, the men who have never troubled about progress, might be trusted perhaps to progress. The particular individuals who talk about progress would certainly fly to the four winds of heaven when the pistol-shot started the race. I do not, therefore, say that the word “progress” is unmeaning; I say it is unmeaning without the previous definition of a moral doctrine, and that it can only be applied to groups of persons who hold that doctrine in common. Progress is not an illegitimate word, but it is logically evident that it is illegitimate for us. It is a sacred word, a word which could only rightly be used by rigid believers and in the ages of faith.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
Chesterton opens with a deliberately shocking claim. Everyone has heard that the visions of hermits and nuns can tip into hysteria, and he grants it. But he says this visionary religion is, in one sense, healthier than our modern, sensible morality. His reason is about what the mind is looking at. The monk meditating on Christ or Buddha has in his head a picture of perfect health, "a thing of clear colours and clean air." He may stare at it too long and become a dreamer or even a driveller, but what he is staring at is wholeness and happiness. As Chesterton puts it, he may go mad, but he is "going mad for the love of sanity." The modern student of ethics, by contrast, may stay sane, but he does so "from an insane dread of insanity." The point is not that monks are right. It is that a person trying to be good by gazing at an ideal is in a different mental place from a person trying to be good by gazing at the wreckage of badness.

He then gives that idea a grotesque and memorable image. A secularist pamphleteer named G. W. Foote had written a pamphlet called Beer and Bible, and argued that a picture of a drunkard's liver would do more for temperance than any prayer. Chesterton says this perfectly captures the incurable morbidity of modern ethics. The altar of the modern temple no longer holds the perfect man, but a diseased body. It is, he says, "the drunkard's liver of the New Testament that is marred for us." It is a joke, a blasphemy and an argument all at once, which is the Chesterton specialty.

From there he turns to literature, and this is where the essay really gets going. Why did so many sane people dislike the realistic writers of the nineteenth century, such as Ibsen and Zola? Chesterton says it was not the frankness. Ordinary men, he says, talk in ways Zola would never print. What bothered them was not the presence of a clear realism but the absence of a clear idealism. Compare Dante, who gives us three moral instruments, Heaven, Purgatory and Hell, with Ibsen, who has only one. In Ibsen's Ghosts we know exactly why the hero is mad. In An Enemy of the People we know Dr. Stockman is sane, but not why. Evil is drawn in uncanny detail while goodness grows "mistier and mistier."

Finally Chesterton widens the lens. Modern slogans such as liberty, progress and education are, he says, dodges to avoid the question of what is good. He translates each one into plain English, and the translations are the heart of the essay. Even his friend Wells, in Mankind in the Making, proposes to study life as a tissue of births, but, Chesterton asks, what is the good of begetting a man until we have settled what is the good of being a man? Hence the title. The negative spirit is a mind that defines itself by what it refuses, and so never has to say what it wants.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
The great strength of this essay is the way Chesterton turns an abstract complaint into pictures you cannot forget. The drunkard's liver on the altar is one. The man answering "To make hammers" when asked the use of a hammer is another. His translations of the modern slogans are a small masterclass in comic logic. "Liberty" becomes "Let us not decide what is good, but let it be considered good not to decide it." That sentence does more work than a page of academic argument, and it is hard to read the word liberty in a political speech afterward without hearing it. His treatment of progress is similarly sharp. Progress, he says, is "a comparative of which we have not settled the superlative." A comparative is a word like "better." You cannot say something is getting better until you know what best would be. It is a real philosophical point delivered as a joke, and it holds up.

The prose also has a kind of generosity that makes the argument harder to resist. He calls Wells "that exceedingly clear-sighted man," credits Shaw with the best defense of Ibsen, and does not pretend that monastic hysteria never happened. He loses very little by conceding things.

But it is fair to say the essay is also uneven and, in places, unfair. The portrait of Ibsen is a caricature. Ibsen did not merely prosecute; plays like A Doll's House end with a person walking out of a door toward a self she has not yet met, and Brand is a demanding idealist if ever there was one. To say Ibsen has only Hell is clever, but it flattens him. Chesterton half admits as much when he insists he does not think Ibsen a pessimist, yet then lets the Hell-only line stand as the headline.

The central argument also contains a slippery step. Chesterton says the monk's morality is more wholesome, and he admits there may be a question about which method is more reasonable or more effective. But wholesome is not the same as true. A skeptic could say that a cheerful picture of perfection is comforting precisely because it may be false, and that a drunkard's liver is at least real. Chesterton does not really answer that here. He is arguing about psychology, not truth, and the essay sometimes lets you forget the difference.

There is also a certain amount of sweeping assertion, such as the claim that the twelfth century agreed about the direction of progress, which no medievalist would accept, and the comparison of realists to bomb-throwing anarchists, which is more a flourish than a point. And the essay, by design, never says what the good life actually is. It diagnoses a gap and walks away. That is satisfying as a provocation but incomplete as an argument.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
Taken on its own, "On the Negative Spirit" is not one of the famous pieces in English literature, and it is honest to say that its impact is mostly the impact of the book it sits in. Heretics was a notable success, and it cemented Chesterton's reputation as a public intellectual who could take on Shaw, Wells and Kipling in print without losing their friendship. It also put him on a clear path. A critic had remarked that it was all very well to attack other people's philosophies, but what was Chesterton's own? He answered with Orthodoxy in 1908, which is the positive half of the argument this chapter sets up. The famous story is that Orthodoxy exists because Heretics left a challenge hanging, and this chapter, with its relentless demand that people state what is good, is where the challenge is most pointed. Chesterton went on to become the leading lay Christian apologist in English, and he joined the Roman Catholic Church in 1922.

Beyond Chesterton's own career, the specific idea in this chapter, that talk of progress or freedom is empty without an account of the good, has a long afterlife. It echoes through later critics of modern moral thinking. C. S. Lewis, who credited Chesterton with helping to change his mind about Christianity, argued in The Abolition of Man that a society can lose the ability to speak about real goodness while still demanding it. The philosopher Alasdair MacIntyre, in After Virtue, made a much more technical case that modern moral language is a set of fragments from a lost shared purpose. These are different writers with different methods, and it would be wrong to say Chesterton caused them, but the family resemblance is real.

In ordinary culture the legacy is less a particular quotation than a habit of mind. When someone asks a politician what, exactly, they mean by "progress," or points out that "freedom" is being used without saying freedom to do what, they are doing a very Chestertonian thing, whether or not they know it. The chapter is also a favourite among readers of Chesterton who come to him through his detective stories or his Christian writing, and it is read in societies devoted to his work.

It is not a standard classroom text. It is more often encountered as a chapter in Heretics or in anthologies of Chesterton's essays than as a set piece in literature courses, and there is little in the way of famous adaptation. Its influence is quiet and intellectual rather than loud.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
People have enjoyed this essay first of all because it is fun. Chesterton wrote with a kind of exuberance that does not wear off. He can describe a man answering "To make hammers" and make you laugh and wince in the same second. Readers who disagree with him completely often say that he is the most enjoyable person to disagree with, because he plays fair about his opponents' virtues and has no malice in him. That tone, argument as a game between friends, is a large part of why he has stayed in print.

Readers have also loved the sharpness of the central diagnosis. Many people have felt, without being able to say it, that public conversation is very good at denouncing and very poor at proposing. Chesterton gave that feeling a shape and a name more than a century ago. The line about the modern mind having "a great silent collapse, an enormous unspoken disappointment" resonates with readers who feel a similar weariness, whatever their politics. The essay is not a complaint that moderns are wicked. It is a charge that they are vague about the very thing they claim to care about most, and readers recognise that charge in themselves.

Writers have admired him too. Jorge Luis Borges was a lifelong enthusiast of Chesterton's essays and stories, and W. H. Auden praised him. C. S. Lewis, as noted, said the book that most helped him was Chesterton's The Everlasting Man. Admirers often say that what they love is how he makes the commonplace look strange: a hammer, a drunkard's liver, a hairdresser.

For religious readers the essay is a joy because it defends the beauty of belief without sneering at doubt. For nonbelieving readers it offers something rarer, which is a challenge made with enough charm that you cannot dismiss it. Even critics who think he is wrong tend to concede that he asks the right question: what are you for? It is a question that applies equally to a monk, a reformer, a scientist or a social media user, and that breadth is part of why people return to the chapter.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
The most common criticism is that Chesterton mistakes style for proof. His method is paradox: take a familiar idea, turn it upside down, and let the surprise do the persuading. That works wonderfully on the page, but critics have long said that an epigram is not an argument. The statement that the monk is sane in his madness while the modern moralist is mad in his sanity is delightful, but it is not demonstrated. Readers who admire him sometimes admit that his best lines persuade them before they have checked whether they are true.

A second objection concerns his picture of the past. Chesterton often paints the Middle Ages, or the age of faith, as a time of shared direction and clear ideals, and sets it against a confused modern world. Historians would say that medieval Europe was full of heresy, war and argument about what was good, and that real moral progress, such as the end of slavery or the expansion of voting rights, has happened in modern societies without a single agreed creed. Critics have also noted that his demand for a clear doctrine could be used to justify dogmatism: if only the certain can be progressive, what happens to those who disagree?

A third complaint is aimed at his treatment of his targets. Ibsen's defenders have argued that Chesterton reads him unfairly, as we have seen. Secularists and rationalists of his own day, such as those who published and read Foote, would have said that preferring a picture of a diseased liver to a prayer is not morbid but honest. They would add that a morality based on evidence has no need to apologise for pointing at consequences.

There is also a moral and political shadow over Chesterton's reputation that readers should be aware of. His later writings on Jews, in particular, have been criticised as antisemitic, and scholars and admirers still argue about how serious the problem is. This chapter is not where that appears, but anyone encountering Chesterton should know that his reputation is complicated.

Finally, some readers simply find him exhausting. The constant stream of reversals and flourishes can feel like being talked at by a brilliant person who will not let you finish a sentence. Even sympathetic readers admit that over a whole book the technique can grow wearing, and that the chapter offers more diagnosis than cure.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
Chesterton belongs to a particular moment, the Edwardian decade, when English journalism was full of brilliant men arguing in public about everything. Shaw, Wells, Belloc, Kipling and Chesterton himself were all, in different ways, essayists and prophets, and Heretics is a portrait gallery of that debate drawn by one of its participants. Behind them stands a longer tradition of English moral critics, from Thomas Carlyle and John Ruskin to John Henry Newman and Matthew Arnold. Arnold's Culture and Anarchy, written in 1869, also worried that the modern world was full of machinery and short of aims. Chesterton's weapon, the paradox, comes from Oscar Wilde, and there is a nice irony in his using Wilde's own tool against the fashionable skepticism that Wilde's heirs represented.

What descends from it? Most directly, Chesterton's own Orthodoxy and the Christian apologetics of Lewis and others. More broadly, a strain of cultural criticism that suspects modern talk of freedom and progress of being hollow, running through writers as different as MacIntyre and many conservative columnists. It is interesting to set the chapter beside W. B. Yeats's famous lines from "The Second Coming," written in 1919, that "the best lack all conviction, while the worst are full of passionate intensity." That is almost the same diagnosis after the First World War, delivered with tragic force rather than comic energy. Chesterton saw the same thing in 1905 and treated it as a problem of philosophy and, a little, of manners.

It is also a useful companion to the nineteenth-century realists he attacks. Read Ibsen's Ghosts first, and then this chapter, and you can feel what Chesterton is reacting to and where he is being unfair. That is a good way to read it: as one half of a conversation.

Why read it now? Partly for the pleasure of watching an unusually joyful mind work. But also because the negative spirit has not gone away. It is easier than ever to say what is wrong, with a thousand voices to say it, and harder than ever to say what we are for. Whether you end up agreeing with Chesterton's answer or not, his question is one worth being asked, and the chapter asks it in about fifteen minutes of lively, funny, provocative reading.

essays.title: On Mr. Rudyard Kipling and Making the World Small
essays.author: G. K. Chesterton
essays.epigraph: There is no such thing on earth as an uninteresting subject; the only thing that can exist is an uninterested person.
essays.keyContext: This is the third chapter of Heretics, the 1905 book in which G. K. Chesterton argued, affectionately and ferociously, with the famous writers of his day. Its subject is Rudyard Kipling, the most celebrated English storyteller and poet of the British Empire. The time matters. The Boer War in South Africa had ended only three years before, and Chesterton had opposed it, while Kipling had cheered it on. You might expect an attack. Instead Chesterton begins with a surprising defense of boredom and of ordinary things, praises Kipling for finding poetry in steam engines and slang, and only then reaches his objection. Kipling, he says, admires England without loving her, because he has seen too much of the world to belong to any piece of it. The essay turns on a paradox. Travelling everywhere can make the world feel smaller, and staying put can make it feel enormous. It is a defense of loving one place, written by a man who clearly loved his own.
paragraphs: There is no such thing on earth as an uninteresting subject; the only thing that can exist is an uninterested person. Nothing is more keenly required than a defence of bores. When Byron divided humanity into the bores and bored, he omitted to notice that the higher qualities exist entirely in the bores, the lower qualities in the bored, among whom he counted himself. The bore, by his starry enthusiasm, his solemn happiness, may, in some sense, have proved himself poetical. The bored has certainly proved himself prosaic.

We might, no doubt, find it a nuisance to count all the blades of grass or all the leaves of the trees; but this would not be because of our boldness or gaiety, but because of our lack of boldness and gaiety. The bore would go onward, bold and gay, and find the blades of grass as splendid as the swords of an army. The bore is stronger and more joyous than we are; he is a demigod⁠—nay, he is a god. For it is the gods who do not tire of the iteration of things; to them the nightfall is always new, and the last rose as red as the first.

The sense that everything is poetical is a thing solid and absolute; it is not a mere matter of phraseology or persuasion. It is not merely true, it is ascertainable. Men may be challenged to deny it; men may be challenged to mention anything that is not a matter of poetry. I remember a long time ago a sensible subeditor coming up to me with a book in his hand, called “Mr. Smith,” or “The Smith Family,” or some such thing. He said, “Well, you won’t get any of your damned mysticism out of this,” or words to that effect. I am happy to say that I undeceived him; but the victory was too obvious and easy. In most cases the name is unpoetical, although the fact is poetical. In the case of Smith, the name is so poetical that it must be an arduous and heroic matter for the man to live up to it. The name of Smith is the name of the one trade that even kings respected, it could claim half the glory of that arma virumque which all epics acclaimed. The spirit of the smithy is so close to the spirit of song that it has mixed in a million poems, and every blacksmith is a harmonious blacksmith.

Even the village children feel that in some dim way the smith is poetic, as the grocer and the cobbler are not poetic, when they feast on the dancing sparks and deafening blows in the cavern of that creative violence. The brute repose of Nature, the passionate cunning of man, the strongest of earthly metals, the wierdest of earthly elements, the unconquerable iron subdued by its only conqueror, the wheel and the ploughshare, the sword and the steam-hammer, the arraying of armies and the whole legend of arms, all these things are written, briefly indeed, but quite legibly, on the visiting-card of Mr. Smith. Yet our novelists call their hero “Aylmer Valence,” which means nothing, or “Vernon Raymond,” which means nothing, when it is in their power to give him this sacred name of Smith⁠—this name made of iron and flame. It would be very natural if a certain hauteur, a certain carriage of the head, a certain curl of the lip, distinguished everyone whose name is Smith. Perhaps it does; I trust so. Whoever else are parvenus, the Smiths are not parvenus. From the darkest dawn of history this clan has gone forth to battle; its trophies are on every hand; its name is everywhere; it is older than the nations, and its sign is the Hammer of Thor. But as I also remarked, it is not quite the usual case. It is common enough that common things should be poetical; it is not so common that common names should be poetical. In most cases it is the name that is the obstacle. A great many people talk as if this claim of ours, that all things are poetical, were a mere literary ingenuity, a play on words. Precisely the contrary is true. It is the idea that some things are not poetical which is literary, which is a mere product of words. The word “signal-box” is unpoetical. But the thing signal-box is not unpoetical; it is a place where men, in an agony of vigilance, light bloodred and sea-green fires to keep other men from death. That is the plain, genuine description of what it is; the prose only comes in with what it is called. The word “pillar-box” is unpoetical. But the thing pillar-box is not unpoetical; it is the place to which friends and lovers commit their messages, conscious that when they have done so they are sacred, and not to be touched, not only by others, but even (religious touch!) by themselves. That red turret is one of the last of the temples. Posting a letter and getting married are among the few things left that are entirely romantic; for to be entirely romantic a thing must be irrevocable. We think a pillar-box prosaic, because there is no rhyme to it. We think a pillar-box unpoetical, because we have never seen it in a poem. But the bold fact is entirely on the side of poetry. A signal-box is only called a signal-box; it is a house of life and death. A pillar-box is only called a pillar-box; it is a sanctuary of human words. If you think the name of “Smith” prosaic, it is not because you are practical and sensible; it is because you are too much affected with literary refinements. The name shouts poetry at you. If you think of it otherwise, it is because you are steeped and sodden with verbal reminiscences, because you remember everything in Punch or Comic Cuts about Mr. Smith being drunk or Mr. Smith being henpecked. All these things were given to you poetical. It is only by a long and elaborate process of literary effort that you have made them prosaic.

Now, the first and fairest thing to say about Rudyard Kipling is that he has borne a brilliant part in thus recovering the lost provinces of poetry. He has not been frightened by that brutal materialistic air which clings only to words; he has pierced through to the romantic, imaginative matter of the things themselves. He has perceived the significance and philosophy of steam and of slang. Steam may be, if you like, a dirty byproduct of science. Slang may be, if you like, a dirty byproduct of language. But at least he has been among the few who saw the divine parentage of these things, and knew that where there is smoke there is fire⁠—that is, that wherever there is the foulest of things, there also is the purest. Above all, he has had something to say, a definite view of things to utter, and that always means that a man is fearless and faces everything. For the moment we have a view of the universe, we possess it.

Now, the message of Rudyard Kipling, that upon which he has really concentrated, is the only thing worth worrying about in him or in any other man. He has often written bad poetry, like Wordsworth. He has often said silly things, like Plato. He has often given way to mere political hysteria, like Gladstone. But no one can reasonably doubt that he means steadily and sincerely to say something, and the only serious question is, What is that which he has tried to say? Perhaps the best way of stating this fairly will be to begin with that element which has been most insisted by himself and by his opponents⁠—I mean his interest in militarism. But when we are seeking for the real merits of a man it is unwise to go to his enemies, and much more foolish to go to himself.

Now, Mr. Kipling is certainly wrong in his worship of militarism, but his opponents are, generally speaking, quite as wrong as he. The evil of militarism is not that it shows certain men to be fierce and haughty and excessively warlike. The evil of militarism is that it shows most men to be tame and timid and excessively peaceable. The professional soldier gains more and more power as the general courage of a community declines. Thus the Pretorian guard became more and more important in Rome as Rome became more and more luxurious and feeble. The military man gains the civil power in proportion as the civilian loses the military virtues. And as it was in ancient Rome so it is in contemporary Europe. There never was a time when nations were more militarist. There never was a time when men were less brave. All ages and all epics have sung of arms and the man; but we have effected simultaneously the deterioration of the man and the fantastic perfection of the arms. Militarism demonstrated the decadence of Rome, and it demonstrates the decadence of Prussia.

And unconsciously Mr. Kipling has proved this, and proved it admirably. For in so far as his work is earnestly understood the military trade does not by any means emerge as the most important or attractive. He has not written so well about soldiers as he has about railway men or bridge builders, or even journalists. The fact is that what attracts Mr. Kipling to militarism is not the idea of courage, but the idea of discipline. There was far more courage to the square mile in the Middle Ages, when no king had a standing army, but every man had a bow or sword. But the fascination of the standing army upon Mr. Kipling is not courage, which scarcely interests him, but discipline, which is, when all is said and done, his primary theme. The modern army is not a miracle of courage; it has not enough opportunities, owing to the cowardice of everybody else. But it is really a miracle of organization, and that is the truly Kiplingite ideal. Kipling’s subject is not that valour which properly belongs to war, but that interdependence and efficiency which belongs quite as much to engineers, or sailors, or mules, or railway engines. And thus it is that when he writes of engineers, or sailors, or mules, or steam-engines, he writes at his best. The real poetry, the “true romance” which Mr. Kipling has taught, is the romance of the division of labour and the discipline of all the trades. He sings the arts of peace much more accurately than the arts of war. And his main contention is vital and valuable. Everything is military in the sense that everything depends upon obedience. There is no perfectly epicurean corner; there is no perfectly irresponsible place. Everywhere men have made the way for us with sweat and submission. We may fling ourselves into a hammock in a fit of divine carelessness. But we are glad that the net-maker did not make the hammock in a fit of divine carelessness. We may jump upon a child’s rocking-horse for a joke. But we are glad that the carpenter did not leave the legs of it unglued for a joke. So far from having merely preached that a soldier cleaning his sidearm is to be adored because he is military, Kipling at his best and clearest has preached that the baker baking loaves and the tailor cutting coats is as military as anybody.

Being devoted to this multitudinous vision of duty, Mr. Kipling is naturally a cosmopolitan. He happens to find his examples in the British Empire, but almost any other empire would do as well, or, indeed, any other highly civilized country. That which he admires in the British army he would find even more apparent in the German army; that which he desires in the British police he would find flourishing, in the French police. The ideal of discipline is not the whole of life, but it is spread over the whole of the world. And the worship of it tends to confirm in Mr. Kipling a certain note of worldly wisdom, of the experience of the wanderer, which is one of the genuine charms of his best work.

The great gap in his mind is what may be roughly called the lack of patriotism⁠—that is to say, he lacks altogether the faculty of attaching himself to any cause or community finally and tragically; for all finality must be tragic. He admires England, but he does not love her; for we admire things with reasons, but love them without reasons. He admires England because she is strong, not because she is English. There is no harshness in saying this, for, to do him justice, he avows it with his usual picturesque candour. In a very interesting poem, he says that
“If England was what England seems”
—that is, weak and inefficient; if England were not what (as he believes) she is⁠—that is, powerful and practical⁠—
“How quick we’d chuck ’er! But she ain’t!”

He admits, that is, that his devotion is the result of a criticism, and this is quite enough to put it in another category altogether from the patriotism of the Boers, whom he hounded down in South Africa. In speaking of the really patriotic peoples, such as the Irish, he has some difficulty in keeping a shrill irritation out of his language. The frame of mind which he really describes with beauty and nobility is the frame of mind of the cosmopolitan man who has seen men and cities.
“For to admire and for to see, For to be’old this world so wide.”

He is a perfect master of that light melancholy with which a man looks back on having been the citizen of many communities, of that light melancholy with which a man looks back on having been the lover of many women. He is the philanderer of the nations. But a man may have learnt much about women in flirtations, and still be ignorant of first love; a man may have known as many lands as Ulysses, and still be ignorant of patriotism.

Mr. Rudyard Kipling has asked in a celebrated epigram what they can know of England who know England only. It is a far deeper and sharper question to ask, “What can they know of England who know only the world?” for the world does not include England any more than it includes the Church. The moment we care for anything deeply, the world⁠—that is, all the other miscellaneous interests⁠—becomes our enemy. Christians showed it when they talked of keeping one’s self “unspotted from the world;” but lovers talk of it just as much when they talk of the “world well lost.” Astronomically speaking, I understand that England is situated on the world; similarly, I suppose that the Church was a part of the world, and even the lovers inhabitants of that orb. But they all felt a certain truth⁠—the truth that the moment you love anything the world becomes your foe. Thus Mr. Kipling does certainly know the world; he is a man of the world, with all the narrowness that belongs to those imprisoned in that planet. He knows England as an intelligent English gentleman knows Venice. He has been to England a great many times; he has stopped there for long visits. But he does not belong to it, or to any place; and the proof of it is this, that he thinks of England as a place. The moment we are rooted in a place, the place vanishes. We live like a tree with the whole strength of the universe.

The globetrotter lives in a smaller world than the peasant. He is always breathing, an air of locality. London is a place, to be compared to Chicago; Chicago is a place, to be compared to Timbuktu. But Timbuktu is not a place, since there, at least, live men who regard it as the universe, and breathe, not an air of locality, but the winds of the world. The man in the saloon steamer has seen all the races of men, and he is thinking of the things that divide men⁠—diet, dress, decorum, rings in the nose as in Africa, or in the ears as in Europe, blue paint among the ancients, or red paint among the modern Britons. The man in the cabbage field has seen nothing at all; but he is thinking of the things that unite men⁠—hunger and babies, and the beauty of women, and the promise or menace of the sky. Mr. Kipling, with all his merits, is the globetrotter; he has not the patience to become part of anything. So great and genuine a man is not to be accused of a merely cynical cosmopolitanism; still, his cosmopolitanism is his weakness. That weakness is splendidly expressed in one of his finest poems, “The Sestina of the Tramp Royal,” in which a man declares that he can endure anything in the way of hunger or horror, but not permanent presence in one place. In this there is certainly danger. The more dead and dry and dusty a thing is the more it travels about; dust is like this and the thistledown and the High Commissioner in South Africa. Fertile things are somewhat heavier, like the heavy fruit trees on the pregnant mud of the Nile. In the heated idleness of youth we were all rather inclined to quarrel with the implication of that proverb which says that a rolling stone gathers no moss. We were inclined to ask, “Who wants to gather moss, except silly old ladies?” But for all that we begin to perceive that the proverb is right. The rolling stone rolls echoing from rock to rock; but the rolling stone is dead. The moss is silent because the moss is alive.

The truth is that exploration and enlargement make the world smaller. The telegraph and the steamboat make the world smaller. The telescope makes the world smaller; it is only the microscope that makes it larger. Before long the world will be cloven with a war between the telescopists and the microscopists. The first study large things and live in a small world; the second study small things and live in a large world. It is inspiriting without doubt to whizz in a motorcar round the earth, to feel Arabia as a whirl of sand or China as a flash of rice-fields. But Arabia is not a whirl of sand and China is not a flash of rice-fields. They are ancient civilizations with strange virtues buried like treasures. If we wish to understand them it must not be as tourists or inquirers, it must be with the loyalty of children and the great patience of poets. To conquer these places is to lose them. The man standing in his own kitchen-garden, with fairyland opening at the gate, is the man with large ideas. His mind creates distance; the motorcar stupidly destroys it. Moderns think of the earth as a globe, as something one can easily get round, the spirit of a schoolmistress. This is shown in the odd mistake perpetually made about Cecil Rhodes. His enemies say that he may have had large ideas, but he was a bad man. His friends say that he may have been a bad man, but he certainly had large ideas. The truth is that he was not a man essentially bad, he was a man of much geniality and many good intentions, but a man with singularly small views. There is nothing large about painting the map red; it is an innocent game for children. It is just as easy to think in continents as to think in cobblestones. The difficulty comes in when we seek to know the substance of either of them. Rhodes’ prophecies about the Boer resistance are an admirable comment on how the “large ideas” prosper when it is not a question of thinking in continents but of understanding a few two-legged men. And under all this vast illusion of the cosmopolitan planet, with its empires and its Reuter’s agency, the real life of man goes on concerned with this tree or that temple, with this harvest or that drinking-song, totally uncomprehended, totally untouched. And it watches from its splendid parochialism, possibly with a smile of amusement, motorcar civilization going its triumphant way, outstripping time, consuming space, seeing all and seeing nothing, roaring on at last to the capture of the solar system, only to find the sun cockney and the stars suburban.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
The essay begins nowhere near Kipling. Chesterton opens with a flat declaration: "There is no such thing on earth as an uninteresting subject; the only thing that can exist is an uninterested person." He then defends the bore. The poet Byron had divided humanity into the bores and the bored, but Chesterton says the bore, with his "starry enthusiasm," is actually closer to the gods, because it is the gods who never tire of repetition. To them the nightfall is always new. This is the engine of the whole piece. Wonder is not a mood that things earn. It is something we bring or fail to bring.

He then proves it with the most ordinary name in English, Smith. A smith is a worker in iron, the trade that even kings respected, with the hammer, the sparks, the sword and the ploughshare all written, he says, "on the visiting-card of Mr. Smith." The same goes for a signal-box, where men light red and green lights to keep other men from death, and a pillar-box, the red post box, which he calls "a sanctuary of human words." The words are dull. The things are not. Poetry has been hiding in plain sight, and only our habit of literary refinement makes it look prosaic.

That is the setup for Kipling, and Chesterton's first move is generous. Kipling, he says, has helped recover "the lost provinces of poetry" by finding romance in steam and slang. Then comes the surprise. Chesterton says Kipling's famous love of soldiers is really a love of discipline, not courage. The modern army is not a miracle of bravery but of organization, and Kipling writes best about engineers, sailors and railway men. In that sense, the baker baking loaves is as military as any soldier, since everything depends on obedience and people doing their jobs well.

So far this is praise. The turn arrives with the word cosmopolitan. Kipling admires England, Chesterton says, because she is strong, not because she is English. He quotes a Kipling line about how we would quickly "chuck" England if she were not what she seems. That, to Chesterton, is a criticism, and love does not criticize first. "We admire things with reasons, but love them without reasons." Kipling is a globetrotter, and "the globetrotter lives in a smaller world than the peasant." The peasant in his cabbage field thinks of what unites men: hunger, babies, the sky. The traveller on the steamer thinks of what divides them: diet, dress, rings in noses. Exploration, he concludes, makes the world smaller. The telescope shrinks things. Only the microscope makes the world larger.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
The first thing to admire is the architecture. It looks like a ramble. The opening third has nothing to do with Kipling, and yet by the end you see that the defense of boredom, the poetry of Smith and the pillar-box were not a digression but the foundation. If everything is interesting when you really look, then the man who rushes past everything to see more of it has not seen more. It is an argument made by building a mood first and cashing it in later, and it is more elegant than it first appears.

The prose is also glorious at its best. "The moss is silent because the moss is alive" is a wonderful sentence, turning an old proverb about rolling stones on its head. The closing paragraph, with motorcars roaring on to capture the solar system "only to find the sun cockney and the stars suburban," is a small masterpiece of comic grandeur. And the distinction between admiring and loving, between reasons and no reasons, is psychologically sharp. Anyone who has loved a family member or a hometown knows it is not a conclusion drawn from a list of virtues.

Chesterton is also fairer to Kipling than the occasion required. He says Kipling's main message is "the only thing worth worrying about" in any man, and he treats Kipling's flaws as an ordinary writer's flaws, comparing them to Wordsworth's bad poetry and Plato's silly remarks.

But the essay has real weaknesses. Its central claim, that Kipling lacks patriotism, is more clever than accurate. Kipling's "Recessional," written for Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee in 1897, is a warning against imperial pride, and he wrote movingly about the English countryside, especially Sussex, where he lived, and said in a poem that every person is given one spot to love above all. A reader who knows Kipling may feel Chesterton has cut out the passages that do not fit. His claim that Kipling writes better about railway men than soldiers also underrates the Barrack-Room Ballads, where the common soldier is vividly courageous.

More troubling is the logic of loving without reasons. It is lovely for a family or a village. Applied to nations, it is exactly the argument of every nationalist who says my country right or wrong. Chesterton admires the patriotism of the Boers and the Irish, but the principle is wide enough to cover patriotisms he would hate. And the peasant, whom he describes as thinking only of hunger and babies, is a rather romantic figure who might not recognise himself. Cecil Rhodes, whom Chesterton describes as essentially good-natured but small-minded, is let off lightly.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
The first consequence was for Chesterton himself. The Kipling chapter gave him one of the clearest statements of a theme that would run through the rest of his work: that the local and ordinary is larger than the global and exotic. He had already written a novel about it, The Napoleon of Notting Hill, in 1904, in which a London suburb goes to war over its own local pride. Heretics, a year later, put the philosophy into essay form, and Orthodoxy, three years after that, built on it whose chapter called "The Flag of the World" compares loving the world to a patriot's loyalty to a homeland, with all its faults. The idea shaped his politics too. He and his friend Hilaire Belloc later argued for distributism, a movement that wanted property and power spread among many small owners rather than concentrated in big states or big companies.

In the wider culture the essay's most durable legacy is its rhetoric. The remark that there is no uninteresting subject, only uninterested people, is still quoted by teachers and writers. The line about the telescope and the microscope turns up in discussions of travel and tourism. And the central reversal, that going everywhere may mean knowing nothing deeply, anticipated a great deal of later writing on place, from the poems and farming essays of Wendell Berry to modern complaints about hurried tourism.

It also fed a longer argument about Kipling himself. In the twentieth century Kipling's reputation went through a steep decline, and then a partial rescue. T. S. Eliot edited a selection of his verse in 1941, and George Orwell wrote a famous essay the following year that called him a jingo imperialist while conceding that he had a real grip on certain truths about responsibility and work. Chesterton's reading, which finds the discipline of ordinary trades at the heart of Kipling and not imperial swagger, is a forerunner of that more nuanced view. Later critics, including Edward Said, discussing Kipling's novel Kim, took a more critical line about the empire in his work.

As for teaching, this is not a chapter usually set in classrooms, and there are no famous adaptations. It lives mostly through Chesterton readers, anthologies of his essays, and quotations that float free of their source. That quiet life is perhaps fitting for an essay that argues for the unglamorous and the small. Its influence has been less a movement than a way of seeing, passed from reader to reader, which is how a defense of ordinary things might be expected to spread.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
