It appeals to anyone who has watched shy people accomplish extraordinary things, and it gives a new reading of adventure stories in which the hero is an ordinary person who happens to be present. It also explains why the heroes of fairy tales are so often youngest sons and tailors and swineherds, never the strongest man in the kingdom. The claim that Romance is a Christian product, the result of believing you do not deserve what you pursue, is stirring even to readers who suspect it is historically too neat.

Finally, readers who share Chesterton's distrust of master plans have found in this chapter a comforting argument that ordinary human things, falling in love, eating, being careless, are not problems to be solved. There is relief in that, and relief is a large part of why people keep going back to him.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
The most direct pushback is from the side of science and philosophy. Wells's claim that knowledge is provisional, that each stronger light shows new darkness, is close to what many scientists and philosophers of science believe. Critics argue that Chesterton's answer, that you need a fixed idea of light to compare lights, does not actually refute it. One can have a direction without having a destination, and one can improve a map without having reached the pole. They add that Chesterton turns Wells's flexible attitude into a claim that nothing is true, which Wells did not say.

Second, the essay's confident glorification of the weak has been questioned. The point that sympathy with the small and defeated is "the first law of practical courage" is stirring, but critics note that underdogs are not always right and that rooting for the weak can curdle into sentimentality. Chesterton's own example, the Boers, whom he and Belloc had championed against the British Empire, were themselves a ruling people whose treatment of Black Africans is a serious blot, and the chapter is silent on it.

Third, there is the assertion that Romance and adventure came from the humility of Christendom, so that the civilization that gained Romance "has gained the habitable globe." Modern readers hear in that line a celebration of European expansion that overlooks conquest, empire and slavery. It sits oddly beside Chesterton's own opposition to imperialism, and it shows how fond he could be of a sweeping claim. A reader who stops to ask how the humility of Christendom explains the conquest of whole continents may find the essay has no answer.

Fourth, his theological detours trouble some readers. Linking original sin to the weakness of Utopia, or the Trinity to the persistence of nationalism, is the kind of move that delights believers and baffles others, and it can feel as if the essay's real purpose is to smuggle in doctrine.

Fifth, there is the charge of unfairness to Wells. Chesterton himself admits the Superman does not loom as large in Wells's thinking as in Shaw's, and that The Food of the Gods is only a half-pantomimic allegory. Critics say he has chosen a minor target and built a large argument on it, and that he leans on Wells's friendly tone to take liberties that a harsher opponent would not be allowed. In the novel, after all, the giants are not conventional villains, and the little people are not conventional heroes.

Finally, the sheer sprawl of the chapter has been criticized: it is a brilliant mind in motion, but not always one that stops to prove its points.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
This chapter belongs to one of the great arguments of its age, between the believers in scientific planning and the defenders of older, more human wisdom. The utopian tradition goes back to Thomas More and, in the nineteenth century, to Edward Bellamy's Looking Backward and William Morris's News from Nowhere, which was itself a reply to Bellamy. Wells's A Modern Utopia was the Edwardian peak of the genre, a vision of a world-state run by a voluntary elite. Chesterton stands on the other side, in the tradition of the fairy tale, Dickens's loyalty to the ordinary, and the Christian conviction that human nature is flawed and that no arrangement of society will cancel the flaw.

Its descendants are many. The dystopian novel of the twentieth century, Huxley's Brave New World and Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four, is a long answer to Wells's optimism, and shares with Chesterton the suspicion of planners who forget what people are like. C. S. Lewis wrote his space trilogy partly as a rebuttal to the kind of science-fiction faith Wells represented, and its last volume, That Hideous Strength, is about a scientific institute that would remake humanity. J. R. R. Tolkien's essay on fairy stories makes a related case for the wisdom of the old tales. In political thought, the Chestertonian suspicion of the rule of experts finds echoes in later writers on local self-government and in critics of technocracy.

It sits beside Shaw's Man and Superman and Nietzsche's Thus Spoke Zarathustra as one of the English-language responses to the Superman idea, and next to Chesterton's own Orthodoxy, whose chapter on the suicide of thought develops the argument about relativism more fully. A good way to read it is with Wells's own The Food of the Gods nearby, to judge how fair the retelling is.

Why does it still matter? Because we live in an age of giants, of enormously powerful companies and individuals whose supporters tell us that their size is proof of their wisdom. Jack's question, whether this giant is any good to us, with its absurd list of what he thinks about politics and children, is exactly the question to put to power. And Chesterton's insistence that the best things in life, love, health, adventure, come when we are not trying to manage them is a refreshing contrast to a culture of optimisation. It is one of the funniest, most wide-ranging chapters in Heretics, and well worth the twenty minutes.

essays.title: Christmas and the Aesthetes
essays.author: G. K. Chesterton
essays.epigraph: Anything that is truly ritual and human must be tied to a concrete hour and a concrete hearth, when the cold wind blows outside.
essays.keyContext: This is the sixth chapter of G. K. Chesterton's Heretics, published in 1905, and despite its title it begins nowhere near Christmas. It starts with two Victorian attempts to replace old religion with something modern. One is the Salvation Army, with its brass bands and street parades, which respectable people tolerated for its charity while sneering at its noise. The other is Positivism, a French philosopher's religion of humanity, complete with its own calendar and holidays, which its English followers embarrassedly kept only for its ideas. Chesterton reverses the usual verdict on both. The Army's loud methods, he says, are the best thing about it, and the Positivists' silly ceremonies were the only sensible part of theirs. Joy, he argues, needs rituals, and rituals need belief. He ends by teasing fashionable aesthetes who dream of revived maypoles but look down on the one great old festival still alive, Christmas. It is a funny, argumentative defense of noise, pudding and faith.
paragraphs: The world is round, so round that the schools of optimism and pessimism have been arguing from the beginning whether it is the right way up. The difficulty does not arise so much from the mere fact that good and evil are mingled in roughly equal proportions; it arises chiefly from the fact that men always differ about what parts are good and what evil. Hence the difficulty which besets “undenominational religions.” They profess to include what is beautiful in all creeds, but they appear to many to have collected all that is dull in them. All the colours mixed together in purity ought to make a perfect white. Mixed together on any human paintbox, they make a thing like mud, and a thing very like many new religions. Such a blend is often something much worse than any one creed taken separately, even the creed of the Thugs. The error arises from the difficulty of detecting what is really the good part and what is really the bad part of any given religion. And this pathos falls rather heavily on those persons who have the misfortune to think of some religion or other, that the parts commonly counted good are bad, and the parts commonly counted bad are good.

It is tragic to admire and honestly admire a human group, but to admire it in a photographic negative. It is difficult to congratulate all their whites on being black and all their blacks on their whiteness. This will often happen to us in connection with human religions. Take two institutions which bear witness to the religious energy of the nineteenth century. Take the Salvation Army and the philosophy of Auguste Comte.

The usual verdict of educated people on the Salvation Army is expressed in some such words as these: “I have no doubt they do a great deal of good, but they do it in a vulgar and profane style; their aims are excellent, but their methods are wrong.” To me, unfortunately, the precise reverse of this appears to be the truth. I do not know whether the aims of the Salvation Army are excellent, but I am quite sure their methods are admirable. Their methods are the methods of all intense and hearty religions; they are popular like all religion, military like all religion, public and sensational like all religion. They are not reverent any more than Roman Catholics are reverent, for reverence in the sad and delicate meaning of the term reverence is a thing only possible to infidels. That beautiful twilight you will find in Euripides, in Renan, in Matthew Arnold; but in men who believe you will not find it⁠—you will find only laughter and war. A man cannot pay that kind of reverence to truth solid as marble; they can only be reverent towards a beautiful lie. And the Salvation Army, though their voice has broken out in a mean environment and an ugly shape, are really the old voice of glad and angry faith, hot as the riots of Dionysus, wild as the gargoyles of Catholicism, not to be mistaken for a philosophy. Professor Huxley, in one of his clever phrases, called the Salvation Army “corybantic Christianity.” Huxley was the last and noblest of those Stoics who have never understood the Cross. If he had understood Christianity he would have known that there never has been, and never can be, any Christianity that is not corybantic.

And there is this difference between the matter of aims and the matter of methods, that to judge of the aims of a thing like the Salvation Army is very difficult, to judge of their ritual and atmosphere very easy. No one, perhaps, but a sociologist can see whether General Booth’s housing scheme is right. But any healthy person can see that banging brass cymbals together must be right. A page of statistics, a plan of model dwellings, anything which is rational, is always difficult for the lay mind. But the thing which is irrational anyone can understand. That is why religion came so early into the world and spread so far, while science came so late into the world and has not spread at all. History unanimously attests the fact that it is only mysticism which stands the smallest chance of being understanded of the people. Common sense has to be kept as an esoteric secret in the dark temple of culture. And so while the philanthropy of the Salvationists and its genuineness may be a reasonable matter for the discussion of the doctors, there can be no doubt about the genuineness of their brass bands, for a brass band is purely spiritual, and seeks only to quicken the internal life. The object of philanthropy is to do good; the object of religion is to be good, if only for a moment, amid a crash of brass.

And the same antithesis exists about another modern religion⁠—I mean the religion of Comte, generally known as Positivism, or the worship of humanity. Such men as Mr. Frederic Harrison, that brilliant and chivalrous philosopher, who still, by his mere personality, speaks for the creed, would tell us that he offers us the philosophy of Comte, but not all Comte’s fantastic proposals for pontiffs and ceremonials, the new calendar, the new holidays and saints’ days. He does not mean that we should dress ourselves up as priests of humanity or let off fireworks because it is Milton’s birthday. To the solid English Comtist all this appears, he confesses, to be a little absurd. To me it appears the only sensible part of Comtism. As a philosophy it is unsatisfactory. It is evidently impossible to worship humanity, just as it is impossible to worship the Savile Club; both are excellent institutions to which we may happen to belong. But we perceive clearly that the Savile Club did not make the stars and does not fill the universe. And it is surely unreasonable to attack the doctrine of the Trinity as a piece of bewildering mysticism, and then to ask men to worship a being who is ninety million persons in one God, neither confounding the persons nor dividing the substance.

But if the wisdom of Comte was insufficient, the folly of Comte was wisdom. In an age of dusty modernity, when beauty was thought of as something barbaric and ugliness as something sensible, he alone saw that men must always have the sacredness of mummery. He saw that while the brutes have all the useful things, the things that are truly human are the useless ones. He saw the falsehood of that almost universal notion of today, the notion that rites and forms are something artificial, additional, and corrupt. Ritual is really much older than thought; it is much simpler and much wilder than thought. A feeling touching the nature of things does not only make men feel that there are certain proper things to say; it makes them feel that there are certain proper things to do. The more agreeable of these consist of dancing, building temples, and shouting very loud; the less agreeable, of wearing green carnations and burning other philosophers alive. But everywhere the religious dance came before the religious hymn, and man was a ritualist before he could speak. If Comtism had spread the world would have been converted, not by the Comtist philosophy, but by the Comtist calendar. By discouraging what they conceive to be the weakness of their master, the English Positivists have broken the strength of their religion. A man who has faith must be prepared not only to be a martyr, but to be a fool. It is absurd to say that a man is ready to toil and die for his convictions when he is not even ready to wear a wreath round his head for them. I myself, to take a corpus vile, am very certain that I would not read the works of Comte through for any consideration whatever. But I can easily imagine myself with the greatest enthusiasm lighting a bonfire on Darwin Day.

That splendid effort failed, and nothing in the style of it has succeeded. There has been no rationalist festival, no rationalist ecstasy. Men are still in black for the death of God. When Christianity was heavily bombarded in the last century upon no point was it more persistently and brilliantly attacked than upon that of its alleged enmity to human joy. Shelley and Swinburne and all their armies have passed again and again over the ground, but they have not altered it. They have not set up a single new trophy or ensign for the world’s merriment to rally to. They have not given a name or a new occasion of gaiety. Mr. Swinburne does not hang up his stocking on the eve of the birthday of Victor Hugo. Mr. William Archer does not sing carols descriptive of the infancy of Ibsen outside people’s doors in the snow. In the round of our rational and mournful year one festival remains out of all those ancient gaieties that once covered the whole earth. Christmas remains to remind us of those ages, whether Pagan or Christian, when the many acted poetry instead of the few writing it. In all the winter in our woods there is no tree in glow but the holly.

The strange truth about the matter is told in the very word “holiday.” A bank holiday means presumably a day which bankers regard as holy. A half-holiday means, I suppose, a day on which a schoolboy is only partially holy. It is hard to see at first sight why so human a thing as leisure and larkiness should always have a religious origin. Rationally there appears no reason why we should not sing and give each other presents in honour of anything⁠—the birth of Michelangelo or the opening of Euston Station. But it does not work. As a fact, men only become greedily and gloriously material about something spiritualistic. Take away the Nicene Creed and similar things, and you do some strange wrong to the sellers of sausages. Take away the strange beauty of the saints, and what has remained to us is the far stranger ugliness of Wandsworth. Take away the supernatural, and what remains is the unnatural.

And now I have to touch upon a very sad matter. There are in the modern world an admirable class of persons who really make protest on behalf of that antiqua pulchritudo of which Augustine spoke, who do long for the old feasts and formalities of the childhood of the world. William Morris and his followers showed how much brighter were the dark ages than the age of Manchester. Mr. W. B. Yeats frames his steps in prehistoric dances, but no man knows and joins his voice to forgotten choruses that no one but he can hear. Mr. George Moore collects every fragment of Irish paganism that the forgetfulness of the Catholic Church has left or possibly her wisdom preserved. There are innumerable persons with eyeglasses and green garments who pray for the return of the maypole or the Olympian games. But there is about these people a haunting and alarming something which suggests that it is just possible that they do not keep Christmas. It is painful to regard human nature in such a light, but it seems somehow possible that Mr. George Moore does not wave his spoon and shout when the pudding is set alight. It is even possible that Mr. W. B. Yeats never pulls crackers. If so, where is the sense of all their dreams of festive traditions? Here is a solid and ancient festive tradition still plying a roaring trade in the streets, and they think it vulgar. If this is so, let them be very certain of this, that they are the kind of people who in the time of the maypole would have thought the maypole vulgar; who in the time of the Canterbury pilgrimage would have thought the Canterbury pilgrimage vulgar; who in the time of the Olympian games would have thought the Olympian games vulgar. Nor can there be any reasonable doubt that they were vulgar. Let no man deceive himself; if by vulgarity we mean coarseness of speech, rowdiness of behaviour, gossip, horseplay, and some heavy drinking, vulgarity there always was wherever there was joy, wherever there was faith in the gods. Wherever you have belief you will have hilarity, wherever you have hilarity you will have some dangers. And as creed and mythology produce this gross and vigorous life, so in its turn this gross and vigorous life will always produce creed and mythology. If we ever get the English back on to the English land they will become again a religious people, if all goes well, a superstitious people. The absence from modern life of both the higher and lower forms of faith is largely due to a divorce from nature and the trees and clouds. If we have no more turnip ghosts it is chiefly from the lack of turnips.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
Chesterton begins with a thought about mixing. The world is so round, he says, that optimists and pessimists cannot even agree which way up it is, because people differ about which parts are good and which are bad. This is why "undenominational religions," which promise to blend the best of every creed, tend to collect the dullest parts of each. "All the colours mixed together in purity ought to make a perfect white. Mixed together on any human paintbox, they make a thing like mud." Worse, some people admire a religion in what he calls a photographic negative, praising what is bad in it and condemning what is good.

His first test case is the Salvation Army. The usual educated view is that they do a lot of good but in a vulgar style, that their aims are fine but their methods wrong. Chesterton says the opposite. He cannot say whether their aims are excellent, but their methods are admirable, because they are the methods of every hearty religion: popular, military, public and sensational. A famous scientist, Thomas Huxley, called the Army "corybantic Christianity," meaning frenzied and noisy, and Chesterton replies that there never has been, and never can be, any Christianity that is not corybantic. Judging aims, like General Booth's housing scheme, takes an expert. Judging a brass band is easy: it is "purely spiritual." The point is a clever one: "The object of philanthropy is to do good; the object of religion is to be good, if only for a moment, amid a crash of brass."

The second test case is Auguste Comte, the French thinker who founded Positivism, a religion that worshipped humanity and came with priests, a new calendar and saints' days for great men. English Positivists like Frederic Harrison kept the philosophy and dropped the ceremonies as absurd. Chesterton says the philosophy is the weak part, for you cannot worship humanity any more than you can worship your club, but the ceremonies were the wise part. Humans are ritual creatures, and "the religious dance came before the religious hymn." He jokes that he would never read Comte's works, but could happily light a bonfire on Darwin Day.

This leads to Christmas. The rationalists attacked Christianity as an enemy of human joy, yet they never set up one new festival. "Mr. Swinburne does not hang up his stocking on the eve of the birthday of Victor Hugo." Only Christmas survives of the old gaieties, and even the word "holiday" shows that leisure was once holy. His last target is the aesthetes, such as Yeats and George Moore, who long for ancient feasts yet may not pull crackers at Christmas. Wherever there is belief, there is hilarity, and with hilarity come dangers.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
The essay's best quality is audacity. The Salvation Army argument reverses a commonplace so neatly that you cannot go back to the old version. The idea that we are comfortable judging the noise of a religion and uncomfortable judging its social program is a real insight, and it works as a comment on the way we all talk about charities, parties and causes. The line about philanthropy and religion, doing good versus being good "amid a crash of brass," is the kind of sentence that Chesterton alone seems to produce.

The material on ritual is also stronger than it first looks. The claim that ritual is older and wilder than thought was not just a joke. The Scottish scholar William Robertson Smith had argued in his 1889 lectures on the religion of the Semites that early religion was mostly something people did, not something they believed, and later scholars often agreed. Chesterton's version, that man was a ritualist before he could speak, anticipates a lot of later thinking about why shared ceremonies matter.

The comedy is dependable. The notion that a bank holiday must mean a day bankers regard as holy, and that a half-holiday is a day on which a schoolboy is only partially holy, is a graceful way to make a historical point. "Take away the supernatural, and what remains is the unnatural" is epigram at its best, and the closing joke about turnip ghosts and the lack of turnips ends the piece with a grin.

But the essay is flawed in ways worth admitting. Structurally, it is lopsided. The title promises Christmas and aesthetes, but Christmas does not really appear until two-thirds through, and the whole first half is a detour through the Army and Comte. The ending is abrupt, a joke and a shrug, and the essay does not so much conclude as stop. A reader may feel that Chesterton had three pieces in his notebook and decided to staple them together.

Fairness is another issue. To say that he does not know whether the Salvation Army's aims are excellent, when its work with the poor was one of the largest charitable efforts of the age, is flippant, and the claim that reverence is "only possible to infidels" is the kind of provocative sentence that falls apart when you press it. The teasing of Yeats and Moore is funny but also a bit unkind, since both were doing serious work reviving old culture, and guessing what they do at Christmas is unanswerable gossip. The claim that all holidays have a religious origin is also overstated, as his own phrase "whether Pagan or Christian" half concedes.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
It is honest to say that this chapter is among the lesser-known parts of Heretics, and its direct influence is hard to trace. It was not a landmark that changed a field. What it did was strengthen a theme that would grow larger in Chesterton's work: the celebration of festivity, noise and the physical side of belief. He returned to Christmas often, in essays, in poems, and in the books on Dickens, and the defense of the loud, crowded, roast-and-pudding Christmas as a real spiritual event, not a degraded one, became part of his public identity. It also fed his larger case in Orthodoxy that Christianity is a joyful faith and not a gloomy one, answering the nineteenth-century charge that it was an enemy of human happiness.

The chapter's quotations have had a life of their own. "Take away the supernatural, and what remains is the unnatural" is widely quoted by religious writers, usually without the context of sausages and Wandsworth. The remark that the dance came before the hymn is a favourite of writers on liturgy and worship.

There are also some happy afterlives for its ideas. Comte's religion of humanity was not just a joke. It lived on in a Positivist Church in Brazil, and the motto of the Brazilian flag, Order and Progress, comes from his thought. The Salvation Army, meanwhile, grew into one of the largest charities in the world, and its brass bands and bell-ringers at Christmas have become part of the season in many countries, which would have delighted Chesterton. And Darwin Day, a celebration of Darwin's birthday on the twelfth of February, is today observed by scientific and humanist groups, as are some secular holidays in December, so the challenge that rationalists had no festivals was, in a small way, eventually taken up.

It is not usually taught in schools and has not been adapted. Its life is in anthologies, Christmas readings, and the reading lists of those who like Chesterton's playful side.

One more effect deserves mention, though it is hard to measure. The chapter taught a certain kind of reader to be unembarrassed. Many people raised among restrained, tasteful believers or tasteful unbelievers found in Chesterton a voice that said loudness and communal silliness were not signs of shallow faith but, often, of deep faith. That is a quiet kind of influence, passed along in conversations and Christmas toasts rather than in footnotes, but it may be the most real one the essay has.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
The easiest thing to say about what readers love is that this is Chesterton having a good time. The chapter is mostly jokes with a spine of conviction, and readers respond to that. A line like "Mr. William Archer does not sing carols descriptive of the infancy of Ibsen outside people's doors in the snow" makes the point about secular festivals better than any argument, because you picture it and laugh, and you realize he is right that it would be absurd.

Readers also love the permission it gives. The people who find Christmas too loud, too commercial, too sentimental, are told that its noisiness is the point and not the flaw. For anyone who has felt faintly embarrassed about enjoying brass bands, carols or an overcooked pudding, the essay is an affectionate defense. Chesterton makes the case that being a bit ridiculous in public, wearing a wreath or lighting a bonfire for what you believe, is a mark of sincerity. "A man who has faith must be prepared not only to be a martyr, but to be a fool" is the sort of line that readers of every belief, or none, have underlined.

There is also the pleasure of the Salvation Army argument. Many readers have felt uneasy about the way respectable people patronize noisy believers, and the essay turns the tables with relish. The Army, he says, has the old voice of "glad and angry faith, hot as the riots of Dionysus, wild as the gargoyles of Catholicism."

And readers with a taste for words enjoy the etymological play on the word holiday, a gentle demonstration that even our most ordinary leisure words carry old religion inside them.

Readers who are not religious sometimes say what they take from it is a question: if we want shared joy, what rituals do we actually have? The essay does not answer that, but it asks it in such a friendly way that people carry it with them. And for those who just love Christmas, it is a lovely thing to read in December, short, warm and a little mischievous.

There is also a gentler thing that readers mention. Chesterton never sounds as though he is lecturing from above. He talks about pudding and crackers as someone who has actually sat at the table, and the humour comes from a man who plainly likes the people he is teasing, including the aesthetes. That fondness is what keeps even his sharpest jokes from turning sour, and it is a good deal of why the essay still feels warm after more than a century.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
The most natural objection is from the people he is writing about. Salvationists took their charity seriously and might have been unhappy to hear that the brass band mattered more than the housing scheme. Social reformers would say that treating the aims of a poverty program as a matter for experts, while the music is for everyone, undersells the real work done to feed and shelter the poor. Chesterton's playful tone about whether the Army's aims are excellent is a joke that can look callous from a distance.

A second line of objection comes from secularists and humanists. They would argue that joy does not require creed. People celebrate birthdays, harvests, sports victories, seasons and weddings without any theology, and even those holidays with religious roots have often absorbed older, non-religious customs. Chesterton's claim that "men only become greedily and gloriously material about something spiritualistic" is a generalization that many anthropologists and historians would find too tidy. The theory that ritual precedes belief is also debated among scholars of religion, and nobody believes it is as simple as Chesterton makes it.

Third, there is the charge of nostalgia. Chesterton's English Christmas, with holly, pudding and crackers, is a comfortable, middle-class one, and critics note that it says nothing about people for whom December was a month of cold and hunger. Dickens at least put the Cratchits in the picture. The essay's fondness for the old Merry England is real but selective, and it does not ask who had the pudding.

Fourth, his treatment of Comte, Yeats and Moore has been seen as more dismissive than fair. Comte's attempt to build a humane, communal secular religion was a serious one, sustained by sincere people, and the aesthetes were doing important cultural work. To mock them by guessing that they do not pull crackers is an effective joke and a poor argument.

Fifth, and generally, there is the question of reputation. Chesterton's later writing on Jews has drawn serious criticism, and readers sometimes find it hard to enjoy his geniality without keeping that in mind. It does not appear in this chapter, but the complication is part of how he is read.

Finally, a plain structural complaint: the title promises more Christmas than it delivers.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
The chapter belongs to a Victorian and Edwardian conversation about what could replace religion once it faded. Matthew Arnold heard the "melancholy, long, withdrawing roar" of the sea of faith, and offered poetry and culture as substitutes. Comte offered a church of humanity. The aesthetes of the 1890s offered beauty for its own sake. Others offered ethical societies and Fabian socialism. Chesterton's wry answer is that none of them could throw a party. They had ideas but not feasts, and a religion is a thing you do with your whole body and a crowd.

That intuition has a distinguished line of relatives. The French sociologist Émile Durkheim argued, in 1912, in The Elementary Forms of Religious Life that shared ritual produces a kind of collective excitement that binds a community, and that religion is at bottom about this. The Russian critic Mikhail Bakhtin wrote about carnival, the loud, grotesque festivity of the Middle Ages, as a form of freedom and renewal. Neither borrowed from Chesterton, but both are working on the same ground. In recent years the writer Alain de Botton has argued in Religion for Atheists that non-believers should learn from religions how to build communal rituals, an echo of Chesterton's complaint that the rationalists never set up a single trophy for the world's merriment.

Among Chesterton's own writing, it connects with his love of Dickens, whose Christmas books helped invent the modern English Christmas, and with the long essays in Orthodoxy about the gladness at the root of faith. It also connects, more distantly, to the distributist longing for a rooted, village life of feasts and customs, which he shared with William Morris, one of the figures he teases here.

Read next to its neighbours in Heretics, it is the lightest chapter. The Wells chapter is about giants, the Shaw chapter about wonder, the Kipling chapter about place. This one is about celebration, and it reminds you that Chesterton's real argument was always that life is a gift to be enjoyed noisily.

Why read it now? Because the question it asks, what do we do together that is joyful and shared, matters to a generation that has plenty of ideas and few communal rites. And because it is December somewhere, and a defense of the pudding is hard to resist.

essays.title: On Sandals and Simplicity
essays.author: G. K. Chesterton
essays.epigraph: There is much more simplicity in the man who eats caviar on impulse than in the man who eats grape-nuts on principle.
essays.keyContext: G. K. Chesterton wrote this short essay in 1905 as a chapter of Heretics, a book in which he argued with the famous thinkers of his day. Its target is the simple life, a fashion among the educated of Edwardian England. People gave up meat, wore plain clothes, and admired Tolstoy, the great Russian novelist who had renounced his wealth and preached peaceful, humble living. Chesterton was a big, jolly, cigar-smoking journalist who loved feasts, and he thought these reformers had the whole idea backward. His claim is that they simplify the things that do not matter, like diet and clothing, while tangling up the things that do, like loyalty, philosophy, and joy. The only simplicity worth having, he says, is simplicity of the heart: the ability to be astonished and glad. As you listen, watch for his famous image of a man in sandals with a raw tomato in his hand, and notice how Chesterton uses humor to make a serious argument about what it means to live well.
paragraphs: The great misfortune of the modern English is not at all that they are more boastful than other people (they are not); it is that they are boastful about those particular things which nobody can boast of without losing them. A Frenchman can be proud of being bold and logical, and still remain bold and logical. A German can be proud of being reflective and orderly, and still remain reflective and orderly. But an Englishman cannot be proud of being simple and direct, and still remain simple and direct. In the matter of these strange virtues, to know them is to kill them. A man may be conscious of being heroic or conscious of being divine, but he cannot (in spite of all the Anglo-Saxon poets) be conscious of being unconscious.

Now, I do not think that it can be honestly denied that some portion of this impossibility attaches to a class very different in their own opinion, at least, to the school of Anglo-Saxonism. I mean that school of the simple life, commonly associated with Tolstoy. If a perpetual talk about one’s own robustness leads to being less robust, it is even more true that a perpetual talking about one’s own simplicity leads to being less simple. One great complaint, I think, must stand against the modern upholders of the simple life⁠—the simple life in all its varied forms, from vegetarianism to the honourable consistency of the Doukhobors. This complaint against them stands, that they would make us simple in the unimportant things, but complex in the important things. They would make us simple in the things that do not matter⁠—that is, in diet, in costume, in etiquette, in economic system. But they would make us complex in the things that do matter⁠—in philosophy, in loyalty, in spiritual acceptance, and spiritual rejection. It does not so very much matter whether a man eats a grilled tomato or a plain tomato; it does very much matter whether he eats a plain tomato with a grilled mind. The only kind of simplicity worth preserving is the simplicity of the heart, the simplicity which accepts and enjoys. There may be a reasonable doubt as to what system preserves this; there can surely be no doubt that a system of simplicity destroys it. There is more simplicity in the man who eats caviar on impulse than in the man who eats grape-nuts on principle. The chief error of these people is to be found in the very phrase to which they are most attached⁠—“plain living and high thinking.” These people do not stand in need of, will not be improved by, plain living and high thinking. They stand in need of the contrary. They would be improved by high living and plain thinking. A little high living (I say, having a full sense of responsibility, a little high living) would teach them the force and meaning of the human festivities, of the banquet that has gone on from the beginning of the world. It would teach them the historic fact that the artificial is, if anything, older than the natural. It would teach them that the loving-cup is as old as any hunger. It would teach them that ritualism is older than any religion. And a little plain thinking would teach them how harsh and fanciful are the mass of their own ethics, how very civilized and very complicated must be the brain of the Tolstoyan who really believes it to be evil to love one’s country and wicked to strike a blow.

A man approaches, wearing sandals and simple raiment, a raw tomato held firmly in his right hand, and says, “The affections of family and country alike are hindrances to the fuller development of human love;” but the plain thinker will only answer him, with a wonder not untinged with admiration, “What a great deal of trouble you must have taken in order to feel like that.” High living will reject the tomato. Plain thinking will equally decisively reject the idea of the invariable sinfulness of war. High living will convince us that nothing is more materialistic than to despise a pleasure as purely material. And plain thinking will convince us that nothing is more materialistic than to reserve our horror chiefly for material wounds.

The only simplicity that matters is the simplicity of the heart. If that be gone, it can be brought back by no turnips or cellular clothing; but only by tears and terror and the fires that are not quenched. If that remain, it matters very little if a few Early Victorian armchairs remain along with it. Let us put a complex entrée into a simple old gentleman; let us not put a simple entrée into a complex old gentleman. So long as human society will leave my spiritual inside alone, I will allow it, with a comparative submission, to work its wild will with my physical interior. I will submit to cigars. I will meekly embrace a bottle of Burgundy. I will humble myself to a hansom cab. If only by this means I may preserve to myself the virginity of the spirit, which enjoys with astonishment and fear. I do not say that these are the only methods of preserving it. I incline to the belief that there are others. But I will have nothing to do with simplicity which lacks the fear, the astonishment, and the joy alike. I will have nothing to do with the devilish vision of a child who is too simple to like toys.

The child is, indeed, in these, and many other matters, the best guide. And in nothing is the child so righteously childlike, in nothing does he exhibit more accurately the sounder order of simplicity, than in the fact that he sees everything with a simple pleasure, even the complex things. The false type of naturalness harps always on the distinction between the natural and the artificial. The higher kind of naturalness ignores that distinction. To the child the tree and the lamppost are as natural and as artificial as each other; or rather, neither of them are natural but both supernatural. For both are splendid and unexplained. The flower with which God crowns the one, and the flame with which Sam the lamplighter crowns the other, are equally of the gold of fairytales. In the middle of the wildest fields the most rustic child is, ten to one, playing at steam-engines. And the only spiritual or philosophical objection to steam-engines is not that men pay for them or work at them, or make them very ugly, or even that men are killed by them; but merely that men do not play at them. The evil is that the childish poetry of clockwork does not remain. The wrong is not that engines are too much admired, but that they are not admired enough. The sin is not that engines are mechanical, but that men are mechanical.

In this matter, then, as in all the other matters treated in this book, our main conclusion is that it is a fundamental point of view, a philosophy or religion which is needed, and not any change in habit or social routine. The things we need most for immediate practical purposes are all abstractions. We need a right view of the human lot, a right view of the human society; and if we were living eagerly and angrily in the enthusiasm of those things, we should, ipso facto, be living simply in the genuine and spiritual sense. Desire and danger make everyone simple. And to those who talk to us with interfering eloquence about Jaeger and the pores of the skin, and about Plasmon and the coats of the stomach, at them shall only be hurled the words that are hurled at fops and gluttons, “Take no thought what ye shall eat or what ye shall drink, or wherewithal ye shall be clothed. For after all these things do the Gentiles seek. But seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things shall be added unto you.” Those amazing words are not only extraordinarily good, practical politics; they are also superlatively good hygiene. The one supreme way of making all those processes go right, the processes of health, and strength, and grace, and beauty, the one and only way of making certain of their accuracy, is to think about something else. If a man is bent on climbing into the seventh heaven, he may be quite easy about the pores of his skin. If he harnesses his wagon to a star, the process will have a most satisfactory effect upon the coats of his stomach. For the thing called “taking thought,” the thing for which the best modern word is “rationalizing,” is in its nature, inapplicable to all plain and urgent things. Men take thought and ponder rationalistically, touching remote things⁠—things that only theoretically matter, such as the transit of Venus. But only at their peril can men rationalize about so practical a matter as health.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
Chesterton opens with a joke that is also an argument. The English, he says, are proud of the wrong things. A Frenchman can boast of being logical and stay logical, but an Englishman who boasts of being simple and direct stops being either. Some virtues die the moment you become conscious of them. You cannot, as he puts it, be conscious of being unconscious. That sets up his target: the fans of the simple life, the vegetarians, the plain dressers, the followers of Tolstoy, even the Doukhobors, a Russian Christian sect that refused to fight in wars or own much property and that Tolstoy helped move to Canada.

His complaint is precise. These reformers, he says, make us simple in the unimportant things and complex in the important ones. They want a plain diet, plain clothes, plain manners, a plain economic system. But in philosophy, loyalty, and spiritual belief they ask for something fiercely elaborate. Then comes one of his best lines: it matters very little whether a man eats a grilled tomato or a plain one, but it matters a great deal whether he eats a plain tomato with a grilled mind. In other words, the menu is trivial and the mind is everything.

From there he flips a famous slogan. The reformers love the phrase plain living and high thinking. Chesterton says they need the opposite: high living and plain thinking. A little high living, a feast or a toast, would teach them that celebration is older than philosophy, that the loving cup is as old as hunger, and that ritual is older than any religion. A little plain thinking would teach them how strange their own ethics are. Here is where the man in sandals appears, holding a raw tomato, declaring that love of family and country are obstacles to universal love. The plain thinker's reply is gentle and devastating: what a great deal of trouble you must have taken to feel like that. Chesterton's point is that ordinary human loyalties are natural, and it takes elaborate effort to talk yourself out of them.

The deeper layer is about wonder. He says the only simplicity that matters is the kind that accepts and enjoys, the kind that sees everything with astonishment and fear and joy. His model is the child, who treats a tree and a lamppost as equally marvelous, so that neither is merely natural or merely artificial. Both are splendid and unexplained. The essay's closing note is that the real problem with machines is not that they are mechanical but that people become mechanical, and that when we lose the childlike poetry of things, no change of habit will bring it back.

A first-time reader might miss how personal this is. Chesterton is not defending luxury as such. He is defending the capacity to be grateful, which he thinks the austere crowd has lost while congratulating itself on its virtue.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
The essay is a good example of Chesterton at his most quotable, and also at his most slippery. Its strengths are obvious. The central distinction, between simplicity of habit and simplicity of heart, is genuinely useful, and he states it in images that stick: the grilled mind, the tomato, the caviar eaten on impulse versus the grape-nuts eaten on principle. That last pairing is a small masterpiece of comic compression. It lets him say, in a dozen words, that spontaneity is a matter of spirit rather than menu, and that a rule followed solemnly can be more artificial than a luxury enjoyed freely.

His method is the paradox, and here the craft is real. He takes a slogan everyone has heard, turns it upside down, and shows that the inverted version is arguably truer. High living and plain thinking is not just a joke. It contains an actual claim: that those who deny themselves pleasure on principle often become the most tangled thinkers, while those who enjoy things honestly tend to see them more clearly. The prose is brisk, the sentences land with a snap, and the humor never fully covers the argument.

But the essay has weaknesses a careful reader should notice. First, Chesterton lumps together very different people. A vegetarian who simply prefers vegetables, a Tolstoyan pacifist who has thought hard about violence, and a health faddist selling cereal are all dropped into one basket. He is far more convincing against the faddist than against Tolstoy, whose moral seriousness he mostly mocks rather than answers. The line about how much trouble the sandal-wearer must have taken is funny, but it is not a refutation of pacifism. It is a rhetorical dodge that makes a disagreement look like a psychological symptom.

Second, there is a convenient circularity. He defines real simplicity as the simplicity of the heart, then assures us that people who cultivate austerity lack it, while people who enjoy cigars and Burgundy have it. That is the sort of claim you cannot easily check, and it conveniently flatters the author's own habits. His later insistence that war is not invariably sinful is stated far more confidently than it is argued here.

Third, the essay can feel dated. Jaeger woolen underclothes, Plasmon, and the coats of the stomach were specific Edwardian fads, and some of the humor requires footnotes. The closing appeal to the Gospel words about taking no thought for food and clothing is moving, but it shifts the argument from persuasion to scripture without warning.

Even so, the essay's core insight survives. It is not a careful treatise. It is a sharp, funny provocation, and it works best when read as one: an invitation to ask whether our habits of virtue have quietly replaced the joy they were meant to protect.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
It is worth being honest that this particular essay did not change history by itself. Its influence is the influence of Heretics as a whole, and of the Chesterton style it helped define. Heretics appeared in 1905, when Chesterton was in his early thirties and already a well-known columnist. The book collected his pieces criticizing the leading ideas of his age, taking on figures like George Bernard Shaw, H. G. Wells, Rudyard Kipling, and the champions of art for art's sake. Its most lasting effect was to provoke a challenge. A critic and friend, G. S. Street, remarked that he would take Chesterton's complaints more seriously once Chesterton had set out his own philosophy. That challenge produced Orthodoxy three years later, the book many readers consider Chesterton's masterpiece. So one of the most concrete results of the Heretics essays, this one included, was to push their author into stating what he actually believed.

On a wider scale, the essay belongs to a long tradition of skepticism about moral fashion. The idea that a lifestyle can become a performance, that virtue can curdle into smugness, has a long afterlife. Later readers will recognize the type Chesterton sketches in every era's version of the earnest self-improver, from health cults to minimalism to fashionable asceticism. His insight that conspicuous simplicity is often a kind of display, and that it can coexist with complicated vanity, is one cultural critics still borrow, whether or not they know where it came from.

It also fed the Distributist and Christian humanist currents that Chesterton led. His defense of feasts, rituals, and ordinary loyalties became part of the case he later made for family, small property, and local life. Writers who shared his temperament, such as Hilaire Belloc, and later admirers like C. S. Lewis and J. R. R. Tolkien, absorbed the idea that the artificial is not the enemy of the natural, and that joy and ceremony are signs of health.

In education, the essay is mostly encountered in anthologies of Chesterton, in courses on the English essay, or as a short, funny example of paradox and argument by reversal. Teachers use it to show how a writer can attack an idea by turning its own slogan against it. It is also read by people interested in the Edwardian debates over socialism, vegetarianism, pacifism, and Tolstoyan communities.

There were no adaptations to speak of, but the lines survive in quotation. The grilled mind remains a stock phrase among people who admire Chesterton, and the contrast between plain living and high living is the sort of thing a reader can carry away intact after a single listen. That portability, more than any political consequence, is the essay's real legacy.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
What readers have most often loved in Chesterton, and in this essay especially, is the sense of being let out of a stuffy room. The Edwardian simple-life movement could be earnest, sanctimonious, and joyless. Chesterton arrived with laughter, a bottle of Burgundy, and an argument that sounded like common sense turned inside out. Many readers, then and now, feel relieved to hear someone say that it is fine to enjoy a good meal, that pleasure is not a betrayal of spirit, and that the habit of constant self-denial can be its own vanity.

They also love the comedy. The man in sandals with the raw tomato is one of the funniest small portraits in English prose. It works because it is specific: the tomato is held firmly in the right hand, as though it were evidence. The reply, what a great deal of trouble you must have taken, is the sort of line people repeat, because it captures a recognizable feeling about performative virtue without being cruel about the person.

Admirers have long praised how Chesterton combines wit with real conviction. Writers as different as Jorge Luis Borges, who admired his stories and paradoxes, and Marshall McLuhan, who credited him as an influence, were drawn to his habit of making the familiar strange. C. S. Lewis later said that reading Chesterton helped open his mind to Christianity, though that credit is for the broader body of his work rather than this single essay. Among general readers, Chesterton is loved for being an optimist who was not a fool: someone who believed in gratitude and wonder but also knew how to argue.

There is another reason this piece resonates. Its central claim, that the childlike capacity to be astonished is the thing to protect, speaks to people who feel the modern world has made them tired and jaded. Chesterton's picture of a child who sees the lamppost and the tree as equally marvelous, and who plays at steam engines in the middle of a field, is genuinely tender. It makes the case for wonder without sentimentality, partly because it is attached to a joke about engines and clockwork.

Finally, readers love the ending's turn. After all the teasing, he lands on something close to a prayer: that the real way to be healthy is to think about something else, to climb toward the seventh heaven and let the pores of the skin look after themselves. It is a lovely, slightly mad sentence, and it leaves the reader feeling that the whole argument has been a way of pointing at joy.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
Chesterton's critics have never been in short supply, and this essay offers several easy targets. The most common charge is that he argues by caricature. The man in sandals with the tomato is a comic type, not a real opponent. Tolstoy was a serious moral thinker who had wrestled with violence, property, and faith, and the Doukhobors had endured persecution for their pacifism. Reducing them to the cranks of the health-food shop lets Chesterton score points without engaging their best reasons. Readers sympathetic to pacifism or to voluntary poverty have found the essay glib on exactly the subjects where glibness is least appropriate.

A second objection is that he treats his own preferences as universal wisdom. The defense of cigars, Burgundy, and a hansom cab is charming, but it comes close to saying that the writer's habits are the habits of a healthy soul. Critics have noticed that the simple-life movement, whatever its absurdities, was partly a response to real problems: industrial squalor, adulterated food, urban poverty, and consumerism. Chesterton's reply, that these are matters of philosophy rather than lifestyle, is reasonable but sidesteps the fact that habits and systems do shape lives.

Third, there is the charge that his paradox method proves less than it seems. Reversing a slogan is a wonderful way to be memorable, but it does not by itself establish that the reversal is true. High living and plain thinking is a delightful phrase, and some readers have felt that it works as a debating trick, leaving the substantive question of how much simplicity is wise unresolved. Similarly, the sweeping assurance that plain thinking will reject the idea that war is always wrong is asserted, not demonstrated.

Fourth, some modern readers are uneasy with the way Chesterton's wider outlook shades into a conservative, religiously confident view of society, with assumptions about nation, family, and ritual that are treated as obviously natural. Critics who admire his style have still found that these assumptions go unexamined. Others have pointed out that the essay passes quickly over the poor, for whom plain living was never a choice, and who are absent from this very comfortable argument.

Finally, a historical caution. The essay's anxieties are Edwardian, and a few of its jokes depend on knowing now-forgotten products and fashions. Some find the humor to have aged better than the argument. A fair summary is that the piece is widely enjoyed for its wit, while its reasoning is regarded as stronger as inspired provocation than as rigorous philosophy.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
Chesterton sits in a particular English tradition: the essayist as public debater, using humor and common sense to puncture the pretensions of intellectual fashion. He descends from writers like Samuel Johnson, William Hazlitt, and Charles Lamb, and shares a family resemblance with Dickens, whom he loved and wrote about with great warmth. Like Dickens, he believes in comfort, hospitality, and the warmth of the hearth, and he is suspicious of reformers who treat ordinary human pleasure as a problem to be solved.

The essay also belongs to a long argument about simplicity itself. On one side stand Rousseau, Thoreau, Tolstoy, and the Arts and Crafts movement, who believed that modern life had grown corrupt and artificial, and who urged a return to nature and plainness. On the other stand thinkers who think this impulse is itself a luxury or a mask. Chesterton is a witty member of the second camp, though he is unusual in that he is no friend of modern industry either. His quarrel is not with simplicity as a value but with simplicity as a method. Thoreau, for example, is a more subtle opponent than Chesterton's caricature suggests, since Walden is much more about attention and wonder than about vegetarian rules, and Chesterton and Thoreau would have agreed more than the essay admits.

What descends from it? You can trace its spirit in later critiques of lifestyle virtue, in essays about consumerism disguised as minimalism, and in the broader suspicion of what is now called virtue signaling. George Orwell, who had a very different politics, made a similar complaint in his own bluntly funny way about the sandal-wearing, fruit-juice-drinking cranks of the left in The Road to Wigan Pier. Orwell and Chesterton disagreed about almost everything, but they shared a dislike of the faddish and the self-righteous, and the comparison is worth making. Within Chesterton's own work, this essay is a preview of the themes of Orthodoxy: wonder, gratitude, the importance of ordinary things, and the idea that the wildest thing in the world is the world itself.

Why read it now? Partly because the target has never gone away. Every generation produces its own tomato-wielding prophet, and every generation needs someone to ask whether the effort of feeling a certain way is a sign of the feeling's reality. It is also worth reading for the pleasure of the prose, which is high-spirited and funny and surprisingly tender.

And finally, it is worth reading because it asks a question that remains open. If simplicity is not about what we eat or wear, what is it about? Chesterton's answer, astonishment and gladness, may not settle the question, but it points toward a way of living that is generous rather than severe, and that is still a pretty good place to start.

essays.title: Science and the Savages
essays.author: G. K. Chesterton
essays.epigraph: You cannot understand a ritual or a poem from the outside by counting pebbles; you can only understand it because you share the common human heart.
essays.keyContext: This essay by G. K. Chesterton appeared in 1905 in his book Heretics, where he took on the prominent ideas of his day. Here his target is the new science of folklore and anthropology, the study of myths, rituals, and so-called primitive peoples. This was the age of scholars who collected customs from around the world and explained them with confident theories about what early humans must have believed. Chesterton, a journalist with a gift for common sense and paradox, thought the scientists were making a basic mistake. They treated human beings like insects, studying them coldly from outside, and so they missed what any ordinary person already knows from the inside: that people do many things, from laying flowers on graves to dancing at balls, without any tidy reason at all. His argument is that to understand human origins, you should look at yourself and your own neighbors. As you listen, notice how funny and how serious he manages to be at once.
paragraphs: A permanent disadvantage of the study of folklore and kindred subjects is that the man of science can hardly be in the nature of things very frequently a man of the world. He is a student of nature; he is scarcely ever a student of human nature. And even where this difficulty is overcome, and he is in some sense a student of human nature, this is only a very faint beginning of the painful progress towards being human. For the study of primitive race and religion stands apart in one important respect from all, or nearly all, the ordinary scientific studies. A man can understand astronomy only by being an astronomer; he can understand entomology only by being an entomologist (or, perhaps, an insect); but he can understand a great deal of anthropology merely by being a man. He is himself the animal which he studies. Hence arises the fact which strikes the eye everywhere in the records of ethnology and folklore⁠—the fact that the same frigid and detached spirit which leads to success in the study of astronomy or botany leads to disaster in the study of mythology or human origins. It is necessary to cease to be a man in order to do justice to a microbe; it is not necessary to cease to be a man in order to do justice to men. That same suppression of sympathies, that same waving away of intuitions or guesswork which make a man preternaturally clever in dealing with the stomach of a spider, will make him preternaturally stupid in dealing with the heart of man. He is making himself inhuman in order to understand humanity. An ignorance of the other world is boasted by many men of science; but in this matter their defect arises, not from ignorance of the other world, but from ignorance of this world. For the secrets about which anthropologists concern themselves can be best learnt, not from books or voyages, but from the ordinary commerce of man with man. The secret of why some savage tribe worships monkeys or the moon is not to be found even by travelling among those savages and taking down their answers in a notebook, although the cleverest man may pursue this course. The answer to the riddle is in England; it is in London; nay, it is in his own heart. When a man has discovered why men in Bond Street wear black hats he will at the same moment have discovered why men in Timbuktu wear red feathers. The mystery in the heart of some savage war-dance should not be studied in books of scientific travel; it should be studied at a subscription ball. If a man desires to find out the origins of religions, let him not go to the Sandwich Islands; let him go to church. If a man wishes to know the origin of human society, to know what society, philosophically speaking, really is, let him not go into the British Museum; let him go into society.

This total misunderstanding of the real nature of ceremonial gives rise to the most awkward and dehumanized versions of the conduct of men in rude lands or ages. The man of science, not realizing that ceremonial is essentially a thing which is done without a reason, has to find a reason for every sort of ceremonial, and, as might be supposed, the reason is generally a very absurd one⁠—absurd because it originates not in the simple mind of the barbarian, but in the sophisticated mind of the professor. The teamed man will say, for instance, “The natives of Mumbojumbo Land believe that the dead man can eat and will require food upon his journey to the other world. This is attested by the fact that they place food in the grave, and that any family not complying with this rite is the object of the anger of the priests and the tribe.” To anyone acquainted with humanity this way of talking is topsy-turvy. It is like saying, “The English in the twentieth century believed that a dead man could smell. This is attested by the fact that they always covered his grave with lilies, violets, or other flowers. Some priestly and tribal terrors were evidently attached to the neglect of this action, as we have records of several old ladies who were very much disturbed in mind because their wreaths had not arrived in time for the funeral.” It may be of course that savages put food with a dead man because they think that a dead man can eat, or weapons with a dead man because they think that a dead man can fight. But personally I do not believe that they think anything of the kind. I believe they put food or weapons on the dead for the same reason that we put flowers, because it is an exceedingly natural and obvious thing to do. We do not understand, it is true, the emotion which makes us think it obvious and natural; but that is because, like all the important emotions of human existence it is essentially irrational. We do not understand the savage for the same reason that the savage does not understand himself. And the savage does not understand himself for the same reason that we do not understand ourselves either.

The obvious truth is that the moment any matter has passed through the human mind it is finally and forever spoilt for all purposes of science. It has become a thing incurably mysterious and infinite; this mortal has put on immortality. Even what we call our material desires are spiritual, because they are human. Science can analyse a pork-chop, and say how much of it is phosphorus and how much is protein; but science cannot analyse any man’s wish for a pork-chop, and say how much of it is hunger, how much custom, how much nervous fancy, how much a haunting love of the beautiful. The man’s desire for the pork-chop remains literally as mystical and ethereal as his desire for heaven. All attempts, therefore, at a science of any human things, at a science of history, a science of folklore, a science of sociology, are by their nature not merely hopeless, but crazy. You can no more be certain in economic history that a man’s desire for money was merely a desire for money than you can be certain in hagiology that a saint’s desire for God was merely a desire for God. And this kind of vagueness in the primary phenomena of the study is an absolutely final blow to anything in the nature of a science. Men can construct a science with very few instruments, or with very plain instruments; but no one on earth could construct a science with unreliable instruments. A man might work out the whole of mathematics with a handful of pebbles, but not with a handful of clay which was always falling apart into new fragments, and falling together into new combinations. A man might measure heaven and earth with a reed, but not with a growing reed.

As one of the enormous follies of folklore, let us take the case of the transmigration of stories, and the alleged unity of their source. Story after story the scientific mythologists have cut out of its place in history, and pinned side by side with similar stories in their museum of fables. The process is industrious, it is fascinating, and the whole of it rests on one of the plainest fallacies in the world. That a story has been told all over the place at some time or other, not only does not prove that it never really happened; it does not even faintly indicate or make slightly more probable that it never happened. That a large number of fishermen have falsely asserted that they have caught a pike two feet long, does not in the least affect the question of whether anyone ever really did so. That numberless journalists announce a Franco-German war merely for money is no evidence one way or the other upon the dark question of whether such a war ever occurred. Doubtless in a few hundred years the innumerable Franco-German wars that did not happen will have cleared the scientific mind of any belief in the legendary war of ’70 which did. But that will be because if folklore students remain at all, their nature will be unchanged; and their services to folklore will be still as they are at present, greater than they know. For in truth these men do something far more godlike than studying legends; they create them.

There are two kinds of stories which the scientists say cannot be true, because everybody tells them. The first class consists of the stories which are told everywhere, because they are somewhat odd or clever; there is nothing in the world to prevent their having happened to somebody as an adventure any more than there is anything to prevent their having occurred, as they certainly did occur, to somebody as an idea. But they are not likely to have happened to many people. The second class of their “myths” consist of the stories that are told everywhere for the simple reason that they happen everywhere. Of the first class, for instance, we might take such an example as the story of William Tell, now generally ranked among legends upon the sole ground that it is found in the tales of other peoples. Now, it is obvious that this was told everywhere because whether true or fictitious it is what is called “a good story;” it is odd, exciting, and it has a climax. But to suggest that some such eccentric incident can never have happened in the whole history of archery, or that it did not happen to any particular person of whom it is told, is stark impudence. The idea of shooting at a mark attached to some valuable or beloved person is an idea doubtless that might easily have occurred to any inventive poet. But it is also an idea that might easily occur to any boastful archer. It might be one of the fantastic caprices of some storyteller. It might equally well be one of the fantastic caprices of some tyrant. It might occur first in real life and afterwards occur in legends. Or it might just as well occur first in legends and afterwards occur in real life. If no apple has ever been shot off a boy’s head from the beginning of the world, it may be done tomorrow morning, and by somebody who has never heard of William Tell.

This type of tale, indeed, may be pretty fairly paralleled with the ordinary anecdote terminating in a repartee or an Irish bull. Such a retort as the famous “Je ne vois pas la necessité” we have all seen attributed to Talleyrand, to Voltaire, to Henri Quatre, to an anonymous judge, and so on. But this variety does not in any way make it more likely that the thing was never said at all. It is highly likely that it was really said by somebody unknown. It is highly likely that it was really said by Talleyrand. In any case, it is not any more difficult to believe that the mot might have occurred to a man in conversation than to a man writing memoirs. It might have occurred to any of the men I have mentioned. But there is this point of distinction about it, that it is not likely to have occurred to all of them. And this is where the first class of so-called myth differs from the second to which I have previously referred. For there is a second class of incident found to be common to the stories of five or six heroes, say to Sigurd, to Hercules, to Rustem, to the Cid, and so on. And the peculiarity of this myth is that not only is it highly reasonable to imagine that it really happened to one hero, but it is highly reasonable to imagine that it really happened to all of them. Such a story, for instance, is that of a great man having his strength swayed or thwarted by the mysterious weakness of a woman. The anecdotal story, the story of William Tell, is as I have said, popular, because it is peculiar. But this kind of story, the story of Samson and Delilah, of Arthur and Guinevere, is obviously popular because it is not peculiar. It is popular as good, quiet fiction is popular, because it tells the truth about people. If the ruin of Samson by a woman, and the ruin of Hercules by a woman, have a common legendary origin, it is gratifying to know that we can also explain, as a fable, the ruin of Nelson by a woman and the ruin of Parnell by a woman. And, indeed, I have no doubt whatever that, some centuries hence, the students of folklore will refuse altogether to believe that Elizabeth Barrett eloped with Robert Browning, and will prove their point up to the hilt by the unquestionable fact that the whole fiction of the period was full of such elopements from end to end.

Possibly the most pathetic of all the delusions of the modern students of primitive belief is the notion they have about the thing they call anthropomorphism. They believe that primitive men attributed phenomena to a god in human form in order to explain them, because his mind in its sullen limitation could not reach any further than his own clownish existence. The thunder was called the voice of a man, the lightning the eyes of a man, because by this explanation they were made more reasonable and comfortable. The final cure for all this kind of philosophy is to walk down a lane at night. Anyone who does so will discover very quickly that men pictured something semi-human at the back of all things, not because such a thought was natural, but because it was supernatural; not because it made things more comprehensible, but because it made them a hundred times more incomprehensible and mysterious. For a man walking down a lane at night can see the conspicuous fact that as long as nature keeps to her own course, she has no power with us at all. As long as a tree is a tree, it is a top-heavy monster with a hundred arms, a thousand tongues, and only one leg. But so long as a tree is a tree, it does not frighten us at all. It begins to be something alien, to be something strange, only when it looks like ourselves. When a tree really looks like a man our knees knock under us. And when the whole universe looks like a man we fall on our faces.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
Chesterton begins with a puzzle about method. Most sciences require the scientist to stand apart from the thing studied. You do not need to feel like a star to understand astronomy. But anthropology and folklore are different, because the scientist is himself the animal under study. A man can understand a great deal about humanity merely by being human. So the cold, detached attitude that helps you dissect a spider actively harms you when you try to understand a person. As Chesterton puts it, the scholar is making himself inhuman in order to understand humanity.

From this he draws a famous consequence: the answer to the riddle of why a distant tribe does a strange thing is to be found not in Africa or the Pacific but in London, and in one's own heart. When you have discovered why men in Bond Street wear black hats, you will have discovered why men in Timbuktu wear red feathers. The secrets of a war dance are better studied at a subscription ball. If you want the origin of religion, go to church. If you want to understand society, go into society rather than the British Museum.

The essay's best illustration concerns ceremony. Learned men, he says, assume every ritual must have a stated reason, so they conclude that a tribe puts food in a grave because they believe the dead can eat. Chesterton imagines a future scholar reading that the English of the twentieth century believed a dead man could smell flowers, because they covered his grave with wreaths, and that old ladies were upset when the wreaths arrived late. The joke exposes the mistake. Ceremony is, in his phrase, something done without a reason. People put food or weapons or flowers with the dead because it is an obvious and natural thing to do, and the emotion behind it is deep and hard to explain, even to the person feeling it.

That leads to his boldest claim: that anything that has passed through the human mind becomes forever unsuitable for strict science. Science can analyze a pork chop, but not a man's wish for one. Desire is mystical whether it is for a chop or for heaven. A science of history or folklore, therefore, rests on unreliable instruments, like trying to measure the world with a growing reed.

Finally he attacks a favorite argument of the folklorists: that a story told in many places must be a myth. That many fishermen claim a two-foot pike does not prove no one ever caught one. Some stories spread because they are good, like William Tell, and some because they happen everywhere. Either way, widespread telling proves nothing about whether it happened. The layer a first-time reader may miss is that Chesterton is defending the dignity of ordinary people, savage and civilized alike, against being treated as specimens.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
This is vintage Chesterton, and it shows both his brilliance and his habit of overreach. Start with what is genuinely excellent. The core insight, that human behavior cannot be understood entirely from outside, is a real one, and anthropology itself eventually absorbed a version of it. The ideas of fieldwork, of taking participants' own understanding seriously, and of avoiding the arrogant assumption that other people's customs are mere mistakes, would all become central to the discipline in the generations after Chesterton wrote. His mockery of the scholar who finds a literal belief behind every gesture hits a genuine weakness of the intellectualist school of the time, which tended to treat ritual as bad science rather than as something else entirely, like expression or habit or feeling.

The craft is delightful. The flowers on the grave, parodied in the language of an ethnographer, are an almost perfect piece of comic argument. It does in a paragraph what a footnote-heavy academic rebuttal might take pages to do: it makes the reader feel the absurdity from the inside. The comparison of Bond Street hats to Timbuktu feathers and the idea of studying war dances at a subscription ball are the kind of lines that make an argument memorable. The pike and the Franco-German war are neat, plain examples that make a logical point without any jargon.

But the essay also has real weaknesses. First, Chesterton slides from a good point to a sweeping one.
