Later conservative thinkers, such as Michael Oakeshott, who wrote about the difference between rationalism and tradition in politics, developed related ideas in a more philosophical key. C. S. Lewis's warning against chronological snobbery, the assumption that whatever is newer is better, echoes Chesterton's point. Outside politics, movements to revive crafts, local food, and older ways of building may be seen as in part carrying out his claim that old tools are not blunted by use.

It is also instructive to compare the chapter with works that take the opposite view. Wells's A Modern Utopia and the futurist manifestos of Marinetti celebrated speed and novelty, while the Victorian Whig historians told the story of history as steady improvement. Chesterton is the mocking counterpoint to both.

Why read it now? We live in an age of constant prediction, from technology forecasts to political promises, and also in an age of intense nostalgia. Chesterton's chapter helps us notice both impulses, and ask whether each is a form of fear. Its most useful gift is a question: are you running toward something, or away from something? Whether or not you agree with his answers, the question, and the laughter along the way, are worth the few minutes it takes to listen.

essays.title: The Wildness of Domesticity
essays.author: G. K. Chesterton
essays.epigraph: If we want wildness and the element of the unpredictable, we do not find it in the regimented office or club, but inside the ordinary family home.
essays.keyContext: G. K. Chesterton wrote this piece in 1910 as part of his book What's Wrong with the World, a fiery, funny argument about how modern England had gone astray. Chesterton was a huge figure in Edwardian London, a journalist, novelist and debater famous for turning common sense upside down to show you something true. Here the target is a very modern assumption: that home life is dull, and that real freedom and adventure live out in the world. Chesterton says that idea comes from the rich, who have servants to run their houses and plenty of money to cushion their escapades. For ordinary working people, he argues, home is the one place where they are actually in charge. The essay is also the opening of a larger case for widespread property and family life, which later grew into a movement called distributism. You do not have to agree with him, and many readers never have. Listen for the jokes, the odd examples, and the surprising claim underneath them.
paragraphs: In the course of this crude study we shall have to touch on what is called the problem of poverty, especially the dehumanised poverty of modern industrialism. But in this primary matter of the ideal the difficulty is not the problem of poverty, but the problem of wealth. It is the special psychology of leisure and luxury that falsifies life. Some experience of modern movements of the sort called “advanced” has led me to the conviction that they generally repose upon some experience peculiar to the rich. It is so with that fallacy of free love of which I have already spoken; the idea of sexuality as a string of episodes. That implies a long holiday in which to get tired of one woman, and a motor car in which to wander looking for others; it also implies money for maintenances. An omnibus conductor has hardly time to love his own wife, let alone other people’s wives. And the success with which nuptial estrangements are depicted in modern “problem plays” is due to the fact that there is only one thing that a drama cannot depict⁠—that is a hard day’s work. I could give many other instances of this plutocratic assumption behind progressive fads. For instance, there is a plutocratic assumption behind the phrase “Why should woman be economically dependent upon man?” The answer is that among poor and practical people she isn’t; except in the sense in which he is dependent upon her. A hunter has to tear his clothes; there must be somebody to mend them. A fisher has to catch fish; there must be somebody to cook them. It is surely quite clear that this modern notion that woman is a mere “pretty clinging parasite,” “a plaything,” etc., arose through the somber contemplation of some rich banking family, in which the banker at least went to the city and pretended to do something, while the banker’s wife went to the Park and did not pretend to do anything at all. A poor man and his wife are a business partnership. If one partner in a firm of publishers interviews the authors while the other interviews the clerks, is one of them economically dependent? Was Hodder a pretty parasite clinging to Stoughton? Was Marshall a mere plaything for Snelgrove?

But of all the modern notions generated by mere wealth the worst is this: the notion that domesticity is dull and tame. Inside the home (they say) is dead decorum and routine; outside is adventure and variety. This is indeed a rich man’s opinion. The rich man knows that his own house moves on vast and soundless wheels of wealth: is run by regiments of servants, by a swift and silent ritual. On the other hand, every sort of vagabondage of romance is open to him in the streets outside. He has plenty of money and can afford to be a tramp. His wildest adventure will end in a restaurant, while the yokel’s tamest adventure may end in a police-court. If he smashes a window he can pay for it; if he smashes a man he can pension him. He can (like the millionaire in the story) buy an hotel to get a glass of gin. And because he, the luxurious man, dictates the tone of nearly all “advanced” and “progressive” thought, we have almost forgotten what a home really means to the overwhelming millions of mankind.

For the truth is, that to the moderately poor the home is the only place of liberty. Nay, it is the only place of anarchy. It is the only spot on the earth where a man can alter arrangements suddenly, make an experiment or indulge in a whim. Everywhere else he goes he must accept the strict rules of the shop, inn, club, or museum that he happens to enter. He can eat his meals on the floor in his own house if he likes. I often do it myself; it gives a curious, childish, poetic, picnic feeling. There would be considerable trouble if I tried to do it in an A.B.C. tea shop. A man can wear a dressing gown and slippers in his house; while I am sure that this would not be permitted at the Savoy, though I never actually tested the point. If you go to a restaurant you must drink some of the wines on the wine list, all of them if you insist, but certainly some of them. But if you have a house and garden you can try to make hollyhock tea or convolvulus wine if you like. For a plain, hardworking man the home is not the one tame place in the world of adventure. It is the one wild place in the world of rules and set tasks. The home is the one place where he can put the carpet on the ceiling or the slates on the floor if he wants to. When a man spends every night staggering from bar to bar or from music-hall to music-hall, we say that he is living an irregular life. But he is not; he is living a highly regular life, under the dull, and often oppressive laws of such places. Some times he is not allowed even to sit down in the bars; and frequently he is not allowed to sing in the music-halls. Hotels may be defined as places where you are forced to dress; and theaters may be defined as places where you are forbidden to smoke. A man can only picnic at home.

Now I take, as I have said, this small human omnipotence, this possession of a definite cell or chamber of liberty, as the working model for the present inquiry. Whether we can give every English man a free home of his own or not, at least we should desire it; and he desires it. For the moment we speak of what he wants, not of what he expects to get. He wants, for instance, a separate house; he does not want a semidetached house. He may be forced in the commercial race to share one wall with another man. Similarly he might be forced in a three-legged race to share one leg with another man; but it is not so that he pictures himself in his dreams of elegance and liberty. Again, he does not desire a flat. He can eat and sleep and praise God in a flat; he can eat and sleep and praise God in a railway train. But a railway train is not a house, because it is a house on wheels. And a flat is not a house, because it is a house on stilts. An idea of earthy contact and foundation, as well as an idea of separation and independence, is a part of this instructive human picture.

I take, then, this one institution as a test. As every normal man desires a woman, and children born of a woman, every normal man desires a house of his own to put them into. He does not merely want a roof above him and a chair below him; he wants an objective and visible kingdom; a fire at which he can cook what food he likes, a door he can open to what friends he chooses. This is the normal appetite of men; I do not say there are not exceptions. There may be saints above the need and philanthropists below it. Opalstein, now he is a duke, may have got used to more than this; and when he was a convict may have got used to less. But the normality of the thing is enormous. To give nearly everybody ordinary houses would please nearly everybody; that is what I assert without apology. Now in modern England (as you eagerly point out) it is very difficult to give nearly everybody houses. Quite so; I merely set up the desideratum; and ask the reader to leave it standing there while he turns with me to a consideration of what really happens in the social wars of our time.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
Chesterton opens by shifting the question. He says that when we talk about the ideal of a good life, the real difficulty is not poverty but wealth. His claim is that a lot of fashionable, so-called advanced ideas rest on experiences that only rich people have. He gives quick, deliberately cheeky examples. Free love, he says, assumes a long holiday in which to get tired of one partner and a motor car in which to go looking for others. An omnibus conductor, he jokes, has hardly time to love his own wife, let alone other people's. Modern problem plays can show a marriage falling apart because, he says, the one thing a drama cannot show is a hard day's work.

The same move is made with the complaint that women are economically dependent on men. Among poor and practical people, he says, that is not how things work: the hunter tears his clothes and someone must mend them, the fisher catches fish and someone must cook them. A poor couple, in his picture, is a business partnership, like two publishers who divide the work between them. Notice that this is a claim about what the rich get wrong, and he is using it to set up the real subject.

That subject arrives with the sentence about domesticity. The worst notion bred by wealth, he says, is that home is dull and tame, with decorum and routine inside and adventure and variety outside. That, he says, is a rich man's opinion, because the rich man's house runs itself on wheels of money and servants, while the streets outside are open to him as a playground. His wildest adventure ends in a restaurant; a poor man's tamest adventure may end in a police court. If the rich man smashes a window he pays for it.

Then comes the central, surprising turn. For the moderately poor, the home is the only place of liberty, and even the only place of anarchy. Everywhere else a person follows the rules of the shop, the inn, the club or the museum. At home you can eat on the floor, wear slippers, brew hollyhock tea, or, in his best joke, put the carpet on the ceiling. The man who goes from bar to bar is not living an irregular life at all, Chesterton says, but a highly regular one under the dull laws of those places. A man can only picnic at home.

Finally he turns that observation into a working model. Everyone, he says, wants a house of his own: a separate house, not a semidetached one, and not a flat, which he calls a house on stilts. He wants what Chesterton calls an objective and visible kingdom, a fire to cook at and a door to open to chosen friends. The excerpt closes by asking the reader to leave that picture standing while he looks at what actually happens in the social conflicts of the age. The layer a first-time reader may miss is that this charming praise of slippers and hollyhock tea is the foundation of a political argument.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
As rhetoric, this is a delight, and it shows why Chesterton was one of the most quoted journalists of his time. The method is the paradox: take a belief everyone holds, turn it over, and show the underside. Home is boring, says the sophisticated modern. No, says Chesterton, home is the one wild place in a world of rules. The examples are concrete and funny enough that you accept the claim before you have decided whether it is true. The line about hotels being places where you are forced to dress and theaters being places where you are forbidden to smoke is a perfect specimen, a definition that is unfair and exactly right at the same time.

The craft is also sharper than the cheerful tone suggests. Chesterton makes his argument by class analysis, which is a surprise from a writer later filed under conservative. He points out that who gets to speak shapes what counts as an idea. Progressive thought, he says, is dictated by the luxurious, so we forget what a home means to the great majority. That is a genuinely interesting insight about how the comfortable mistake their own situation for universal truth, and it still applies.

The weaknesses are real, though. The argument leans on sweeping generalizations that he never supports. When he says every normal man desires a house of his own, or that this is the normal appetite of men, he is announcing a fact rather than demonstrating it, and the escape hatch of allowing for saints and philanthropists does not fix that. The word man does a great deal of work here. The home he describes is a place where a man is king, and the woman who mends the clothes and cooks the fish appears only as part of a business partnership in which she has nothing to say. Today that reads as a blind spot, because the essay praises home as liberty without asking whose liberty.

His comparisons also rig the game. He sets the actual conditions of a dim tea shop or a bar against the best imaginable version of a private home, and neglects that the poor home of 1910 could mean a crowded, damp, exhausting place where the freedom to put the carpet on the ceiling was not the first thing on anyone's mind. He admits that the difficulty of giving everyone a house is a real one, but he sets it aside, which is honest and also convenient.

And the jokes occasionally substitute for reasoning. The three-legged race comparison is wonderful, but it does not tell us why a shared wall actually matters. Still, as a piece of writing, the energy is infectious, and the logic underneath is more disciplined than it first appears. You can be unconvinced and still admire how skilfully he gets you to nod along.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
What's Wrong with the World, published in 1910, was one of Chesterton's most important books of social argument, and this chapter is a good sample of its spirit. The book sets out an argument that the real problem of modern society is that most people have been deprived of the small, solid kinds of property and independence that make a free life possible. That idea did not stay on the page. Chesterton and his friend Hilaire Belloc, a writer who shared his convictions, developed it into a movement called distributism, which argued for spreading ownership of land and workshops widely rather than concentrating it in the hands of a few capitalists or a state. In the 1920s Chesterton helped found a Distributist League, and the movement had its own newspaper. It never won power, but it left a distinctive third voice in debates that were otherwise a contest between capitalism and socialism.

The influence also traveled through Catholic social thought. Chesterton was not yet a Catholic when he wrote this book, since he joined the Church in 1922, but his arguments about family, property and the dignity of ordinary work run close to ideas that church teachers developed in the same era. Later writers who think about the value of local, small-scale life, from advocates of land reform to some environmental and community-minded thinkers, have drawn on this tradition, sometimes without knowing his name. His phrase about the home being the one wild place in a world of rules is the sort of line that gets passed along from writer to writer.

Chesterton's career as a whole was shaped by books like this one. They established him as a public moralist who could argue with the most famous intellectuals of his day, including George Bernard Shaw and H. G. Wells, who were frequent friendly opponents. The essay's style, in which a surprising definition does the work of an argument, became his trademark. Later essayists who love paradox, such as those writing for opinion pages, owe something to his example.

As for how it is taught, it is more often read as a piece of rhetoric and a cultural document than as policy. Students of the Edwardian period read it to see what thoughtful people made of the housing crisis, women's changing roles and the rise of the very rich. It has also turned up in recent debates about work-from-home life, small property and the meaning of a house versus an apartment, because people keep rediscovering that the place where you can make your own rules matters. Its direct political legacy is modest, and its lasting power is mainly in the way it taught readers to question the assumptions of the comfortable.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
The first thing readers have loved is the sheer pleasure of the prose. Chesterton could make an argument feel like a conversation with the funniest person at the table. Admirers, including writers who disagreed with his politics, have often said that he was a master of surprise: he gives you a sentence that sounds absurd, and by the end of the paragraph it feels like something you had always half known. The image of eating dinner on the floor because you can is the kind of thing readers remember decades later.

Second, readers appreciated his defense of ordinary life. In an age when many progressive and artistic circles treated the family home as a trap or a convention to be escaped, Chesterton spoke up for the small, unglamorous pleasures of cooking at your own fire and welcoming your own friends. People who felt that their domestic life was undervalued, or condescended to by clever commentators, found in him an ally. For many readers, the essay offers a kind of permission to take the home seriously as a place of creativity, not just comfort.

Third, readers have admired the way he connects the private and the political. The essay moves from a joke about slippers to a vision of a society in which most people have a stake. Even those who dispute his conclusions often respect that he saw the link between how people live in their kitchens and how they are treated by the economy. His insight that the rich often mistake their own freedom from drudgery for a universal condition resonates with readers from many parts of the political spectrum.

Finally, there is a lasting affection for his tone. He is argumentative but not bitter, and he laughs at himself, too: he admits that he eats on the floor, and that he has never actually tested whether the Savoy would permit a dressing gown. That self-mocking honesty makes the radical claim easy to accept. Many readers have said that reading Chesterton feels like being let in on a joke that happens to be true.

Fans of the broader book have often singled out passages like this as the heart of it, where the author is most himself, playful and pointed together. Writers from many backgrounds have also praised his gift for making an abstract principle feel like something you could touch, like a carpet on a ceiling or a fire to cook at. For readers who come to him for the first time, that concreteness is often the entry point, and it is why a hundred-year-old argument about housing can still feel fresh.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
The most serious and most lasting objection concerns women. Chesterton wrote this book in the middle of the campaign for women's suffrage, and he opposed it, arguing that women's true sphere was the home and that the vote was a distraction. Feminist readers then and now have pointed out that his picture of the home as a place of liberty is a picture of liberty for the man of the house. The woman in his examples mends and cooks, and her freedom is never discussed. When he describes the poor couple as a business partnership, critics reply that a partnership in which one partner has no vote and no independent income is a strange one. Many readers who love his wit stumble here.

A second line of criticism is that he romanticizes poverty and domestic life. The home of a working family in 1910 could be overcrowded, unhealthy and dependent on a landlord, and a man with no savings might not be free to alter much at all. Socialists and reformers of his day argued that the way to freedom for ordinary people was better housing, shared services and stronger wages, not a nostalgic ideal of the detached cottage. Chesterton does acknowledge that it is hard to give everyone a house, but critics felt he then glided past the hardest part of the problem.

Third, many commentators have questioned his sweeping claims about what normal people want. By declaring that every normal man wants a separate house with an objective kingdom, he treats his own taste as a law of human nature. Others have pointed out that people want many different things, including flats, lodgings and communal life, and that the chance to live near neighbors or in a city can feel like liberty to some. The remark that a flat is a house on stilts is funny, but it does not prove that those who live in flats are unhappy.

There is also the broader complaint that Chesterton's arguments rely more on wit than on evidence. Opponents, including some of his friendly sparring partners, felt that a clever reversal can prove almost anything. A paradox sounds like a discovery but can be only a rearrangement. Readers who prefer data and statistics find little of either here.

Finally, some later historians have noted that the distributist politics that grew from these ideas never offered a clear, workable program for an industrial economy. Admirers say that is unfair to a vision more moral than technical. But it is fair to say that the essay is stronger as a challenge to our assumptions than as a plan, and that its charm sometimes hides its gaps.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
Chesterton belongs to a tradition of English essayists who combine humor with moral argument, running from Samuel Johnson and William Hazlitt through Charles Dickens's journalism, and on to George Orwell. Like Dickens, he defends the small domestic world against forces that would flatten it. Like Orwell, a later essayist who also wrote about Chesterton, he wants to describe how ordinary people actually live. Where Orwell approaches the subject through observation and plain prose, Chesterton approaches it through paradox and parable.

His ideas also descend from the Victorian critics of industrial society, especially John Ruskin and William Morris, who had argued that modern factory life damaged both work and home. Chesterton shares their suspicion of the machine age and their love of craft and local life, though his remedy is more cheerful and more devoted to the family. In a different register, the essay anticipates later writing on the meaning of a house, from the philosopher Gaston Bachelard's reflections on the poetics of domestic space to modern writing on housing and ownership. The idea that a home is a zone of personal sovereignty has become part of many political traditions, from conservative arguments about property to left-leaning ones about tenants' rights.

Comparisons are instructive. Virginia Woolf's A Room of One's Own, written nearly two decades later, also treats a private space as the foundation of freedom, but it asks exactly the question Chesterton skips: who gets that room, and who has been denied it? Reading the two together shows both how much the idea of a place of one's own matters and how easily it can be blind to who is left out. Chesterton's jokes about the rich belong to a long English habit of laughing at the comfortable.

Why read it now? First, because the central insight, that the powerful tend to mistake their own situation for everyone's, is permanently useful. Second, because the essay still captures something true about the small freedoms of private life that remote work, rising rents and crowded cities have made newly visible. And third, because it is simply a pleasure to hear a writer defend something as unfashionable as a kitchen floor picnic with such conviction.

Read it with both admiration and caution. Take the paradox seriously, enjoy the energy, and then ask the questions Chesterton leaves open. That is what the best essays invite you to do, and it is part of why this one has lasted.

essays.title: On the Enjoyment of Unpleasant Places
essays.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
essays.epigraph: Things looked at patiently from one side after another generally end by showing a side that is beautiful.
essays.keyContext: Robert Louis Stevenson was only about twenty-three when this essay appeared in 1874, in a magazine called The Portfolio, long before Treasure Island made him famous. He was a sickly young Scotsman from a family of lighthouse engineers, training for a career he did not want, and writing was already his private ambition. This essay shows him teaching himself how to see. His idea is simple and a little cheeky: any place, however bleak, can give you something, if you stay long enough and look in the right spirit. He builds the case from his own memory of a windswept, treeless stretch of the northern Scottish coast, where he found his deepest feeling of peace in a sheltered hollow between two ruined castles. It is an early example of the warm, conversational style he later perfected, and it is a gentle reminder that happiness in a landscape is partly something you bring with you. Listen for how he moves from argument to memory to a small moment of real stillness.
paragraphs: It is a difficult matter to make the most of any given place, and we have much in our own power. Things looked at patiently from one side after another generally end by showing a side that is beautiful. A few months ago some words were said in the Portfolio as to an “austere regimen in scenery”; and such a discipline was then recommended as “healthful and strengthening to the taste.” That is the text, so to speak, of the present essay. This discipline in scenery, it must be understood, is something more than a mere walk before breakfast to whet the appetite. For when we are put down in some unsightly neighbourhood, and especially if we have come to be more or less dependent on what we see, we must set ourselves to hunt out beautiful things with all the ardour and patience of a botanist after a rye plant. Day by day we perfect ourselves in the art of seeing nature more favourably. We learn to live with her, as people learn to live with fretful or violent spouses: to dwell lovingly on what is good, and shut our eyes against all that is bleak or inharmonious. We learn, also, to come to each place in the right spirit. The traveller, as Brantôme quaintly tells us, “fait des discours en soi pour se soutenir en chemin”; and into these discourses he weaves something out of all that he sees and suffers by the way; they take their tone greatly from the varying character of the scene; a sharp ascent brings different thoughts from a level road; and the man’s fancies grow lighter as he comes out of the wood into a clearing. Nor does the scenery any more affect the thoughts than the thoughts affect the scenery. We see places through our humours as through differently coloured glasses. We are ourselves a term in the equation, a note of the chord, and make discord or harmony almost at will. There is no fear for the result, if we can but surrender ourselves sufficiently to the country that surrounds and follows us, so that we are ever thinking suitable thoughts or telling ourselves some suitable sort of story as we go. We become thus, in some sense, a centre of beauty; we are provocative of beauty, much as a gentle and sincere character is provocative of sincerity and gentleness in others. And even where there is no harmony to be elicited by the quickest and most obedient of spirits, we may still embellish a place with some attraction of romance. We may learn to go far afield for associations, and handle them lightly when we have found them. Sometimes an old print comes to our aid; I have seen many a spot lit up at once with picturesque imaginations, by a reminiscence of Callot, or Sadeler, or Paul Brill. Dick Turpin has been my lay figure for many an English lane. And I suppose the Trossachs would hardly be the Trossachs for most tourists if a man of admirable romantic instinct had not peopled it for them with harmonious figures, and brought them thither with minds rightly prepared for the impression. There is half the battle in this preparation. For instance: I have rarely been able to visit, in the proper spirit, the wild and inhospitable places of our own Highlands. I am happier where it is tame and fertile, and not readily pleased without trees. I understand that there are some phases of mental trouble that harmonise well with such surroundings, and that some persons, by the dispensing power of the imagination, can go back several centuries in spirit, and put themselves into sympathy with the hunted, houseless, unsociable way of life that was in its place upon these savage hills. Now, when I am sad, I like nature to charm me out of my sadness, like David before Saul; and the thought of these past ages strikes nothing in me but an unpleasant pity; so that I can never hit on the right humour for this sort of landscape, and lose much pleasure in consequence. Still, even here, if I were only let alone, and time enough were given, I should have all manner of pleasures, and take many clear and beautiful images away with me when I left. When we cannot think ourselves into sympathy with the great features of a country, we learn to ignore them, and put our head among the grass for flowers, or pore, for long times together, over the changeful current of a stream. We come down to the sermon in stones, when we are shut out from any poem in the spread landscape. We begin to peep and botanise, we take an interest in birds and insects, we find many things beautiful in miniature. The reader will recollect the little summer scene in Wuthering Heights⁠—the one warm scene, perhaps, in all that powerful, miserable novel⁠—and the great feature that is made therein by grasses and flowers and a little sunshine: this is in the spirit of which I now speak. And, lastly, we can go indoors; interiors are sometimes as beautiful, often more picturesque, than the shows of the open air, and they have that quality of shelter of which I shall presently have more to say.

With all this in mind, I have often been tempted to put forth the paradox that any place is good enough to live a life in, while it is only in a few, and those highly favoured, that we can pass a few hours agreeably. For, if we only stay long enough we become at home in the neighbourhood. Reminiscences spring up, like flowers, about uninteresting corners. We forget to some degree the superior loveliness of other places, and fall into a tolerant and sympathetic spirit which is its own reward and justification. Looking back the other day on some recollections of my own, I was astonished to find how much I owed to such a residence; six weeks in one unpleasant countryside had done more, it seemed, to quicken and educate my sensibilities than many years in places that jumped more nearly with my inclination.

The country to which I refer was a level and treeless plateau, over which the winds cut like a whip. For miles and miles it was the same. A river, indeed, fell into the sea near the town where I resided; but the valley of the river was shallow and bald, for as far up as ever I had the heart to follow it. There were roads, certainly, but roads that had no beauty or interest; for, as there was no timber, and but little irregularity of surface, you saw your whole walk exposed to you from the beginning: there was nothing left to fancy, nothing to expect, nothing to see by the wayside, save here and there an unhomely-looking homestead, and here and there a solitary, spectacled stone-breaker; and you were only accompanied, as you went doggedly forward, by the gaunt telegraph-posts and the hum of the resonant wires in the keen sea-wind. To one who had learned to know their song in warm pleasant places by the Mediterranean, it seemed to taunt the country, and make it still bleaker by suggested contrast. Even the waste places by the side of the road were not, as Hawthorne liked to put it, “taken back to Nature” by any decent covering of vegetation. Wherever the land had the chance, it seemed to lie fallow. There is a certain tawny nudity of the South, bare sunburnt plains, coloured like a lion, and hills clothed only in the blue transparent air; but this was of another description⁠—this was the nakedness of the North; the earth seemed to know that it was naked, and was ashamed and cold.

It seemed to be always blowing on that coast. Indeed, this had passed into the speech of the inhabitants, and they saluted each other when they met with “Breezy, breezy,” instead of the customary “Fine day” of farther south. These continual winds were not like the harvest breeze, that just keeps an equable pressure against your face as you walk, and serves to set all the trees talking over your head, or bring round you the smell of the wet surface of the country after a shower. They were of the bitter, hard, persistent sort, that interferes with sight and respiration, and makes the eyes sore. Even such winds as these have their own merit in proper time and place. It is pleasant to see them brandish great masses of shadow. And what a power they have over the colour of the world! How they ruffle the solid woodlands in their passage, and make them shudder and whiten like a single willow! There is nothing more vertiginous than a wind like this among the woods, with all its sights and noises; and the effect gets between some painters and their sober eyesight, so that, even when the rest of their picture is calm, the foliage is coloured like foliage in a gale. There was nothing, however, of this sort to be noticed in a country where there were no trees and hardly any shadows, save the passive shadows of clouds or those of rigid houses and walls. But the wind was nevertheless an occasion of pleasure; for nowhere could you taste more fully the pleasure of a sudden lull, or a place of opportune shelter. The reader knows what I mean; he must remember how, when he has sat himself down behind a dyke on a hillside, he delighted to hear the wind hiss vainly through the crannies at his back; how his body tingled all over with warmth, and it began to dawn upon him, with a sort of slow surprise, that the country was beautiful, the heather purple, and the faraway hills all marbled with sun and shadow. Wordsworth, in a beautiful passage of the “Prelude,” has used this as a figure for the feeling struck in us by the quiet by-streets of London after the uproar of the great thoroughfares; and the comparison may be turned the other way with as good effect:⁠—
“Meanwhile the roar continues, till at length, Escaped as from an enemy, we turn Abruptly into some sequester’d nook, Still as a shelter’d place when winds blow loud!”

I remember meeting a man once, in a train, who told me of what must have been quite the most perfect instance of this pleasure of escape. He had gone up, one sunny, windy morning, to the top of a great cathedral somewhere abroad; I think it was Cologne Cathedral, the great unfinished marvel by the Rhine; and after a long while in dark stairways, he issued at last into the sunshine, on a platform high above the town. At that elevation it was quite still and warm; the gale was only in the lower strata of the air, and he had forgotten it in the quiet interior of the church and during his long ascent; and so you may judge of his surprise when, resting his arms on the sunlit balustrade and looking over into the Place far below him, he saw the good people holding on their hats and leaning hard against the wind as they walked. There is something, to my fancy, quite perfect in this little experience of my fellow-traveller’s. The ways of men seem always very trivial to us when we find ourselves alone on a church-top, with the blue sky and a few tall pinnacles, and see far below us the steep roofs and foreshortened buttresses, and the silent activity of the city streets; but how much more must they not have seemed so to him as he stood, not only above other men’s business, but above other men’s climate, in a golden zone like Apollo’s!

This was the sort of pleasure I found in the country of which I write. The pleasure was to be out of the wind, and to keep it in memory all the time, and hug oneself upon the shelter. And it was only by the sea that any such sheltered places were to be found. Between the black worm-eaten headlands there are little bights and havens, well screened from the wind and the commotion of the external sea, where the sand and weeds look up into the gazer’s face from a depth of tranquil water, and the seabirds, screaming and flickering from the ruined crags, alone disturb the silence and the sunshine. One such place has impressed itself on my memory beyond all others. On a rock by the water’s edge, old fighting men of the Norse breed had planted a double castle; the two stood wall to wall like semidetached villas; and yet feud had run so high between their owners, that one, from out of a window, shot the other as he stood in his own doorway. There is something in the juxtaposition of these two enemies full of tragic irony. It is grim to think of bearded men and bitter women taking hateful counsel together about the two hall-fires at night, when the sea boomed against the foundations and the wild winter wind was loose over the battlements. And in the study we may reconstruct for ourselves some pale figure of what life then was. Not so when we are there; when we are there such thoughts come to us only to intensify a contrary impression, and association is turned against itself. I remember walking thither three afternoons in succession, my eyes weary with being set against the wind, and how, dropping suddenly over the edge of the down, I found myself in a new world of warmth and shelter. The wind, from which I had escaped, “as from an enemy,” was seemingly quite local. It carried no clouds with it, and came from such a quarter that it did not trouble the sea within view. The two castles, black and ruinous as the rocks about them, were still distinguishable from these by something more insecure and fantastic in the outline, something that the last storm had left imminent and the next would demolish entirely. It would be difficult to render in words the sense of peace that took possession of me on these three afternoons. It was helped out, as I have said, by the contrast. The shore was battered and bemauled by previous tempests; I had the memory at heart of the insane strife of the pygmies who had erected these two castles and lived in them in mutual distrust and enmity, and knew I had only to put my head out of this little cup of shelter to find the hard wind blowing in my eyes; and yet there were the two great tracts of motionless blue air and peaceful sea looking on, unconcerned and apart, at the turmoil of the present moment and the memorials of the precarious past. There is ever something transitory and fretful in the impression of a high wind under a cloudless sky; it seems to have no root in the constitution of things; it must speedily begin to faint and wither away like a cut flower. And on those days the thought of the wind and the thought of human life came very near together in my mind. Our noisy years did indeed seem moments in the being of the eternal silence; and the wind, in the face of that great field of stationary blue, was as the wind of a butterfly’s wing. The placidity of the sea was a thing likewise to be remembered. Shelley speaks of the sea as “hungering for calm,” and in this place one learned to understand the phrase. Looking down into these green waters from the broken edge of the rock, or swimming leisurely in the sunshine, it seemed to me that they were enjoying their own tranquillity; and when now and again it was disturbed by a wind ripple on the surface, or the quick black passage of a fish far below, they settled back again (one could fancy) with relief.

On shore too, in the little nook of shelter, everything was so subdued and still that the least particular struck in me a pleasurable surprise. The desultory crackling of the whin-pods in the afternoon sun usurped the ear. The hot, sweet breath of the bank, that had been saturated all day long with sunshine, and now exhaled it into my face, was like the breath of a fellow-creature. I remember that I was haunted by two lines of French verse; in some dumb way they seemed to fit my surroundings and give expression to the contentment that was in me, and I kept repeating to myself⁠—
“Mon cœur est un luth suspendu, Sitôt qu’on le touche, il résonne.”

I can give no reason why these lines came to me at this time; and for that very cause I repeat them here. For all I know, they may serve to complete the impression in the mind of the reader, as they were certainly a part of it for me.

And this happened to me in the place of all others where I liked least to stay. When I think of it I grow ashamed of my own ingratitude. “Out of the strong came forth sweetness.” There, in the bleak and gusty North, I received, perhaps, my strongest impression of peace. I saw the sea to be great and calm; and the earth, in that little corner, was all alive and friendly to me. So, wherever a man is, he will find something to please and pacify him: in the town he will meet pleasant faces of men and women, and see beautiful flowers at a window, or hear a cage-bird singing at the corner of the gloomiest street; and for the country, there is no country without some amenity⁠—let him only look for it in the right spirit, and he will surely find.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
The essay begins with a thesis, and the thesis is practical. It is hard to make the most of any given place, Stevenson says, but we have much in our own power, and things looked at patiently from one side after another usually end up showing a beautiful side. He calls this an austere regimen in scenery, a discipline for the eyes. That is the text, as he puts it, of the whole piece. The point is not to take a brisk walk before breakfast. If we are stuck somewhere ugly, we must hunt out beauty with the patience of a botanist, and learn to see nature more favourably, the way people learn to live with a difficult spouse: dwell on what is good, and close your eyes to the rest.

Then he adds something more interesting. We are not just looking at scenery; we are part of it. We see places through our moods as through coloured glass. We are, he says, a term in the equation, a note in the chord. If we surrender to the country around us and tell ourselves suitable stories as we go, we can become a centre of beauty, as a gentle person draws gentleness out of others. And when the landscape will not cooperate, we have fallbacks: borrow romance from old prints, as he does with Dick Turpin on an English lane, or shrink our attention down to flowers in the grass, birds and insects, or step indoors.

From there he reaches his paradox: any place is good enough to live a life in, though only a few are good enough to pass a few hours agreeably. Stay long enough and memories grow up around the dullest corners like flowers. He then tells the story that proves it. Six weeks in one unpleasant countryside, a level treeless plateau where the wind cut like a whip, taught him more than years in places he liked better. The locals greeted each other with Breezy, breezy, and the telegraph wires hummed bleakly overhead.

The heart of the essay is a sheltered cove he visited on three afternoons, where two ruined castles stood wall to wall like semidetached villas, and one owner had once shot the other in his own doorway. The place offered something precisely because of the wind: the joy of escaping it. He compares this to Wordsworth's quiet side street after the roar of the main road and to a traveller on a cathedral roof who found the air still while people far below leaned into a gale.

The layer a first reader might miss is the final turn. The peace Stevenson felt came from contrast, from knowing the hard wind was just over the edge. The wind became almost a gift. He closes ashamed of his ingratitude for a place he liked least, and with the quiet moral that wherever a man is, he will find something to please him, if he looks in the right spirit.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
This is a young man's essay, and it has both the charm and the flaws that implies. The strongest thing about it is the movement. It starts as an argument, slides into reminiscence, and by the end has become a small piece of lyric prose, so that the thesis is demonstrated rather than merely stated. The cove passage is the best writing in it. The rocks, the green water, the crackling whin-pods in the afternoon sun, and the warm breath of a bank that has soaked up sunshine all day and gives it back like the breath of a fellow creature, are sharply observed and truly felt. The comparison of the wind to the wind of a butterfly's wing, set against a great field of still blue, is a lovely way to turn a scene into a thought about human life.

There is also craft in the structure of the paradox. Most of us would say that pretty places make us happy. Stevenson shows that our happiness depends on contrast and on attention, which is a more subtle claim and a more useful one. The advice is memorable because it comes in concrete form: look at the grass, listen to the pods, hug yourself behind the dyke.

The weaknesses are equally visible. The opening is stiff and overloaded with borrowed learning. There are references to Brantôme in French, to Callot and Sadeler and Paul Brill, to Hawthorne, Wordsworth, Shelley, Emily Brontë and a couplet of French verse, and some of them feel like a young writer showing off his reading. The prose can slip into the ornamental, with pairs of adjectives and balanced clauses that look more like exercises in the style of the Victorian essayists he admired than the loose, personal voice he would soon develop. The Wuthering Heights aside is charming, but a reader without that novel in mind might feel left out.

There is a more serious limit as well. The philosophy is a comfortable one. To advise a reader to find pleasure in an unpleasant place assumes that the reader is a visitor with the freedom to leave, and with the leisure to walk to a cove three afternoons running. For the people who actually live and work in a bleak district, with no choice of residence, the advice would sound easy. Stevenson partly acknowledges this by calling it a paradox, but he does not wrestle with it.

Finally, the argument wobbles in the middle. He says any place is good enough to live in, yet the evidence is mostly about a shelter from the wind, which is a pleasure available only in some corners. Even so, these are the faults of a gifted apprentice. The best of the essay is already the real Stevenson, and the rest is a promising sketch.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
It would be an overstatement to say that this essay changed the course of literature. It appeared in a specialist magazine, The Portfolio, which was devoted mainly to the visual arts, and it was among the first pieces Stevenson published at a time when he was still known only to family and friends. Its main importance is as an early marker. It shows that the writer who would later produce Travels with a Donkey in the Cevennes, Treasure Island and Kidnapped already had a distinctive habit of mind: a belief that attention and spirit can transform a place, and a fondness for the moral drawn lightly from an anecdote.

Within Stevenson's own career, the essay belongs to the group of early pieces on landscape and travel that taught him how to write about places. The training mattered. When he later wrote about the Scottish coast, the Cevennes, the American West and eventually the South Seas, he drew on the same method of attending closely to small details and letting mood colour the scene. His fiction also owes a debt, since the vivid sense of weather, tide and coastline that gives Kidnapped and Treasure Island their atmosphere was first practised here. And his family's work building lighthouses along the Scottish coast supplied the setting, since he first went to the northern harbours as a trainee engineer.

Beyond Stevenson, the essay is part of a large tradition of writing that treats the experience of place as something we make as well as find. Later nature writers and travel writers have made similar arguments, that attention is a form of love and that even drab landscapes reward patient looking. The idea has an echo in modern talk of mindfulness, though Stevenson's version is much more literary and less self-improving. Readers who enjoy the contemporary genre of the walking essay will recognise its ancestry.

The documented record here is limited. There is little evidence of a specific, dramatic public reaction to this particular essay when it first appeared, and it has never been a headline work. It has mostly survived as part of the collected essays and travel pieces, where it is read for its quality and for what it tells us about the young author.

In teaching, it is sometimes used as a gentle model of the personal essay: it has a clear thesis, a vivid example, and a graceful close. Students can see the structure plainly, and the cove passage is a fine specimen of descriptive writing. Its modest reputation makes it a discovery for many readers rather than a set text.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
What readers seem to value most is the generosity of the idea. Many people have had the experience of being stuck in a place they disliked, a dull town, a rented room, a wet holiday, and Stevenson tells them that the experience may not be wasted. That is a consoling message, and he delivers it without preaching. The tone is of a friend who has tried the thing himself and is a little ashamed to report that it worked.

Readers also love the cove. The passage about the two ruined castles, the hot breath of the sunny bank and the green water enjoying its own tranquillity gives a clear and physical sense of a particular afternoon, and it does so in language that is musical without being showy. The detail of the man on the cathedral top, standing above other men's business and above their climate in a golden zone like Apollo's, is one of those images that stays with people. Anthologists have often been drawn to such passages, and they work especially well read aloud.

Another source of affection is the honesty of the narrator. He admits that he cannot find the right humour for wild Highland scenery, that sad thoughts of past ages bring him only an unpleasant pity, and that he likes nature to charm him out of sadness like David playing before Saul. He also admits that he does not know why two lines of French verse came to him in the cove, and repeats them because he cannot explain them. This candour about the limits of his own taste makes his advice feel earned. Readers tend to trust a guide who confesses his own preferences.

There is also real pleasure in the form. The essay lets a thought wander, and takes the reader along from argument to anecdote to memory, so that the effect is of conversation rather than lecture. Admirers of Stevenson's later essays, including the famous ones in Virginibus Puerisque, often find in this early piece the seeds of that conversational charm.

It is fair to say that general readers and later admirers of Stevenson have tended to treat the early landscape essays as small pleasures: slight, but graceful, and bearing the unmistakable mark of a writer in the making. For those who love walking, weather or quiet places, the essay often becomes a quiet favourite.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
Because this essay has never been a famous battleground, there is no dramatic body of controversy to report. What can be said is that readers and critics of Stevenson's early work have raised a few recurring reservations, and some of them apply fairly here.

The first is the charge of literary self-consciousness. Stevenson himself later described his youthful years as a time of playing the sedulous ape, imitating admired writers in order to learn their tricks. Critics have seen the same apprenticeship in these early essays: the elaborate sentences, the allusions to painters and poets, and the careful balance of phrases. Some readers find the opening paragraphs mannered and a little cold compared with the later, warmer Stevenson. The essay is a graceful performance, they say, but it sometimes feels like a performance.

The second is the matter of slightness. The argument that we can find beauty almost anywhere is attractive, but it can seem thin, even complacent. A reader who has lived in real hardship, in an ugly industrial town or a place of poverty, may feel that the advice trivialises the difficulty. Seeing beauty in a windswept coast for six weeks is not the same as living there for life. This objection is not fatal, since Stevenson presents his view as a paradox and an exercise rather than a law, but it is a fair one.

Third, there is a note of class and privilege in the traveller's stance. The narrator wanders, selects, and goes home to reflect. His dismissal of the Highlands as a place where he cannot find the right humour assumes that landscape exists to supply pleasant moods to the visitor, and some modern readers find that outlook too consumerist. The people who actually lived in those places appear only as the passing figures of a stone-breaker or a homestead.

Fourth, the passage about the old feud, with its bearded men and bitter women taking hateful counsel, leans on a romantic and slightly stagey picture of the past that a historian might find thin.

None of this makes the essay a failure. Most criticism of it amounts to saying that it is a young man's work, polished but not yet deep, and that its pleasures are modest. That is likely a fair verdict, and the essay's quiet success lies in how well it does a small thing.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
This essay sits in the great tradition of the English familiar essay, the conversational, personal piece that wanders from observation to reflection. That tradition runs from Montaigne, the sixteenth-century Frenchman who invented the form, through Addison and Steele, Charles Lamb and William Hazlitt, to Stevenson's own contemporaries. Stevenson was a conscious heir of Lamb and Hazlitt, and he wrote essays throughout his life. This one, from his early twenties, shows him finding his voice within that tradition.

It also belongs to the Romantic and Victorian habit of writing about landscape as a matter of feeling. Wordsworth stands behind it, and is quoted directly, as does Shelley, and the allusion to Wuthering Heights shows that Stevenson knew how a novel could use a little patch of sunshine and grass. At the same time, the essay is a reaction against the grand Romantic taste for sublime mountains. Stevenson prefers the tame and the small. In that he anticipates a modern sensibility that values the ordinary landscape, from the nature writing of the twentieth century to the growing interest in everyday places.

Among his own works, it belongs with the pieces that grew out of his early wandering in Scotland and France, and it points ahead to the travel books that made him known. It also foreshadows a moral thread that runs through much of his writing, an optimistic doctrine that happiness is a duty and a skill that can be practised. His later essays on that theme are better known and stronger, but the seed is here.

If you compare it with other writers on place, you can see the contrast. Henry David Thoreau, writing a couple of decades earlier, also urged close attention to a modest local landscape, though with a more severe and challenging spirit. Stevenson is gentler and more social. Later essayists of walking and place, from Virginia Woolf's London wanderings to modern nature writers, share his faith that the quality of attention changes the quality of a place.

Why read it now? Because most of us spend much of our lives in places we did not choose, and because the habit it recommends, looking again, patiently, from one side after another, costs nothing and works more often than we expect. It is short, it is lovely in its last pages, and it leaves you a little more willing to find the shelter in whatever wind you are standing in.

essays.title: Roads
essays.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
essays.epigraph: Nothing captures the unrest and poetry of the human spirit like the white ribbon of a country road winding over the hill into the unknown.
essays.keyContext: In 1873 a young Robert Louis Stevenson, then in his early twenties and still half-heartedly training to be an engineer in Edinburgh, published this essay in a magazine called The Portfolio. It is one of his earliest pieces of published prose, and it is about something so ordinary we hardly notice it: the road. Stevenson was the son and grandson of builders of lighthouses and harbours, so he grew up around people who made things out of rock and engineering, but he wanted to write. Here he argues that the best way to learn to love landscape is not through grand mountains but through quiet country, where a winding road becomes endless company. A road, he says, has life and character, it connects us to other people, and above all it carries our longing for whatever lies beyond the next hill. The essay is slow, ornate and a little bookish, but it contains the seed of his lifelong love of walking and travel. Listen for the way an everyday thing turns into a kind of poetry.
paragraphs: No amateur will deny that he can find more pleasure in a single drawing, over which he can sit a whole quiet forenoon, and so gradually study himself into humour with the artist, than he can ever extract from the dazzle and accumulation of incongruous impressions that send him, weary and stupefied, out of some famous picture-gallery. But what is thus admitted with regard to art is not extended to the (so-called) natural beauties no amount of excess in sublime mountain outline or the graces of cultivated lowland can do anything, it is supposed, to weaken or degrade the palate. We are not at all sure, however, that moderation, and a regimen tolerably austere, even in scenery, are not healthful and strengthening to the taste; and that the best school for a lover of nature is not to the found in one of those countries where there is no stage effect⁠—nothing salient or sudden⁠—but a quiet spirit of orderly and harmonious beauty pervades all the details, so that we can patiently attend to each of the little touches that strike in us, all of them together, the subdued note of the landscape. It is in scenery such as this that we find ourselves in the right temper to seek out small sequestered loveliness. The constant recurrence of similar combinations of colour and outline gradually forces upon us a sense of how the harmony has been built up, and we become familiar with something of nature’s mannerism. This is the true pleasure of your “rural voluptuary,”⁠—not to remain awestricken before a Mount Chimborazo; not to sit deafened over the big drum in the orchestra, but day by day to teach himself some new beauty⁠—to experience some new vague and tranquil sensation that has before evaded him. It is not the people who “have pined and hungered after nature many a year, in the great city pent,” as Coleridge said in the poem that made Charles Lamb so much ashamed of himself; it is not those who make the greatest progress in this intimacy with her, or who are most quick to see and have the greatest gusto to enjoy. In this, as in everything else, it is minute knowledge and long-continued loving industry that make the true dilettante. A man must have thought much over scenery before he begins fully to enjoy it. It is no youngling enthusiasm on hilltops that can possess itself of the last essence of beauty. Probably most people’s heads are growing bare before they can see all in a landscape that they have the capability of seeing; and, even then, it will be only for one little moment of consummation before the faculties are again on the decline, and they that look out of the windows begin to be darkened and restrained in sight. Thus the study of nature should be carried forward thoroughly and with system. Every gratification should be rolled long under the tongue, and we should be always eager to analyse and compare, in order that we may be able to give some plausible reason for our admirations. True, it is difficult to put even approximately into words the kind of feelings thus called into play. There is a dangerous vice inherent in any such intellectual refining upon vague sensation. The analysis of such satisfactions lends itself very readily to literary affectations; and we can all think of instances where it has shown itself apt to exercise a morbid influence, even upon an author’s choice of language and the turn of his sentences. And yet there is much that makes the attempt attractive; for any expression, however imperfect, once given to a cherished feeling, seems a sort of legitimation of the pleasure we take in it. A common sentiment is one of those great goods that make life palatable and ever new. The knowledge that another has felt as we have felt, and seen things, even if they are little things, not much otherwise than we have seen them, will continue to the end to be one of life’s choicest pleasures.

Let the reader, then, betake himself in the spirit we have recommended to some of the quieter kinds of English landscape. In those homely and placid agricultural districts, familiarity will bring into relief many things worthy of notice, and urge them pleasantly home to him by a sort of loving repetition; such as the wonderful life-giving speed of windmill sails above the stationary country; the occurrence and recurrence of the same church tower at the end of one long vista after another: and, conspicuous among these sources of quiet pleasure, the character and variety of the road itself, along which he takes his way. Not only near at hand, in the lithe contortions with which it adapts itself to the interchanges of level and slope, but far away also, when he sees a few hundred feet of it upheaved against a hill and shining in the afternoon sun, he will find it an object so changeful and enlivening that he can always pleasurably busy his mind about it. He may leave the riverside, or fall out of the way of villages, but the road he has always with him; and, in the true humour of observation, will find in that sufficient company. From its subtle windings and changes of level there arises a keen and continuous interest, that keeps the attention ever alert and cheerful. Every sensitive adjustment to the contour of the ground, every little dip and swerve, seems instinct with life and an exquisite sense of balance and beauty. The road rolls upon the easy slopes of the country, like a long ship in the hollows of the sea. The very margins of waste ground, as they trench a little farther on the beaten way, or recede again to the shelter of the hedge, have something of the same free delicacy of line⁠—of the same swing and wilfulness. You might think for a whole summer’s day (and not have thought it any nearer an end by evening) what concourse and succession of circumstances has produced the least of these deflections; and it is, perhaps, just in this that we should look for the secret of their interest. A footpath across a meadow⁠—in all its human waywardness and unaccountability, in all the grata protervitas of its varying direction⁠—will always be more to us than a railroad well engineered through a difficult country. No reasoned sequence is thrust upon our attention: we seem to have slipped for one lawless little moment out of the iron rule of cause and effect; and so we revert at once to some of the pleasant old heresies of personification, always poetically orthodox, and attribute a sort of freewill, an active and spontaneous life, to the white ribbon of road that lengthens out, and bends, and cunningly adapts itself to the inequalities of the land before our eyes. We remember, as we write, some miles of fine wide highway laid out with conscious aesthetic artifice through a broken and richly cultivated tract of country. It is said that the engineer had Hogarth’s line of beauty in his mind as he laid them down. And the result is striking. One splendid satisfying sweep passes with easy transition into another, and there is nothing to trouble or dislocate the strong continuousness of the main line of the road. And yet there is something wanting. There is here no saving imperfection, none of those secondary curves and little trepidations of direction that carry, in natural roads, our curiosity actively along with them. One feels at once that this road has not has been laboriously grown like a natural road, but made to pattern; and that, while a model may be academically correct in outline, it will always be inanimate and cold. The traveller is also aware of a sympathy of mood between himself and the road he travels. We have all seen ways that have wandered into heavy sand near the seacoast, and trail wearily over the dunes like a trodden serpent. Here we too must plod forward at a dull, laborious pace; and so a sympathy is preserved between our frame of mind and the expression of the relaxed, heavy curves of the roadway. Such a phenomenon, indeed, our reason might perhaps resolve with a little trouble. We might reflect that the present road had been developed out of a tract spontaneously followed by generations of primitive wayfarers; and might see in its expression a testimony that those generations had been affected at the same ground, one after another, in the same manner as we are affected today. Or we might carry the reflection further, and remind ourselves that where the air is invigorating and the ground firm under the traveller’s foot, his eye is quick to take advantage of small undulations, and he will turn carelessly aside from the direct way wherever there is anything beautiful to examine or some promise of a wider view; so that even a bush of wild roses may permanently bias and deform the straight path over the meadow; whereas, where the soil is heavy, one is preoccupied with the labour of mere progression, and goes with a bowed head heavily and unobservantly forward. Reason, however, will not carry us the whole way; for the sentiment often recurs in situations where it is very hard to imagine any possible explanation; and indeed, if we drive briskly along a good, well-made road in an open vehicle, we shall experience this sympathy almost at its fullest. We feel the sharp settle of the springs at some curiously twisted corner; after a steep ascent, the fresh air dances in our faces as we rattle precipitately down the other side, and we find it difficult to avoid attributing something headlong, a sort of abandon, to the road itself.

The mere winding of the path is enough to enliven a long day’s walk in even a commonplace or dreary countryside. Something that we have seen from miles back, upon an eminence, is so long hid from us, as we wander through folded valleys or among woods, that our expectation of seeing it again is sharpened into a violent appetite, and as we draw nearer we impatiently quicken our steps and turn every corner with a beating heart. It is through these prolongations of expectancy, this succession of one hope to another, that we live out long seasons of pleasure in a few hours’ walk. It is in following these capricious sinuosities that we learn, only bit by bit and through one coquettish reticence after another, much as we learn the heart of a friend, the whole loveliness of the country. This disposition always preserves something new to be seen, and takes us, like a careful cicerone, to many different points of distant view before it allows us finally to approach the hoped-for destination.

In its connection with the traffic, and whole friendly intercourse with the country, there is something very pleasant in that succession of saunterers and brisk and businesslike passersby, that peoples our ways and helps to build up what Walt Whitman calls “the cheerful voice of the public road, the gay, fresh sentiment of the road.” But out of the great network of ways that binds all life together from the hill-farm to the city, there is something individual to most, and, on the whole, nearly as much choice on the score of company as on the score of beauty or easy travel. On some we are never long without the sound of wheels, and folk pass us by so thickly that we lose the sense of their number. But on others, about little-frequented districts, a meeting is an affair of moment; we have the sight far off of someone coming towards us, the growing definiteness of the person, and then the brief passage and salutation, and the road left empty in front of us for perhaps a great while to come. Such encounters have a wistful interest that can hardly be understood by the dweller in places more populous. We remember standing beside a countryman once, in the mouth of a quiet by-street in a city that was more than ordinarily crowded and bustling; he seemed stunned and bewildered by the continual passage of different faces; and after a long pause, during which he appeared to search for some suitable expression, he said timidly that there seemed to be a great deal of meeting thereabouts. The phrase is significant. It is the expression of town-life in the language of the long, solitary country highways. A meeting of one with one was what this man had been used to in the pastoral uplands from which he came; and the concourse of the streets was in his eyes only an extraordinary multiplication of such “meetings.”

And now we come to that last and most subtle quality of all, to that sense of prospect, of outlook, that is brought so powerfully to our minds by a road. In real nature, as well as in old landscapes, beneath that impartial daylight in which a whole variegated plain is plunged and saturated, the line of the road leads the eye forth with the vague sense of desire up to the green limit of the horizon. Travel is brought home to us, and we visit in spirit every grove and hamlet that tempts us in the distance. Sehnsucht⁠—the passion for what is ever beyond⁠—is livingly expressed in that white ribbon of possible travel that severs the uneven country; not a ploughman following his plough up the shining furrow, not the blue smoke of any cottage in a hollow, but is brought to us with a sense of nearness and attainability by this wavering line of junction. There is a passionate paragraph in Werther that strikes the very key. “When I came hither,” he writes, “how the beautiful valley invited me on every side, as I gazed down into it from the hilltop! There the wood⁠—ah, that I might mingle in its shadows! there the mountain summits⁠—ah, that I might look down from them over the broad country! the interlinked hills! the secret valleys! Oh to lose myself among their mysteries! I hurried into the midst, and came back without finding aught I hoped for. Alas! the distance is like the future. A vast whole lies in the twilight before our spirit; sight and feeling alike plunge and lose themselves in the prospect, and we yearn to surrender our whole being, and let it be filled full with all the rapture of one single glorious sensation; and alas! when we hasten to the fruition, when there is changed to here, all is afterwards as it was before, and we stand in our indigent and cramped estate, and our soul thirsts after a still ebbing elixir.” It is to this wandering and uneasy spirit of anticipation that roads minister. Every little vista, every little glimpse that we have of what lies before us, gives the impatient imagination rein, so that it can outstrip the body and already plunge into the shadow of the woods, and overlook from the hilltop the plain beyond it, and wander in the windings of the valleys that are still far in front. The road is already there⁠—we shall not be long behind. It is as if we were marching with the rear of a great army, and, from far before, heard the acclamation of the people as the vanguard entered some friendly and jubilant city. Would not every man, through all the long miles of march, feel as if he also were within the gates?

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
Stevenson begins with an analogy from art. Anyone who loves pictures knows that you can get more pleasure from sitting a whole quiet morning with a single drawing than from rushing through a famous gallery and leaving stupefied. We admit that for art, he says, but we do not extend the point to nature. We assume no amount of sublime mountains can dull the palate. He suggests the opposite: a rather austere regimen even in scenery may be healthy for the taste, and the best school for a lover of nature is a country with no stage effects, where a quiet harmony runs through all the details.

In such quiet scenery, he says, we learn patience and the habit of small observation. The true pleasure of what he calls the rural voluptuary is not to stand awestruck before a great peak or sit deafened by the big drum in an orchestra, but to teach oneself some new beauty every day. He adds that it takes years: most people's heads are growing bare before they can see all that a landscape holds. Notice his humility about the difficulty of putting such feelings into words, and his remark that sharing a feeling with another person is one of life's choicest pleasures.

Then he turns to his subject. In placid farm country, the road becomes the chief object of interest. Its curves adapt to the slopes, it shines in the distance against a hill, and it follows the ground like a long ship in the hollows of the sea. Its edges have a free delicacy. A footpath across a meadow, with all its human waywardness, will always mean more to us than a railway engineered through hard country, because it seems to slip us out of the iron rule of cause and effect. Here is the key idea: natural roads are alive because they have been grown by countless travellers' choices. He contrasts a highway laid out to follow Hogarth's line of beauty, which is correct but cold, with the saving imperfection of real tracks.

He goes on to say that the mood of a road matches the mood of the walker, and that winding paths prolong expectancy. A road hides what it will show next, and so, step by step, we learn the country as we learn the heart of a friend. Roads also carry company: the traveller, the farmer, a countryman who once said that there seemed a great deal of meeting in the city.

The last and most important layer is longing. The road leads the eye toward the horizon and stands for what the Germans call Sehnsucht, the passion for what is always beyond. Quoting Goethe's Werther, he says distance is like the future. The road lets imagination run ahead of the body, so that we feel as if we were already within the gates, like a soldier marching at the rear of an army that hears the cheering as the vanguard enters a city.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
At its best this essay is graceful, and its core idea is original: a road is a living line, not merely a means of getting somewhere. The sentence about the road rolling on the easy slopes like a long ship in the hollows of the sea is the kind of image that makes an argument memorable. So is the comparison of a straight, engineered highway to a model that is academically correct but inanimate and cold. Stevenson has a fine gift for finding a general truth inside a small observation, and the contrast between a footpath and a railway is a lovely way to express a worry about modern life that was only beginning to be voiced.

The structure is also sound. It moves from a general principle about art and scenery to the particular subject, then through a sequence of qualities, form, mood, expectation, company, and finally the metaphysical longing that closes it. The countryman's remark about a great deal of meeting is a small masterpiece of anecdote: it makes the point about solitude and town life in one strange, sweet phrase.

But the weaknesses show, and some of them are the weaknesses of youth. The prose is heavily ornamented. Sentences stretch and double back on themselves, quotations pile up, and Latin and German phrases are dropped in without help. A modern reader meeting grata protervitas, Sehnsucht, a rural voluptuary and a quotation from Werther in a few pages may feel that the author is performing for an audience of educated Victorians. The royal we, which Stevenson uses throughout, adds to the stiffness. He later wrote far more plainly and warmly, and this essay is not yet that writer.

The argument also loses focus. The opening, about the gallery and the drawing, takes a long time to reach roads, and the long discussion of why a road's mood matches ours, with its tentative explanations about generations of wayfarers and bushes of wild roses, wanders without settling. There is a charming reasonableness in his admission that reason will not carry us all the way, but it also reads as an unfinished thought.

There is, too, a slight sentimentality in the treatment of country life. The countryman is a figure of quaint simplicity, and the solitary meetings on the road are made to sound more poetic than they might feel to those who walked them out of necessity. This is the view of a young man who can choose his walks.

Still, the ending is excellent. The image of the marching army, hearing the cheers of a city not yet reached, is both original and moving, and it lifts the essay above its mannerisms. A flawed piece, then, but one with a real idea at its centre and a few lines of lasting beauty.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
Roads was one of Stevenson's first published essays, and its significance lies mainly in what it shows about the writer he would become.
