At the time he was a young Edinburgh man, the son of a family of famous lighthouse engineers, who was expected to follow them into the profession. He studied engineering, then law, and was called to the Scottish bar in 1875, but he spent his energy on writing. Appearing in The Portfolio, an art magazine, in 1873, this essay was an early public step on that path.

The essay is a statement of an attitude that stayed with him: that travel is not about arriving, that the journey itself is the substance, and that a walker sees more than a person in a hurry. In his later book Virginibus Puerisque, he wrote the famous line that to travel hopefully is a better thing than to arrive. That idea is already present here in the claim that it is through the prolongations of expectancy that we live out long seasons of pleasure in a few hours' walk. His first travel book, An Inland Voyage, and then Travels with a Donkey in the Cevennes, which many consider the founding classic of modern walking literature, carry this outlook into practice.

Beyond Stevenson's own career, the essay joins a stream of writing about walking and roads that has grown ever since. Writers on walking from Thoreau before him to many modern authors share his conviction that the slow pace reveals the world. It is also an early example of an aesthetic argument for the irregular, the grown and the organic over the planned and engineered, a theme that would be taken up in discussions of town planning, garden design and the picturesque. His contrast between the natural road and the highway built to a theoretical line anticipates later debates about whether designed landscapes can ever feel alive.

I must be careful here. There is little documented evidence of how this particular essay was received on publication, and it did not make Stevenson famous. It has survived as part of his collected essays and travel writing, and is read by admirers of his work and by anyone interested in the literature of walking. That is a modest legacy, but a real one.

As for teaching, it is sometimes used as an example of Victorian descriptive prose and as an early look at Stevenson's style, valued more for its place in his development than for its status as a standalone classic.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
Readers who love Stevenson's essays tend to prize the way he turns attention into a kind of pleasure. Roads gives them a vocabulary for something they already feel: the way a path curving out of sight pulls us forward, and the particular joy of seeing a bit of road far off, shining on a hillside, long before we reach it. The idea that we learn the country bit by bit, as we learn the heart of a friend, through one coquettish reticence after another, is an image that readers have found delightful, and it applies to more than roads.

The central metaphor of longing also lands for many. The road as a white ribbon of possible travel that cuts through the uneven country, bringing the ploughman and the cottage smoke close to us, expresses an almost universal human feeling, the pull of the horizon. The quotation from Werther about distance being like the future gives this a philosophical depth, and the closing image of marching at the rear of an army that hears the cheers from the front is the sort of ending that readers remember. For people who love to walk, drive or cycle, the essay feels like a small confirmation that their pleasure is a real and respectable one.

Readers have also enjoyed the humour and humanity that peek out between the ornate sentences. The countryman who found that there seemed to be a great deal of meeting in the city is a perfect little story. The road that trails wearily over the dunes like a trodden serpent, matching the walker's heavy mood, is vivid and funny. And the contrast between the life-giving natural road and the one made to pattern gives the essay an argument that anyone who has been disappointed by a too-perfect planned town will recognise.

Admirers of Stevenson's work as a whole often point to the essay as evidence of how early his gift for observation and rhythm appeared. Even in a youthful piece, the cadence of the sentences has a musical quality that makes it a pleasure to read aloud. This essay drew little specific famous praise, but it is generally regarded by Stevenson readers as a charming and revealing early work.

For those who come to it fresh, the surprise is how much a piece about roads has to say about desire, expectation and the way imagination outruns the body. That unexpected depth is what many readers say they love.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
As with many of Stevenson's early essays, there is no famous controversy attached to Roads. The criticisms that can fairly be made are the ones that readers of his early prose have tended to raise.

The most common is that the style is overworked. The essay is full of long, balanced sentences, learned allusions and decorative adjectives. In later life Stevenson himself was frank about having learned to write by imitating admired authors, and critics have seen that apprenticeship here. Some find the result more like an exercise in Victorian fine writing than the natural voice of a man talking. A reader who has just enjoyed the plain vigour of Treasure Island may be surprised by the stately, slightly breathless manner of this earlier essay.

A related complaint is that the argument is loose. The essay drifts from art to scenery, to roads, to the psychology of walking and finally to longing, with little to bind these together except the writer's enthusiasm. Some of the speculation, about why the shape of a road should echo our mood, is tentative and unresolved. A more disciplined essayist might have cut it.

There is also a question of tone. The essay speaks for a cultivated, leisured traveller, and its talk of the rural voluptuary and of studying nature for a lifetime assumes time, money and education. For most people who used roads in the 1870s, a road was a way to get to work, to market or to the next town, not a source of aesthetic delight. The quaint figure of the countryman who has never seen a crowd condescends a little to the people it admires.

Some modern readers also object to the nostalgia of the piece, with its preference for the winding natural road over the engineered highway or railway. Whatever the charm of that view, it can be seen as a romantic resistance to a modern world that offered real benefits, from faster travel to better access. Stevenson himself, the child of engineers, was not so simple, and it is a little ironic that the engineer's son praises the road that no engineer designed.

None of these complaints is severe. They add up to the verdict that the essay is a gifted beginner's work, richer in promise than in perfection. The promise, though, is considerable.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
Roads belongs to the long literary tradition of the walker's essay, in which a person on foot finds in the commonplace a reason for reflection. Behind it stand the Romantic poets, above all Wordsworth, who walked thousands of miles and made walking a source of poetry, and the English essayists William Hazlitt and Charles Lamb, whom Stevenson admired. Hazlitt's essay on going a journey is an obvious relation. Through Stevenson, the tradition passes forward to later writers who treat walking as a way of seeing, among them Edward Thomas, who wrote beautifully of English paths, and many modern authors of the long walk and the journey on foot.

The essay also draws on the German Romantic idea of longing, the Sehnsucht Stevenson explicitly names, and the quotation from Goethe's The Sorrows of Young Werther ties it to the European Romantic mood. Walt Whitman's Song of the Open Road, quoted in the essay, shows a link to the American celebration of the road as a symbol of freedom, a symbol that would later reappear in the literature of the highway, the tramp and the journey across a continent. Stevenson's own time in America would deepen that connection.

What descends from it is, in part, the very modern idea that the way we move through a landscape shapes how we see it. Writers on cycling, hiking and slow travel echo his argument, and so do critics of the modern motorway who complain that fast, straight roads cut us off from the country. His preference for the grown path over the planned line also has kinship with later thinkers on cities and gardens, who prize the organic over the imposed.

Compare it with Thoreau's essay Walking, written in the 1850s. Thoreau also treats walking as a form of wisdom, but he is more fierce and prophetic, and reaches for wildness. Stevenson is gentler, prizes the tame and the moderate, and finds his transcendence not in wilderness but in a farm road bending around a hill. The difference tells you something about the two temperaments and the two landscapes.

Why read it now? Partly for the fresh sentences and the image of the marching army. Partly because in a time of satnavs and straight lines, it reminds us of the pleasure of not knowing what is around the bend. And partly to see a famous writer at the start, already looking up the road, and already, as his essay says, a little ahead of his own body.

essays.title: A Winter’s Walk in Carrick and Galloway
essays.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
essays.epigraph: Through frosted glens and beside dark Scottish sea-lochs in January, the solitary walker tastes the ancient quiet of the winter earth.
essays.keyContext: Robert Louis Stevenson wrote A Winter's Walk in Carrick and Galloway in the mid-1870s, when he was in his mid-twenties, a young Edinburgh lawyer-in-name who was really becoming a professional writer. It describes a cold January walk along the Ayrshire coast in the southwest of Scotland, Robert Burns country, the week after the New Year. What makes it interesting is that Stevenson is not writing a cheerful guidebook. He sees the beauty of snow on ruined castles, but also the poverty of an old man gathering cockles, the grim history of a castle where a man was roasted over a fire, and the heavy drinking in a market town. The piece mixes landscape painting, social observation, history and dry humour, and it shows him learning to turn a walk into literature. What you are given here is the first part of a longer essay, so it stops mid-journey. Listen for the sharp little portraits of people, and for the moment the weather changes.
paragraphs: At the famous bridge of Doon, Kyle, the central district of the shire of Ayr, marches with Carrick, the most southerly. On the Carrick side of the river rises a hill of somewhat gentle conformation, cleft with shallow dells, and sown here and there with farms and tufts of wood. Inland, it loses itself, joining, I suppose, the great herd of similar hills that occupies the centre of the Lowlands. Towards the sea it swells out the coastline into a protuberance, like a bay-window in a plan, and is fortified against the surf behind bold crags. This hill is known as the Brown Hill of Carrick, or, more shortly, Brown Carrick.

It had snowed overnight. The fields were all sheeted up; they were tucked in among the snow, and their shape was modelled through the pliant counterpane, like children tucked in by a fond mother. The wind had made ripples and folds upon the surface, like what the sea, in quiet weather, leaves upon the sand. There was a frosty stifle in the air. An effusion of coppery light on the summit of Brown Carrick showed where the sun was trying to look through; but along the horizon clouds of cold fog had settled down, so that there was no distinction of sky and sea. Over the white shoulders of the headlands, or in the opening of bays, there was nothing but a great vacancy and blackness; and the road as it drew near the edge of the cliff seemed to skirt the shores of creation and void space.

The snow crunched under foot, and at farms all the dogs broke out barking as they smelt a passerby upon the road. I met a fine old fellow, who might have sat as the father in “The Cottar’s Saturday Night,” and who swore most heathenishly at a cow he was driving. And a little after I scraped acquaintance with a poor body tramping out to gather cockles. His face was wrinkled by exposure; it was broken up into flakes and channels, like mud beginning to dry, and weathered in two colours, an incongruous pink and grey. He had a faint air of being surprised⁠—which, God knows, he might well be⁠—that life had gone so ill with him. The shape of his trousers was in itself a jest, so strangely were they bagged and ravelled about his knees; and his coat was all bedaubed with clay as tough he had lain in a rain-dub during the New Year’s festivity. I will own I was not sorry to think he had had a merry New Year, and been young again for an evening; but I was sorry to see the mark still there. One could not expect such an old gentleman to be much of a dandy or a great student of respectability in dress; but there might have been a wife at home, who had brushed out similar stains after fifty New Years, now become old, or a round-armed daughter, who would wish to have him neat, were it only out of self-respect and for the ploughman sweetheart when he looks round at night. Plainly, there was nothing of this in his life, and years and loneliness hung heavily on his old arms. He was seventy-six, he told me; and nobody would give a day’s work to a man that age: they would think he couldn’t do it. “And, ’deed,” he went on, with a sad little chuckle, “ ’deed, I doubt if I could.” He said goodbye to me at a footpath, and crippled wearily off to his work. It will make your heart ache if you think of his old fingers groping in the snow.

He told me I was to turn down beside the schoolhouse for Dunure. And so, when I found a lone house among the snow, and heard a babble of childish voices from within, I struck off into a steep road leading downwards to the sea. Dunure lies close under the steep hill: a haven among the rocks, a breakwater in consummate disrepair, much apparatus for drying nets, and a score or so of fishers’ houses. Hard by, a few shards of ruined castle overhang the sea, a few vaults, and one tall gable honeycombed with windows. The snow lay on the beach to the tidemark. It was daubed on to the sills of the ruin: it roosted in the crannies of the rock like white seabirds; even on outlying reefs there would be a little cock of snow, like a toy lighthouse. Everything was grey and white in a cold and dolorous sort of shepherd’s plaid. In the profound silence, broken only by the noise of oars at sea, a horn was sounded twice; and I saw the postman, girt with two bags, pause a moment at the end of the clachan for letters. It is, perhaps, characteristic of Dunure that none were brought him.

The people at the public-house did not seem well pleased to see me, and though I would fain have stayed by the kitchen fire, sent me “ben the hoose” into the guestroom. This guestroom at Dunure was painted in quite aesthetic fashion. There are rooms in the same taste not a hundred miles from London, where persons of an extreme sensibility meet together without embarrassment. It was all in a fine dull bottle-green and black; a grave harmonious piece of colouring, with nothing, so far as coarser folk can judge, to hurt the better feelings of the most exquisite purist. A cherry-red half window-blind kept up an imaginary warmth in the cold room, and threw quite a glow on the floor. Twelve cockleshells and a halfpenny china figure were ranged solemnly along the mantelshelf. Even the spittoon was an original note, and instead of sawdust contained seashells. And as for the hearthrug, it would merit an article to itself, and a coloured diagram to help the text. It was patchwork, but the patchwork of the poor; no glowing shreds of old brocade and Chinese silk, shaken together in the kaleidoscope of some tasteful housewife’s fancy; but a work of art in its own way, and plainly a labour of love. The patches came exclusively from people’s raiment. There was no colour more brilliant than a heather mixture; “My Johnny’s grey breeks,” well polished over the oar on the boat’s thwart, entered largely into its composition. And the spoils of an old black cloth coat, that had been many a Sunday to church, added something (save the mark!) of preciousness to the material.

While I was at luncheon four carters came in⁠—long-limbed, muscular Ayrshire Scots, with lean, intelligent faces. Four quarts of stout were ordered; they kept filling the tumbler with the other hand as they drank; and in less time than it takes me to write these words the four quarts were finished⁠—another round was proposed, discussed, and negatived⁠—and they were creaking out of the village with their carts.

The ruins drew you towards them. You never saw any place more desolate from a distance, nor one that less belied its promise near at hand. Some crows and gulls flew away croaking as I scrambled in. The snow had drifted into the vaults. The clachan dabbled with snow, the white hills, the black sky, the sea marked in the coves with faint circular wrinkles, the whole world, as it looked from a loophole in Dunure, was cold, wretched, and out-at-elbows. If you had been a wicked baron and compelled to stay there all the afternoon, you would have had a rare fit of remorse. How you would have heaped up the fire and gnawed your fingers! I think it would have come to homicide before the evening⁠—if it were only for the pleasure of seeing something red! And the masters of Dunure, it is to be noticed, were remarkable of old for inhumanity. One of these vaults where the snow had drifted was that “black voute” where “Mr. Alane Stewart, Commendatour of Crossraguel,” endured his fiery trials. On the 1st and 7th of September 1570 (ill dates for Mr. Alan!), Gilbert, Earl of Cassilis, his chaplain, his baker, his cook, his pantryman, and another servant, bound the Poor Commendator “betwix an iron chimlay and a fire,” and there cruelly roasted him until he signed away his abbacy. It is one of the ugliest stories of an ugly period, but not, somehow, without such a flavour of the ridiculous as makes it hard to sympathise quite seriously with the victim. And it is consoling to remember that he got away at last, and kept his abbacy, and, over and above, had a pension from the Earl until he died.

Some way beyond Dunure a wide bay, of somewhat less unkindly aspect, opened out. Colzean plantations lay all along the steep shore, and there was a wooded hill towards the centre, where the trees made a sort of shadowy etching over the snow. The road went down and up, and past a blacksmith’s cottage that made fine music in the valley. Three compatriots of Burns drove up to me in a cart. They were all drunk, and asked me jeeringly if this was the way to Dunure. I told them it was; and my answer was received with unfeigned merriment. One gentleman was so much tickled he nearly fell out of the cart; indeed, he was only saved by a companion, who either had not so fine a sense of humour or had drunken less.

“The toune of Mayboll,” says the inimitable Abercrummie, “stands upon an ascending ground from east to west, and lyes open to the south. It hath one principall street, with houses upon both sides, built of freestone; and it is beautifyed with the situation of two castles, one at each end of this street. That on the east belongs to the Erle of Cassilis. On the west end is a castle, which belonged sometime to the laird of Blairquan, which is now the tolbuith, and is adorned with a pyremide [conical roof], and a row of ballesters round it raised from the top of the staircase, into which they have mounted a fyne clock. There be four lanes which pass from the principall street; one is called the Black Vennel, which is steep, declining to the southwest, and leads to a lower street, which is far larger than the high chiefe street, and it runs from the Kirkland to the Well Trees, in which there have been many pretty buildings, belonging to the severall gentry of the countrey, who were wont to resort thither in winter, and divert themselves in converse together at their owne houses. It was once the principall street of the town; but many of these houses of the gentry having been decayed and ruined, it has lost much of its ancient beautie. Just opposite to this vennel, there is another that leads northwest, from the chiefe street to the green, which is a pleasant plott of ground, enclosed round with an earthen wall, wherein they were wont to play football, but now at the Gowff and byasse-bowls. The houses of this towne, on both sides of the street, have their several gardens belonging to them; and in the lower street there be some pretty orchards, that yield store of good fruit.” As Patterson says, this description is near enough even today, and is mighty nicely written to boot. I am bound to add, of my own experience, that Maybole is tumbledown and dreary. Prosperous enough in reality, it has an air of decay; and though the population has increased, a roofless house every here and there seems to protest the contrary. The women are more than well-favoured, and the men fine tall fellows; but they look slipshod and dissipated. As they slouched at street corners, or stood about gossiping in the snow, it seemed they would have been more at home in the slums of a large city than here in a country place betwixt a village and a town. I heard a great deal about drinking, and a great deal about religious revivals: two things in which the Scottish character is emphatic and most unlovely. In particular, I heard of clergymen who were employing their time in explaining to a delighted audience the physics of the Second Coming. It is not very likely any of us will be asked to help. If we were, it is likely we should receive instructions for the occasion, and that on more reliable authority. And so I can only figure to myself a congregation truly curious in such flights of theological fancy, as one of veteran and accomplished saints, who have fought the good fight to an end and outlived all worldly passion, and are to be regarded rather as a part of the Church Triumphant than the poor, imperfect company on earth. And yet I saw some young fellows about the smoking-room who seemed, in the eyes of one who cannot count himself straitlaced, in need of some more practical sort of teaching. They seemed only eager to get drunk, and to do so speedily. It was not much more than a week after the New Year; and to hear them return on their past bouts with a gusto unspeakable was not altogether pleasing. Here is one snatch of talk, for the accuracy of which I can vouch⁠—
“Ye had a spree here last Tuesday?”
“We had that!”
“I wasna able to be oot o’ my bed. Man, I was awful bad on Wednesday.”
“Ay, ye were gey bad.”

And you should have seen the bright eyes, and heard the sensual accents! They recalled their doings with devout gusto and a sort of rational pride. Schoolboys, after their first drunkenness, are not more boastful; a cock does not plume himself with a more unmingled satisfaction as he paces forth among his harem; and yet these were grown men, and by no means short of wit. It was hard to suppose they were very eager about the Second Coming: it seemed as if some elementary notions of temperance for the men and seemliness for the women would have gone nearer the mark. And yet, as it seemed to me typical of much that is evil in Scotland, Maybole is also typical of much that is best. Some of the factories, which have taken the place of weaving in the town’s economy, were originally founded and are still possessed by self-made men of the sterling, stout old breed⁠—fellows who made some little bit of an invention, borrowed some little pocketful of capital, and then, step by step, in courage, thrift and industry, fought their way upwards to an assured position.

Abercrummie has told you enough of the Tolbooth; but, as a bit of spelling, this inscription on the Tolbooth bell seems too delicious to withhold: “This bell is founded at Maiboll Bi Danel Geli, a Frenchman, the 6th November, 1696, Bi appointment of the heritors of the parish of Maiyboll.” The Castle deserves more notice. It is a large and shapely tower, plain from the ground upwards, but with a zone of ornamentation running about the top. In a general way this adornment is perched on the very summit of the chimney-stacks; but there is one corner more elaborate than the rest. A very heavy string-course runs round the upper story, and just above this, facing up the street, the tower carries a small oriel window, fluted and corbelled and carved about with stone heads. It is so ornate it has somewhat the air of a shrine. And it was, indeed, the casket of a very precious jewel, for in the room to which it gives light lay, for long years, the heroine of the sweet old ballad of “Johnnie Faa”⁠—she who, at the call of the gipsies’ songs, “came tripping down the stair, and all her maids before her.” Some people say the ballad has no basis in fact, and have written, I believe, unanswerable papers to the proof. But in the face of all that, the very look of that high oriel window convinces the imagination, and we enter into all the sorrows of the imprisoned dame. We conceive the burden of the long, lacklustre days, when she leaned her sick head against the mullions, and saw the burghers loafing in Maybole High Street, and the children at play, and ruffling gallants riding by from hunt or foray. We conceive the passion of odd moments, when the wind threw up to her some snatch of song, and her heart grew hot within her, and her eyes overflowed at the memory of the past. And even if the tale be not true of this or that lady, or this or that old tower, it is true in the essence of all men and women: for all of us, some time or other, hear the gipsies singing; over all of us is the glamour cast. Some resist and sit resolutely by the fire. Most go and are brought back again, like Lady Cassilis. A few, of the tribe of Waring, go and are seen no more; only now and again, at springtime, when the gipsies’ song is afloat in the amethyst evening, we can catch their voices in the glee.

By night it was clearer, and Maybole more visible than during the day. Clouds coursed over the sky in great masses; the full moon battled the other way, and lit up the snow with gleams of flying silver; the town came down the hill in a cascade of brown gables, bestridden by smooth white roofs, and sprangled here and there with lighted windows. At either end the snow stood high up in the darkness, on the peak of the Tolbooth and among the chimneys of the Castle. As the moon flashed a bull’s-eye glitter across the town between the racing clouds, the white roofs leaped into relief over the gables and the chimney-stacks, and their shadows over the white roofs. In the town itself the lit face of the clock peered down the street; an hour was hammered out on Mr. Geli’s bell, and from behind the red curtains of a public-house someone trolled out⁠—a compatriot of Burns, again!⁠—“The saut tear blin’s my e’e.”

Next morning there was sun and a flapping wind. From the street corners of Maybole I could catch breezy glimpses of green fields. The road underfoot was wet and heavy⁠—part ice, part snow, part water, and anyone I met greeted me, by way of salutation, with “A fine thowe” (thaw). My way lay among rather bleak bills, and past bleak ponds and dilapidated castles and monasteries, to the Highland-looking village of Kirkoswald. It has little claim to notice, save that Burns came there to study surveying in the summer of 1777, and there also, in the kirkyard, the original of Tam o’ Shanter sleeps his last sleep. It is worth noticing, however, that this was the first place I thought “Highland-looking.” Over the bill from Kirkoswald a farm-road leads to the coast. As I came down above Turnberry, the sea view was indeed strangely different from the day before. The cold fogs were all blown away; and there was Ailsa Craig, like a refraction, magnified and deformed, of the Bass Rock; and there were the chiselled mountaintops of Arran, veined and tipped with snow; and behind, and fainter, the low, blue land of Cantyre. Cottony clouds stood in a great castle over the top of Arran, and blew out in long streamers to the south. The sea was bitten all over with white; little ships, tacking up and down the Firth, lay over at different angles in the wind. On Shanter they were ploughing lea; a cart foal, all in a field by himself, capered and whinnied as if the spring were in him.

The road from Turnberry to Girvan lies along the shore, among sandhills and by wildernesses of tumbled bent. Every here and there a few cottages stood together beside a bridge. They had one odd feature, not easy to describe in words: a triangular porch projected from above the door, supported at the apex by a single upright post; a secondary door was hinged to the post, and could be hasped on either cheek of the real entrance; so, whether the wind was north or south, the cotter could make himself a triangular bight of shelter where to set his chair and finish a pipe with comfort. There is one objection to this device; for, as the post stands in the middle of the fairway, anyone precipitately issuing from the cottage must run his chance of a broken head. So far as I am aware, it is peculiar to the little corner of country about Girvan. And that corner is noticeable for more reasons: it is certainly one of the most characteristic districts in Scotland. It has this movable porch by way of architecture; it has, as we shall see, a sort of remnant of provincial costume, and it has the handsomest population in the Lowlands.⁠ ⁠…

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
On the surface this is a travel sketch: a man walks south along the coast of Ayrshire in the snow, stays a night, and walks on. But Stevenson is doing several things at once. The first is painting a landscape, and the opening is full of it. The snow has tucked the fields in like children under a counterpane, the wind has made ripples in it like sand left by the sea, and the road near the cliff edge seems to skirt the shores of creation and void space. That last phrase tells you that this is not a postcard. The world is empty, grey and white, a cold and dolorous sort of shepherd's plaid.

The second thing is human. Stevenson meets an old man gathering cockles, with a face broken into flakes and channels like drying mud, and a faint air of being surprised that life had gone so ill with him. He is seventy-six and cannot find work, because nobody believes a man that age can do it. His reply, that he doubts whether he could, with a sad little chuckle, is the emotional heart of the first half. The narrator imagines the wife or daughter who might have brushed the clay from his coat, and recognises that there is none. Look closely and you see that Stevenson is moved, and that he refuses to hide it, while still letting the old man keep his dignity.

The third layer is history and the uncomfortable truth about the picturesque. The ruined castle at Dunure looks romantic, but it is the place where, in 1570, a powerful earl roasted a church official between an iron chimney and a fire to make him sign away his lands. Stevenson tells the story with a tone that is half horror and half black comedy, noting that the victim survived and kept his post and a pension. The point is that the beauty of ruins sits on top of cruelty.

Then the walk reaches the town of Maybole, where Stevenson sets the quotation of an old topographer's loving description beside his own verdict that the town is tumbledown and dreary. The men boast of their drinking spree like schoolboys, and the talk of religious revivals seems beside the point. Yet he balances this by praising the self-made manufacturers. The Johnnie Faa ballad, about a lady who left her lord to follow gypsies, gives him a moment of real insight: all of us, sooner or later, hear the gipsies singing.

Finally the weather turns, with a thaw and a view of Ailsa Craig and Arran, and the mood lifts. The essay's meaning lies in this range: a winter walk as an education in seeing both the beauty and the hardness of a place.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
The strongest quality here is the eye. Stevenson looks at a scene and finds the exact, surprising comparison. The snow roosting in the crannies of the rock like white seabirds, the little cock of snow on an outlying reef like a toy lighthouse, and the lit clock face peering down the street of Maybole under racing clouds are all images that make the scene visible. The moonlit paragraph, with the town coming down the hill in a cascade of brown gables bestridden by smooth white roofs, is a small tour de force of light and shadow. His sentences move with the pace of walking, and the sequence of impressions has the unforced rhythm of someone who is simply noticing.

The humour is also well judged. The description of the inn's guestroom, painted in what he calls aesthetic fashion, with twelve cockleshells and a china figure on the mantelpiece, a spittoon filled with seashells and a patchwork hearthrug made of people's old clothes, is a clever way of making fun of fashionable taste in London while showing real respect for the poor housewife's labour of love. The hearthrug passage is the best joke in the piece because it turns into a tenderness. The four carters finishing four quarts of stout in less time than it takes to write the sentence is pure comic timing.

The structure, however, is loose, and that is partly the nature of the form. The essay is a series of episodes strung along a road, and some are much stronger than others. The long quotation from the old description of Maybole, in antique spelling, is a gift to a topographer but a pause for a general reader. The ballad and castle sections drift into antiquarian detail that depends on the reader's interest in local history. The passage about Scottish drinking and revivals, while lively, borders on a sermon, and the tone shifts uneasily between mockery and moral disapproval.

There is also a question of how well Stevenson handles the poor. The old cockle-gatherer is rendered with real feeling, but the portraits of the drunk carters, the men on the street corners and the people at the inn who do not seem well pleased to see a stranger are seen from outside, with the amused detachment of a young gentleman. The wit sometimes keeps people at arm's length.

Even so, the best passages are first rate. The wicked baron stuck in the ruin all afternoon, who would have heaped up the fire and gnawed his fingers, is a witty way of making a cold room feel cold. Overall it is an uneven but deeply attractive piece, with moments of real power surrounded by good, lively filler.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
This is not one of Stevenson's famous works, and its influence is modest and indirect. It was written when he was beginning to publish regularly in magazines, and it belongs to the group of early travel and landscape essays that trained him as a writer. After his death it was gathered with other pieces of this kind in a posthumous collection of travel essays, which is where most readers meet it today.

Its significance in his career is as a stage in his development. In these years he was learning to combine description, anecdote and reflection in a way that would carry over into his first books of travel. An Inland Voyage appeared in 1878 and Travels with a Donkey in the Cevennes in 1879, and the qualities that make them work, the quick portrait of a stranger, the mocking self-awareness, the sense of landscape as mood, are all practised here. You can see the same eye at work in the passages of his novels set in Scotland, where weather and coastline are almost characters. Kidnapped and The Master of Ballantrae in particular carry the Scottish landscape and the Scottish past, with their mixture of beauty and violence, that this essay already weighs in the balance.

The essay also adds to the picture of Scotland as a place of layered history. Stevenson's interest in the dark stories lying under picturesque ruins, the cruelty of old lords, the zeal of religious factions, the feuds of families, runs through his fiction and his essays. The Dunure episode is a miniature of that habit of mind.

The record of its reception is thin. There is no recorded famous reaction to this particular essay, and it has not been the subject of major critical controversy. It has survived chiefly among Stevenson enthusiasts, Scottish literature scholars and readers interested in Burns country, as a vivid snapshot of the Ayrshire coast in the 1870s. As a record of what Scottish rural life looked like, with its drinking, its revivalist religion, its poverty and its manufacturing beginnings, it has some value for social historians.

In teaching, it appears mainly as an example of Victorian travel writing and of the Scottish essay tradition, and is less often assigned than his more famous works. It remains a pleasant discovery, and a good introduction to his gift for noticing.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
The first thing that readers enjoy is the sheer sensory quality of the winter scene. The crunch of snow underfoot, dogs barking at every farm, the profound silence broken only by the sound of oars at sea, and the postman who blows his horn and finds no letters waiting, all give a convincing impression of a cold day on a quiet coast. Stevenson's trick of noticing the small thing, such as the tiny cock of snow on a reef, makes the scene believable and charming. For readers who love the Scottish coast, it is a vivid portrait of a place at a particular moment.

They also love the people. The old man gathering cockles is a small, unforgettable portrait, handled with a delicate mix of humour and pity. The passage ends with the line that it will make your heart ache if you think of his old fingers groping in the snow, and it is the sort of sentence that readers carry away. The contrasting comic scenes, the carters and their stout, the three drunken men in a cart who think it hilarious that a traveller is asking the way to Dunure, give a sense of lively, unvarnished Scottish life.

Readers also admire the way Stevenson plays with the reader. The mock-solemn description of the guestroom, with its cockleshells and its seashell spittoon, is comedy of a high order, and the sly aside that the hearthrug would merit an article to itself, and a coloured diagram to help the text, is a joke aimed at the fashion for aesthetic home decoration.

Another source of affection is the way the piece moves between darkness and light. The gloomy Dunure episode, with its grim history and its savage joke about the wicked baron, gives way to the moonlit night in Maybole and the sunny morning of the thaw, with Ailsa Craig and the peaks of Arran, a colt capering in a field as though spring were in him. The change of weather lifts the essay, and readers feel it. It is a satisfying shape, a journey from stifling cold to open sea air.

The ballad passage about the lady who left her home for the gypsies is also a favourite for many. Stevenson's meditation that all of us hear the gipsies singing, that some resist, most go and are brought back, and a few are never seen again, is a lovely piece of reflection, and one that readers often quote. Admirers of his work say that you can feel the future novelist in this humane, imaginative aside.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
Since this essay has not been a prominent subject of criticism, there are no particular reviewers or famous arguments to cite. What can be said honestly is what readers have found less successful, drawn from the text and from general assessments of Stevenson's early work.

The first complaint is about structure. The essay is episodic and, in the version we have, unfinished, breaking off in mid-journey with an ellipsis. Some readers find the stretches of antiquarian description, especially the long quotation from an old description of Maybole in seventeenth-century spelling and the tangents about the bell and the castle, a drag on the pace. A traveller's notebook is not always a shapely essay.

The second concerns tone. Stevenson's comments on Scottish drinking and religious revivals are brisk and judgmental. He calls the Scottish character in these matters emphatic and most unlovely, and he makes fun of clergymen explaining the physics of the Second Coming. For some readers this sounds like the superiority of a young middle-class man from Edinburgh looking down on country people, and a few have seen a streak of snobbery in the way he describes the Maybole men as slipshod and dissipated. Others, of course, find his candour refreshing, and defenders point out that he is also a Scot criticizing his own people, and that he balances the picture with praise of the self-made manufacturers.

A third line of criticism, more common today, concerns the treatment of poverty. Stevenson shows real compassion for the old cockle-gatherer, but he also finds the roasting of the commendator ridiculous and keeps up a comic mood throughout. A modern reader may feel that the essay is too ready to turn hardship into material, or too quick to aestheticise a cold, bare room.

Finally, the essay's reliance on dense local reference, to Burns, to ballads, to particular families and places, makes it harder for readers outside Scotland. Without that knowledge some of the allusions fall flat.

None of this has made the essay a battleground. It is regarded as a minor but charming work, which is exactly how it should be read. The faults are those of a young writer's notebook, and the virtues are those of an observer with a remarkable eye.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
This essay belongs to the great nineteenth-century tradition of the walking tour and the travel sketch, a tradition that runs from the Romantic poets, who tramped the Lake District and the Alps, through Hazlitt and Thoreau to Stevenson's own generation. Stevenson was one of the form's finest practitioners, and his best-known travel books helped define it. This early essay is a smaller version of the same enterprise: a solitary walker, a few days on the road, the pleasure of casual meetings and the shift of mood with the weather.

It also sits within Scottish literature, in the long conversation with Robert Burns that the essay makes explicit by repeatedly invoking the poet. The old man who might have sat as the father in The Cottar's Saturday Night, the drunken men who are compatriots of Burns, and the walk through Kirkoswald where Burns studied surveying and where the original of Tam o' Shanter lies buried, all place Stevenson in conscious relation to that heritage. The Scots tradition of mixing humour, sentiment and dark history, the same that you find in Burns, in Walter Scott and later in Stevenson's own fiction, is unmistakable.

Among the works it relates to, perhaps the nearest are Stevenson's other essays of place and his account of walking in the Cevennes. Beyond him, writers of the English and Scottish landscape and of the winter walk, from Dorothy Wordsworth's journals to later nature writers, share this combination of exact description and personal feeling. Writers on rural poverty and social observation, from Dickens in his travel sketches to the later documentary writers, might also be placed alongside the old man and the cockles.

The reader may also notice an early example of what would be called psychogeography, the interest in how a place's history and atmosphere shape the mood of one who passes through it, though Stevenson would not have used the word. The idea that ruins carry buried cruelty beneath their picturesque outlines has a long afterlife.

Why read it now? For the moonlit paragraph, for the cockle-gatherer, for the hearthrug, and for the pleasure of a writer discovering that a walk is a story. It also stands as a reminder of how to travel, with all senses open, and with a willingness to be moved, amused and disturbed by what lies on the road. It is short on polish but long on life, and that is a fine reason to read.

essays.title: The Coast of Fife
essays.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
essays.epigraph: Every old town along the Firth of Forth keeps its own salty memory of witches, Covenanters, smugglers, and sea-captains.
essays.keyContext: The Coast of Fife is a memory piece by Robert Louis Stevenson, written in 1888 when he was already famous for Treasure Island and Jekyll and Hyde, and living far from the Scotland he describes. It looks back to a trip he took as a boy in 1863, when his father, a builder and inspector of lighthouses, took him around the shores of Fife to visit the harbour lights. Stevenson's family had made their name and fortune building lighthouses along the Scottish coast, and this essay is partly about what it meant to grow up in that profession, and to know from childhood that he would not follow it. But it is also something stranger and more playful: a rambling tour of local legends, from an assassination on a lonely moor to a shipwrecked Spanish duke. Beneath the stories lies an idea about how writers think, which is that history grips us through a single picturesque image. What you are given is the opening stretch of a longer piece, so it ends on a lively Fair Isle anecdote.
paragraphs: Many writers have vigorously described the pains of the first day or the first night at school; to a boy of any enterprise, I believe, they are more often agreeably exciting. Misery⁠—or at least misery unrelieved⁠—is confined to another period, to the days of suspense and the “dreadful looking-for” of departure; when the old life is running to an end, and the new life, with its new interests, not yet begun: and to the pain of an imminent parting, there is added the unrest of a state of conscious preexistence. The area railings, the beloved shopwindow, the smell of semi-suburban tanpits, the song of the church bells upon a Sunday, the thin, high voices of compatriot children in a playing-field⁠—what a sudden, what an overpowering pathos breathes to him from each familiar circumstance! The assaults of sorrow come not from within, as it seems to him, but from without. I was proud and glad to go to school; had I been let alone, I could have borne up like any hero; but there was around me, in all my native town, a conspiracy of lamentation: “Poor little boy, he is going away⁠—unkind little boy, he is going to leave us”; so the unspoken burden followed me as I went, with yearning and reproach. And at length, one melancholy afternoon in the early autumn, and at a place where it seems to me, looking back, it must be always autumn and generally Sunday, there came suddenly upon the face of all I saw⁠—the long empty road, the lines of the tall houses, the church upon the hill, the woody hillside garden⁠—a look of such a piercing sadness that my heart died; and seating myself on a doorstep, I shed tears of miserable sympathy. A benevolent cat cumbered me the while with consolations⁠—we two were alone in all that was visible of the London Road: two poor waifs who had each tasted sorrow⁠—and she fawned upon the weeper, and gambolled for his entertainment, watching the effect it seemed, with motherly eyes.

For the sake of the cat, God bless her! I confessed at home the story of my weakness; and so it comes about that I owed a certain journey, and the reader owes the present paper, to a cat in the London Road. It was judged, if I had thus brimmed over on the public highway, some change of scene was (in the medical sense) indicated; my father at the time was visiting the harbour lights of Scotland; and it was decided he should take me along with him around a portion of the shores of Fife; my first professional tour, my first journey in the complete character of man, without the help of petticoats.

The Kingdom of Fife (that royal province) may be observed by the curious on the map, occupying a tongue of land between the firths of Forth and Tay. It may be continually seen from many parts of Edinburgh (among the rest, from the windows of my father’s house) dying away into the distance and the easterly haar with one smoky seaside town beyond another, or in winter printing on the gray heaven some glittering hilltops. It has no beauty to recommend it, being a low, sea-salted, wind-vexed promontory; trees very rare, except (as common on the east coast) along the dens of rivers; the fields well cultivated, I understand, but not lovely to the eye. It is of the coast I speak: the interior may be the garden of Eden. History broods over that part of the world like the easterly haar. Even on the map, its long row of Gaelic place-names bear testimony to an old and settled race. Of these little towns, posted along the shore as close as sedges, each with its bit of harbour, its old weather-beaten church or public building, its flavour of decayed prosperity and decaying fish, not one but has its legend, quaint or tragic: Dunfermline, in whose royal towers the king may be still observed (in the ballad) drinking the bloodred wine; somnolent Inverkeithing, once the quarantine of Leith; Aberdour, hard by the monastic islet of Inchcolm, hard by Donibristle where the “bonny face was spoiled”; Burntisland where, when Paul Jones was off the coast, the Reverend Mr. Shirra had a table carried between tidemarks, and publicly prayed against the rover at the pitch of his voice and his broad lowland dialect; Kinghorn, where Alexander “brak’s neckbane” and left Scotland to the English wars; Kirkcaldy, where the witches once prevailed extremely and sank tall ships and honest mariners in the North Sea; Dysart, famous⁠—well famous at least to me for the Dutch ships that lay in its harbour, painted like toys and with pots of flowers and cages of songbirds in the cabin windows, and for one particular Dutch skipper who would sit all day in slippers on the break of the poop, smoking a long German pipe; Wemyss (pronounce Weems) with its bat-haunted caves, where the Chevalier Johnstone, on his flight from Culloden, passed a night of superstitious terrors; Leven, a bald, quite modern place, sacred to summer visitors, whence there has gone but yesterday the tall figure and the white locks of the last Englishman in Delhi, my uncle Dr. Balfour, who was still walking his hospital rounds, while the troopers from Meerut clattered and cried “Deen Deen” along the streets of the imperial city, and Willoughby mustered his handful of heroes at the magazine, and the nameless brave one in the telegraph office was perhaps already fingering his last despatch; and just a little beyond Leven, Largo Law and the smoke of Largo town mounting about its feet, the town of Alexander Selkirk, better known under the name of Robinson Crusoe. So on, the list might be pursued (only for private reasons, which the reader will shortly have an opportunity to guess) by St. Monance, and Pittenweem, and the two Anstruthers, and Cellardyke, and Crail, where Primate Sharpe was once a humble and innocent country minister: on to the heel of the land, to Fife Ness, overlooked by a sea-wood of matted elders and the quaint old mansion of Balcomie, itself overlooking but the breach or the quiescence of the deep⁠—the Carr Rock beacon rising close in front, and as night draws in, the star of the Inchcape reef springing up on the one hand, and the star of the May Island on the other, and farther off yet a third and a greater on the craggy foreland of St. Abb’s. And but a little way round the corner of the land, imminent itself above the sea, stands the gem of the province and the light of medieval Scotland, St. Andrews, where the great Cardinal Beaton held garrison against the world, and the second of the name and title perished (as you may read in Knox’s jeering narrative) under the knives of true-blue Protestants, and to this day (after so many centuries) the current voice of the professor is not hushed.

Here it was that my first tour of inspection began, early on a bleak easterly morning. There was a crashing run of sea upon the shore, I recollect, and my father and the man of the harbour light must sometimes raise their voices to be audible. Perhaps it is from this circumstance, that I always imagine St. Andrews to be an ineffectual seat of learning, and the sound of the east wind and the bursting surf to linger in its drowsy classrooms and confound the utterance of the professor, until teacher and taught are alike drowned in oblivion, and only the seagull beats on the windows and the draught of the sea-air rustles in the pages of the open lecture. But upon all this, and the romance of St. Andrews in general, the reader must consult the works of Mr. Andrew Lang; who has written of it but the other day in his dainty prose and with his incommunicable humour, and long ago in one of his best poems, with grace, and local truth, and a note of unaffected pathos. Mr. Lang knows all about the romance, I say, and the educational advantages, but I doubt if he had turned his attention to the harbour lights; and it may be news even to him, that in the year 1863 their case was pitiable. Hanging about with the east wind humming in my teeth, and my hands (I make no doubt) in my pockets, I looked for the first time upon that tragicomedy of the visiting engineer which I have seen so often reenacted on a more important stage. Eighty years ago, I find my grandfather writing: “It is the most painful thing that can occur to me to have a correspondence of this kind with any of the keepers, and when I come to the Light House, instead of having the satisfaction to meet them with approbation and welcome their Family, it is distressing when one is obliged to put on a most angry countenance and demeanour.” This painful obligation has been hereditary in my race. I have myself, on a perfectly amateur and unauthorised inspection of Turnberry Point, bent my brows upon the keeper on the question of storm-panes; and felt a keen pang of self-reproach, when we went downstairs again and I found he was making a coffin for his infant child; and then regained my equanimity with the thought that I had done the man a service, and when the proper inspector came, he would be readier with his panes. The human race is perhaps credited with more duplicity than it deserves. The visitation of a lighthouse at least is a business of the most transparent nature. As soon as the boat grates on the shore, and the keepers step forward in their uniformed coats, the very slouch of the fellows’ shoulders tells their story, and the engineer may begin at once to assume his “angry countenance.” Certainly the brass of the handrail will be clouded; and if the brass be not immaculate, certainly all will be to match⁠—the reflectors scratched, the spare lamp unready, the storm-panes in the storehouse. If a light is not rather more than middling good, it will be radically bad. Mediocrity (except in literature) appears to be unattainable by man. But of course the unfortunate of St. Andrews was only an amateur, he was not in the Service, he had no uniform coat, he was (I believe) a plumber by his trade and stood (in the medieval phrase) quite out of the danger of my father; but he had a painful interview for all that, and perspired extremely.

From St. Andrews, we drove over Magus Muir. My father had announced we were “to post,” and the phrase called up in my hopeful mind visions of top-boots and the pictures in Rowlandson’s Dance of Death; but it was only a jingling cab that came to the inn door, such as I had driven in a thousand times at the low price of one shilling on the streets of Edinburgh. Beyond this disappointment, I remember nothing of that drive. It is a road I have often travelled, and of not one of these journeys do I remember any single trait. The fact has not been suffered to encroach on the truth of the imagination. I still see Magus Muir two hundred years ago; a desert place, quite uninclosed; in the midst, the primate’s carriage fleeing at the gallop; the assassins loose-reined in pursuit, Burley Balfour, pistol in hand, among the first. No scene of history has ever written itself so deeply on my mind; not because Balfour, that questionable zealot, was an ancestral cousin of my own; not because of the pleadings of the victim and his daughter; not even because of the live bum-bee that flew out of Sharpe’s ’bacco-box, thus clearly indicating his complicity with Satan; nor merely because, as it was after all a crime of a fine religious flavour, it figured in Sunday books and afforded a grateful relief from Ministering Children or the Memoirs of Mrs. Kathatine Winslowe. The figure that always fixed my attention is that of Hackston of Rathillet, sitting in the saddle with his cloak about his mouth, and through all that long, bungling, vociferous hurly-burly, revolving privately a case of conscience. He would take no hand in the deed, because he had a private spite against the victim, and “that action” must be sullied with no suggestion of a worldly motive; on the other hand, “that action,” in itself, was highly justified, he had cast in his lot with “the actors,” and he must stay there, inactive but publicly sharing the responsibility. “You are a gentleman⁠—you will protect me!” cried the wounded old man, crawling towards him. “I will never lay a hand on you,” said Hackston, and put his cloak about his mouth. It is an old temptation with me, to pluck away that cloak and see the face⁠—to open that bosom and to read the heart. With incomplete romances about Hackston, the drawers of my youth were lumbered. I read him up in every printed book that I could lay my hands on. I even dug among the Wodrow manuscripts, sitting shamefaced in the very room where my hero had been tortured two centuries before, and keenly conscious of my youth in the midst of other and (as I fondly thought) more gifted students. All was vain: that he had passed a riotous nonage, that he was a zealot, that he twice displayed (compared with his grotesque companions) some tincture of soldierly resolution and even of military common sense, and that he figured memorably in the scene on Magus Muir, so much and no more could I make out. But whenever I cast my eyes backward, it is to see him like a landmark on the plains of history, sitting with his cloak about his mouth, inscrutable. How small a thing creates an immortality! I do not think he can have been a man entirely commonplace; but had he not thrown his cloak about his mouth, or had the witnesses forgot to chronicle the action, he would not thus have haunted the imagination of my boyhood, and today he would scarce delay me for a paragraph. An incident, at once romantic and dramatic, which at once awakes the judgment and makes a picture for the eye, how little do we realise its perdurable power! Perhaps no one does so but the author, just as none but he appreciates the influence of jingling words; so that he looks on upon life, with something of a covert smile, seeing people led by what they fancy to be thoughts and what are really the accustomed artifices of his own trade, or roused by what they take to be principles and are really picturesque effects. In a pleasant book about a school-class club, Colonel Fergusson has recently told a little anecdote. A “Philosophical Society” was formed by some Academy boys⁠—among them, Colonel Fergusson himself, Fleeming Jenkin, and Andrew Wilson, the Christian Buddhist and author of The Abode of Snow. Before these learned pundits, one member laid the following ingenious problem: “What would be the result of putting a pound of potassium in a pot of porter?” “I should think there would be a number of interesting bi-products,” said a smatterer at my elbow; but for me the tale itself has a bi-product, and stands as a type of much that is most human. For this inquirer who conceived himself to burn with a zeal entirely chemical, was really immersed in a design of a quite different nature; unconsciously to his own recently breeched intelligence, he was engaged in literature. Putting, pound, potassium, pot, porter; initial p, mediant t⁠—that was his idea, poor little boy! So with politics and that which excites men in the present, so with history and that which rouses them in the past: there lie at the root of what appears, most serious unsuspected elements.

The triple town of Anstruther Wester, Anstruther Easter, and Cellardyke, all three Royal Burghs⁠—or two Royal Burghs and a less distinguished suburb, I forget which⁠—lies continuously along the seaside, and boasts of either two or three separate parish churches, and either two or three separate harbours. These ambiguities are painful; but the fact is (although it argue me uncultured), I am but poorly posted upon Cellardyke. My business lay in the two Anstruthers. A tricklet of a stream divides them, spanned by a bridge; and over the bridge at the time of my knowledge, the celebrated Shell House stood outpost on the west. This had been the residence of an agreeable eccentric; during his fond tenancy, he had illustrated the outer walls, as high (if I remember rightly) as the roof, with elaborate patterns and pictures, and snatches of verse in the vein of exegi monumentum; shells and pebbles, artfully contrasted and conjoined, had been his medium; and I like to think of him standing back upon the bridge, when all was finished, drinking in the general effect and (like Gibbon) already lamenting his employment.

The same bridge saw another sight in the seventeenth century. Mr. Thomson, the “curat” of Anstruther Easter, was a man highly obnoxious to the devout: in the first place, because he was a “curat”; in the second place, because he was a person of irregular and scandalous life; and in the third place, because he was generally suspected of dealings with the Enemy of Man. These three disqualifications, in the popular literature of the time, go hand in hand; but the end of Mr. Thomson was a thing quite by itself, and in the proper phrase, a manifest judgment. He had been at a friend’s house in Anstruther Wester, where (and elsewhere, I suspect) he had partaken of the bottle; indeed, to put the thing in our cold modern way, the reverend gentleman was on the brink of delirium tremens. It was a dark night, it seems; a little lassie came carrying a lantern to fetch the curate home; and away they went down the street of Anstruther Wester, the lantern swinging a bit in the child’s hand, the barred lustre tossing up and down along the front of slumbering houses, and Mr. Thomson not altogether steady on his legs nor (to all appearance) easy in his mind. The pair had reached the middle of the bridge when (as I conceive the scene) the poor tippler started in some baseless fear and looked behind him; the child, already shaken by the minister’s strange behaviour, started also; in so doing, she would jerk the lantern; and for the space of a moment the lights and the shadows would be all confounded. Then it was that to the unhinged toper and the twittering child, a huge bulk of blackness seemed to sweep down, to pass them close by as they stood upon the bridge, and to vanish on the farther side in the general darkness of the night. “Plainly the devil come for Mr. Thomson!” thought the child. What Mr. Thomson thought himself, we have no ground of knowledge; but he fell upon his knees in the midst of the bridge like a man praying. On the rest of the journey to the manse, history is silent; but when they came to the door, the poor caitiff, taking the lantern from the child, looked upon her with so lost a countenance that her little courage died within her, and she fled home screaming to her parents. Not a soul would venture out; all that night, the minister dwelt alone with his terrors in the manse; and when the day dawned, and men made bold to go about the streets, they found the devil had come indeed for Mr. Thomson.

This manse of Anstruther Easter has another and a more cheerful association. It was early in the morning, about a century before the days of Mr. Thomson, that his predecessor was called out of bed to welcome a Grandee of Spain, the Duke of Medina Sidonia, just landed in the harbour underneath. But sure there was never seen a more decayed grandee; sure there was never a duke welcomed from a stranger place of exile. Halfway between Orkney and Shetland, there lies a certain isle; on the one hand the Atlantic, on the other the North Sea, bombard its pillared cliffs; sore-eyed, short-living, inbred fishers and their families herd in its few huts; in the graveyard pieces of wreck-wood stand for monuments; there is nowhere a more inhospitable spot. Belle-Isle-en-Mer⁠—Fair-Isle-at-Sea⁠—that is a name that has always rung in my mind’s ear like music; but the only “Fair Isle” on which I ever set my foot, was this unhomely, rugged turret-top of submarine sierras. Here, when his ship was broken, my lord Duke joyfully got ashore; here for long months he and certain of his men were harboured; and it was from this durance that he landed at last to be welcomed (as well as such a papist deserved, no doubt) by the godly incumbent of Anstruther Easter; and after the Fair Isle, what a fine city must that have appeared! and after the island diet, what a hospitable spot the minister’s table! And yet he must have lived on friendly terms with his outlandish hosts. For to this day there still survives a relic of the long winter evenings when the sailors of the great Armada crouched about the hearths of the Fair-Islanders, the planks of their own lost galleon perhaps lighting up the scene, and the gale and the surf that beat about the coast contributing their melancholy voices. All the folk of the north isles are great artificers of knitting: the Fair-Islanders alone dye their fabrics in the Spanish manner. To this day, gloves and nightcaps, innocently decorated, may be seen for sale in the Shetland warehouse at Edinburgh, or on the Fair Isle itself in the catechist’s house; and to this day, they tell the story of the Duke of Medina Sidonia’s adventure.

It would seem as if the Fair Isle had some attraction for “persons of quality.” When I landed there myself, an elderly gentleman, unshaved, poorly attired, his shoulders wrapped in a plaid, was seen walking to and fro, with a book in his hand, upon the beach. He paid no heed to our arrival, which we thought a strange thing in itself; but when one of the officers of the Pharos, passing narrowly by him, observed his book to be a Greek Testament, our wonder and interest took a higher flight. The catechist was cross-examined; he said the gentleman had been put across some time before in Mr. Bruce of Sumburgh’s schooner, the only link between the Fair Isle and the rest of the world; and that he held services and was doing “good.” So much came glibly enough; but when pressed a little farther, the catechist displayed embarrassment. A singular diffidence appeared upon his face: “They tell me,” said he, in low tones, “that he’s a lord.” And a lord he was; a peer of the realm pacing that inhospitable beach with his Greek Testament, and his plaid about his shoulders, set upon doing good, as he understood it, worthy man! And his grandson, a good-looking little boy, much better dressed than the lordly evangelist, and speaking with a silken English accent very foreign to the scene, accompanied me for a while in my exploration of the island. I suppose this little fellow is now my lord, and wonder how much he remembers of the Fair Isle. Perhaps not much; for he seemed to accept very quietly his savage situation; and under such guidance, it is like that this was not his first nor yet his last adventure.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
The essay starts with a small, true piece of psychology. Writers often describe the misery of the first night at school, Stevenson says, but for an enterprising boy that is more exciting than painful. The real misery comes earlier, in the days of dreadful waiting before leaving, when the old life is ending and the new has not begun. Every familiar thing, the area railings, the shop window, the church bells, suddenly breathes pathos. And around him in his native town was a conspiracy of lamentation: everyone saying poor little boy, he is going away. One autumn afternoon on the London Road, the whole scene took on a look of such piercing sadness that he sat on a doorstep and cried, while a kindly cat tried to console him. Because of that cat, he jokes, his father decided a change of scene was medically indicated, and took him along on a tour of the Fife lighthouses. That is why, he says, the reader owes the present paper to a cat.

Then the tone shifts into an enormous, loving list of the little towns along the Fife coast, each with its legend, quaint or tragic. Stevenson crams in ballads, witches, Dutch ships with songbirds in the cabin windows, a family uncle who walked his hospital rounds in Delhi during the mutiny of 1857, and the town of the real man behind Robinson Crusoe. The effect is to show a coast thick with history, which broods over it like the sea mist.

The central scene comes on the road across Magus Muir. Stevenson cannot remember the drive itself, but he vividly pictures the murder of Archbishop Sharp there in the seventeenth century, and especially one man who did not take part: Hackston of Rathillet, sitting on his horse with his cloak about his mouth, wrestling privately with a case of conscience. The old, wounded man crawled to him and said you are a gentleman, you will protect me, and Hackston replied that he would never lay a hand on him. Stevenson spent his youth trying and failing to find the man behind the cloak. Out of this he draws the essay's main idea: how small a thing creates an immortality. A single dramatic gesture can fix a person in memory for centuries.

He then widens the point with a comic story about schoolboys discussing potassium in a pot of porter, and shows that the boy was really delighting in the sound of the letter p. Under what seems like science, or politics, or history, there lies the writer's love of pictures and sounds.

Finally he tours Anstruther, with a shell-covered house, a drunken minister who dies after seeing what he takes for the devil, a stranded Spanish duke, and a lord reading a Greek Testament on a remote island beach.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
What works best in the essay is the voice. Stevenson speaks with a mixture of mock-grandeur and affection, and his sense of comic timing is superb. The cat who consoles the weeping boy and gets credit for the entire essay is a perfect opening, humane and funny, and it earns the reader's trust. The self-mockery runs through it: his hands, he says, were no doubt in his pockets, and he cannot quite remember whether the Anstruthers are two or three burghs. This casual confession of ignorance is a kind of charm that makes the learning lighter.

The catalogue of Fife towns is a remarkable set piece, a single sweeping paragraph that makes a landscape out of anecdotes. Each little burst of story, the minister praying against Paul Jones at the top of his voice, the Dutch skipper in slippers smoking a long pipe, is chosen with a novelist's eye for the vivid detail. The Hackston passage is the finest thing in the extract: the image of the cloak, and the exchange between the dying man and the one who would not help, have the force of a scene from a novel. And the essay's reflection on it, that the author knows how much picturesque effect and jingling words lead people while they imagine they are led by principles, is a real insight, delivered lightly.

The weaknesses are of a particular kind. The essay is digressive, and the digressions sometimes exceed their value. The lengthy list of places, with names that mean little to a reader outside Scotland, can feel like a roll call, and the references to Andrew Lang, Colonel Fergusson and a handful of school friends assume a knowledge that most readers lack. The joke about potassium and porter, although it ends in a clever point about alliteration, is a long way round to get there.

There is also a question of coherence. The title promises a coast, and the opening promises a story of the boy's departure, but the essay turns out to be a gallery of tales held together by personality. Readers who want a tidy argument may feel that the thread is lost between the lighthouse, the murder, the minister and the Spanish duke. The link between the cat and the eventual stories is whimsical rather than logical.

Finally, the extract ends in the middle of the Fair Isle story with no conclusion, so it is hard to judge the whole. But what we have is a rich, gleaming, slightly overstuffed piece, saved by its warmth and its wit.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
The Coast of Fife is not one of the works for which Stevenson is chiefly remembered, and its impact is quieter than that of his novels. It belongs to the late essays and memoirs through which he looked back on Scotland from a distance. In 1888 Stevenson left Britain for good, setting out on the voyage that would take him across the Pacific to Samoa, where he died in 1894. These memories of Edinburgh, Fife and the family profession, written with a sharpened sense of loss, are among his most personal writings. Pieces in this vein were gathered into collections of his essays and memories, which kept his reputation as a stylist alive.

Its importance for his career lies in how it records the pressures of his upbringing. The Stevensons were the great lighthouse family of Scotland, and the essay names the grandfather who wrote of the painful duty of putting on an angry countenance at the lighthouse, and the father who inspected the lights. Stevenson's decision to abandon engineering for literature was a famous break with family expectation, and the mock-serious account of inheriting the engineer's role gives a glimpse of what he had turned away from. It also shows how rich a store of material the profession gave him, since stories like Kidnapped, with its Scottish coasts and tides, and the poetry of the lights, drew from it.

The essay has a further interest for students of the writing craft. Its central reflection, that a single dramatic image or gesture can fix itself in the imagination more strongly than a mass of fact, and that authors know how much people are led by picturesque effects, is an idea that later writers on narrative have echoed. The notion that history works on us through scenes and gestures rather than arguments is a useful one, and Stevenson states it with unusual clarity.

There is no well-documented wave of reaction to this piece and no famous reviews of it. It has remained part of the body of his essays, read by admirers and by readers interested in Scotland, the Covenanters and the lighthouse service. In teaching it appears occasionally as an example of personal essay and memoir, and for the Hackston passage in particular, which is sometimes read as a short study in how narrative stays in the mind.

Its main afterlife is as a source for readers curious about Stevenson's inner life, a bridge between the Edinburgh child and the exile who wrote his last books in the South Seas.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
Readers who come to this essay often say they love the voice. It is the sound of an excellent talker who knows his audience, one who can move from tears on a doorstep to a roll call of towns to a murder on the moor without losing the thread of intimacy. The joke that the reader owes the paper to a cat in the London Road is the kind of line that makes a reader lean in and smile.

They love the sense of a place saturated with stories. The paragraph that sweeps along the Fife coast, town after town, each with its legend, is both a joke about Stevenson's own obsession and a real gift. The Dutch ships painted like toys with pots of flowers and cages of songbirds in the cabin windows are the sort of image that stays with you. The quiet reference to his uncle Dr. Balfour, walking his hospital rounds in Delhi while the rebels cried in the streets, is a startling swerve into world history, made small by the family connection.

Many admirers single out the Hackston passage. The portrait of a man on a horse with a cloak over his mouth, caught between conscience and complicity, is dramatic and ambiguous, and Stevenson's candid account of how he hunted for the man behind the cloak through books and manuscripts, sitting shamefaced among cleverer students, is endearing. The moment where he declares how small a thing creates an immortality is regarded as one of the finest lines in the extract. People who care about how stories work find the observation, that the writer sees people led by picturesque effects while they think they follow principles, a wise and slightly wicked insight.

The comic stories also delight. The Anstruther curate who mistakes a shadow for the devil, and the child who runs screaming home with the lantern, make a perfect little ghost tale, told with perfect timing and ending on a dry, wicked joke. The decayed Spanish duke finding a warm welcome after the bleak Fair Isle, and the lord with his Greek Testament and his silken-accented grandson on the beach, have the charm of well-chosen anecdotes. Readers say they feel they are being taken on a walk by a very good companion.

Beyond that, many readers love the underlying warmth. The essay reveals a family, a childhood and a boyish self, all treated with a mixture of irony and tenderness, and that humane quality is what draws people back.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
It would be misleading to claim a famous critical storm around this essay, since there isn't one that I can document. What follows are the reservations that readers tend to have, based on the text and on general views of Stevenson's late essays.

The most common complaint is that the essay is a ramble. The structure is loose, a chain of anecdotes held together by the narrator's personality, and a reader looking for a firm argument or a clear arc may find it frustrating. The title suggests a travelogue of the coast, and the early pages suggest a story about leaving home, but the middle wanders through Covenanter history, school anecdotes and a minister's death. Even the more tolerant reader may feel that some of these threads are indulgent.

A second complaint is the assumption of knowledge. Stevenson writes for readers who know Scottish history, who have heard of Archbishop Sharp, Paul Jones, Knox and Culloden, and who recognise Andrew Lang and the old school friends. For a modern reader outside Scotland, the density of names and allusions can be daunting, and the humour sometimes depends on an inside knowledge that is no longer shared.

Third, a few readers object to the tone toward the religious and historical material. The Covenanting world, with its zeal, its murders and its Sunday-book morality, is treated with a wry detachment that some find too flippant. The mocking account of the curate's end, with its suggestion that the poor man was on the brink of delirium tremens, is amusing but also a little callous. Others would say that the irony is exactly the point, a gentle undermining of the pieties of Stevenson's strict upbringing.
