Paine asserts that aristocracy began in robbery and monarchy in usurpation, and he declares the English landed estates to have been plundered at the conquest. Historians point out that the real stories are far more complicated, involving consent, custom, and gradual development. His rhetoric is powerful, but it is not careful scholarship, and some of the claims have to be taken as polemic rather than proof.

Third, there is the limit of his equality. The essay speaks of every man, and it never takes up the case of women or enslaved people, even though the logic of the argument points in that direction. Later feminists and anti-slavery writers took his principles further than he did, and some modern critics hold that his silence shows the limits of the revolutionary imagination. Others reply that he should be judged by the direction of his argument rather than its immediate conclusions.

A fourth line of criticism concerns the treatment of the executive. Paine suggests that the executive is a merely subordinate function, the arm that carries out the will of the legislature, and he treats the arrangement of that office as a matter of opinion. Critics, including many of the American founders, felt that he underrated the need for checks and balances and for a strong, independent executive. His distrust of mixed government made him less sympathetic to the kind of separation of powers that the American Constitution adopted.

Finally, contemporary opponents attacked Paine himself. In Britain he had been prosecuted for seditious libel over Rights of Man, and in France he had been imprisoned. Conservatives treated his principles as an invitation to revolution, while some radicals thought him too moderate, since he opposed vengeance and rejected the execution of the king. That position, which he held in the Convention, cost him dearly. So the essay was attacked from several sides at once, which may be the best sign that it said something of importance.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
The Dissertation belongs to the Age of Democratic Revolution, the era of the American and French revolutions in which political thought moved from theory to practice. Its ancestors include John Locke's argument that government rests on consent, Jean-Jacques Rousseau's doctrine that sovereignty belongs to the people, and the English radical tradition of the seventeenth century. Paine takes those ideas and strips them of their scholarly trappings, offering them to a general audience as a few simple claims.

The most important companion work is Paine's own Rights of Man, from which the essay quotes at length. Together they form his case against hereditary rule. Another useful comparison is with the Federalist Papers, written a few years earlier. The authors of those essays shared Paine's belief in representation but were warier of unchecked majorities, and they built an elaborate system of balance to restrain them. The two works are a good pair, showing the democratic and the cautious sides of the founding age.

Looking forward, the essay descends into the great democratic movements of the nineteenth century: the Chartists, the reformers who widened the franchise in Britain and across Europe, and the American arguments over property qualifications that gradually disappeared. John Stuart Mill, though he wanted weighted votes for the educated, drew on the same tradition when he defended representative government. Paine's belief that the right to vote belongs to persons, not property, ultimately became the standard assumption of modern democracy.

In a literary sense, the essay belongs to the tradition of plain-style political prose that runs from Jonathan Swift and Daniel Defoe to William Cobbett and George Orwell. Paine's gift is to make abstract principle sound like common sense. He wrote as if a skilled tradesman were explaining something to neighbors, and that voice has been imitated ever since.

Why does it still matter? Because it asks questions that every generation must answer again. What gives a government the right to rule? May the past bind the future? Is it fair to link voting to wealth, education, or birth? And how can a movement for freedom avoid becoming a machine for punishment? Paine does not settle all these questions, but he frames them with a force that remains startling. Reading him today, it is easy to forget how new these ideas were. The essay is a reminder that what we now take for granted had to be argued for, line by line, by someone who knew it might cost him his life.

essays.title: Anti-Monarchal Essay
essays.author: Thomas Paine
essays.epigraph: Why is Royalty an absurd and detestable government? Why is the Republic a government accordant with nature and reason?
essays.keyContext: This short, fiery essay argues that kings are not just bad but absurd, and that France was right to get rid of its own. It dates from 1792, just after the French Convention abolished the monarchy and proclaimed a republic. Collections of political writing have long printed it under the name of Thomas Paine, the English-born pamphleteer of the American and French revolutions. A careful reader should know, however, that the essay refers to Paine in the third person, so its authorship is uncertain and it may have come from someone in his French circle. Whoever wrote it, the aim is clear. The author wants new republicans to understand why they should celebrate, not just that they should. The essay mocks the idea of inherited rule, answers the standard defenses of monarchy one by one, and argues that royalty and priestcraft rest on the same trick. It is a vivid example of revolutionary rhetoric at full volume.
paragraphs: When we reach some great good, long desired, we begin by felicitating ourselves. We triumph, we give ourselves up to this joy without rendering to our minds any full account of our reasons for it. Then comes reflection: we pass in review all the circumstances of our new happiness; we compare it in detail with our former condition; and each of these thoughts becomes a fresh enjoyment. This satisfaction, elucidated and well-considered, we now desire to procure for our readers.

In seeing Royalty abolished and the Republic established, all France has resounded with unanimous plaudits. Yet some who clap their hands do not sufficiently understand the condition they are leaving or that which they are assuming.

The perjuries of Louis, the conspiracies of his court, the wildness of his worthy brothers, have filled every Frenchman with horror, and this race was dethroned in their hearts before its fall by legal decree. But it is little to throw down an idol; it is the pedestal that above all must be broken down; it is the regal office rather than the incumbent that is murderous. All do not realize this.

Why is Royalty an absurd and detestable government? Why is the Republic a government accordant with nature and reason? At the present time a Frenchman should put himself in a position to answer these two questions clearly. For, in fine, if you are free and contented it is yet needful that you should know why.
Let us first discuss Royalty or Monarchy. Although one often wishes to distinguish between these names, common usage gives them the same sense.

Bands of brigands unite to subvert a country, place it under tribute, seize its lands, enslave its inhabitants. The expedition completed, the chieftain of the robbers adopts the title of monarch or king. Such is the origin of Royalty among all tribes⁠—huntsmen, agriculturists, shepherds.

A second brigand arrives who finds it equitable to take away by force what was conquered by violence: he dispossesses the first; he chains him, kills him, reigns in his place. Ere long time effaces the memory of this origin; the successors rule under a new form; they do a little good, from policy; they corrupt all who surround them; they invent fictitious genealogies to make their families sacred; the knavery of priests comes to their aid; they take Religion for a lifeguard: thenceforth tyranny becomes immortal, the usurped power becomes an hereditary right.

The effects of Royalty have been entirely harmonious with its origin. What scenes of horror, what refinements of iniquity, do the annals of monarchies present! If we should paint human nature with a baseness of heart, an hypocrisy, from which all must recoil and humanity disavow, it would be the portraiture of kings, their ministers and courtiers.

And why should it not be so? What should such a monstrosity produce but miseries and crimes? What is monarchy? It has been finely disguised, and the people familiarized with the odious title: in its real sense the word signifies the absolute power of one single individual, who may with impunity be stupid, treacherous, tyrannical, etc. Is it not an insult to nations to wish them so governed?

Government by a single individual is vicious in itself, independently of the individual’s vices. For however little a State, the prince is nearly always too small: where is the proportion between one man and the affairs of a whole nation?

True, some men of genius have been seen under the diadem; but the evil is then even greater: the ambition of such a man impels him to conquest and despotism, his subjects soon have to lament his glory, and sing their Te-Deums while perishing with hunger. Such is the history of Louis XIV and so many others.

But if ordinary men in power repay you with incapacity or with princely vices? But those who come to the front in monarchies are frequently mere mean mischief-makers, commonplace knaves, petty intriguers, whose small wits, which in courts reach large places, serve only to display their ineptitude in public, as soon as they appear. In short, monarchs do nothing, and their ministers do evil: this is the history of all monarchies.

But if Royalty as such is baneful, as hereditary succession it is equally revolting and ridiculous. What! there exists among my kind a man who pretends that he is born to govern me? Whence derived he such right? From his and my ancestors, says he. But how could they transmit to him a right they did not possess? Man has no authority over generations unborn. I cannot be the slave of the dead, more than of the living. Suppose that instead of our posterity, it was we who should succeed ourselves: we should not today be able to despoil ourselves of the rights which would belong to us in our second life: for a stronger reason we cannot so despoil others.

An hereditary crown! A transmissible throne! What a notion! With even a little reflection, can anyone tolerate it? Should human beings then be the property of certain individuals, born or to be born? Are we then to treat our descendants in advance as cattle, who shall have neither will nor rights of their own? To inherit government is to inherit peoples, as if they were herds. It is the basest, the most shameful fantasy that ever degraded mankind.

It is wrong to reproach kings with their ferocity, their brutal indifference, the oppressions of the people, and molestations of citizens: it is hereditary succession that makes them what they are: this breeds monsters as a marsh breeds vipers.

The logic on which the hereditary prince rests is in effect this: I derive my power from my birth; I derive my birth from God; therefore I owe nothing to men. It is little that he has at hand a complacent minister, he continues to indulge, conscientiously, in all the crimes of tyranny. This has been seen in all times and countries.

Tell me, then, what is there in common between him who is master of a people, and the people of whom he is master? Are these masters really of their kind? It is by sympathy that we are good and human: with whom does a monarch sympathize? When my neighbor suffers I pity, because I put myself in his place: a monarch pities none, because he has never been, can never be, in any other place than his own.

A monarch is an egoist by nature, the egoist par excellence. A thousand traits show that this kind of men have no point of contact with the rest of humanity. There was demanded of Charles II the punishment of Lauderdale, his favorite, who had infamously oppressed the Scotch. “Yes,” said Charles coolly, “this man has done much against the Scotch, but I cannot see that he has done anything against my interests.” Louis XIV often said: “If I follow the wishes of the people, I cannot act the king.” Even such phrases as “misfortunes of the State,” “safety of the State,” filled Louis XIV with wrath.

Could nature make a law which should assure virtue and wisdom invariably in these privileged castes that perpetuate themselves on thrones, there would be no objection to their hereditary succession. But let us pass Europe in review: all of its monarchs are the meanest of men. This one a tyrant, that one an imbecile, another a traitor, the next a debauchee, while some muster all the vices. It looks as if fate and nature had aimed to show our epoch, and all nations, the absurdity and enormity of Royalty.

But I mistake: this epoch has nothing peculiar. For, such is the essential vice of this royal succession by animal filiation, the peoples have not even the chances of nature⁠—they cannot even hope for a good prince as an alternative. All things conspire to deprive of reason and justice an individual reared to command others. The word of young Dionysius was very sensible: his father, reproaching him for a shameful action, said, “Have I given thee such example?” “Ah,” answered the youth, “thy father was not a king!”

In truth, were laughter on such a subject permissible, nothing would suggest ideas more burlesque than this fantastic institution of hereditary kings. Would it not be believed, to look at them, that there really exist particular lineages possessing certain qualities which enter the blood of the embryo prince, and adapt him physically for royalty, as a horse for the racecourse? But then, in this wild supposition, it yet becomes necessary to assure the genuine family descent of the heir presumptive. To perpetuate the noble race of Andalusian chargers, the circumstances pass before witnesses, and similar precautions seem necessary, however indecent, to make sure that the trickeries of queens shall not supply thrones with bastards, and that the kings, like the horses, shall always be thoroughbreds.

Whether one jests or reasons, there is found in this idea of hereditary royalty only folly and shame. What then is this office, which may be filled by infants or idiots? Some talent is required to be a simple workman; to be a king there is need to have only the human shape, to be a living automaton. We are astonished when reading that the Egyptians placed on the throne a flint, and called it their king. We smile at the dog Barkouf, sent by an Asiatic despot to govern one of his provinces. But monarchs of this kind are less mischievous and less absurd than those before whom whole peoples prostrate themselves. The flint and the dog at least imposed on nobody. None ascribed to them qualities or characters they did not possess. They were not styled “Father of the People,”⁠—though this were hardly more ridiculous than to give that title to a rattle-head whom inheritance crowns at eighteen. Better a mute than an animate idol. Why, there can hardly be cited an instance of a great man having children worthy of him, yet you will have the royal function pass from father to son! As well declare that a wise man’s son will be wise. A king is an administrator, and an hereditary administrator is as absurd as an author by birthright.

Royalty is thus as contrary to common sense as to common right. But it would be a plague even if no more than an absurdity; for a people who can bow down in honor of a silly thing is a debased people. Can they be fit for great affairs who render equal homage to vice and virtue, and yield the same submission to ignorance and wisdom? Of all institutions, none has caused more intellectual degeneracy. This explains the often-remarked abjectness of character under monarchies.

Such is also the effect of this contagious institution that it renders equality impossible, and draws in its train the presumption and the evils of “Nobility.” If you admit inheritance of an office, why not that of a distinction? The Nobility’s heritage asks only homage, that of the Crown commands submission. When a man says to me, “I am born illustrious,” I merely smile; when he says “I am born your master,” I set my foot on him.

When the Convention pronounced the abolition of Royalty none rose for the defence that was expected. On this subject a philosopher, who thought discussion should always precede enactment, proposed a singular thing; he desired that the Convention should nominate an orator commissioned to plead before it the cause of Royalty, so that the pitiful arguments by which it has in all ages been justified might appear in broad daylight. Judges give one accused, however certain his guilt, an official defender. In the ancient Senate of Venice there existed a public officer whose function was to contest all propositions, however incontestible, or however perfect their evidence. For the rest, pleaders for Royalty are not rare: let us open them, and see what the most specious of royalist reasoners have said.
A king is necessary to preserve a people from the tyranny of powerful men.

Establish the Rights of Man; enthrone Equality; form a good Constitution; divide well its powers; let there be no privileges, no distinctions of birth, no monopolies; make safe the liberty of industry and of trade, the equal distribution of [family] inheritances, publicity of administration, freedom of the press: these things all established, you will be assured of good laws, and need not fear the powerful men. Willingly or unwillingly, all citizens will be under the Law.
The Legislature might usurp authority, and a king is needed to restrain it.

With representatives, frequently renewed, who neither administer nor judge, whose functions are determined by the laws; with national conventions, with primary assemblies, which can be convoked any moment; with a people knowing how to read, and how to defend itself; with good journals, guns, and pikes; a Legislature would have a good deal of trouble in enjoying any months of tyranny. Let us not suppose an evil for the sake of its remedy.
A king is needed to give force to executive power.

This might be said while there existed nobles, a priesthood, parliaments, the privileged of every kind. But at present who can resist the Law, which is the will of all, whose execution is the interest of all? On the contrary the existence of an hereditary prince inspires perpetual distrust among the friends of liberty; his authority is odious to them; in checking despotism they constantly obstruct the action of government. Observe how feeble the executive power was found, after our recent pretence of marrying Royalty with Liberty.

Take note, for the rest, that those who talk in this way are men who believe that the King and the Executive Power are only one and the same thing: readers of La Feuille Villageoise are more advanced.

Others use this bad reasoning: “Were there no hereditary chief there would be an elective chief: the citizens would side with this man or that, and there would be a civil war at every election.” In the first place, it is certain that hereditary succession alone has produced the civil wars of France and England; and that beyond this are the pretended rights, of royal families which have twenty times drawn on these nations the scourge of foreign wars. It is, in fine, the heredity of crowns that has caused the troubles of Regency, which Thomas Paine calls Monarchy at nurse.

But above all it must be said, that if there be an elective chief, that chief will not be a king surrounded by courtiers, burdened with pomp, inflated by idolatries, and endowed with thirty millions of money; also, that no citizen will be tempted to injure himself by placing another citizen, his equal, for some years in an office without limited income and circumscribed power.
In a word, whoever demands a king demands an aristocracy, and thirty millions of taxes. See why Franklin described Royalism as a crime like poisoning.

Royalty, its fanatical éclat, its superstitious idolatry, the delusive assumption of its necessity, all these fictions have been invented only to obtain from men excessive taxes and voluntary servitude. Royalty and Popery have had the same aim, have sustained themselves by the same artifices, and crumble under the same Light.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
The essay begins with a clever psychological observation. When we win some long-desired good, we celebrate first and think later. Then reflection arrives, and by comparing our new happiness with our old condition, we double our pleasure. The writer wants to give his readers that second, reasoned joy. France has just abolished royalty and set up a republic, and everyone is applauding. But some of those applauding do not fully understand what they have left behind or what they have taken on.

The first big idea follows. It is little to throw down an idol; it is the pedestal that must be broken. In other words, the fault is not Louis XVI the man, whose perjuries and conspiracies had made him hated, but the office itself. It is the regal office rather than the incumbent that is murderous. The writer wants Frenchmen to be able to answer two questions clearly: why is royalty absurd and detestable, and why is a republic in accord with nature and reason?

To answer the first, he attacks monarchy from several angles. One is sympathy. We are good because we can put ourselves in another's place, and a king, he says, never has been and never can be in any place but his own, so he is an egoist by nature. He illustrates with a story of Charles II, who said that a favorite who had oppressed the Scots had done nothing against his interests, and with a remark attributed to Louis XIV. Another is character. All the monarchs of Europe, he claims, are the meanest of men, and even if one were good, the system gives the people no chance of choosing one.

The sharpest ridicule is directed at heredity. The writer asks us to imagine that royal blood really produced a special ability to rule, the way a racehorse is bred for speed. In that case, he jokes, one would have to verify the lineage as carefully as breeders do. The comic point is that an office which may be filled by an infant or an idiot cannot require talent. He compares it to the Egyptians placing a flint on the throne, or an Asian despot sending a dog to govern a province, and says those at least deceived nobody. A king is an administrator, and an hereditary administrator is as absurd as an author by birthright.

The final part takes up the best arguments for monarchy and answers them. A king is said to protect people from powerful men, to restrain a legislature, to give force to the executive, and to prevent civil war at elections. To each the writer replies that a good constitution, equal rights, frequent elections, a literate people, and a free press do those jobs better, and that it is hereditary succession that has caused wars. He closes with a bold equation. Royalty and popery have had the same aim, have sustained themselves by the same artifices, and will crumble under the same light.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
As rhetoric, the essay is vigorous and often very funny. The opening is a real strength: starting with the psychology of celebration is a disarming way into a polemic, and it signals that the writer is addressing readers' minds as well as their feelings. The line that it is the pedestal that must be broken, and not just the idol, is memorable and exactly right, because it makes the argument structural rather than personal. It tells new republicans that dethroning one king is not enough.

The structure of the second half is also effective. By stating the royalist arguments in plain, short headings and answering each in a paragraph, the writer gives the piece the feel of a catechism for new citizens. This is a smart design for a text meant, in the subtitle that some editions give it, for the use of new republicans. It teaches by repeated drill, and it is easy to remember. The proposal that the Convention appoint an official defender of royalty, like the devil's advocate or the officer in the old Venetian senate who contested every motion, is a neat way of showing confidence in the argument.

The jokes are the highlight. The flint, the dog, and the thoroughbred are vivid pictures, and the remark that when a man says he is born illustrious one merely smiles, but when he says he is born your master one sets a foot on him, has real punch. These lines make the argument vivid and portable.

But there are weaknesses. The breeding joke, though funny, rests on an insinuation about queens that is coarse and lazily sexist, and it relies on a stereotype rather than on evidence. The claim that all the monarchs of Europe are the meanest of men is a sweeping insult that no historian could support, and the argument from the bad character of kings is the weakest in the piece, since a defender could simply point to a good one. The writer half-sees this and pivots to the structural argument, but the rhetoric lingers.

More seriously, the answers to the royalist objections are quick, and sometimes too quick. The claim that a good constitution and a free press will make powerful men harmless is optimistic, and the remark that an elected chief would never be surrounded by courtiers or burdened with pomp was soon tested. Within a dozen years, the French Republic produced Napoleon, who had himself crowned emperor. It is a bitter irony for an essay so confident. Readers today admire the vigor but notice that the author is more interested in winning than in weighing the possible dangers of what he proposes.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
Here honesty requires a caveat: the documented reception of this particular piece is thin. It is not a famous, widely reviewed work like Common Sense or Rights of Man, and its specific reviewers and sales are not on record. What can be said is something about its setting and its afterlife.

Its setting is the autumn of 1792. On the twenty-first of September the Convention abolished the monarchy, and the next day the French counted the beginning of a republican era. Thomas Paine, who had been elected to the Convention, was at the center of the debate, and the essay's references to his name show how closely the new republicans associated his ideas with their cause. The piece belongs to a flood of pamphlets and newspaper articles that tried to explain the new order to ordinary people, including peasants, whose papers like the Feuille Villageoise, mentioned in the essay, aimed to teach them politics in plain language.

Its afterlife has been largely through anthologies. Collections of Paine's writings have printed it, so students and readers interested in the revolution encounter it as a compact sample of republican argument. It is useful in teaching because it shows how revolutionaries tried to move from a feeling to a justification, and how they used humor and plain logic against an institution that had been protected by awe.

The essay also illustrates a theme that did shape later events: the idea that the monarchy itself, not just a bad monarch, was the problem. That view helped drive the push toward the trial and execution of Louis XVI in January 1793. Paine himself, famously, opposed the execution, arguing that the king should be exiled, a stand that contributed to his own imprisonment under the Terror. It is a reminder that the arguments of 1792 had consequences that even their advocates did not control.

Beyond that, the impact is the general one of republican polemic. Pieces like this helped make it normal to ask of any ruler by what right he rules, and to answer by appeal to reason rather than tradition. That habit of mind spread across Europe and the Americas through the nineteenth century, and this essay is one small, vivid piece of the evidence.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
Because this essay is obscure compared with its famous cousins, there is little recorded praise. What can be said is what readers tend to like in it today.

First, they like the energy. The writer is plainly delighted by the argument, and the delight is catching. Reading it, one feels the mood of 1792, when the abolition of a thousand-year institution seemed like the dawn of a new age. That sense of exhilaration is rare in political writing, which is usually cautious, and it gives the piece a youthful charm.

Second, they like the humor. For modern readers the jokes about the flint, the dog, and the thoroughbred are the high points. They are irreverent in a way that still feels fresh, and they show that mockery can be a serious political tool. The line about being born your master is the sort of sentence people copy into notebooks.

Third, the writer's confidence in ordinary people is appealing. The essay assumes that readers can follow an argument, that they can distinguish between a person and an office, and that a people who know how to read and defend themselves can govern without a monarch. It treats the audience as citizens rather than subjects, and many readers admire that respect.

Fourth, the essay gives a clear and compressed account of why hereditary rule is troubling, which is useful for students. The point that an office passing by birth is as absurd as an author by birthright can be grasped immediately, and it opens up larger questions about inherited privilege that are still alive today, in debates about wealth, titles, and political dynasties.

Finally, there is a historical pleasure in hearing a revolution explain itself. The reader gets a glimpse of the arguments that circulated in the streets and journals of Paris, with all their bravado and their blind spots. For a person trying to understand how people actually talked in 1792, the essay is a vivid document, and that is reason enough to read it.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
The first problem is the one a careful reader meets immediately: who wrote it? The essay is widely printed among Paine's works, but its text speaks of Thomas Paine in the third person, saying that he calls monarchy at nurse the regency of a child king, and it refers to Franklin and to readers of a French journal as if from outside. It also talks about the French in the first person plural, as a Frenchman would. These details suggest that it was written by a French republican, or translated from one, and that the attribution to Paine may be loose. The question is unsettled, and readers should treat the authorship as uncertain rather than as established.

The more substantive criticism is aimed at the argument. Defenders of monarchy then and later have said that the essay confuses the worst kings with the institution, and that it ignores the stabilizing function of a hereditary head of state who stands above party. Modern constitutional monarchies, such as Britain, the Netherlands, and Sweden, are among the most stable democracies, which makes the claim that royalty is inherently an engine of servitude look overstated. The writer would answer that these are not true monarchies, but that is a debatable rejoinder.

A second criticism is about moral tone. The essay's ridicule can slide into contempt, and the line about setting one's foot on a man who says he is born your master is the language of a revolution that was becoming violent. Critics have pointed out that a movement which begins with jokes about an idol can end by treating the idol's people as enemies, and the next year did bring the Terror. The essay does not foresee that, and its cheerful confidence now reads with a shadow.

Third, there is the historical record. The writer predicts that an elected head of state would never be a king surrounded by courtiers, but within years the French republic ended in an empire. Historians note that revolutions often produce new forms of personal rule, and that dismissing the risk, as the writer does, was naive.

Fourth, the essay's anti-clerical ending has drawn objections. The equation of royalty and popery treats religion as a mere trick of tax collectors, which many believers and many historians find reductive. The same impulse, applied in the Revolution's dechristianization campaigns, produced real persecution. So the essay is read both as a spirited defense of republican principle and as a case study in the blind spots of revolutionary certainty.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
This essay belongs to the great tradition of anti-monarchical writing that stretches across the early modern period. Its ancestors include John Milton's Tenure of Kings and Magistrates, written to justify the trial of Charles I, and John Locke's attack on the divine right theory of Robert Filmer, which argued that kings inherit their power from Adam. Voltaire and the French philosophes mocked kings and priests for decades before the Revolution, and Jonathan Swift's Gulliver's Travels turned the courts of Europe into objects of satire. The essay's jokes about absurd rulers belong to this line of satire.

The closest relative is Paine's own Common Sense of 1776, which also ridiculed hereditary monarchy and declared that one honest man is worth more to society than all the crowned ruffians that ever lived. Paine's Rights of Man followed in 1791 and 1792, and the essay we have read applies the same logic to the French case. If the work is indeed by another hand, it shows how widely that style had spread and how readily the new republicans borrowed Paine's plain manner.

Looking forward, the essay descends into the nineteenth-century republican movements of France, Spain, Italy, and Latin America, which kept arguing that an inherited head of state is incompatible with equality. It also anticipates later arguments about inherited privilege in general, including the case against hereditary titles and dynasties, and the modern movements in countries such as Australia and Britain that debate whether to keep a monarch at all.

For comparison, one can set it against Edmund Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France, which defended inherited institutions as the accumulated wisdom of ages and warned that tearing down the old order would unleash chaos. Burke's prediction proved partly right, and this essay's optimism partly wrong. Reading them together gives a fuller picture of the argument that shaped modern politics. It is the argument between those who think institutions should justify themselves to reason and those who think reason should be humble before inheritance.

Why read it today? Not because it is the best argument against monarchy, but because it shows the moment when such an argument became a popular passion. It captures the excitement, the humor, the overconfidence, and the moral energy of a new republic in its first weeks. It is a short, lively document, and it reminds us that political change begins with someone persuading an audience that a thing they always accepted is, when you look at it, a little ridiculous.

essays.title: Discourses I.1: Of the Things Which Are in Our Power, and Not in Our Power
essays.author: Epictetus
essays.epigraph: You may fetter my leg, but my will not even Zeus himself can overpower.
essays.keyContext:
This is the very first chapter of the Discourses, the classroom lectures of Epictetus, a Greek philosopher who lived in the Roman Empire around the year 100. Epictetus began life as a slave, was lame, and later became one of the most respected teachers of Stoicism, an ancient school that taught calm, courage and self-command. He never wrote anything himself. A devoted student named Arrian took notes, and that is why we have these talks, roughly as he delivered them, in blunt and sometimes funny spoken language.

The chapter lays down the idea the whole Stoic way of life rests on: some things are up to us, and most things are not. Your judgments and choices belong to you. Your body, your money, your reputation and other people do not. Epictetus argues that nearly all our misery comes from mixing the two up. The idea later shaped Marcus Aurelius, modern therapy, and a military prisoner in Vietnam. As you listen, watch for the stories of men who faced Nero and kept their composure.
paragraphs: Of all the faculties (except that which I shall soon mention), you will find not one which is capable of contemplating itself, and, consequently, not capable either of approving or disapproving. How far does the grammatic art possess the contemplating power? As far as forming a judgment about what is written and spoken. And how far music? As far as judging about melody. Does either of them then contemplate itself? By no means. But when you must write something to your friend, grammar will tell you what words you should write; but whether you should write or not, grammar will not tell you. And so it is with music as to musical sounds; but whether you should sing at the present time and play on the lute, or do neither, music will not tell you. What faculty then will tell you? That which contemplates both itself and all other things. And what is this faculty? The rational faculty; for this is the only faculty that we have received which examines itself, what it is, and what power it has, and what is the value of this gift, and examines all other faculties: for what else is there which tells us that golden things are beautiful, for they do not say so themselves? Evidently it is the faculty which is capable of judging of appearances. What else judges of music, grammar, and the other faculties, proves their uses, and points out the occasions for using them? Nothing else.

As then it was fit to be so, that which is best of all and supreme over all is the only thing which the gods have placed in our power, the right use of appearances; but all other things they have not placed in our power. Was it because they did not choose? I indeed think that, if they had been able, they would have put these other things also in our power, but they certainly could not. For as we exist on the earth, and are bound to such a body and to such companions, how was it possible for us not to be hindered as to these things by externals?

But what says Zeus? “Epictetus, if it were possible, I would have made both your little body and your little property free and not exposed to hindrance. But now be not ignorant of this: this body is not yours, but it is clay finely tempered. And since I was not able to do for you what I have mentioned, I have given you a small portion of us, this faculty of pursuing an object and avoiding it, and the faculty of desire and aversion, and, in a word, the faculty of using the appearances of things; and if you will take care of this faculty and consider it your only possession, you will never be hindered, never meet with impediments; you will not lament, you will not blame, you will not flatter any person.”

Well, do these seem to you small matters? I hope not. Be content with them then and pray to the gods. But now when it is in our power to look after one thing, and to attach ourselves to it, we prefer to look after many things, and to be bound to many things, to the body and to property, and to brother and to friend, and to child and to slave. Since then we are bound to many things, we are depressed by them and dragged down. For this reason, when the weather is not fit for sailing, we sit down and torment ourselves, and continually look out to see what wind is blowing. It is north. What is that to us? When will the west wind blow? When it shall choose, my good man, or when it shall please Aeolus; for God has not made you the manager of the winds, but Aeolus. What then? We must make the best use that we can of the things which are in our power, and use the rest according to their nature. What is their nature then? As God may please.

Must I then alone have my head cut off? What, would you have all men lose their heads that you may be consoled? Will you not stretch out your neck as Lateranus did at Rome when Nero ordered him to be beheaded? For when he had stretched out his neck, and received a feeble blow, which made him draw it in for a moment, he stretched it out again. And a little before, when he was visited by Epaphroditus, Nero’s freedman, who asked him about the cause of offense which he had given, he said, “If I choose to tell anything, I will tell your master.”

What then should a man have in readiness in such circumstances? What else than this? What is mine, and what is not mine; and what is permitted to me, and what is not permitted to me. I must die. Must I then die lamenting? I must be put in chains. Must I then also lament? I must go into exile. Does any man then hinder me from going with smiles and cheerfulness and contentment? Tell me the secret which you possess. I will not, for this is in my power. But I will put you in chains. Man, what are you talking about? Me in chains? You may fetter my leg, but my will not even Zeus himself can overpower. I will throw you into prison. My poor body, you mean. I will cut your head off. When then have I told you that my head alone cannot be cut off? These are the things which philosophers should meditate on, which they should write daily, in which they should exercise themselves.

Thrasea used to say, I would rather be killed today than banished tomorrow. What then did Rufus say to him? If you choose death as the heavier misfortune, how great is the folly of your choice? But if, as the lighter, who has given you the choice? Will you not study to be content with that which has been given to you?

What then did Agrippinus say? He said, “I am not a hindrance to myself.” When it was reported to him that his trial was going on in the Senate, he said, “I hope it may turn out well; but it is the fifth hour of the day”⁠—this was the time when he was used to exercise himself and then take the cold bath⁠—“let us go and take our exercise.” After he had taken his exercise, one comes and tells him, You have been condemned. To banishment, he replies, or to death? To banishment. What about my property? It is not taken from you. Let us go to Aricia then, he said, and dine.

This it is to have studied what a man ought to study; to have made desire, aversion, free from hindrance, and free from all that a man would avoid. I must die. If now, I am ready to die. If, after a short time, I now dine because it is the dinner-hour; after this I will then die. How? Like a man who gives up what belongs to another.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
Epictetus opens in an odd way, with a question about how a mind can examine itself. He points out that no skill can judge itself. Grammar can tell you how to spell a word in a letter to a friend, but it cannot tell you whether you should write the letter. Music can tell you how to play the lute, but it cannot tell you whether this is the right moment to play. Something else has to make those calls, and that something is reason, the faculty that looks at everything, including itself. Specifically, it is the faculty that judges "appearances," his word for the way things strike us. A thing shows up in your mind as frightening, or insulting, or desirable, and reason is what decides whether to accept that first impression.

From there he makes the move that defines the whole chapter. Of everything in life, the gods placed only one thing fully in our power: the right use of appearances. Everything else, the body, property, family, friends, reputation, even our own lifespan, is tangled up with the outside world, and the outside world cannot be ordered around. Epictetus has Zeus speak to him directly in a small imaginary scene. Zeus says, in effect, that he would have liked to make the body and property free too, but could not. The body is "clay finely tempered," not truly yours. What you were given instead is a small portion of the divine itself, the ability to choose, to reach for things and turn away from them, and to handle impressions well.

Then comes the diagnosis. We are unhappy because we attach ourselves to many things we do not control, and so we are dragged down by each of them. His example is the sailor tormenting himself over the wind. The winds belong to Aeolus, he says, not to you.

The second half turns the idea into a drill for hard moments, and it is where the chapter gets its force. Epictetus imagines a tyrant threatening him. I will put you in chains. You may fetter my leg, he answers, but my will not even Zeus can overpower. I will throw you into prison. That is my poor body you mean. I will cut off your head. When did I ever say my head was the one part of me that could not be cut off?

The closing story of Agrippinus is the picture of how this looks in practice. Told that his trial is under way in the Senate, he says he hopes it goes well, but it is time for his exercise and cold bath. Told he has been condemned, he asks whether it is to death or exile. Exile. Is his property taken? No. Then, he says, let us go to Aricia and dine.

A first-time reader may miss that this is not a call to passivity. Epictetus still wants you to act, to write the letter, to sail the ship. What he wants removed is the demand that the result obey you. That is the difference between effort and anxiety, and the whole chapter is built to make you feel it.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
As rhetoric, this chapter is very good, and much of the credit goes to its pacing. It starts with a dry, almost technical point about faculties that cannot examine themselves, which could easily put a listener off. Then it turns it into a theology, then into a theatrical dialogue with Zeus, then into a series of sharp little exchanges with an imaginary tyrant, and finally into a short, funny, human story. Each step makes the abstract idea more concrete.

The tyrant dialogue is the best piece of writing here. It works because it is so quick and so cheeky. Epictetus does not argue that chains are pleasant or that death is nothing. He simply keeps correcting the grammar of the threat. You are threatening my leg, not me. This is a clever trick of redescription, and it is memorable because it can be repeated in your head at three in the morning.

The weaknesses are real, though. The opening argument, that reason alone can judge reason, is a little too neat. It moves from "no skill judges itself" to "reason is the only thing in our power" without much of a bridge, and a skeptical reader could object that our judgments are shaped by upbringing, mood and the people around us, so they are not so cleanly ours. Epictetus half admits this elsewhere by insisting that the ability needs training, but here he states the claim with more confidence than he earns.

There is also a hardness in the examples. He speaks of loved ones in the same breath as property. "Brother and friend, and child" sit in a list with "slave" and the body, all of them things that drag you down. Modern readers often find this chilling, and it is hard to defend it as simple good sense. A parent who is calm at a child's illness because the child is "not in my power" has, many would say, lost something that makes a life worth living. The chapter has no room for grief that is a form of love.

And the stories of Lateranus and Agrippinus, while inspiring, are selected from the survivors of a very specific kind of danger: Roman aristocrats facing the emperor. They sound better than they would feel.

Even so, the sheer practicality of the method keeps this chapter on the list of the best short pieces of moral writing. It is unsentimental, quick, and it asks the reader to do something rather than merely agree. Where it is weakest, it is weak the way a strong, confident teacher is weak: he gives the medicine at full dose and trusts you to adjust it. That makes it sometimes severe, but also very clear.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
The Discourses were never published by Epictetus, so their influence is in a way an accident of loyalty. Arrian, a young Greek who later became a Roman governor and a historian of Alexander the Great, attended Epictetus's school at Nicopolis in northwestern Greece and wrote down what he heard. He later said he had not meant to make a book of it, which is partly why the voice is so alive. Four of the original eight books survive, along with a short handbook of the main ideas called the Enchiridion, which Arrian also compiled. This first chapter, with its split between what is and is not in our power, is the foundation of both.

The first great reader was probably Marcus Aurelius, the emperor, who in his private notebook, now called the Meditations, credits his teacher Rusticus for lending him a copy of Epictetus's lectures. Much of the calm, self-addressed tone of Marcus's writing is Epictetus's training turned inward. Through the late Roman world, Epictetus was widely read, and in the Middle Ages his handbook was adapted by Christian monks. Its ideas of detachment and acceptance of providence fit comfortably into monastic life, and a version of the Enchiridion was reworked for use in religious communities.

The twentieth century gave him two famous second lives. In the 1960s, the American psychologists Albert Ellis and Aaron Beck, who founded rational emotive therapy and cognitive behavioral therapy, both said they had drawn on Epictetus. The central idea is the same one that opens the Discourses: it is our judgments about events, not the events themselves, that disturb us. Much of modern cognitive therapy, which teaches people to catch a distressing thought and examine it, is a clinical version of treating appearances with suspicion.

The second life belongs to Admiral James Stockdale, a navy pilot shot down over North Vietnam in 1965 who spent about seven and a half years as a prisoner of war, much of it in torture and isolation. Before his capture he had read Epictetus under the guidance of a philosophy professor. In captivity, Stockdale later wrote and said, the idea that you control your own will but not your body or circumstances was what kept him intact. He wrote about this in essays and lectures, and the story brought Epictetus to a very wide audience, including the military.

More recently, the broad revival of Stoicism has made this chapter common reading. Books and online communities promote what is often called the dichotomy of control, a sentence that sums up the chapter's opening lines. The phrase is modern, but the habit it describes, sorting your worries into "mine" and "not mine," is straight out of this text.

In schools, the chapter is often taught as a primer on Stoic ethics, and it serves historians as a window into the dangers of life under Nero, naming real men who lived and died under tyranny.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
What people have loved in this chapter is, first of all, its usefulness. Most philosophy asks you to consider an idea. Epictetus asks you to try it out before breakfast. Readers across nearly two thousand years have reported that this single move, asking whether a given worry is within their power, has actually changed how a bad day feels. That is a rare thing for a text that old to claim, and many readers have said so in their own words.

Admirers also love the voice. Epictetus does not sound like a professor handing down conclusions. He sounds like a sharp, slightly sarcastic coach who has heard every excuse. "My good man," he says to the person fretting about the wind, and the little phrase tells you he has seen this before and finds it a bit funny. This humor makes the severity bearable. He lets the reader laugh at their own foolishness, and that laughter is a first step toward changing.

Another loved quality is the dignity he gives to ordinary people. Epictetus was born a slave, lived with a damaged leg, and had no property to speak of. His teaching says that the inner freedom a person needs is available to the poor, the sick and the powerless just as much as to the rich. For a reader in a tight spot, there is something very moving about hearing this from someone who actually lived through the tight spot, and not from a comfortable aristocrat. This is why prisoners, soldiers and people in hospital have turned to him so often.

The Agrippinus story in particular has delighted generations. It is a few sentences long, it has an almost comic timing, and it leaves a picture in the mind: a man receiving his sentence and asking, in effect, where is lunch. Readers have enjoyed it as an image of grace under pressure. The same goes for Lateranus stretching his neck out a second time after the first blow fell weakly, a story that is shocking but also, in a grim way, almost admirable.

Many people also love how compact the chapter is. It lays out a whole philosophy of daily life in about a thousand words.

Finally, there is the consolation. People who love this chapter frequently speak of it as something they return to in a crisis. The reasoning is that if you cannot control the outcome, you are released from the exhausting job of controlling it, and what is left is a clear, small task: act well and accept the rest. For anyone worn out by anxiety, that is a real relief. Epictetus does not promise that things will turn out fine. He promises that you can be fine whether or not they do, and a great many readers have found that promise worth the harshness that comes with it.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
The best-known objection to Epictetus came from Blaise Pascal, the seventeenth-century French mathematician and religious thinker. In a conversation recorded about his reading, Pascal praised Epictetus for understanding duty but charged him with pride. In Pascal's view, telling people that they can master themselves by willpower alone ignores human weakness and our need for grace. A philosophy that makes you the owner of your own peace, he thought, flatters the reader. The charge has echoed ever since, in various forms.

A second line of criticism is about emotion. Critics have long argued that Stoic detachment asks people to cut off their feelings for others. If you train yourself to treat your children, friends and spouse as things you do not control and should not be too attached to, you may protect yourself from pain but also from love. The philosopher Martha Nussbaum has written in detail about the Stoic effort to remove strong emotion and has asked whether the resulting life is truly better. Many readers, hearing a parent told not to grieve, feel that something has gone wrong.

A third criticism is political. If a person is taught that only their inner attitude matters, they may stop caring about changing unjust conditions. The German philosopher Hegel, in his account of the history of consciousness, described Stoic freedom as a kind of retreat, a freedom that exists only in thought and leaves the real chains in place. A slave who feels free inside is still a slave. Later readers have worried that such teaching can be used to make people accept oppression. Epictetus, to be fair, was no apologist for tyranny, and his examples show men resisting emperors. But the emphasis falls on how to endure, not how to reform.

Nietzsche attacked the Stoics from another side. He thought that telling people to live according to nature was a self-deception, since the Stoics in fact wanted to impose their own values on nature. He also disliked what he saw as an ethic of self-protection rather than greatness.

There are also more ordinary objections. Many things are partly in our power, such as our health and our work, so the line looks sharper than life allows. And the theology, Zeus speaking to his student, will not persuade anyone who does not share the assumption of a caring divine order.

Finally, there is the question of tone. Epictetus is sometimes harsh, and his willingness to call his listeners fools or wretches can feel more like scolding than help. Modern self-help versions of Stoicism, in turn, have been criticized for turning a demanding ancient discipline into a productivity trick, a way to keep calm at work and endure an unfair system. That criticism is aimed at today's popularizers more than at Epictetus, but it has become part of the conversation around him.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
This chapter belongs to the school of philosophy called Stoicism, founded in Athens around 300 BC by Zeno of Citium and named after the painted porch, the stoa, where he taught. The early Stoics, above all Chrysippus, built a large system of logic, physics and ethics. By the time of the Roman Empire, the emphasis had narrowed to ethics, and Stoicism had become a practical discipline for living under uncertain and often dangerous rulers. Seneca, a wealthy statesman and Nero's tutor, Musonius Rufus, Epictetus's own teacher, Epictetus himself and the emperor Marcus Aurelius are the main voices of this late phase. Of the four, Epictetus is the most plainspoken and the most severe.

He also descends from Socrates, whom he treats as the model of the good man. Socrates accepted his execution calmly and said, as Plato reports, that his accusers could harm him in body but not in the things that count. Epictetus returns to that idea again and again. The Stoics took it and built a whole system around it, and the cheerful way Epictetus talks about death and exile is a direct echo.

Compared with its neighbors, this chapter has a different flavor than Marcus Aurelius, who writes privately and wrestles with doubt. Epictetus is a teacher in a room, speaking to students with a challenge in his voice. Compared with Seneca, he is less polished and less literary, and he lacks the rich man's perspective. His sentences are the sentences of someone who has had very little and does not envy anyone.

Outside the Stoic tradition, similar ideas appear in other places. The Serenity Prayer, with its request for the wisdom to tell the changeable from the unchangeable, is a close relative of this chapter, though it has a different origin. The Bhagavad Gita counsels acting without clinging to the fruits of action, which sounds very much like Epictetus's advice to do your part and leave the outcome alone.

Among descendants, cognitive behavioral therapy is the clearest, and the modern Stoic revival, with its books, podcasts and daily practices, is the most visible. Philosophers such as Pierre Hadot, who wrote about ancient philosophy as a way of life and not only a set of arguments, have used Epictetus as a central example. Hadot's point was that these lectures were spiritual exercises, to be repeated, memorized and lived.

Why does it still matter to read? Partly because it is short and clear and forceful. Partly because we live in a time of constant alarm, when the news makes us feel responsible for things we cannot touch. And partly because it asks a question that never stops being useful: what, right now, is actually up to me? Even if you decide, with Pascal or Nussbaum, that Epictetus asks too much, you will have to think hard to find out exactly where you disagree. A text that makes you do that has earned its place in the great conversation.

essays.title: Discourses I.2: How a Man on Every Occasion Can Maintain His Proper Character
essays.author: Epictetus
essays.epigraph: It is you who know yourself, how much you are worth to yourself, and at what price you sell yourself; for men sell themselves at various prices.
essays.keyContext:
This chapter of the Discourses asks a question that sounds simple: how can a person stay true to who they are, whatever happens? It comes from Epictetus, a Greek teacher of Stoic philosophy who worked in the Roman Empire around the year 100. He was born a slave, became free, and ended up teaching ambitious young men, some of them future officials, in a school in northwestern Greece. A student named Arrian wrote down his talks, so we hear him roughly as he spoke.

The backdrop matters. Under emperors like Nero and Vespasian, honest men could be ordered to stay silent, play along, or die. Epictetus tells the true stories of senators and philosophers who were given exactly those orders. His answer is that each of us has a character, and that the real question is not what is safe but what we are willing to sell ourselves for. As you listen, notice how he turns a price tag into a test of identity.
paragraphs: To the rational animal only is the irrational intolerable; but that which is rational is tolerable. Blows are not naturally intolerable. How is that? See how the Lacedaemonians endure whipping when they have learned that whipping is consistent with reason. To hang yourself is not intolerable. When then you have the opinion that it is rational, you go and hang yourself. In short, if we observe, we shall find that the animal man is pained by nothing so much as by that which is irrational; and, on the contrary, attracted to nothing so much as to that which is rational.

But the rational and the irrational appear such in a different way to different persons, just as the good and the bad, the profitable and the unprofitable. For this reason, particularly, we need discipline, in order to learn how to adapt the preconception of the rational and the irrational to the several things conformably to nature. But in order to determine the rational and the irrational, we use not only the estimates of external things, but we consider also what is appropriate to each person. For to one man it is consistent with reason to hold a chamber pot for another, and to look to this only: that if he does not hold it, he will receive stripes, and he will not receive his food; but if he shall hold the pot, he will not suffer anything hard or disagreeable. But to another man not only does the holding of a chamber pot appear intolerable for himself, but intolerable also for him to allow another to do this office for him. If then you ask me whether you should hold the chamber pot or not, I shall say to you that the receiving of food is worth more than the not receiving of it, and the being scourged is a greater indignity than not being scourged; so that if you measure your interests by these things, go and hold the chamber pot. “But this,” you say, “would not be worthy of me.” Well then, it is you who must introduce this consideration into the inquiry, not I; for it is you who know yourself, how much you are worth to yourself, and at what price you sell yourself; for men sell themselves at various prices.

For this reason, when Florus was deliberating whether he should go down to Nero’s spectacles, and also perform in them himself, Agrippinus said to him, “Go down:” and when Florus asked Agrippinus, “Why do not you go down?” Agrippinus replied, “Because I do not even deliberate about the matter. For he who has once brought himself to deliberate about such matters, and to calculate the value of external things, comes very near to those who have forgotten their own character. For why do you ask me the question, whether death is preferable or life? I say life. Pain or pleasure? I say pleasure. But if I do not take a part in the tragic acting, I shall have my head struck off.” “Go then and take a part, but I will not.” “Why?” “Because you consider yourself to be only one thread of those which are in the tunic. Well then it was fitting for you to take care how you should be like the rest of men, just as the thread has no design to be anything superior to the other threads. But I wish to be purple, that small part which is bright, and makes all the rest appear graceful and beautiful. Why then do you tell me to make myself like the many? and if I do, how shall I still be purple?”

Priscus Helvidius also saw this, and acted conformably. For when Vespasian sent and commanded him not to go into the senate, he replied, “It is in your power not to allow me to be a member of the senate, but so long as I am, I must go in.” “Well, go in then,” says the emperor, “but say nothing.” “Do not ask my opinion, and I will be silent.” “But I must ask your opinion.” “And I must say what I think right.” “But if you do, I shall put you to death.” “When then did I tell you that I am immortal? You will do your part, and I will do mine: it is your part to kill; it is mine to die, but not in fear: yours to banish me; mine to depart without sorrow.”

What good then did Priscus do, who was only a single person? And what good does the purple do for the toga? Why, what else than this, that it is conspicuous in the toga as purple, and is displayed also as a fine example to all other things? But in such circumstances another would have replied to Caesar who forbade him to enter the senate, “I thank you for sparing me.” But such a man Vespasian would not even have forbidden to enter the senate, for he knew that he would either sit there like an earthen vessel, or, if he spoke, he would say what Caesar wished, and add even more.

In this way an athlete also acted who was in danger of dying unless his private parts were amputated. His brother came to the athlete, who was a philosopher, and said, “Come, brother, what are you going to do? Shall we amputate this member and return to the gymnasium?” But the athlete persisted in his resolution and died. When someone asked Epictetus how he did this, as an athlete or a philosopher? As a man, Epictetus replied, and a man who had been proclaimed among the athletes at the Olympic games and had contended in them, a man who had been familiar with such a place, and not merely anointed in Baton’s school. Another would have allowed even his head to be cut off, if he could have lived without it. Such is that regard to character which is so strong in those who have been accustomed to introduce it of themselves and conjoined with other things into their deliberations.
“Come then, Epictetus, shave yourself.” If I am a philosopher, I answer, I will not shave myself. “But I will take off your head!” If that will do you any good, take it off.

Some person asked, “how then shall every man among us perceive what is suitable to his character?” How, he replied, does the bull alone, when the lion has attacked, discover his own powers and put himself forward in defense of the whole herd? It is plain that with the powers the perception of having them is immediately conjoined: and, therefore, whoever of us has such powers will not be ignorant of them. Now a bull is not made suddenly, nor a brave man; but we must discipline ourselves in the winter for the summer campaign, and not rashly run upon that which does not concern us.

Only consider at what price you sell your own will: if for no other reason, at least for this, that you sell it not for a small sum. But that which is great and superior perhaps belongs to Socrates and such as are like him. Why then, if we are naturally such, are not a very great number of us like him? Is it true then that all horses become swift, that all dogs are skilled in tracking footprints? What then, since I am naturally dull, shall I, for this reason, take no pains? I hope not. Epictetus is not superior to Socrates; but if he is not inferior, this is enough for me; for I shall never be a Milo, and yet I do not neglect my body; nor shall I be a Croesus, and yet I do not neglect my property; nor, in a word, do we neglect looking after anything because we despair of reaching the highest degree.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
The chapter begins with a strange claim: only a rational animal finds the irrational intolerable. Epictetus means that suffering is rarely about the raw event. Blows, he says, are not naturally unbearable. The Spartans take a whipping calmly because they have learned that enduring it fits their idea of what is reasonable. A man who decides that hanging himself is reasonable goes and does it. What truly pains a human being, in other words, is whatever seems senseless to him, and what attracts him is whatever seems sensible. So everything depends on what you have taught yourself to count as sensible.

But people differ on this, and Epictetus faces that squarely with his chamber pot example. To one man, holding another man's chamber pot is perfectly reasonable if the alternative is a beating and no dinner. To another man it would be unthinkable. Epictetus does not scold either one. He says food is worth more than none and a beating is a worse indignity than no beating, so if those are your measures, go and hold the pot. But if you say "that would not be worthy of me," then you are the one bringing a new consideration into the question, a consideration about who you are. Men, he says, "sell themselves at various prices." The phrase is the key to the chapter. Everyone has a price, and what matters is knowing yours.

The stories that follow show what it looks like to have set the price so high that nothing is for sale. Florus wonders whether to appear in Nero's theatrical shows, which was a humiliating thing for a Roman of rank to do. Agrippinus tells him to go. Why will you not go yourself, asks Florus? Because, says Agrippinus, I do not even deliberate about it. Once you start weighing such things, you have already come close to forgetting your character. The image he uses is a robe. Most people are content to be one thread in the tunic. Agrippinus wants to be the purple stripe, the small bright band that makes the whole garment look fine.

Then comes Priscus Helvidius, ordered by the emperor Vespasian to stay out of the Senate. If I am a senator, I must go in, he says. Then say nothing. Then do not ask my opinion. But I must ask. Then I must say what I think is right. Then I will have you killed. "When then did I tell you that I am immortal?" Priscus answers. You do your part, which is to kill, and I will do mine, which is to die without fear.

What a first-time reader may miss is that Epictetus is not praising stubbornness. The point is that a settled sense of who you are makes some questions simply not open for discussion, and that this frees you. The bull senses its strength when the lion arrives. Character, like muscle, is built in the winter for the summer campaign. And he closes with a refusal to be crushed by comparison: he will never be the wrestler Milo or the rich king Croesus, yet he still looks after his body and his property. Falling short of the greatest does not excuse neglect.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
This is one of the most dramatic chapters in the Discourses, and its dramatic quality is a strength. Epictetus does not argue in the abstract that integrity matters. He puts real names and real confrontations on the table and lets the dialogue carry the point. The exchange between Priscus and Vespasian, with its neat pairs of "I must" and "I will," has the compression of a short play. The line about not being immortal is one of the best retorts in ancient prose, because it deflates the threat without denying it.

The chamber pot passage is also unusually honest. Many moralists would simply declare that a dignified person would never do such a thing. Epictetus, who as a slave surely knew the reality of the act, refuses to be so glib. He lets the person choose and says the choice reveals a price. That frankness makes the later demands feel earned. It is hard to dismiss a teacher who has not pretended that humiliation is imaginary.

The purple thread metaphor is exactly the kind of image that sticks. It is visual, brief and slightly flattering, which is why people remember it. It makes the case for being different without sounding vain.

Yet there are real flaws. The chapter can feel arbitrary about what counts as a point of honor. Why is appearing in a Nero show a line that cannot be crossed, while holding a chamber pot is fine for the right person? The answer is meant to be "whatever your own character says," but that makes the standard curiously private. A reader could ask whether a person with poor judgment would simply find their own vices to be part of their character. Epictetus gives no outside test beyond the example of the great, and the great are men like Socrates, whom he admits are rare.

The athlete anecdote is also puzzling. A philosopher-athlete dies rather than submit to an amputation, and Epictetus praises him for acting "as a man." Many readers will find this obscure and perhaps grotesque, since it is hard to see what principle was served by refusing medical treatment. It is the one story in the chapter where admiration seems to override judgment. The "shave yourself" retort, where Epictetus says that if he is a philosopher he will not shave, and that the emperor may take his head if it helps, is amusing but shows a certain swagger too. Philosophers in his day were known for beards, so it is partly about the costume of the profession, which makes the heroic gesture a little smaller.

There is also the oddly confident assertion that a person who has the powers will know it, like a bull. This leaves out the many people who discover their courage late, or fail it and are sorry. The chapter is better at celebrating the people who passed the test than helping the rest of us who are not sure.

Still, the final paragraph rescues the chapter from elitism. By saying that being dull by nature is no reason to give up effort, Epictetus turns an aristocratic ideal into a daily practice. It is a very good ending to a chapter that might otherwise have been only a gallery of heroes.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
The chapter's influence is part of the larger story of the Discourses, which Arrian recorded and which survived in four of eight original books. Epictetus himself wrote nothing, and without Arrian we would not know this particular teacher at all. Arrian later served as a Roman governor and wrote a famous history of Alexander the Great, so his decision to preserve these classroom talks is itself a mark of how seriously a worldly, educated man took them.

The chapter's central question, how to stay one's self under pressure, ran through the late Stoic tradition. Marcus Aurelius, who read Epictetus closely, wrote repeatedly in his private notebook about keeping his own mind clear amid the demands of empire. The image of the person who refuses to bend even when the emperor commands has a long line of descendants, from accounts of martyrs in the early Christian centuries to later stories of conscience against power.

Helvidius Priscus and the other Stoic senators in these pages became a recurring symbol. Historians of Rome, especially Tacitus, describe a circle of Stoic opposition to tyrannical emperors, and writers in later centuries, when dealing with their own authoritarian governments, returned to these figures as models. The phrase "the Stoic opposition" is now standard in histories of the early empire, and whenever someone argues that philosophy has a role in public courage, Priscus's reply to Vespasian is likely to be cited.

In the twentieth century, Admiral James Stockdale, a navy officer who was held prisoner in North Vietnam for years, said he had Epictetus in mind during his captivity. He referred to the Discourses in speeches about leadership and integrity, and his example brought this kind of thinking into military education and business writing. The idea of a "price" for your will appears in modern discussions of corruption and ethics, where it is common to ask what a person would do under pressure and what would be enough to make them give in.

In modern therapy, the part about perceiving things as reasonable or unreasonable fits with cognitive approaches, which treat distress as dependent on beliefs about what is acceptable. Some therapists use the chamber pot passage as an example of how values shape what feels like humiliation.

The chapter is also taught in philosophy and classics courses as a primer on Stoic ethics and on the question of moral identity, sometimes called "integrity" in the sense of wholeness. Philosophers in the twentieth century, among them those interested in how our commitments define us, have written about the idea that some actions are unthinkable for a person, not because a calculation forbids them but because they are not options. Agrippinus's remark that he does not even deliberate is a classic ancient version of that idea.

Finally, the purple thread line has entered the language of ethics lectures and graduation speeches, where it is a popular way to encourage students to stand out for good reasons.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
Readers have loved this chapter first for its courage, and for the fact that the courage is shown instead of preached. The scene of Priscus Helvidius walking toward the Senate house, knowing the emperor has forbidden it, and answering threats of death with calm logic has the power of a good scene in a film. People remember it. They remember that the answer to "I will have you put to death" is a kind of joke about mortality, and the combination of lightness and steel is deeply attractive.

They have also loved its lack of illusion about money and comfort. Epictetus does not pretend that principle is free. He admits that holding the pot gets you food and refusing gets you beaten, and he says so in plain terms. For readers tired of lofty moralizing, this realism is refreshing. The reader is treated as an adult who can decide for themselves, with the one condition that they know what they are paying.

The image of the purple stripe is a favorite. Readers like that it gives a graceful reason for individuality. Instead of saying "be different for the sake of it," it says that a small bright part makes the whole cloth look better. This has made it a popular quotation among people who feel pressure to blend in.

Another point of affection is the humane ending. After a series of near-heroic examples, Epictetus says that he is naturally dull and will still make an effort. The honesty here is disarming. It tells the reader that the goal is not to be Socrates but to do what one can, as one tends one's body and property without hoping to become a champion or a king. Readers often say they find this consoling, and it helps them take on the harder passages that came before.

Many people also love the line about the bull and the lion for its simplicity. It makes the case that courage is something that shows itself when needed, and that preparation in quiet seasons matters. Athletes, soldiers and teachers have all been drawn to the idea that you must "discipline ourselves in the winter for the summer campaign." It has the ring of a coaching maxim, and in a sense it is one, since Epictetus often borrows language from the gymnasium.

Finally, readers appreciate that the chapter takes the reader's inner life seriously. It does not assume that character is a given. It treats it as something you can examine, name and protect. For anyone who has been asked to compromise at work or in a community, and who felt a quiet sense that something would be lost, the chapter gives words for that feeling.
