This is why it is often recommended to young people starting careers, who are about to be offered their first prices.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
Critics of Epictetus, and of this chapter in particular, have raised several objections over the centuries. The most familiar is that his ideal is elitist and, in practice, available mostly to the strong. The stories involve senators, athletes and philosophers, people with standing, education and sometimes the safety of a famous name. A poor person with a family to feed, in a world with no protection, cannot easily say "I do not deliberate about this." Epictetus does acknowledge that men differ in price and that he will not condemn the man who holds the pot, but the heroes he praises are the ones who refuse.

A related objection is that the chapter is weak on how a person actually comes to know their own character. It assumes that you will know, the way the bull does. Critics note that people often deceive themselves about what they are made of, and that a standard that rests on self-knowledge is only as good as the self-knowledge. History includes many men who were certain of their principles until the moment they were tested.

Others have criticized the Stoic readiness to die. The philosopher-athlete story strikes many modern readers as pointlessly stubborn. More broadly, some have said that treating death as simply "my part" can shade into a kind of fatalism that makes resistance less practical. Priscus did not reform Vespasian. Within a few years, according to the historical accounts, he was exiled and then killed. A skeptic can ask what the gesture achieved, and Epictetus's own answer, that the purple makes the garment look fine, is more aesthetic than political.

The Stoics also faced the charge, going back to antiquity, that their ideal was too severe to be human. Pascal, in the seventeenth century, said that Epictetus understood duty but flattered human pride by suggesting we could meet it alone. The English-speaking world of the eighteenth century, which loved Stoic writing, still often found it cold.

There is also a more recent unease about how this kind of thinking can be used. Corporate and self-help writers have turned the language of character and price into a motivational vocabulary, which some critics think drains it of its context. In its original setting the "price" in question was one's life, one's freedom and one's honor in front of an emperor, not the cost of a promotion.

Finally, scholars point out that Arrian's notes give us a single, selective record, and that the speeches attributed to people like Priscus come to us through a teacher's retelling and not from neutral sources. Historians who have compared these stories with Tacitus find some agreement but also a heightened, teaching quality. The stories are probably true in outline, but they are polished to make a point, and readers should keep that in mind.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
This chapter sits in the tradition of Stoicism, the school founded in Athens by Zeno around 300 BC and carried to Rome by thinkers like Seneca and Musonius Rufus. Its special interest is in what scholars call the "roles" or "personae" a person plays. Earlier Stoics, notably Panaetius, taught that each person has several roles: as a human being, as a member of a family or city, as an individual with particular talents and as someone with a chosen path. Epictetus draws on this when he speaks of being appropriate "to each person." The chapter is a vivid example of Roman Stoicism applied to politics and daily conduct.

It descends, too, from Socrates, who in Plato's account preferred to die rather than give up his philosophical work. Epictetus mentions him at the end, with a modest comparison, and the whole chapter has a Socratic cast: the claim that goodness is a matter of what you value, and that the person who values the right things cannot be truly harmed by those who value the wrong ones.

In literature, the idea of the person who will not cooperate with tyranny echoes in many later works. Thomas More, who refused to approve Henry VIII's divorce and was executed, was described by admirers in language that recalls Priscus. Sophocles had already given the world Antigone, who defies a king's order because she cannot do otherwise. In modern times, the conscientious objector, the dissident and the whistleblower are all kin to the characters in this chapter. Writers like Vaclav Havel, with his essays on living in truth under an oppressive state, work in the same spirit, although he did not take his ideas from Epictetus alone.

In philosophy, the idea that some things are unthinkable for a person shows up in twentieth-century discussions of moral character, in the work of Bernard Williams, for instance, who wrote about "one thought too many" and about integrity. Epictetus's notion that a person's character sets limits on deliberation is a remarkable ancient anticipation of those discussions.

Compared with the Enchiridion, the short handbook drawn from the Discourses, this chapter is richer and more concrete. Compared with Seneca's letters, it is rougher and less comfortable. Compared with Marcus Aurelius, it is public, not private: a story told for a class of students who might soon face official power.

Why read it today? Because the situation it describes has not gone away. People still face pressure to go along, to stay quiet, to take part in something they find degrading, and to tell themselves that it is reasonable. The chapter does not tell you what to decide. It tells you that the decision is also a statement about who you are, and that you are setting a price whether you admit it or not. That is an idea worth spending ten minutes with before bed.

essays.title: Discourses I.12: Of Contentment
essays.author: Epictetus
essays.epigraph: Freedom is secured not by the fulfilling of men's desires, but by the removal of desire.
essays.keyContext:
This short chapter from the Discourses of Epictetus deals with a question people in every age ask: how should we feel about the way the world is run? Epictetus was a Greek Stoic teacher in the Roman Empire around the year 100. He had been a slave, and he taught in a small school in northwestern Greece. A student named Arrian wrote down his talks, which is how we have them in their lively, argumentative spoken style.

Here he begins with a quick survey of what people believe about the gods, from outright denial to the belief that the divine cares about everything. Then he argues that a wise person should willingly accept the order of the world, as a good citizen accepts the law. This is not resignation, he insists, but real freedom. The chapter is one of the clearest statements of the Stoic idea that peace comes not from changing the world but from changing what we ask of it.
paragraphs: With respect to gods, there are some who say that a divine being does not exist: others say that it exists, but is inactive and careless, and takes no forethought about anything; a third class say that such a being exists and exercises forethought, but only about great things and heavenly things, and about nothing on the earth; a fourth class say that a divine being exercises forethought both about things on the earth and heavenly things, but in a general way only, and not about things severally. There is a fifth class to whom Ulysses and Socrates belong, who say: “I move not without thy knowledge” (Iliad x 278).

Before all other things then it is necessary to inquire about each of these opinions, whether it is affirmed truly or not truly. For if there are no gods, how is it our proper end to follow them? And if they exist, but take no care of anything, in this case also how will it be right to follow them? But if indeed they do exist and look after things, still if there is nothing communicated from them to men, nor in fact to myself, how even so is it right (to follow them)? The wise and good man then after considering all these things, submits his own mind to him who administers the whole, as good citizens do to the law of the state. He who is receiving instruction ought to come to be instructed with this intention: How shall I follow the gods in all things, how shall I be contented with the divine administration, and how can I become free? For he is free to whom everything happens according to his will, and whom no man can hinder. What then is freedom madness? Certainly not: for madness and freedom do not consist. But, you say, I would have everything result just as I like, and in whatever way I like. You are mad, you are beside yourself. Do you not know that freedom is a noble and valuable thing? But for me inconsiderately to wish for things to happen as I inconsiderately like, this appears to be not only not noble, but even most base. For how do we proceed in the matter of writing? Do I wish to write the name of Dion as I choose? No, but I am taught to choose to write it as it ought to be written. And how with respect to music? In the same manner. And what universally in every art or science? Just the same. If it were not so, it would be of no value to know anything, if knowledge were adapted to every man’s whim. Is it then in this alone, in this which is the greatest and the chief thing, I mean freedom, that I am permitted to will inconsiderately? By no means; but to be instructed is this, to learn to wish that everything may happen as it does. And how do things happen? As the disposer has disposed them? And he has appointed summer and winter, and abundance and scarcity, and virtue and vice, and all such opposites for the harmony of the whole; and to each of us he has given a body, and parts of the body, and possessions, and companions.

Remembering then this disposition of things, we ought to go to be instructed, not that we may change the constitution of things⁠—for we have not the power to do it, nor is it better that we should have the power⁠—but in order that, as the things around us are what they are and by nature exist, we may maintain our minds in harmony with the things which happen. For can we escape from men? and how is it possible? And if we associate with them, can we change them? Who gives us the power? What then remains, or what method is discovered of holding commerce with them? Is there such a method by which they shall do what seems fit to them, and we not the less shall be in a mood which is conformable to nature? But you are unwilling to endure and are discontented: and if you are alone, you call it solitude; and if you are with men, you call them knaves and robbers; and you find fault with your own parents and children, and brothers and neighbours. But you ought when you are alone to call this condition by the name of tranquillity and freedom, and to think yourself like to the gods; and when you are with many, you ought not to call it crowd, nor trouble, nor uneasiness, but festival and assembly, and so accept all contentedly.

What then is the punishment of those who do not accept? It is to be what they are. Is any person dissatisfied with being alone? let him be alone. Is a man dissatisfied with his parents? let him be a bad son, and lament. Is he dissatisfied with his children? let him be a bad father. Cast him into prison. What prison? Where he is already, for he is there against his will; and where a man is against his will, there he is in prison. So Socrates was not in prison, for he was there willingly. Must my leg then be lamed? Wretch, do you then on account of one poor leg find fault with the world? Will you not willingly surrender it for the whole? Will you not withdraw from it? Will you not gladly part with it to him who gave it? And will you be vexed and discontented with the things established by Zeus, which he with the Moirae (fates) who were present and spinning the thread of your generation, defined and put in order? Know you not how small a part you are compared with the whole. I mean with respect to the body, for as to intelligence you are not inferior to the gods nor less; for the magnitude of intelligence is not measured by length nor yet by height, but by thoughts.

Will you not then choose to place your good in that in which you are equal to the gods? “Wretch that I am to have such a father and mother.” What then, was it permitted to you to come forth and to select and to say: Let such a man at this moment unite with such a woman that I may be produced? It was not permitted, but it was a necessity for your parents to exist first, and then for you to be begotten. Of what kind of parents? Of such as they were. Well then, since they are such as they are, is there no remedy given to you? Now if you did not know for what purpose you possess the faculty of vision, you would be unfortunate and wretched if you closed your eyes when colors were brought before them; but in that you possess greatness of soul and nobility of spirit for every event that may happen, and you know not that you possess them, are you not more unfortunate and wretched? Things are brought close to you which are proportionate to the power which you possess, but you turn away this power most particularly at the very time when you ought to maintain it open and discerning. Do you not rather thank the gods that they have allowed you to be above these things which they have not placed in your power, and have made you accountable only for those which are in your power? As to your parents, the gods have left you free from responsibility; and so with respect to your brothers, and your body, and possessions, and death and life. For what then have they made you responsible? For that which alone is in your power: the proper use of appearances. Why then do you draw on yourself the things for which you are not responsible? It is, indeed, a giving of trouble to yourself.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
The chapter opens like a lecture on theology. Epictetus sorts people into five camps. Some say there is no divine being. Some say there is but it does nothing. Some say it looks after heaven and great matters but not the earth. Some say it looks after everything only in a general way, not in detail. And a fifth group, which includes Odysseus and Socrates, says, in a line from the Iliad, that "I move not without thy knowledge." Epictetus belongs with the fifth. He thinks the first job of a student is to decide which of these is true, because everything else depends on it. If there are no gods, or they do not care, there is nothing to follow.

Once that is settled, he turns to the question of freedom, and the argument becomes surprising. A free person, he says, is one to whom everything happens according to his will, whom no one can hinder. Does that mean doing whatever you like? No, that is madness. He compares it to writing. When you write the name of Dion, you do not spell it as you please, you learn to spell it as it ought to be written. The same goes for music and every other craft. Knowledge would be worthless if it bent to anyone's whim. So the greatest skill, freedom, must work the same way. To be educated in it is "to learn to wish that everything may happen as it does."

That phrase is the center of the chapter and it is easy to misread. Epictetus does not say that you should stop trying to improve things. He says that the pattern of events, summer and winter, abundance and scarcity, even virtue and vice, was arranged as a whole, and you were handed a body, possessions and companions as part of it. You cannot escape other people or fix them. What you can do is keep your own mind in harmony with what occurs.

The rest of the chapter works out what that means in daily life. The person who is alone calls it loneliness, and the person who is with others calls them thieves and rogues. Epictetus suggests renaming: call being alone tranquillity, and call a crowd a festival. The punishment for not accepting is simply to be what you are, discontented. Someone who is in a place against his will is in prison, whatever the building. Socrates, by contrast, was not in prison, because he was there willingly.

He ends by turning to what we cannot pick: our parents, our bodies, our births. You did not choose your mother and father, so complaining is pointless. What the gods did make you answerable for is the one thing in your power, the right use of appearances, meaning how you handle what comes to you.

A first-time reader might miss that the argument is partly an argument about responsibility. The more we blame, the more we claim control we do not have, and the less we use the control we do. Contentment here is not mood but accuracy.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
The chapter's best idea, that freedom means wanting what is real and not what is whimsical, is subtle and surprisingly modern. The comparison to spelling a name is a clever way of making it concrete. We all accept that a craft has rules that do not bend to our feelings. Epictetus asks why the art of living should be the one exception. It is a good, plain argument and it comes at exactly the right moment, after he has raised the suspicion that "wish things to happen as they do" sounds like surrender.

The renaming trick is also well observed. Anyone who has felt lonely in a quiet house and relaxed once they called it peace, or been irritated in a crowd and enjoyed it once they thought of it as a party, knows there is some truth here. It anticipates later psychological ideas about reframing, and it is practical enough to try tonight.

The weak points are fairly clear. The opening survey of beliefs about the gods is brisk to the point of being unfair. The five positions are lined up so that only the last survives, and the arguments against the others take a couple of sentences. A reader who is not already inclined to believe in a caring divine order will find the foundation of the chapter shaky. Everything that follows, the claim that the world has been arranged for harmony, rests on it.

There is a deeper problem. The same argument that tells you to accept your parents and your bad leg also tells you to accept cruelty and injustice, since "virtue and vice" are said to be part of the harmony. Epictetus does not quite say that evil is good, but his line that these opposites exist "for the harmony of the whole" sits uncomfortably next to the suffering of real people. Many readers will feel that a harmony that includes vice has been defined too generously. The chapter does not answer the question of why anyone should rebuild a flawed world if it is already in order.

The passage about the lame leg is another place where the logic is strained. "Must my leg then be lamed? Wretch, do you then on account of one poor leg find fault with the world?" Epictetus was himself lame, which gives the line a certain authority and a certain edge. But it is delivered with a scolding force that may not help someone in pain. The tone moves between comforting and hectoring, and a reader may prefer one or the other.

Still, the writing has energy. The questions come at you quickly, the examples are drawn from daily life, and the best lines, about calling a crowd a festival, are the sort of thing you remember. As teaching it is persuasive. As a proof, it is not, and Epictetus would probably say that this is not the job of a lecture. Its job is to change what you do when the wind blows from the wrong direction.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
This chapter has had its largest effect through the way it distills a central Stoic doctrine, usually described as living in agreement with nature or with providence, into something a person can practice. The doctrine goes back to the founders of Stoicism, who held that the universe is governed by a rational order, and that wisdom lies in aligning one's will with it. Epictetus puts it in an everyday key, and that version became the one most people read.

Marcus Aurelius, the Roman emperor, drew heavily on this idea. His private notebook, the Meditations, returns again and again to accepting what happens as part of the whole, to loving what fate brings. It is likely that his teacher introduced him to Epictetus's lectures, and the habit of addressing yourself sternly, as this chapter does, shaped the emperor's style.

In Christian thought, the idea that a person should submit to a wise divine administration and find freedom in doing so found a ready audience. Early Christian writers admired Stoic ethics even where they disagreed on theology, and a handbook of Epictetus's teaching was adapted for monastic use in the Middle Ages. The phrase "thy will be done" has an obvious cousin in Epictetus's "if so it pleases God, so let it be," which appears elsewhere in the Discourses.

In the modern era the chapter fed into several streams. Some of the language of the Serenity Prayer, associated with the twentieth-century theologian Reinhold Niebuhr and widely used in recovery programs, echoes the Stoic division between what can and cannot be changed, though its immediate origin is Christian. Modern cognitive therapy, whose founders cited Epictetus, shares his idea that distress depends on how we interpret events.

More recently, the so-called Stoic revival has made this sort of teaching popular again. Writers and speakers promote the idea of embracing what happens, sometimes using the Latin phrase "amor fati," a love of fate, which comes from later writers but fits the spirit of this text. Nietzsche, who disliked the Stoics, still used that phrase for his own purposes.

In education, the chapter has served as a classic text for introducing Stoic ethics to students because it is short and covers a lot of ground: theology, freedom, family, solitude and responsibility. It is often paired with the Enchiridion in classes.

Within the Discourses it is also a useful bridge. It links the opening ideas about what is in our power to the later, more practical advice about the relationships and roles we hold, so scholars treat it as a hinge in the argument of the first book.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
Readers have most often loved the chapter's consoling reframing. The line about calling a crowd a festival and solitude tranquillity is the kind of thing people copy into notebooks. It gives an immediate practice to try, and many readers report that it works at least some of the time. A person stuck in traffic, a crowded train or a lonely evening can use it at once.

They also love its picture of freedom. Most people think of freedom as having options and getting what you want. Epictetus suggests that real freedom is being unbothered, a mind that cannot be hindered because it asks only for what is possible. That reversal is bracing. For a reader worn down by wanting, the idea that they might simply stop being at war with reality comes as a relief. Writers in the tradition of self-improvement have returned to it for that reason.

The comparison between life and craft is another favorite. People appreciate the plain sense of it: you accept that a spelling or a musical note must be right, so why complain that the world does not follow your preferences? It is argued in a way that does not require anyone to share Stoic physics, though the theology is there for those who want it.

Readers also admire the courage behind the calm. Because Epictetus was a former slave with a lame leg, his talk of contentment cannot be dismissed as the comfort of a rich man. When he tells the listener not to blame the world for one leg, many people feel the weight of what he has himself endured. His teaching carries more credibility because it was lived in conditions most of us would find hard.

The image of the mind as large, though the body is small, is often cited. "The magnitude of intelligence is not measured by length nor yet by height, but by thoughts" is one of the most quoted lines for readers who feel small in the face of larger forces. It says that your size in the universe is not your size in the room.

Finally, there is the sense of dignity. Epictetus calls us to thank the gods for having made us responsible only for what is in our power. It turns a limitation into a gift. The same set of facts that might look like helplessness is shown as a kind of lightness, and readers who take it in often describe feeling that a weight has lifted. That emotional effect is a large part of why the chapter has lasted.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
The strongest objection is moral and political. If you are taught that the order of the world is harmonious and that you should wish for things to happen as they do, you may become less willing to resist injustice. Critics from Hegel onward have argued that Stoicism's inner freedom is a way of living with chains rather than breaking them. When Epictetus tells someone dissatisfied with their lot to stop complaining, the line can sound uncomfortably like what a powerful person would like a powerless one to hear.

A second objection concerns the claim that everything happens according to a divine plan. The existence of cruelty, plague, war and the deaths of children has led many readers to find the Stoic confidence unconvincing. The traditional problem of evil is not answered here, only waved at through the remark that opposites exist for the harmony of the whole. Philosophers who share Epictetus's ethics but not his theology have often tried to keep the practice and drop the cosmic claims.

Third, there is the charge that the teaching is cold toward family. The passage on parents, saying that you did not choose them and so are not to blame, is a kind of comfort. But the language of "responsibility" and "not in your power" can read as dismissive. Critics such as the philosopher Martha Nussbaum have asked whether a person who has trained themselves to accept the loss of loved ones as part of the natural order has lost the kind of attachment that makes life valuable.

Fourth, some readers find the tone off-putting. "You are mad, you are beside yourself," he says to the person who wants things to go his way. "Wretch" is a favorite word. This is classroom language, meant to shake students up, but it can come across as bullying. Seneca's gentler letters, or the private doubts of Marcus Aurelius, can feel more humane by contrast.

There is also the historical caution that the words come to us secondhand. Arrian's notes were not an authorized text, and scholars debate how closely they reflect Epictetus's actual words. The chapter may have been polished in the writing.

Finally, a few critics have said that the chapter's claim about freedom plays with words. When Epictetus defines a free person as one to whom everything happens according to his will, and then says that the way to achieve that is to will whatever happens, it can seem like a trick, a definition that makes freedom easy by shrinking what we ask of it. Defenders reply that this is exactly the point, and that the shrinking is the lesson. Still, the dispute is real, and it is part of how the chapter is read and argued over today.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
This chapter belongs to Stoicism, the school that began in Athens around 300 BC and flourished in Rome. The Stoics held that the universe is a single living, rational whole, sometimes called by the names of Zeus, God or providence, and that a good human life consists in living in agreement with it. Epictetus, writing in the late first and early second century, represents the later Roman phase, which concentrated on ethics and daily practice more than on the system of physics and logic. This chapter is especially close to the Stoic theme of "following God," found in the famous hymn of Cleanthes, whose line is quoted elsewhere in the Discourses.

It descends from Socrates, whom Epictetus mentions here as one who was never truly in prison, and from the broader Greek tradition that the wise person fits themselves to the order of things. It also relates to the Homeric background, as with the line from the Iliad about Odysseus asking for the goddess to know his every move.

Its relatives in other traditions are many. Buddhist teaching about the cause of suffering as craving, and the cure as releasing it, treats similar ground. The Book of Job in the Hebrew Bible confronts the question of whether one can accept a world one did not make, though it ends with a very different answer, one in which God speaks out of the whirlwind. Taoist writings, with their stress on going with the way of things, have a similar flavor. Spinoza, the seventeenth-century philosopher, argued that freedom is understanding necessity, an idea that is close to Epictetus and was likely shaped by Stoic sources.

Among later works, Boethius wrote his Consolation of Philosophy in prison in the sixth century, drawing on Stoic ideas about fortune and acceptance. Montaigne in the sixteenth century wrote essays on how to accept death and ill fortune, with plenty of Stoic echoes. In our own time, Viktor Frankl's account of his experience in Nazi camps, with its claim that we keep the last of human freedoms, the choice of our attitude, is regularly compared to Epictetus.

Compared with other chapters in the Discourses, this one is more theological and more concerned with attitude to the world as a whole. It is less about specific acts than about the background mood in which we act.

Why read it? Because it names a problem we all share, the sense that the world should be otherwise, and offers a practical response. You do not have to agree with the theology to feel the force of the exercise. Even a skeptic can try, tonight, to call a noisy room a festival and see what changes.

essays.title: Discourses I.29: On Constancy (Or Firmness)
essays.author: Epictetus
essays.epigraph: The essence of the Good is a certain kind of moral will; the essence of the Bad is a certain kind of moral will. What then are external things? Materials for the will.
essays.keyContext:
This is a long, fierce lecture from the Discourses of Epictetus, a Greek Stoic teacher who lived under the Roman emperors around the year 100. Born a slave and later freed, he taught in a school in northwestern Greece, and a student named Arrian took down his words. Epictetus never published anything himself, so we hear a living classroom voice, with its jokes, jabs and sudden stories.

The subject is constancy, meaning steadiness of mind when someone more powerful threatens you. His argument is that a tyrant can take your body, your property and your freedom of movement, but cannot touch your will, your power to judge and choose. Along the way he draws on Socrates, on a stolen lamp, and on the stage and the athletic arena. The chapter is demanding, even stern, but it is also a vivid account of how people have faced prison and death with their dignity intact.
paragraphs: The being (nature) of the Good is a certain Will; the being of the Bad is a certain kind of Will. What then are externals? Materials for the Will, about which the will being conversant shall obtain its own good or evil. How shall it obtain the good? If it does not admire (overvalue) the materials; for the opinions about the materials, if the opinions are right, make the will good: but perverse and distorted opinions make the will bad. God has fixed this law, and says, “If you would have anything good, receive it from yourself.” You say, “No, but I will have it from another.” Do not so: but receive it from yourself. Therefore when the tyrant threatens and calls me, I say, “Whom do you threaten?” If he says, “I will put you in chains,” I say, “You threaten my hands and my feet.” If he says, “I will cut off your head,” I reply, “You threaten my head.” If he says, “I will throw you into prison,” I say, “You threaten the whole of this poor body.” If he threatens me with banishment, I say the same. Does he then not threaten you at all? If I feel that all these things do not concern me, he does not threaten me at all; but if I fear any of them, it is I whom he threatens. Whom then do I fear? the master of what? The master of things which are in my own power? There is no such master. Do I fear the master of things which are not in my power? And what are these things to me?

“Do you philosophers then teach us to despise kings?” I hope not. Who among us teaches to claim against them the power over things which they possess? Take my poor body, take my property, take my reputation, take those who are about me. If I advise any persons to claim these things, they may truly accuse me. “Yes, but I intend to command your opinions also.” And who has given you this power? How can you conquer the opinion of another man? “By applying terror to it,” he replies, “I will conquer it.” Do you not know that opinion conquers itself, and is not conquered by another? But nothing else can conquer Will except the Will itself. For this reason too the law of God is most powerful and most just, which is this: Let the stronger always be superior to the weaker. Ten are stronger than one. For what? For putting in chains, for killing, for dragging whither they choose, for taking away what a man has. The ten therefore conquer the one in this in which they are stronger. In what then are the ten weaker? If the one possesses right opinions and the others do not. Well then, can the ten conquer in this matter? How is it possible? If we were placed in the scales, must not the heavier draw down the scale in which it is?

How strange then that Socrates should have been so treated by the Athenians. Slave, why do you say Socrates? Speak of the thing as it is: how strange that the poor body of Socrates should have been carried off and dragged to prison by stronger men, and that anyone should have given hemlock to the poor body of Socrates, and that it should breathe out the life. Do these things seem strange, do they seem unjust, do you on account of these things blame God? Had Socrates then no equivalent for these things? Where then for him was the nature of good? Whom shall we listen to, you or him? And what does Socrates say? Anytus and Melitus can kill me, but they cannot hurt me: and further, he says, “If it so pleases God, so let it be.”

But show me that he who has the inferior principles overpowers him who is superior in principles. You will never show this, nor come near showing it; for this is the law of nature and of God that the superior shall always overpower the inferior. In what? In that in which it is superior. One body is stronger than another: many are stronger than one: the thief is stronger than he who is not a thief. This is the reason why I also lost my lamp, because in wakefulness the thief was superior to me. But the man bought the lamp at this price: for a lamp he became a thief, a faithless fellow, and like a wild beast. This seemed to him a good bargain. Be it so. But a man has seized me by the cloak, and is drawing me to the public place: then others bawl out, “Philosopher, what has been the use of your opinions? see you are dragged to prison, you are going to be beheaded.” And what system of philosophy (εἰσαγωγήν) could I have made so that, if a stronger man should have laid hold of my cloak, I should not be dragged off; that if ten men should have laid hold of me and cast me into prison, I should not be cast in? Have I learned nothing else then? I have learned to see that everything which happens, if it be independent of my will, is nothing to me. I may ask, if you have not gained by this. Why then do you seek advantage in anything else than in that in which you have learned that advantage is?

Then sitting in prison I say: The man who cries out in this way neither hears what words mean, nor understands what is said, nor does he care at all to know what philosophers say or what they do. Let him alone.

But now he says to the prisoner, “Come out from your prison.”⁠—If you have no further need of me in prison, I come out: if you should have need of me again, I will enter the prison.⁠—“How long will you act thus?”⁠—So long as reason requires me to be with the body: but when reason does not require this, take away the body, and fare you well. Only we must not do it inconsiderately, nor weakly, nor for any slight reason; for, on the other hand, God does not wish it to be done, and he has need of such a world and such inhabitants in it. But if he sounds the signal for retreat, as he did to Socrates, we must obey him who gives the signal, as if he were a general.

Well then, ought we to say such things to the many? Why should we? Is it not enough for a man to be persuaded himself? When children come clapping their hands and crying out, “Today is the good Saturnalia,” do we say, “The Saturnalia are not good”? By no means, but we clap our hands also. Do you also then, when you are not able to make a man change his mind, be assured that he is a child, and clap your hands with him; and if you do not choose to do this, keep silent.

A man must keep this in mind; and when he is called to any such difficulty, he should know that the time is come for showing if he has been instructed. For he who is come into a difficulty is like a young man from a school who has practiced the resolution of syllogisms; and if any person proposes to him an easy syllogism, he says: rather propose to me a syllogism which is skillfully complicated that I may exercise myself on it. Even athletes are dissatisfied with slight young men, and say, “He cannot lift me.”⁠—“This is a youth of noble disposition.” [You do not so]; but when the time of trial is come, one of you must weep and say, “I wish that I had learned more.” A little more of what? If you did not learn these things in order to show them in practice, why did you learn them? I think that there is someone, among you who are sitting here, who is suffering like a woman in labor, and saying, “Oh, that such a difficulty does not present itself to me as that which has come to this man; oh, that I should be wasting my life in a corner, when I might be crowned at Olympia. When will anyone announce to me such a contest?” Such ought to be the disposition of all of you. Even among the gladiators of Caesar (the Emperor) there are some who complain grievously that they are not brought forward and matched, and they offer up prayers to God and address themselves to their superintendents entreating that they may fight. And will no one among you show himself such? I would willingly take a voyage [to Rome] for this purpose and see what my athlete is doing, how he is studying his subject.⁠—I do not choose such a subject, he says. Why, is it in your power to take what subject you choose? There has been given to you such a body as you have, such parents, such brethren, such a country, such a place in your country:⁠—then you come to me and say, “Change my subject.” Have you not abilities which enable you to manage the subject which has been given to you? [You ought to say]: “It is your business to propose; it is mine to exercise myself well.” However, you do not say so, but you say, “Do not propose to me such a tropic, but such [as I would choose]: do not urge against me such an objection, but such [as I would choose].” There will be a time perhaps when tragic actors will suppose that they are [only] masks and buskins and the long cloak. I say, these things, man, are your material and subject. Utter something that we may know whether you are a tragic actor or a buffoon; for both of you have all the rest in common. If anyone then should take away the tragic actor’s buskins and his mask, and introduce him on the stage as a phantom, is the tragic actor lost, or does he still remain? If he has voice, he still remains.

An example of another kind: “Assume the governorship of a province.” I assume it, and when I have assumed it, I show how an instructed man behaves. “Lay aside the laticlave (the mark of senatorial rank), and clothing yourself in rags, come forward in this character.” What then, have I not the power of displaying a good voice (that is, of doing something that I ought to do)? How then do you now appear (on the stage of life)? As a witness summoned by God. “Come forward, you, and bear testimony for me, for you are worthy to be brought forward as a witness by me: is anything external to the will good or bad? do I hurt any man? have I made every man’s interest dependent on any man except himself? What testimony do you give for God?”⁠—I am in a wretched condition, Master (Lord), and I am unfortunate; no man cares for me, no man gives me anything; all blame me, all steak ill of me.⁠—Is this the evidence that you are going to give, and disgrace his summons, who has conferred so much honor on you, and thought you worthy of being called to bear such testimony?

But suppose that he who has the power has declared, “I judge you to be impious and profane.” What has happened to you? I have been judged to be impious and profane? Nothing else? Nothing else. But if the same person had passed judgment on a hypothetical syllogism (συνημμένου), and had made a declaration, “the conclusion that, if it is day, it is light, I declare to be false,” what has happened to the hypothetical syllogism? who is judged in this case? who has been condemned? the hypothetical syllogism, or the man who has been deceived by it? Does he then who has the power of making any declaration about you know what is pious or impious? Has he studied it, and has he learned it? Where? From whom? Then is it the fact that a musician pays no regard to him who declares that the lowest chord in the lyre is the highest; nor yet a geometrician, if he declares that the lines from the centre of a circle to the circumference are not equal; and shall he who is really instructed pay any regard to the uninstructed man when he pronounces judgment on what is pious and what is impious, on what is just and unjust? Oh, the signal wrong done by the instructed. Did they learn this here?

Will you not leave the small arguments (λογάρια) about these matters to others, to lazy fellows, that they may sit in a corner and receive their sorry pay, or grumble that no one gives them anything; and will you not come forward and make use of what you have learned? For it is not these small arguments that are wanted now: the writings of the Stoics are full of them. What then is the thing which is wanted? A man who shall apply them, one who by his acts shall bear testimony to his words. Assume, I entreat you, this character, that we may no longer use in the schools the examples of the ancients, but may have some example of our own.

To whom then does the contemplation of these matters (philosophical inquiries) belong? To him who has leisure, for man is an animal that loves contemplation. But it is shameful to contemplate these things as runaway slaves do: we should sit, as in a theatre, free from distraction, and listen at one time to the tragic actor, at another time to the lute-player; and not do as slaves do. As soon as the slave has taken his station he praises the actor and at the same time looks round: then if anyone calls out his master’s name, the slave is immediately frightened and disturbed. It is shameful for philosophers thus to contemplate the works of nature. For what is a master? Man is not the master of man; but death is, and life and pleasure and pain; for if he comes without these things, bring Caesar to me and you will see how firm I am. But when he shall come with these things, thundering and lightning, and when I am afraid of them, what do I do then except to recognize my master like the runaway slave? But so long as I have any respite from these terrors, as a runaway slave stands in the theatre, so do I: I bathe, I drink, I sing; but all this I do with terror and uneasiness. But if I shall release myself from my masters, that is from those things by means of which masters are formidable, what further trouble have I, what master have I still?

What then, ought we to publish these things to all men? No, but we ought to accommodate ourselves to the ignorant (τοῖς ἰδιώταις) and to say: “This man recommends to me that which he thinks good for himself: I excuse him.” For Socrates also excused the jailor, who had the charge of him in prison and was weeping when Socrates was going to drink the poison, and said, “How generously he laments over us.” Does he then say to the jailor that for this reason we have sent away the women? No, but he says it to his friends who were able to hear (understand) it; and he treats the jailor as a child.

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
The chapter begins with a bold claim: the good and the bad are both located in the will, the faculty of choosing and judging. Everything outside the will, the body, property, reputation, other people, is only raw material. A person becomes good or bad by the opinions they form about that material. If you overvalue it, you will be at its mercy. If you judge it rightly, you cannot be hurt. God, Epictetus says, has given a simple law: if you want something good, take it from yourself.

The famous demonstration is the tyrant. When someone threatens to chain him, he replies that they threaten his hands and feet. When they threaten his head, his head. When they threaten prison, the whole poor body. If I truly feel that none of this concerns me, then he threatens me not at all. If I fear any of it, then I have handed over the power myself. The man who threatens is the master only of things I should not have made my masters.

Epictetus then asks a subtler question: what about the claim that the ten always beat the one? He accepts it, but only in the area where they are stronger. Ten men can drag you off, chain you, kill you. They cannot make you believe something false against your will, because opinion is conquered only by itself. The law that the stronger prevails is true, he says, but it applies strictly: the superior overcomes the inferior in that in which he is superior. A thief is stronger than a sleeper, and that is how he lost his lamp. But the thief, who bought a lamp at the price of becoming a thief, made a poor bargain, since he gave up his honesty for a cheap object.

Socrates is the proof case. He was dragged to prison and given hemlock, and people call it strange. Epictetus says to speak accurately: it was the poor body of Socrates that was dragged. Socrates himself said that his accusers could kill him but not harm him.

The second half turns from defense to practice. When a hard moment comes, he says, it is the moment to show you have learned something. He compares it to an athlete who is bored by weak opponents, and to a student who wants a hard logic puzzle. He mocks those who say they wish for different material, a different body, parents or country. The material is what it is, and the test is how you work with it. Stoic philosophers who only write clever arguments, he says, have missed the point. What the world needs is someone whose acts testify to their words.

He ends with the runaway slave watching a play, who enjoys it while looking over his shoulder for his master. Philosophy done in fear, he says, is like that. The real masters are death, life, pleasure and pain, and only when we are free of those can we watch the world with calm.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
This chapter is one of the most forceful things in the Discourses, and its force comes from the combination of logic and theatre. The argument is simple enough to state in a sentence, but Epictetus makes it live through a rapid string of scenes: the tyrant, the cloak, the lamp, the prison, the stage. A mind that might nod at an abstract claim is made to hear it said in a threatening voice and answered back.

The repeated answer to the tyrant is the best of these. It is almost a formula, and the turn from "you threaten me" to "you threaten my leg" is a memorable piece of reframing. It also teaches by repetition, which suits a spoken lecture. A listener can leave with a short script to hold.

The stolen lamp is also well chosen. It is a tiny loss, treated seriously enough to make a point and lightly enough to be funny. The domestic touch helps. He does not mourn the lamp. He says the thief paid a high price for it in honesty. That inversion of who has lost what is clever and stays in the mind.

The chapter's weaknesses are in its length and its argument. It is very long for what it says, and it circles. Several of the same moves, the athlete, the actor, the tyrant, come back in different clothes. In a classroom this repetition would have helped. On the page it can feel loose, and some of the sections, such as the comparison of logic exercises to trials in life, do not add much.

The central claim also depends on a very strong view: that only the will matters, and that the body is not truly "me." A reader who thinks of the body as part of the self, and of torture as an attack on a person rather than on a possession, may feel that Epictetus has made things too easy. He is describing an ideal in which pain and loss simply do not count. Even sympathetic readers wonder how many people can truly live that way under real torture, and the chapter gives little help for the case where the will itself begins to break.

There is also a rhetorical problem. He often puts objections in the mouths of fools, "Slave, why do you say Socrates?" and the scolding can seem unfair. The imagined opponent is always weaker than a real one would be.

And yet the ending, with its quiet distinction between what to tell philosophers and what to tell the jailer, shows a gentler side. Epictetus says that we should not trumpet these ideas to everyone, and that when someone cannot be persuaded, we may treat them as a child and clap along. That final note of tact tempers the severity and is the most humane part of the chapter.

analysis.heading: III. The Impact It Had
analysis.paragraph:
This lecture contains perhaps the best-known statement of what later writers have called the Stoic "inner citadel," the idea that there is a part of a person that no external force can reach. That phrase belongs to the French scholar Pierre Hadot, who used it as the title of his book on Marcus Aurelius, but it fits Epictetus equally well, and this chapter is one of its sources.

Marcus Aurelius, who knew Epictetus's teaching through Arrian's notes or through his teacher, repeats the point again and again in the Meditations, reminding himself that what is not in his power cannot hurt his character. The idea of a mind protected from tyranny also shaped the life and death of other Romans. Stoic senators who defied emperors drew on this tradition, and later historians celebrated them as figures of moral resistance.

In Christian thought, the picture of Socrates drinking hemlock and the idea that a good man cannot be truly harmed influenced early writers who spoke of martyrdom. Boethius, writing in prison, used similar arguments to console himself. In the Renaissance and Enlightenment, the Stoic image of the free mind in a captive body was echoed by writers on liberty and conscience, including Montaigne, and the idea that tyrants control only what is external became part of the vocabulary of resistance.

The most striking modern case is Admiral James Stockdale, a United States Navy pilot shot down over North Vietnam in 1965 who spent more than seven years as a prisoner. Stockdale had studied Epictetus before his capture, and he later said that the Enchiridion and the Discourses helped him endure torture and isolation. He taught the lesson to other prisoners and described it in lectures on leadership. His account made this very chapter, the one about tyrants threatening the body while the will remains free, an unusually practical text for soldiers.

Elsewhere, therapists who follow cognitive approaches draw on the passage about how we respond to threats. The idea that we are disturbed by our judgments of events, and not by events themselves, appears throughout Stoic writing and was cited by Albert Ellis and Aaron Beck. In the recent revival of Stoicism, this chapter is often quoted for its tyrant scripts.

In teaching, the chapter is used to introduce the Stoic division between things in our power and things not in it, and also to illustrate how ancient philosophy was understood as a way of life. Scholars of Roman history use it as evidence for what it felt like to live under emperors who could, and did, order the deaths of philosophers.

analysis.heading: IV. What Readers Loved
analysis.paragraph:
What readers have loved most in this chapter is the sheer nerve of it. Here is a man who was once a slave, speaking calmly about chains and prison and beheading as if they were minor inconveniences. The repeated answer to the tyrant, that he threatens only my leg, my head, my poor body, has a bracing effect. It makes fear seem smaller. People who face intimidating situations, whether a bully, a boss or a regime, often find that rehearsing these lines is steadying.

They also love the Socrates passage. By saying that it was only the poor body of Socrates that was dragged off, Epictetus cuts through the sense of tragedy and replaces it with admiration. Readers who know Plato's account of the trial and death of Socrates find that this reframing gives them a way to think about his end as a victory, not a defeat. The line "Anytus and Meletus can kill me, but they cannot hurt me" is a favorite of those who have to bear injustice.

The humor is another source of affection. The stolen lamp is a nice example: a philosopher mildly pointing out that the thief got a bad bargain. The scenes of men crying, "I wish I had learned more," or of gladiators begging to fight, have the grit of real teaching. Epictetus is funny in the way a good coach is funny, by naming what everyone is thinking.

Readers also respond to the challenge. The chapter is not a comfort for the idle. It tells the reader that difficulty is the moment philosophy was made for, and that wishing for easy material is a kind of cowardice. Many people say they have taken on a hard task partly because of the athlete comparison, in which an athlete is displeased by weak opponents and wants someone who can really test him.

The image of the tragic actor stripped of mask and costume, who still has his voice, is often admired. It says that when everything external is taken away, what is left is the thing that mattered, and that you can find out whether you are a real actor or a buffoon only when the props are gone.

Finally, readers have valued the tact of the ending. The idea that we do not need to argue with everyone, that we can let a weeping jailer be and not correct him, strikes many as wise. It suggests that the Stoic is not a preacher but a person who has quietly worked something out and is content to live by it.

analysis.heading: V. What Critics Pushed Back On
analysis.paragraph:
The classic criticism is that this kind of teaching leaves injustice standing. If a tyrant can only threaten what is not truly yours, then there is no reason to oppose him. Hegel, in his account of ancient philosophy, treated Stoic freedom as a retreat inward, a freedom that is only in thought. A slave who has learned to say "you threaten only my body" is still in chains. Marxist and other readers have made the same charge: that Stoicism makes oppression easier to bear and therefore easier to maintain.

A defense is available. Stoic senators did resist emperors, and some died for it. Epictetus's students were being prepared for public life. But the chapter itself emphasizes endurance and says little about changing laws or ending tyranny. It tells you to accept your arrest, not to organize against it. When he says that the tyrant is not to be opposed over body and property, "take my poor body, take my property," it seems an easy surrender of everything people might fight for.

A second criticism is about psychology. It is one thing to say that the will is free, and another to live as though pain were nothing. Many who have experienced torture or grief say that the mind does not stay detached on command. Critics ask whether the teaching sets a standard that makes suffering people feel they have failed. Epictetus has little patience for tears, and a person weeping for a lost child might find his words unkind. Even Stockdale, in his own writing, acknowledged that the discipline was hard and that he felt the weight of what he had endured.

Third, Pascal in the seventeenth century said that Epictetus knew our duties but not our weakness, and flattered us by suggesting we could be self-sufficient. This is a religious critique, but it points to something real: the chapter has a heroic picture of human beings that does not fit everyone.

Fourth, the tone is often harsh. The chapter calls listeners slaves, women in labor, buffoons, cowards. It is meant to shake them, but readers sometimes find it bullying and preachy. Philosophers of a gentler temper have found Seneca or Marcus Aurelius easier company.

Finally, some scholars note the limits of what we know. These are notes taken by a student, and nobody can say how much was Epictetus and how much Arrian's shaping. The ending, in which we should not tell these ideas to everyone, has also been read as elitist, as though wisdom were for a few and the many were children to be humored. That remark has troubled modern readers more than it did ancient ones.

analysis.heading: VI. Its Place in the Bigger Picture
analysis.paragraph:
This chapter sits within Roman Stoicism, which began as a Greek school founded in Athens around 300 BC and became, under the Roman emperors, a philosophy of survival and dignity. The Stoics taught that virtue is the only real good and that the universe is governed by reason. Under Nero and later emperors, the school became associated with a small, principled opposition, and its teachers were exiled or killed. Epictetus himself was banished from Rome when the emperor Domitian expelled philosophers, which is why he ended up teaching in Greece.

The chapter's chief ancestor is Socrates, who in Plato's Apology says that no harm can come to a good man, and who in the Crito and the Phaedo walks calmly to his death. Epictetus treats him as a model, and the claim that Socrates' accusers could not hurt him is a direct echo of Plato.

Its descendants include almost every tradition that locates freedom inside. Early Christian martyr accounts, from the second century onward, depict believers calmly facing wild beasts and executioners. Boethius' Consolation of Philosophy was written while he awaited execution. Modern writing from prison, such as the letters of Dietrich Bonhoeffer or Viktor Frankl's account of the camps, with his claim that the last human freedom is to choose one's attitude, belong to the same family, although their authors had different sources.

In the history of ideas, the line that opinion cannot be conquered by force also resonates with early modern defenses of freedom of conscience, and with political thinkers who argue that tyranny can control bodies but not minds. The counter-argument, that regimes do succeed in shaping minds by terror and propaganda, is a reminder that the claim is an ideal.

In relation to other chapters of the Discourses, this is among the longest and most varied. It contains in miniature several of Epictetus's favorite devices: the imagined opponent, the athletic comparison, the stage metaphor, the appeal to Socrates. It is therefore a good representative of his style.

Why read it now? Because the situation it addresses has not disappeared. People still face threats, from governments, employers and crowds, and they still ask what part of them is beyond reach. The chapter will not settle that for you, and you may end up agreeing with Pascal or Hegel against it. But it makes you decide what you would actually protect, and that is a question worth asking before you have to.

essays.title: Discourses IV.4: To Those Who Are Desirous of Passing Life in Tranquillity
essays.author: Epictetus
essays.epigraph: Remember that not only the desire of power and of riches makes us mean and subject to others, but even the desire of quiet, and leisure, and travel, and book-learning.
essays.keyContext:
This chapter of the Discourses, by the Greek Stoic teacher Epictetus, takes on a surprising target: the person who longs for peace and quiet. Epictetus lived around the year 100 in the Roman Empire. He was born a slave, later freed, and taught philosophy in a school in northwestern Greece, where a student named Arrian took notes that became this book.

The chapter is aimed at people, perhaps people like us, who tell themselves they would be happy if only they had more time to read, to travel, to study, or to be left alone. Epictetus answers that wanting leisure is just another way of being enslaved to something outside you. Reading, he says, is meant to prepare you for living, not to replace it. The overall message is that tranquillity is something you practice in the middle of the crowd, not something you escape to. It is a surprisingly modern complaint, and a useful one for anyone who reads for a living or for fun.
paragraphs: Remember that not only the desire of power and of riches makes us mean and subject to others, but even the desire of tranquillity, and of leisure, and of travelling abroad, and of learning. For to speak plainly, whatever the external thing may be, the value which we set upon it places us in subjection to others. What then is the difference between desiring to be a senator or not desiring to be one; what is the difference between desiring power or being content with a private station; what is the difference between saying, “I am unhappy, I have nothing to do, but I am bound to my books as a corpse”; or saying, “I am unhappy, I have no leisure for reading”? For as salutations and power are things external and independent of the will, so is a book. For what purpose do you choose to read? Tell me. For if you only direct your purpose to being amused or learning something, you are a silly fellow and incapable of enduring labor. But if you refer reading to the proper end, what else is this than a tranquil and happy life (εὔσοια)? But if reading does not secure for you a happy and tranquil life, what is the use of it? “But it does secure this,” the man replies, “and for this reason I am vexed that I am deprived of it.”⁠—And what is this tranquil and happy life, which any man can impede, I do not say Caesar or Caesar’s friend, but a crow, a piper, a fever, and thirty thousand other things? But a tranquil and happy life contains nothing so sure as continuity and freedom from obstacle. Now I am called to do something: I will go then with the purpose of observing the measures (rules) which I must keep, of acting with modesty, steadiness, without desire and aversion to things external; and then that I may attend to men, what they say, how they are moved; and this not with any bad disposition, or that I may have something to blame or to ridicule; but I turn to myself, and ask if I also commit the same faults. How then shall I cease to commit them? Formerly I also acted wrong, but now I do not: thanks to God.

Come, when you have done these things and have attended to them, have you done a worse act than when you have read a thousand verses or written as many? For when you eat, are you grieved because you are not reading? are you not satisfied with eating according to what you have learned by reading, and so with bathing and with exercise? Why then do you not act consistently in all things, both when you approach Caesar, and when you approach any person? If you maintain yourself free from perturbation, free from alarm, and steady; if you look rather at the things which are done and happen than are looked at yourself; if you do not envy those who are preferred before you; if surrounding circumstances (ὕλαι) do not strike you with fear or admiration, what do you want? Books? How or for what purpose? for is not this (the reading of books) a preparation for life? and is not life itself (living) made up of certain other things than this? This is just as if an athlete should weep when he enters the stadium, because he is not being exercised outside of it. It was for this purpose that you used to practice exercise; for this purpose were used the halteres (weights), the dust, the young men as antagonists; and do you seek for those things now when it is the time of action? This is just as if in the topic (matter) of assent when appearances present themselves, some of which can be comprehended, and some cannot be comprehended, we should not choose to distinguish them but should choose to read what has been written about comprehension (κατάληψις).

What then is the reason of this? The reason is that we have never read for this purpose, we have never written for this purpose, so that we may in our actions use in a way conformable to nature the appearances presented to us; but we terminate in this, in learning what is said, and in being able to expound it to another, in resolving a syllogism, and in handling the hypothetical syllogism. For this reason where our study (purpose) is, there alone is the impediment. Would you have by all means the things which are not in your power? Be prevented then, be hindered, fail in your purpose. But if we read what is written about action (efforts, ὁρμή), not that we may see what is said about action, but that we may act well: if we read what is said about desire and aversion (avoiding things), in order that we may neither fail in our desires, nor fall into that which we try to avoid; if we read what is said about duty (officium), in order that remembering the relations (of things to one another) we may do nothing irrationally nor contrary to these relations; we should not be vexed in being hindered as to our readings, but we should be satisfied with doing the acts which are conformable (to the relations), and we should be reckoning not what so far we have been accustomed to reckon: “Today I have read so many verses, I have written so many;” but (we should say), “Today I have employed my action as it is taught by the philosophers; I have not employed my desire; I have used avoidance (ἐκκλίσει) only with respect to things which are within the power of my will; I have not been afraid of such a person, I have not been prevailed upon by the entreaties of another; I have exercised my patience, my abstinence, my cooperation with others;” and so we should thank God for what we ought to thank him.

But now we do not know that we also in another way are like the many. Another man is afraid that he shall not have power: you are afraid that you will. Do not do so, my man; but as you ridicule him who is afraid that he shall not have power, so ridicule yourself also. For it makes no difference whether you are thirsty like a man who has a fever, or have a dread of water like a man who is mad. Or how will you still be able to say as Socrates did, “If so it pleases God, so let it be?” Do you think that Socrates if he had been eager to pass his leisure in the Lyceum or in the Academy and to discourse daily with the young men, would have readily served in military expeditions so often as he did; and would he not have lamented and groaned, “Wretch that I am; I must now be miserable here, when I might be sunning myself in the Lyceum?” Why, was this your business, to sun yourself? And is it not your business to be happy, to be free from hindrance, free from impediment? And could he still have been Socrates, if he had lamented in this way: how would he still have been able to write Paeans in his prison?

In short remember this, that what you shall prize which is beyond your will, so far you have destroyed your will. But these things are out of the power of the will, not only power (authority), but also a private condition: not only occupation (business), but also leisure.⁠—“Now then must I live in this tumult?”⁠—Why do you say tumult?⁠—“I mean among many men.”⁠—Well what is the hardship? Suppose that you are at Olympia: imagine it to be a panegyris (public assembly), where one is calling out one thing, another is doing another thing, and a third is pushing another person; in the baths there is a crowd: and who of us is not pleased with this assembly, and leaves it unwillingly? Be not difficult to please nor fastidious about what happens.⁠—“Vinegar is disagreeable, for it is sharp; honey is disagreeable, for it disturbs my habit of body. I do not like vegetables. So also I do not like leisure; it is a desert: I do not like a crowd; it is confusion.”⁠—But if circumstances make it necessary for you to live alone or with a few, call it quiet, and use the thing as you ought: talk with yourself, exercise the appearances (presented to you), work up your preconceptions. If you fall into a crowd, call it a celebration of games, a panegyris, a festival: try to enjoy the festival with other men. For what is a more pleasant sight to him who loves mankind than a number of men? We see with pleasure herds of horses or oxen: we are delighted when we see many ships: who is pained when he sees many men?⁠—“But they deafen me with their cries.”⁠—Then your hearing is impeded. What then is this to you? Is then the power of making use of appearances hindered? And who prevents you from using according to nature inclination to a thing and aversion from it; and movement towards a thing and movement from it? What tumult (confusion) is able to do this?

Do you only bear in mind the general rules: what is mine? what is not mine? what is given (permitted) to me? what does God will that I should do now? what does he not will? A little before he willed you to be at leisure, to talk with yourself, to write about these things, to read, to hear, to prepare yourself. You had sufficient time for this. Now he says to you: Come now to the contest, show us what you have learned, how you have practiced the athletic art. How long will you be exercised alone? Now is the opportunity for you to learn whether you are an athlete worthy of victory, or one of those who go about the world and are defeated. Why then are you vexed? No contest is without confusion. There must be many who exercise themselves for the contest, many who call out to those who exercise themselves, many masters, many spectators.⁠—“But my wish is to live quietly.”⁠—Lament then and groan as you deserve to do. For what other is a greater punishment than this to the untaught man and to him who disobeys the divine commands: to be grieved, to lament, to envy, in a word to be disappointed and to be unhappy? Would you not release yourself from these things?⁠—“And how shall I release myself?”⁠—Have you not often heard that you ought to remove entirely desire, apply aversion (turning away) to those things only which are within your power, that you ought to give up everything: body, property, fame, books, tumult, power, private station? for whatever way you turn, you are a slave, you are subjected, you are hindered, you are compelled, you are entirely in the power of others. But keep the words of Cleanthes in readiness:
Lead me, O Zeus, and thou necessity.

Is it your will that I should go to Rome? I will go to Rome. To Gyara? I will go to Gyara. To Athens? I will go to Athens. To prison? I will go to prison. If you should once say, “When shall a man go to Athens?” you are undone. It is a necessary consequence that this desire, if it is not accomplished, must make you unhappy; and if it is accomplished, it must make you vain, since you are elated at things at which you ought not to be elated; and on the other hand, if you are impeded, it must make you wretched because you fall into that which you would not fall into. Give up then all these things.⁠—“Athens is a good place.”⁠—But happiness is much better; and to be free from passions, free from disturbance, for your affairs not to depend on any man. “There is tumult at Rome and visits of salutation.” But happiness is an equivalent for all troublesome things. If then the time comes for these things, why do you not take away the wish to avoid them? what necessity is there to carry a burden like an ass, and to be beaten with a stick? But if you do not so, consider that you must always be a slave to him who has it in his power to effect your release, and also to impede you, and you must serve him as an evil genius.

There is only one way to happiness, and let this rule be ready both in the morning and during the day and by night: the rule is not to look towards things which are out of the power of our will, to think that nothing is our own, to give up all things to the Divinity, to Fortune; to make them the superintendents of these things, whom Zeus also has made so; for a man to observe that only which is his own, that which cannot be hindered; and when we read, to refer our reading to this only, and our writing and our listening. For this reason I cannot call the man industrious if I hear this only: that he reads and writes; and even if a man adds that he reads all night, I cannot say so, if he knows not to what he should refer his reading. For neither do you say that a man is industrious if he keeps awake for a girl; nor do I. But if he does it (reads and writes) for reputation, I say that he is a lover of reputation. And if he does it for money, I say that he is a lover of money, not a lover of labor; and if he does it through love of learning, I say that he is a lover of learning. But if he refers his labor to his own ruling power (ἡγεμονικόν), that he may keep it in a state conformable to nature and pass his life in that state, then only do I say that he is industrious. For never commend a man on account of these things which are common to all, but on account of his opinions (principles); for these are the things which belong to each man, which make his actions bad or good. Remembering these rules, rejoice in that which is present, and be content with the things which come in season. If you see anything which you have learned and inquired about occurring to you in your course of life (or opportunely applied by you to the acts of life), be delighted at it. If you have laid aside or have lessened bad disposition and a habit of reviling; if you have done so with rash temper, obscene words, hastiness, sluggishness; if you are not moved by what you formerly were, and not in the same way as you once were, you can celebrate a festival daily, today because you have behaved well in one act, and tomorrow because you have behaved well in another. How much greater is this a reason for making sacrifices than a consulship or the government of a province? These things come to you from yourself and from the gods. Remember this: who gives these things and to whom, and for what purpose. If you cherish yourself in these thoughts, do you still think that it makes any difference where you shall be happy, where you shall please God? Are not the gods equally distant from all places? Do they not see from all places alike that which is going on?

analysis.heading: I. What It Really Means
analysis.paragraph:
Epictetus starts with a provocation. We usually think that wanting power or wealth makes us dependent on others, and that wanting quiet and books is a nobler wish. He says no. Whatever external thing you value, whether power, riches, tranquillity, leisure, travel or learning, puts you in subjection to the people and events that control it. There is no real difference, he says, between the man who is unhappy because he has no leisure to read and the man who is unhappy because he has no office. A book, like a salutation from a senator, is an external thing.

He then asks the question that gives the chapter its bite: why do you read? If it is only to be amused or to learn something, you are a "silly fellow." If you read to achieve a tranquil and happy life, then you must admit that a life any crow, piper or fever can interrupt is not much of a tranquillity. Real tranquillity, he says, has a quality of continuity and freedom from obstacle, so it cannot depend on conditions that anyone can hinder.

The key is that reading is preparation for life, and life is made of other things. He uses the picture of an athlete who weeps on entering the stadium because he is not being trained outside it. All the training, with its weights, dust and sparring partners, was for this moment. So when you are called away to do something, whether to approach the emperor or deal with a neighbor, that is the contest itself. The point of study is to act "with modesty, steadiness, without desire and aversion to things external."

The chapter then redefines industry. A man who reads all night is not necessarily industrious. If he reads for reputation, he loves reputation, if for money, money, if for the pleasure of learning, learning. Only the person who directs his work toward keeping his own ruling power, his governing mind, in order is truly industrious. The daily review he suggests is not "I read so many verses today" but "I did not fear that person, I was not swayed by that plea, I practiced patience."

Another movement answers those who say they cannot bear the crowd. Epictetus asks them to imagine Olympia, with its shoving and shouting and baths full of people, and to call it a festival. Solitude, similarly, can be called quiet. The Stoic prayer from Cleanthes, "Lead me, O Zeus," lets him say that he will go to Rome, Gyara, Athens or prison as he is led.

What a first-time reader may miss is how self-implicating the chapter is. Epictetus is talking to students who loved books, and he is pointing at their own comfortable form of slavery.

analysis.heading: II. How Well It Works: A Critique
analysis.paragraph:
This chapter has a sharp, clear idea at its center, and the best parts are the ones that apply it to a scholar's life. The line that a book is as external as a salutation is startling because it turns a flattering image of the reader upside down. Many of us feel virtuous when we say we need more time to read or think. Epictetus points out that this is just another form of the old complaint, "if only I had what I want, I would be well." It is a genuinely perceptive piece of psychology, and still stings.

The athlete image is also well chosen. It is concrete, and it makes the point about preparation without much argument. The idea that life itself is the stadium, and that books are the training, is one that readers retain for years.

The idea of reviewing your day by what you did and not what you read is another strength. It gives a practical test: not how many pages, but whether you were afraid, whether you gave in, whether you were patient. It makes philosophy into a daily accounting, which is its main purpose in this school.

Yet the chapter has weaknesses. It is somewhat repetitive. The same point, that you should stop wanting what is not in your power, is made again and again with new examples, and the structure wanders, moving from reading to crowds to Socrates to Cleanthes and back to reading. A reader who wanted a tight argument will find it loose.

There is also a real tension in its contempt for learning. Epictetus devotes his life to teaching and to a kind of reading, and the chapter itself is part of a school of books. Yet he sneers at those who love learning for its own sake and calls them silly. That seems too harsh.
